purpose: Mistakes found in published sources by the atlas's workers (research/blueprint/PROTOCOL.md section 18).

issues.locator: §1.5 Notation, p. 8
issues.printed: "Sp2r(R) denotes the standard symplectic group, i.e., the automorphisms of the free R-module on generators e_i, f_i (1 ≤ i ≤ g) with form ⟨e_i, f_j⟩ = δ_ij and ⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 1. … Sp(R) := lim_g Sp2r(R). … automorphisms of R^{2g}"
issues.correction: ⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 0, with 1 ≤ i ≤ r, the limit over r and R^{2r}.
issues.reason: With ⟨e_i, e_i⟩ = 1 the form is not alternating, so its automorphism group is not a symplectic group; the index g is the genus elsewhere in the paper, while the rank parameter is r.

issues.locator: §2.7, Lemma 2.7.1 and its proof, pp. 16–17; proof of Lemma 3.5.1, p. 30
issues.printed: "Both sides are groups of order 2, and both Sp2r(Fq) and SL2r(Fq) have vanishing integral H2. Proof. The vanishing of integral H2 for both groups is well known, see e.g. [57]."; and "MSO2 coincides with second (integral) homology … and since ℓ is finite, this group vanishes by [57]."
issues.correction: H_2(Sp_{2r}(F_q), Z) and H_2(SL_{2r}(F_q), Z) have odd order for odd q; they vanish except for r = 1, q = 9, where H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3. Odd order suffices for both uses.
issues.reason: SL_2(F_9) = Sp_2(F_9) is the double cover 2·A_6 of A_6 ≅ PSL_2(F_9), whose Schur multiplier is Z/6; the universal central extension 6·A_6 of SL_2(F_9) has kernel Z/3, so H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3. Independently: a Sylow 3-subgroup P ≅ (F_9, +) is abelian with H_2(P, Z) = Λ²P ≅ Z/3, and diag(t, t^{−1}) acts on it by the determinant of u ↦ t²u over F_3, namely N_{F_9/F_3}(t)² = 1; by Swan's theorem H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z)_{(3)} ≅ H_2(P, Z)^{N(P)} ≅ Z/3. (For SL_2(F_{p²}) with p ≥ 5 the same computation gives 0, since N(t)² ≠ 1 for some t.) This is the exceptional A_1(9) case in Steinberg's list, reference [57] of the paper. In Lemma 2.7.1 only H_2 ⊗ Z/2 = 0 is needed (to identify H_3(−, Z)/2 with H_3(−, Z/2)), and in Lemma 3.5.1 any homomorphism from Z/3 to ℓ^×/2 is zero.

issues.locator: §5.1, Lemma 5.1.1 and its proof, p. 40; hence §5.3 (Lemma 5.3.1), §5.6 and Theorem 3.1 in the case r = 1, #ℓ = 9
issues.printed: "Lemma 5.1.1. (Irreducibility in large genus). There exists g0(ℓ, r) such that for g ≥ g0(r, ℓ) the Q̄-fiber of M^G is irreducible. Proof. This follows from a result of Dunfield–Thurston [18, Theorem 6.25] since H2(G, Z) is trivial in the case at hand"
issues.correction: Lemma 5.1.1 holds when H_2(Sp_{2r}(ℓ), Z) = 0, i.e. unless r = 1 and #ℓ = 9. For G = SL_2(F_9) the Q̄-fibre of 𝔐^G_g has at least three components for every large g, so the proof of Step A, and with it of Theorem 3.1, does not cover r = 1, #ℓ = 9. That case must be excluded or treated one component at a time.
issues.reason: The case r = 1, #ℓ = 9 satisfies the hypothesis #ℓ ≡ ±1 (mod 8) of Theorem 3.1, and H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3 (see E3). For a surjection φ : π_1(Σ_g) → G, the class φ_*[Σ_g] ∈ H_2(G, Z) is invariant under the mapping class group and under conjugation by G. Every class occurs for g large: realize it by some surface, then add handles mapped onto generators. So the orbits of the mapping class group on Epi(π_1Σ_g, G)/G, which by Example 5.2 are the components of 𝔐^G_g(C), number at least |H_2(G, Z)| = 3. Galois acts on the invariant through the cyclotomic character (the fundamental class lives in Ẑ(1)), so for q ≡ 1 (mod 3) all three components are defined over F_q, and for q large they carry admissible pairs. Lemma 5.3.1 uses H^0(𝔐^{G*}_{Q̄}, Z/2) = Z/2, which then fails. Theorem 3.1 may still hold in this case, but the paper does not prove it.

issues.printed: "ε = (−qt)^{dim H1} ∏ det(F|H1) = (−√q t)^{dim H1} det(F̄)"
issues.correction: ε = (−qt)^{dim H^1} det(F | H^1)^{−1} = (−√q t)^{dim H^1} det(F̄).
issues.reason: With n = dim H^1 and qF^{−1} conjugate to F (from ⟨Fx, Fy⟩ = q⟨x, y⟩), L(1/(qt)) = det(1 − F/(qt)) = (−qt)^{−n} det(F) L(t), so ε(t) = L(t)/L(1/(qt)) = (−qt)^n det(F)^{−1}. Since det F = q^{n/2} det F̄ and det F̄ = ±1, this equals (−√q t)^n det F̄; the printed middle expression is q^n times too large. The conclusion (ε(ρ, 1/√q) = det F̄) is unaffected.

issues.locator: §5.5, proof of the Claim, p. 46
issues.printed: "(a) Each m ∈ M is larger than ℓ, q and the size of the Picard group of X." and "Since the order of A is also prime to the order of the last group and to q, we get an isomorphism: Hom(class group, A) ≃ ∏_x Hom(k_x^×, A)"
issues.correction: (a) should bound m by the class number #Pic^0(X)(k). The map Hom(class group, A) → ∏_{x∈S} Hom(k_x^×, A) is surjective, not an isomorphism, which is all the argument needs.
issues.reason: Pic(X) is infinite (degree gives Pic(X) → Z with finite kernel Pic^0(X)(k)), and Hom(Pic(X), A) ⊇ Hom(Z, A) = A ≠ 0 corresponds to constant-field extensions, so the displayed map is not injective. Surjectivity holds: Ext^1(Pic(X), A) = 0 because Pic(X) ≅ Z ⊕ Pic^0(X)(k) and #Pic^0(X)(k) is prime to #A = M by (a). The chosen local characters therefore extend to the ray class group, and the resulting A-cover is geometrically connected because the inertia groups generate A.

issues.locator: §6.4, the choice of D in (6.18), p. 58, and Lemma 6.4.2, p. 58
issues.printed: "Let D be the smallest integer such that (6.18) E := dim Γ(S°_{Fq}, O(D)) ≥ 6N." and "Lemma 6.4.2 … the condition of vanishing at all x_i defines a codimension r subspace of Γ(S°_{Fq}, O(D)) whenever D is sufficiently large; it suffices that the x_i are contained in the complement of a Fq-hyperplane of dim Γ(S°, O(D)) ≥ r + 1."
issues.correction: Choose D ≥ max(D_E, 2N − 1), where D_E is the least D with E ≥ 6N; Lemma 6.4.1 already allows every D ≥ D_0. Then r ≤ 2N distinct points impose independent conditions on degree-D forms (Poonen, Lemma 2.1: surjectivity for D ≥ r − 1), and the rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: The smallest D with E ≥ 6N can be 1 (hyperplane sections of a surface in a large projective space), and distinct points need not impose independent conditions on hyperplanes: three collinear points of S° impose only two. Then the proportion of slices through them exceeds q^{−r}, which the evaluation of (6.21) needs to exclude. The cited Lemma 2.1 of Poonen gives independence once D ≥ r − 1, and r ≤ 2N = 8 here.

The prime (2) is inert in F/ℚ, so F_(2) = ℚ_4 is unramified over ℚ_2 with residue field 𝔽_4. F_(2)(i)/F_(2) has conductor exponent 2, so 𝔪 = (4). This is a contradiction. An exhaustive search over the 12 units of ℤ[ζ_3]/4 confirms it. Inertness of a principal prime (p) in K is detected by χ(p) = (−1)^{(N(p)−1)/2}, where N is the norm to ℚ; this is the Hilbert symbol (p, −1) at (2), trivial on global units. issues.locator: Published §2.2.4, second paragraph, p. 13; the same assertion and proof are in arXiv:1609.00320v1 §2.2.4, p. 12
issues.printed: On en déduit qu'une K-algèbre A admet au plus une norme spectrale pour laquelle elle est complète : en effet, si || 1, || 2 sont deux telles normes, on peut supposer, en remplaçant la première par le supremum des deux, que le morphisme identique (A,|| 1) → (A,|| 2) est continu. Par le théorème de l'image ouverte de Banach [7, I.3.3, th. 1], || 1 est équivalente à || 2, donc ce morphisme est bicontinu et l'on conclut de ce qui précède que || 1 = || 2.
issues.correction: The assertion is false as stated. Keep the preceding sentence, which is what the paper actually needs and which is true: the spectral norm of a uniform normed algebra is the unique spectral norm compatible with its topology. A completeness variant must add a hypothesis making the two norms comparable — for instance that the identity is continuous in one direction, or that the maximum of the two is complete.
issues.reason: Take K = Q_p and A = C_p as an abstract Q_p-algebra. Choose t in a transcendence basis B of C_p over the algebraic closure F of Q_p; since F(pt) = F(t), the set (B∖{t}) ∪ {pt} is again a transcendence basis, so there is a field automorphism σ of C_p over F with σ(t) = pt. Then |x|' := |σ(x)| is again a multiplicative Q_p-algebra norm, and (C_p,|·|') is complete because σ is an isometric bijection onto (C_p,|·|); but |t|' = |pt| = p^{-1}|t| ≠ |t|. So C_p carries two distinct complete spectral — indeed multiplicative — norms. The step that fails is the replacement of ||1 by the supremum: for a_n ∈ F converging to t for |·|, one has |a_n − x|' = |a_n − σ(x)|, so the same sequence converges to σ^{-1}(t) = p^{-1}t for |·|'; it is Cauchy for the maximum of the two norms and has two different limits, so the maximum is not complete and the open mapping theorem does not apply to it. Downstream audit (every occurrence of the assertion in the paper is on pp. 13, 22 and 41): it is USED once, in the proof of Lemme 2.4.1(2) p. 22 — « Notons par ailleurs que si la norme est spectrale complète, elle est unique avec cette propriété (cf. 2.2.2), donc préservée par G » — and the counterexample above is exactly of that shape, a non-continuous automorphism moving the norm. That use is repairable by the paper's own part (3): γ(b) satisfies the same monic polynomial ∏_{γ∈G}(T−γ(b)) ∈ A[T] as b, whose coefficients determine the spectral value by [6, 3.1.2, prop. 1], so |·|_sp is G-invariant for that reason. On p. 41 the assertion is invoked for the perfectoidness of a finite étale extension, but the valid reason — uniqueness of the spectral norm compatible with the canonical topology of a finite projective module — is given in the same parenthesis. No main theorem is affected.

issues.reason: For F_9=F_3(i), i^2=-1, the normal basis (1+i,1-i) has trace Gram matrix G=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Multiplication by i has matrix A=[[0,1],[2,0]], so A!=A^T although it is self-adjoint for the trace pairing: A=G^(-1)A^TG. Taking a Carlitz reduction with iota(t)=i already disproves the constant-coefficient matrix-transpose claim. The trace duality repair preserves the desired module-dual comparison.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.9.5 (published: Theorem 4.90), the statement; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version
issues.printed: Then the prismatic Dieudonné functor M_Δ(−) : BT(R) → DM^adm(R) from the category of p-divisible groups over R to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystals over R is essentially surjective.
issues.correction: … to the category of admissible prismatic Dieudonné modules over R …
issues.reason: R is assumed quasi-regular semiperfectoid and the displayed functor is the non-calligraphic M_Δ(−), which Definition 4.42 (arXiv Definition 4.2.8) defines as Ext^1_{(R)_qsyn}(G, O^pris) with values in prismatic Dieudonné modules over R; DM^adm(R) is used for both categories by the deliberate overloading of Definitions 4.8 and 4.19 (arXiv Definitions 4.1.8 and 4.1.15), but the words in the statement name the wrong one. The proof settles it: it begins 'let M ∈ DM^adm(R)' and speaks of 'a descent datum for expressing that it comes from an admissible prismatic Dieudonné module over R (namely, M)'. The crystal version of the same statement is Theorem 4.74 (arXiv Theorem 4.6.10), for a general quasi-syntomic ring.

issues.locator: Example 6.0.4 (published: Example A.4), the displayed chain of equalities; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version
issues.printed: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.correction: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i−1}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.reason: The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct.

issues.locator: the proof of Proposition 5.3.5 (published: Proposition 5.23), the step asserting topological nilpotence of the divided Frobenius; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version, and corrected by the 2025 erratum
issues.printed: We claim that the divided Frobenius is topologically nilpotent on its kernel. It suffices to show the same for the surjection A_crys(R) → W(R) coming from the PD-thickening W(R) → R. We recall that A_crys(R) is obtained from W(R^♭) by passing to the PD-envelope for the ideal ker(W(R^♭) → R). This kernel is (topologically) generated by the elements V^m([x]) for m ≥ 0 and x ∈ I := ker(R^♭ → R).
issues.correction: The claim is false. The erratum states: 'The key step in the proof of Proposition 5.23 is to show that for a quasiregular semiperfect ring R, the divided Frobenius φ_1 acts topologically nilpotently on the kernel of the map A_crys(R) → W(R). This is not true.' The counterexample, due to Andrew Senger, is R = F_p[x^{1/p^∞}]/x with the element Σ_{k ∈ Z} p^k [x^{1/p^k}] of A_crys(R), which is fixed by the divided Frobenius and lies in the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R). The erratum diagnoses the gap: 'While the generators of the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R) used in the proof do topologically generate the kernel in the p-adic topology of A_crys(R), they fail to do so in the p-adic topology of the kernel itself.' The statement of Proposition 5.23 is unaffected: it was already known by the different proofs of Lau, Displays and formal p-divisible groups, and of Zink, The display of a formal p-divisible group, both cited immediately before it, and the erratum records that 'the arguments of this fallacious proof are not used anywhere else in the paper, so this mistake does not affect any of the results stated in the paper'.
issues.reason: Verified against the erratum itself, which was published for exactly this proposition; the mistake was pointed out to the authors by Akhil Mathew and Andrew Senger. Note that the paper proves a similar topological-nilpotence statement twice more, in Lemma 4.88 (arXiv Lemma 4.9.3) for the kernel of Δ_S → Δ_{S̃} and in Lemma 5.15 (arXiv Lemma 5.2.8) for the Breuil–Kisin prism; neither is retracted, and the erratum's sentence that the fallacious argument is used nowhere else applies to them.

issues.locator: Example 7.3, the two stated ranges in the computation of the cyclic homology of k over W(k); in arXiv v2, the version read (the published version could not be consulted)
issues.printed: Using the filtrations of [antieauperiodic], we conclude for i ≤ 2p−1, π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} if i = 2s ≥ 0, 0 otherwise. … Thus, in the range 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, we deduce that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) if i = 2s, 0 if i is odd.
issues.correction: The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).
issues.reason: Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds.

issues.locator: Published Theorem9.1/Definition9.2 pp48–50; arXiv v4 pp52–54
issues.printed: There exists a unique function
issues.correction: Replace the unique-choice definition by a solution-set/existence interface pending a repaired theorem with extra conditions. The two printed test conditions alone do not determine a vector for n=m=2. Also remove the assertion that all restricted Speh vectors lie in Pi.
issues.reason: For n=m=2, G'=GL2,V'=1,T'=id and all formal W^0 are left-N'-invariant. With u=[[1,varpi^-1],[0,1]], f=1_(uK')-1_K' is a nonzero right-K'-invariant compact function annihilated by every test integral by left translation (det u=1). Extend f to D=V iota(G') using Psi. Lapid–Mao20 Cor3.13/3.15 supplies a Shalika vector with this restriction; right averaging preserves f. Adding it to the L=1 essential vector gives a second solution. The proof's character claim fails explicitly: (I+tE13)(I+bE32)(I-tE13)=I+bE32+tbE12, so Psi changes by psi(tb). See report for full argument and limits. The continuation verifies the compact-induction hypothesis directly against Lapid–Mao Cor3.13/3.15 and obtains infinitely many independent perturbations using u_r=I+varpi^-r E12. These vectors satisfy precisely the printed right-iota(Kprime) condition; no K^(c_pi)-invariance is claimed.

issues.reason: Differentiate W_Ze^0(x exp(t),x exp(-t)) at t=0. issues.locator: Theorem 4.1, JAMS p.928, proof p.929; author p.13–14
issues.printed: "Theorem 4.1. Let V be a polarized variation of pure Hodge structures of weight k over the punctured polydisk (∆*)^n, with period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M}. Then Φ is R_an,exp-definable." (∆ is the unit disk, p.4.)
issues.correction: Definability holds only after shrinking. For some radius 0 < ρ < 1, the restriction of Φ to (∆*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable, and then for every ρ < 1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces. The reduction in §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover the compactification.
issues.reason: Counterexample (n = 1, trivial monodromy). Let f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) on the unit disk, so |f| < 1, and τ = 2i + εf with ε small, so that τ(∆) lies in a disk on which π: H → Γ\H is injective (Γ torsion-free, e.g. Γ(3)). τ is the period map of a polarized weight-one integral VHS. But Φ^{−1}(π(2i + ε/e)) contains the points z_n = 2πin/(2 + 2πin), n ≠ 0, where f = 1/e. These form an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1, which is impossible for a fibre of a definable map. The proof itself allows for this: it says 'after maybe shrinking the polydisk' (p.14), and its Siegel set S_H (y > 1) covers only |q| < e^{−2π}. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected, since §4.1 can use finitely many shrunken charts. Checked numerically: |f(z_n) − 1/e| < 1e−8 for 0 < |n| ≤ 2000. Noted by the extraction (item local-outer-boundary-obstruction).

issues.locator: Lemma 4.5 proof, JAMS p.930; author p.15
issues.printed: "Consider for each positive integer m and real number c the function f_{m,c} which we obtain from f by setting z_1 = mz_2 + c. Note that the assumptions of the lemma still apply to f_{m,c}, and it follows by induction on n that f_{m,c} ≪ 1 on all of Σ_{n−1}"
issues.correction: State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on wider sectors Σ_n^R={|x_i|<R,y₁≥⋯≥y_n>1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution maps Σ_(n−1)^R′ into Σ_n^(mR′+|c|). The application needs original-source bounded-real-width uniformity for Schmid Corollary 5.29 and the CKS/Kashiwara norm estimates; G3 records that this is still unverified. The R-quantifier of the target Theorem 1.5 is not evidence for its prerequisites.
issues.reason: Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation.

issues.correction: Choose smaller semialgebraic corner boxes whose closures lie inside larger analytic charts. Prove definability of the compact matching graph and cover it by finitely many neighborhoods of analytic transition extensions. Mere boundedness of the smaller domains is insufficient.
issues.reason: Analytic coordinate changes between relatively compact domains need not be R_an-definable: F(x)=x+(x²/4)sin(1/x), 0<x<1, has derivative greater than 1/4 and maps diffeomorphically to a bounded interval. Thus a buffer in larger charts is necessary for the printed immediate inference. The new buffered-transition-graph item supplies a proof of the theorem, not a counterexample to its conclusion.

issues.locator: Inventiones mathematicae 222 (2020), Theorem 3.16 (ii), p. 55, and its introduction form Theorem A (ii), p. 4
issues.printed: dim(X) > 0
issues.correction: Part (ii) needs dim(X) ≥ 2 whenever X(R) ≠ ∅. The hypothesis dim(X) > 0 of Theorem 3.16, and the hypothesis d ≥ 1 of Theorem A, are too weak: the case dim(X) = 1 with X(R) ≠ ∅ must be excluded. Part (i) is not affected by this counterexample.
issues.reason: Take X = E the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 - x over R = ℝ, with its rational point at infinity. All the printed hypotheses hold: dim(X) = 1 > 0; H^2(X,O_X) = 0 because X is a curve; and the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles is the codimension-0 case, which holds trivially, since X is geometrically irreducible, so H^0_G(X(ℂ),ℤ(0)) = ℤ and the class of the codimension-0 cycle [X] generates it. The left-hand side of (ii) fails: the only integral closed subscheme of dimension 1 in a curve is the curve itself, and E has geometric genus 1, which is odd, so X contains no geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus. The right-hand side holds: by Hochschild–Serre, Pic(X) → Pic(X_ℂ)^G is injective with cokernel embedding in Br(ℝ), and that obstruction is killed by the real point, so the map is an isomorphism and is in particular onto on 2-primary torsion. Hence (ii) is false as printed. The proof combines Theorems3.3 and3.6 with Proposition3.9, whose real-point argument assumes dimension at least2. Prior worker checked the published and arXiv statements; retained here without an independent-review verdict.

issues.reason: The cited result is BPLZZ Theorem 4.14(4): if the weak base change of π exists and is hermitian, the base change of χ_{π_∞} is χ_{BC(π)_∞}. Its proof reduces to BPLZZ Proposition 4.13(1), whose argument by contradiction only rules out 'weak base change does not exist'. When the weak base change exists but is not cuspidal, the T-character χ′ is CAP, Theorem 3.6 does not apply, and nothing in the printed argument reaches the archimedean component. This paper applies the theorem to σ whose weak base change is a Hermitian Arthur parameter Π. In the endoscopic case, the one the paper is about, Π is not cuspidal. The common infinitesimal character is needed to choose the multipliers μ^h with μ^h(σ) = 1 for all (U_h, σ) ∈ 𝔛^h_0, compatible with μ(Π) = 1 under base change, which (10.1.6.6) uses. issues.locator: §1, p.4 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "Then p² strongly divides ∆(f) if and only if f modulo p has at least two distinct multiple roots in F̄_p, or has a root in F_p of multiplicity at least 3; and p² weakly divides ∆(f) if p² | ∆(f) but f modulo p has only one multiple root in F_p and this root is a simple double root."
issues.correction: This holds for odd p. For p = 2, 4 always divides Δ(f) strongly when 2 | Δ(f), so W^{(2)}_m is empty for even m.
issues.reason: By Stickelberger's congruence, the discriminant of a monic integer polynomial is ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4, so 2 | Δ(f + 2g) implies 4 | Δ(f + 2g) for every g. For example f = x² + 1 ≡ (x + 1)² mod 2 has a single simple double root, yet Δ(x² + a_1x + a_2) = a_1² − 4a_2 ≡ 0 mod 4 whenever a_1 is even. A brute-force check over all f mod p confirms the criterion for p = 3 (n ≤ 5) and p = 5 (n ≤ 4), and finds failures at p = 2 for every n = 2, …, 5. The proofs only use the implication "two multiple roots or a triple root ⇒ strong", which holds at p = 2 as well (in Proposition 2.2), and the tail estimates concern large primes, so nothing else changes.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.1, (41), p.23 (arXiv v3)
issues.correction: The middle term should be O(Σ_{m≤X^{1/κ}} θ̄(m)m^κX^{n(n+1)/2−1}). Since θ̄(p) ≤ 1 − λ_n(p) ≪ 1/p² for p > N, this is O_ε(X^{n(n+1)/2−1/κ+ε}), which the stated error term O_ε(X^{n(n+1)/2−min{1/5,1/(2κ)}+ε}) absorbs.
issues.reason: W_m(Σ) is a union of θ̄(m)m^{κn} residue classes modulo m^κ ≤ X. Each class meets the region {H < X} in Vol/m^{κn} + O(X^{n(n+1)/2−1}/m^{κ(n−1)}) points, the error coming from the a_1-direction, of length ≍ X. An error X^{n(n+1)/2−n} per m cannot hold: already for m = 1 the count #{H(f) < X} = 2^nX^{n(n+1)/2} + O(X^{n(n+1)/2−1}) of the introduction has an error of exact order X^{n(n+1)/2−1}, since the number of a_1 in (−X, X) fluctuates by O(1). Summing the corrected errors: Σ_{m≤X^{1/κ}} C^{ω(m)}m^{κ−2} ≪ X^{(κ−1)/κ+ε}, giving X^{n(n+1)/2−1/κ+ε} ≤ X^{n(n+1)/2−1/(2κ)+ε}. So Theorem 4.1 stands.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.3, p.22 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "When n ≥ 4 is even and the polynomial factors as g(x)ḡ(x) over a quadratic extension, the splitting field has degree at most 2(n/2)! and so the index of the corresponding Galois group in S_n is again at least n(n−1)/2."
issues.correction: The splitting field has degree at most 2((n/2)!)², so the index is at least C(n, n/2)/2. That is ≥ n(n − 1)/2 only for n ≥ 8. For n = 6 the index can be 10, but n/[S_n : H] ≤ 3/5 < 1 still gives the stated bound. For n = 4 the index can be 3 (Galois group D_4), and the argument yields O_ε(X^{6+4/3+ε}) = O_ε(X^{22/3+ε}) for these quartics. So Proposition 4.3 is proved for n = 4 only in the weaker form #V_4(Z)^red_X = O_ε(X^{22/3+ε}) = O(X^{n(n+1)/2−8/3+ε}).
issues.reason: Over K = Q(√d) the splitting fields of g and ḡ have degree up to (n/2)! each, and their compositum up to ((n/2)!)². The Galois group of f lies in S_{n/2} ≀ S_2, of order 2((n/2)!)². Example: x⁴ − 2 = (x² − √2)(x² + √2) over Q(√2) has Galois group D_4 of order 8 > 2·2! = 4. With [S_4 : D_4] = 3, Dietmann's bound for |a_4| ≤ X⁴ is X^{4/3+ε} per (a_1, a_2, a_3), against the X^{2/(n−1)} = X^{2/3} the proof claims. Every use of Proposition 4.3 (§§2.4, 3.4, (4)) needs only O(X^{n(n+1)/2−1/5}), which X^{10−8/3+ε} satisfies. No main result is affected.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.1 and proof, p.24 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "By the uniqueness of Minkowski-reduced bases for these rings, φ must map Minkowski basis elements to Minkowski basis elements, i.e., φ(h_i(θ)) = h*_i(θ*) for all i. In particular, this is true for i = 1, so φ(θ) = θ* + c for some c ∈ Z … It follows that g(x) = g*(x), a contradiction."
issues.correction: A Minkowski-reduced basis is unique at best up to the signs of its vectors: with α_1, …, α_n, every ±α_1, …, ±α_n is also Minkowski-reduced. So φ(h_1(θ)) = ±h*_1(θ*), φ(θ) = ±θ* + c, and the correct conclusion is g*(x) = g(x) or g*(x) = (−1)^ng(−x). Lemma 5.1 holds as stated only for pairs not related by x ↦ −x. In Corollaries 1.3 and 1.4 each field then comes from at most two of the counted polynomials, so the lower bounds are unchanged. Remark 5.6 already counts θ ↦ ±θ + c.
issues.reason: Counterexample: g = x³ − 50x + 7 and g* = x³ − 50x − 7 are distinct, have vanishing x²-coefficients and are strongly quasi-reduced. For both, an exhaustive search gives the Minkowski-reduced basis 1, θ, θ² − 33, unique up to sign, with squared lengths 3, 100, 1667. Yet x ↦ −x is an isomorphism Z[x]/(g) ≅ Z[x]/(g*). If "unique" were meant literally, including signs, no lattice would be strongly quasi-reduced and Lemma 5.3 would fail instead.

issues.locator: Proofs of Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3, p.25 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "The condition that Q is Minkowski reduced is equivalent to the condition that γ belongs to F_SL. The condition that Q be quasi-reduced is simply then that t_i ≤ c t_{i+1} (with no condition on ν)." (Lemma 5.2); "… shows that the density of monic integer polynomials f … that have nonzero discriminant and are strongly quasi-reduced is greater than 1 − ε." (Lemma 5.3)
issues.correction: Lemma 5.2: F_SL is a Siegel set, which contains the Minkowski domain but is not equal to it. The proof needs the converse direction for well-separated tori: if t_{i+1}/t_i ≥ C_n for all i (C_n depending on n), then a basis with these Gram–Schmidt lengths is Minkowski-reduced after a unipotent integral change of basis. This holds because each successive shortest extending vector must then have the form ±b_i + Σ_{j<i}c_jb_j. Since the ratios for g(ρx) grow like ρ, the lemma follows. Lemma 5.3: the proof yields quasi-reduction only. Uniqueness of the reduced basis up to sign must be added. For well-separated tori it fails only on the locus where two candidates ±b_i + Σc_jb_j have equal length, a proper closed semialgebraic subset of V_n(R), whose integer points in ρ·B are o(ρ^{n(n+1)/2}).
issues.reason: As written, the equivalence is false, and "strongly" in Lemma 5.3 is asserted without argument. Both steps are standard, and with them the lemmas and Corollaries 1.3–1.4 stand.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.6 and proof, pp.11–12
issues.printed: "Proposition 3.6. We have det(A^top(A^top)^t) det(B^top(B^top)^t) | Δ as elements in Z[W_0]." Proof: "Suppose (A, B) ∈ W_0(C) with det(B^top(B^top)^t) = 0. Then B^top does not have full rank."
issues.correction: Over C, det(MM^t) = 0 does not imply rank M < g (for M = (1, i), MM^t = 0), so the Nullstellensatz argument fails and the statement is false. What the argument does prove: Δ vanishes on the complex locus where B^top (or A^top) has rank < g. So Δ lies in the ideal generated by the g × g minors of B^top (a prime determinantal ideal), and likewise for A^top. On bounded sets this gives |Δ| ≪ Σ|minors| ≪ det(B^top(B^top)^t)^{1/2}, by Cauchy–Binet, and that suffices for Lemma 6.25 with the exponent doubled.
issues.reason: Counterexample for n = 3 (g = 1): A = [[0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]] and B = [[0, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0]] lie in W_0(Z). Then f_{A,B} = −y(x² − 3xy + y²) and Δ = 5, while det(A^top(A^top)^t)det(B^top(B^top)^t) = 1·2 = 2 ∤ 5. At random integral points the claimed divisibility held in only 6 of 37 cases for n = 3 and 0 of 40 for n = 5. Δ vanished at all 12 random points with rank-1 B^top for n = 5.

issues.locator: Lemma 7.2 and proof, pp.52–53; proof of Theorem 3, p.53
issues.printed: "Lemma 7.2 … Suppose the corresponding rank-n rings R_f and R_{f*} are isomorphic. Then f(x, y) and f*(x, y) are SL_2(Z)-equivalent. Proof. … By the uniqueness of Minkowski-reduced bases, φ must map the basis elements 1, ζ_1, …, ζ_{n−1} for R_f to the corresponding basis elements 1, ζ*_1, …, ζ*_{n−1}."
issues.correction: Minkowski-reduced bases are unique at best up to the signs of their vectors, so φ(ζ_i) = ±ζ*_i. The conclusion is only that f* is GL_2(Z)-equivalent to f, e.g. f*(x, y) = f(−x, y). In the proof of Theorem 3, choose B so that no two of its elements are GL_2(Z)-equivalent (GL_2(Z) also acts discretely). The bound is unchanged.
issues.reason: Counterexample for n = 3: f = x³ − x²y + xy² + y³, an S_3 cubic (disc −44), is strongly Minkowski-reduced. An exhaustive search gives the reduced basis 1, ζ_1, ζ_2 with unique minima up to sign. f*(x, y) = f(−x, y) = −x³ − x²y − xy² + y³ has the same lattice R_{f*} = R_f, since ζ*_i = ±ζ_i, so it is strongly Minkowski-reduced too. But f* is not SL_2(Z)-equivalent to f. Otherwise f would have a stabilizer element δ of determinant −1, and −δ would be a nontrivial automorphism of R_f in the twisted GL_2(Z)-action, which is impossible for an order in a non-Galois cubic field. Part I's Lemma 5.1 has the same sign gap (its E10).

issues.locator: Lemma 2.56, second assertion, p.101 of the published version; the same wording is arXiv v1 Lemma 2.37 (p.20), v2 Lemma 2.50 (p.26) and v3 Lemma 2.56 (p.29)
issues.printed: "More generally, let D be a fixed divisor and let A be a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor such that A ∼_Q M + Λ, where M is an effective Cartier divisor with no exceptional curve of Y → X in its support, and −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD for δ > 0. Take x ∈ F ∩ M of multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M. Then ε_sa(A; x) converges to k when δ → 0."
issues.correction: Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This is exactly what the printed proof establishes; there is no upper bound.
issues.reason: Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic A, gap-seshadri-limit); verified and proved in the corrected form by this continuation.

issues.printed: "Let Δ ≥ 0 be a Q-divisor on X such that (X, Δ) is globally +-regular (completely purely globally +-regular over R, resp.). Suppose that Δ_Y ≥ 0, where K_Y + Δ_Y = f*(K_X + Δ). Then (Y, Δ_Y) is globally +-regular (globally +-regular, resp.)."
issues.correction: The conclusion in the resp. case is "completely purely globally +-regular over R", with the pure boundary S_Y the strict transform of S and B_Y = Δ_Y − S_Y. This is what arXiv v2 (Proposition 6.28, p.64) prints, and arXiv v1 (Proposition 6.22, p.48) prints "purely ... purely".
issues.reason: The printed resp. conclusion is false. Take R = k[[t]] with k of characteristic p, X = Y = Spec R, f = id and Δ = S = V(t). Then (X, S) is purely globally +-regular. For a finite normal R′ ⊇ R with uniformizer s and ramification e, the map R → s^{1−e}R′ splits because R′ is R-free and 1 ∉ t·s^{1−e}R′ = sR′. But (X, S) is not globally +-regular: already for the identity cover, a splitting of O_X → O_X(S) = t^{−1}R would send 1 = t·t^{−1} into tR. The cited proof (Proposition 6.26, which applies because R is complete, together with Lemma 4.27 with B′ = B_Y) proves the pure conclusion. The consumer in Theorem 7.14 (p.165) uses the pure conclusion. In arXiv v3 the qualifier is visibly garbled as "( ly globally +-regular, resp.)", so the published wording is a typesetting slip. Checked on the page images of v3 p.71 and published p.154. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic B, gap-pure-birational); the version history was established by this continuation.

issues.printed: Fix a complete and algebraically closed nonarchimedean field K. Let A be a classical affinoid K-algebra of dimension d. Theorem 7.3, which Theorem 1.19 is labelled as, proves the vanishing above degree d only for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic; the smooth case is claimed only in Remark 7.4(2), only for constant coefficients, and only as an adaptation: 'The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant, thanks to [Elkik, Theorem 7 and Remark 2 on page 587].' issues.reason: Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. No proof of the smooth case for non-constant ℓ-power torsion sheaves appears in Section 7, and the reduction of Theorem 7.3 to constant coefficients runs through Proposition 7.9 for the two cases actually stated there, not for the smooth case.

issues.locator: Proposition 51 and Theorem 9, Appendix A, pp.36–37 (published version)
issues.printed: "Proposition 51. Suppose L is defined over a number field. Then inf_{φ ∈ Aut(ℙ¹)} ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = e^{−poly_n(δ_L)}. Proof. … Now the operator L′ := L + 1 is also Fuchsian …"
issues.correction: Assume in addition that L + 1 is Fuchsian. This holds when every finite zero of a₀ has order ≤ n and deg a₀ ≥ n, and in particular for the Legendre Picard–Fuchs operator (87), a₀ = λ(1−λ), n = 2, which is the only operator to which the paper applies Theorem 9. Under this normalization the proof of Proposition 51 is correct, and Theorem 9 follows as written.
issues.reason: For a general Fuchsian operator, L + 1 need not be Fuchsian, and both statements fail. Take L = ∂_t, which is Fuchsian: its only singular point ∞ is regular singular (∂_t = −z(z∂_z), z = 1/t). Then φ(s) = κs gives φ*L = κ^{-1}∂_s and inf_φ ‖a₀(φ*L)‖ = 0. In Theorem 9 take b(t) = (t − t₀)/(2r) (|b| ≤ 1 on D^{1/2}) and f = (t − t₀)²/(4r), so j_z f(t₀) = 0 while |∂_z f(t₀ + r/2)| = r/4, unbounded in r. Here L + 1 = ∂ + 1 has an irregular singularity at ∞. Theorems 1–8 are unaffected.

issues.printed: (a) p. 21: "This is the same argument we have already applied in the case G = SL_n in the proof of Theorem 5.13"; (b) p. 25: "Let W denote the Weyl group of G, let Λ = ZΦ(H,T) ⊂ X^*(T)"; (c) p. 26: "we have a tautological isomorphism j_0 : Ĝ_{Q̄_λ} ≅ G_{λ_0}"; (d) p. 32: "conjugating ρ_{U_0} by an element of Ĝ(R_U) with trivial image in Ĝ(k), that ρ_{U_0}|_{W_K} = ιχ^∨ for some character χ^∨ : W_K → T̂(R_U)"
issues.correction: (a) Ĝ = SL_n, the hypothesis of Theorem 5.13; (b) the Weyl group of H; (c) j_0 : Ĝ_{Q̄_{λ_0}} ≅ G_{λ_0}; (d) Ĝ(R_{U_0}) and T̂(R_{U_0}).
issues.reason: (a) G is the automorphic group over F_q and plays no role in §5. (b) The whole paragraph works with the reductive group H over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero — Φ(H,T), H⫽H ≅ T/W, the Dynkin diagram of H. (c) G_{λ_0} is the Zariski closure of the image of α_{λ_0} = R∘ρ inside GL(V)(Q̄_{λ_0}), and φ_{λ_0}∘j_0 is formed three lines later, so the source must be Ĝ over Q̄_{λ_0}. (d) ρ_{U_0} is valued in Ĝ(R_{U_0}), of which R_U is a quotient; the parallel statement in Proposition 7.9 correctly writes Ĝ(R_{U_1}) and T(K) → R^×_{U_1}.

issues.locator: §§2–4, pp. 15, 16, 17 (arXiv v2): four hat- and index-slips in the proofs of Theorems 4.5, 4.8 and Proposition 4.7
issues.printed: (a) p. 15: "Since QN_P is a parabolic subgroup of G, we obtain n(δ) = N ≤ dim QN_P"; (b) p. 15: "We claim that there exist g, g′ ∈ G(k) such that (g_1, …, g_n, g, g′) is Ĝ(k)-conjugate to T(δ_1, …, δ_n, γ, γ′)"; (c) p. 15: "for any m ≥ 1, γ = (γ_1, …, γ_m) ∈ Γ^m, and f ∈ Z[Ĝ^n]^Ĝ, we have the formula f(ρ(γ_1), …, ρ(γ_m)) = Θ_m(f)(γ)"; (d) p. 16: "ρ(γ) is the unique element g ∈ Ĝ(k) such that (g_1, …, g_n, g) has a closed orbit in Ĝ(k)"; (e) p. 17: "Let Ĝ(E)^0 denote the subgroup of elements g ∈ G(E) such that for all χ ∈ X^*(Ĝ), χ(g) ∈ O_E^×"
issues.correction: (a) a parabolic subgroup of Ĝ_k; (b) g, g′ ∈ Ĝ(k); (c) f ∈ Z[Ĝ^m]^Ĝ; (d) a closed orbit in Ĝ^{n+1}_k; (e) g ∈ Ĝ(E).
issues.reason: Throughout §4 the ambient group is Ĝ over Z and no group G is in play, so the unhatted G of (a), (b) and (e) is undefined; in (b) the elements are conjugated inside Ĝ(k) in the very same sentence, and in (e) Ĝ(E)^0 is being defined as a subgroup of Ĝ(E). In (c) the tuple and Θ_m are indexed by m, so f must be an invariant function of m variables for both sides to be defined; n is an unrelated integer fixed earlier in the proof. In (d) the tuple has n + 1 entries and the relevant orbit, throughout §§3–4, is the diagonal conjugation orbit in Ĝ^{n+1}.

issues.locator: §§2–3, pp. 5, 10, 11, 12, 13 (arXiv v2): five slips with mathematical content
issues.printed: (a) p. 5: "We write Art_{K_v} : K^× → Γ^{ab}_{K_v} for the Artin map of local class field theory"; (b) p. 10: "self-dual as a representation of G (because there exists a non-degenerate G-invariant symmetric bilinear form on G; see for example [SS70, Lemma I.5.3])"; (c) p. 11: "let f(T) = T^n + a_1T^{n−1} + ⋯ + a_n ∈ K[X] denote the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by a"; (d) p. 12: "S is an integral locally closed subscheme of X, smooth over O, such that O_{S,x}/(λ) = O_{S_0,x}"; (e) p. 13: "Indeed, G_k·φ(x) is closed inside X, by hypothesis, and η is finite, so η^{-1}(G_k·φ(x)) is a closed subset of X′_k"
issues.correction: (a) Art_{K_v} : K_v^× → Γ^{ab}_{K_v}; (b) a symmetric bilinear form on 𝔤; (c) ∈ K[T]; (d) O_{S,x}/(̟) = O_{S_0,x}; (e) G_k·x, twice.
issues.reason: (a) The local Artin map has the local multiplicative group as its source; K^× is the global one. (b) The assertion being justified is that the **Lie algebra** 𝔤 is self-dual as a G-representation, which needs an invariant form on 𝔤; [SS70, Lemma I.5.3] is about the Lie algebra. (c) The polynomial is in the variable T over K, whereas K[X] would be functions on the scheme X being acted on. (d) One divides by the uniformizer ̟ of O fixed in §2 to pass to the special fibre; λ is never introduced as an element of O and denotes a cocharacter in Proposition 3.6. (e) Here φ : G × S → X and x ∈ X(k), so φ(x) is not defined; the hypothesis of Proposition 3.13 is that G_k·x is closed, and the point of G × S in play is (1, x), as the last line of the same proof writes.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 10.2, p. 54 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: "It now follows from the facts that t̂^{ẇ}_k = 0 and that dim_k ĝ_k ≥ r that dim_k ĝ^{ẇ}_k = #R = r"
issues.correction: dim_k ĝ^{ẇ}_k ≥ r.
issues.reason: As printed the middle clause is vacuous, since dim ĝ_k ≥ r holds for any reductive group of rank r and gives no information about the ẇ-invariants. The fact being used is that the invariants of a lift of a Coxeter element have dimension at least the rank, which with the free action of ẇ on the roots forces equality and hence regularity of ẇ.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 6.5, p. 48 (arXiv v2 p. 54)
issues.printed: Then ψκ^{−1}(ζ) = 1 … Moreover, ψ is crystalline by the above. Note that ψκ^{−1} ≡ 1 (mod ϖ).

On O_F^× the congruence does hold (ψκ^{−1} is trivial on the roots of unity and 1 + 𝔪_F is pro-p). issues.printed: "Let L/K be any wildly ramified extension of degree p. … the same calculation as before shows that rsw_{e′_L}(res_{L/K} A) = [c̄_L ω, 0]_{π_L, e′_L}, where π_L is a uniformiser of L, e′_L = pe′ and c̄_L is some non-zero element of F."
issues.correction: Let L/K be a totally ramified extension of degree p, e.g. L = K(π^{1/p}) (K contains ζ_p). Then F_L = F, ω stays non-zero, e′_L = pe′, and the rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: With an imperfect residue field, a degree-p extension can be wildly ramified with e(L/K) = 1 and purely inseparable residue extension (ferociously ramified, the paper's own term in the proof of Lemma 10.5). For such L, e′_L = e′, not pe′. Concretely, take L = K(x̃^{1/p}), where x̃ lifts the x in ω = dx/x ∧ dy/y. This is wildly ramified of degree p, and x̃ is a p-th power in L, so res_{L/K}A = (x̃, ỹ)_p = 0 and the claimed rsw_{e′_L}(res A) = [c̄_L ω, 0] with c̄_L ≠ 0 fails (ω also dies in Ω²_{F_L}, since dx = 0 there). The proposition asserts failure for some L, so one totally ramified L suffices and the stated result stands.

issues.locator: Introduction, paragraph before Theorem C, p. 823 (Invent. Math.); same text in arXiv v5
issues.printed: "Our next result owes its existence to Wittenberg's suggestion that our methods could be used to address Question 1.4. It gives a positive answer to that question, and also shows that the answer to Question 1.3 is no, in general."
issues.correction: Theorem C gives a positive answer to Question 1.4 for every V that has good ordinary reduction at some prime of L, for example abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. In general the positive answer is conditional on the existence of such a prime, conjectured by Serre and recorded by the authors right after Theorem C. The negative answer to Question 1.3 is unconditional, e.g. via K3 surfaces.
issues.reason: Theorem C assumes a prime 𝔭 of good ordinary reduction, and its proof uses ordinarity through [BK, Theorem 0.7(iii)] to get gr⁰ H²(V̄_𝔭, Q_p) ≠ 0. For a smooth projective V with H²(V, O_V) ≠ 0 (so H⁰(Ω²) ≠ 0 by Hodge symmetry), nothing in the paper supplies such a prime. Ordinarity is geometric and does not change under finite extension of L. The paper itself says, after Theorem C, that ordinary reduction at a positive density of primes is only conjectured in general (Joshi, attributing it to Serre), and known for abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. So the claim holds only for varieties with an ordinary prime.

issues.locator: Abstract (p. 298) and §1 Introduction (p. 305), compared with the §4.1 set-up for Theorem 4.8 (p. 361) and Lemma 4.11 (pp. 364–365). arXiv v2 has the same text ("completely solved", l. 316; same parenthetical on twisting before Thm 4.8). arXiv v1 is also the same: intro, and §3.8 Theorem 3.25 with the same twist-minimal hypothesis.
issues.printed: p. 305 (§1): "In the process of proving our main result, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N*)[m], where N* is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two. In particular, we prove that when ρ̄ is unramified at p and ρ̄(Frob_p) is a scalar, then the multiplicity of ρ̄ is two (see Theorem 4.8). (In all other cases, the multiplicity was already known to be one—and in the exceptional cases we consider, the multiplicity was also known to be ≥2)." Abstract, p. 298: "Moreover, we also completely solve the problem (for p odd) of determining the multiplicity of an irreducible modular representation ρ̄ in the Jacobian J_1(N), where N is the minimal level such that ρ̄ arises in weight two." p. 361 (§4.1, set-up before Thm 4.8): "Assume that ρ̄ has minimal conductor amongst all its twists at all other primes (one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)."
issues.correction: In the abstract and introduction, limit the multiplicity claim to ρ̄ that have minimal conductor amongst their twists at primes ≠ p. That is the hypothesis of Theorem 4.8. Twist-minimality at p is automatic in the scalar case, where ρ̄|G_p is unramified. The alternative is to give a separate argument for non-twist-minimal ρ̄. Theorem 4.8 as stated in §4.1 needs no change.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 298, 305 and 361–366 and checked them against the text above.

1. The claims do not match. The abstract and introduction claim multiplicity two for every irreducible modular ρ̄ (p odd) at its own minimal weight-2 level. The classical multiplicity-one results cited in Remark 4.9 (Mazur, Gross, Edixhoven, ...) are stated without twist-minimality. Theorem 4.8, however, is proved only under the hypothesis that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists. The only link between the two is the parenthetical "(one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)". That remark is true, but it does not show that multiplicity is unchanged by twisting: ρ̄ and ρ̄⊗ψ̄ sit at different levels N(ρ̄)p and N(ρ̄⊗ψ̄)p, with different Jacobians and Hecke algebras.

2. The multiplicity depends on the Hecke algebra. The proof of Theorem 4.8 uses T_pG^0 ≅ T_m and T_pG^e = Hom(T_m, Z_p), so dim J[m] = 1 + (number of generators of ω_{T_m}). Multiplicity two therefore means T_m has type 3. This is a property of T_m, and T_m changes under twisting.

3. A concrete example where T_m changes. Let ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄, with ρ̄_0 twist-minimal and unramified at a prime v ∤ N_0 p, and χ̄ tame of conductor v. Then ρ̄^{I_v} = 0, so every lift has conductor exactly v² and every lift appears at level N(ρ̄)p, with U_v = 0. If ρ̄_0(Frob_v) has eigenvalue ratio ≡ v, then Ribet's level-raised forms (Steinberg at v, level N_0vp) twisted by χ̃ are extra newforms of conductor v² in T_m(ρ̄). They have no counterpart in T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) at level N_0p. So T_m(ρ̄) corresponds to the unrestricted deformation problem at v, while T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) corresponds to the unramified one.

4. The proof does not carry over word for word. The proof of Lemma 4.11 lists the non-smooth cases only under twist-minimality. In the example above, R_v ≅ R_v^unrestricted(ρ̄_0|G_v). Its unramified and Steinberg components meet at characteristic-0 points (unramified lifts with eigenvalue ratio v), where H^2(G_v, ad^0ρ) ≠ 0. So "R_v[1/p] formally smooth" fails, and that property is what the text uses when applying Kisin's method to get R̃[1/p] = T[1/p]. The paper's own remark on p. 363 also uses twist-minimality to exclude v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄^{I_v} = 0.

5. The result is probably still true. R_v is still a complete intersection, and weight-2 points avoid the intersection locus by Ramanujan. So multiplicity two is plausible at non-minimal level too, but the paper gives no argument for it.

Conclusion: this is a gap in the reduction to the twist-minimal case, and it affects the claim in the abstract and introduction. Theorem 4.8 itself, as stated, is correct. Defence tried and failed. (1) The quantity is not twist-invariant by any formal argument. Twisting ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄ (χ̄ of conductor x ≠ p) changes N(ρ̄), N*, the curve J_1(N*) and the Hecke algebra T. (2) If ρ̄ is not twist-minimal at x, then ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. Every lift then has conductor cond(ρ̄|G_x), so every lift of ρ̄|G_x shows up at level Γ_1(N). After twisting back, m at level N(ρ̄)p also sees non-minimal forms for ρ̄_0. Examples are χ-twists of forms that are Steinberg at x (conductor x²) when the level-raising condition holds, or of ramified principal series of p-power type when x ≡ 1 mod p. So T_m is not the twist of T_{m_0} at level N(ρ̄_0)p. When no such extra forms exist, a Chebotarev/trace argument does identify the two Hecke algebras, but not in general. (3) The paper's proof really does use minimality. On p. 362, Φ is 'the only twists' preserving minimal-conductor lifts only under minimality; when x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ is non-minimal at x, the characters of Z_p⊗(Z/x)^× also qualify. On p. 363 the paper itself says the twist-uniqueness 'is not true when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v' and removes this case by the minimality assumption. Lemma 4.11 lists only the non-smooth cases that can occur for twist-minimal ρ̄. For a non-minimal ρ̄|G_x = χ̄⊗(unramified, Frobenius-eigenvalue ratio ≡ x mod p), R_{x,φ} is isomorphic to the unrestricted fixed-determinant ring of an unramified representation. Its unramified and Steinberg components meet in the generic fibre at the points μ⊕με, where H²(G_x, ad⁰ρ) ≠ 0. So the claim that the generic fibre is formally smooth fails, and with it the stated input to Kisin's R[1/p] = T[1/p]. (4) No nearby statement closes the gap. Remark 4.12 concerns J_H, and the parenthetical '(one can always twist ρ̄…)' only says that a twist-minimal twist exists. The general statement is very plausibly true: the extra local rings are complete intersections of type 1, and modular points avoid the singular locus. But the paper gives no proof of it, so the introduction and abstract claim more than Theorem 4.8 proves. Consequences: §4.1 opens with 'Although this is not needed for our main results', and nothing later cites Theorem 4.8. Only the claim in the abstract and introduction is affected, and the proposed restriction is right and minimal.

issues.printed: Betti: "To Galois representations conjecturally arising from tempered π of cohomological type associated to G, where G is reductive with a maximal compact K, maximal Q-split torus A, and l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) − rank(A) is arbitrary," ... paragraph after: "In practice, however, what we really need is that (after localizing at a suitable maximal ideal m of the Hecke algebra T) the cohomology is concentrated in l0 + 1 consecutive degrees. (This is certainly true of the tempered representations which occur in Betti cohomology. According to [9], the range of cohomological degrees to which they occur has length l0 + 1. In the coherent case, the value of l0 will depend on the infinity components πv allowed. That tempered representations occur in a range of length l0, then follows from [10, Theorems 3.4 and 3.5] together with knowledge of L-packets at infinite primes)." (p. 300 = PDF page 4; the same wording is in arXiv v2, lines 131-145.)
issues.correction: Main fix: "maximal Q-split torus A" should read "maximal Q-split torus A in the centre of G" (the usual A_G). Then l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) − rank(A), with rank meaning absolute rank of the real group, as in §8.4. This is the qualifier the paper itself uses in §8.2, p. 419: "the maximal Q-split torus in the centre". Minor wording fix: "has length l0 + 1" counts degrees, while the rest of the paper uses "range of length l0" for the interval [q0, q0 + l0]. So that sentence would be clearer as "consists of the l0 + 1 consecutive degrees [q0, q0 + l0]". This second change is only terminology; no mathematics depends on it.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered page (p. 300 = PDF p. 4) against the transcription above. Read literally, A is a maximal Q-split torus of G. "rank" must mean absolute rank here: §8.4 computes l0 from rank(SL_n(R)) − rank(SO_n(R)), and with real rank you would get Hilbert modular surfaces wrong. Under that reading my own computations give:
(a) GL2/Q: rank G = 2, rank O(2) = 1, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = −1, which is impossible.
(b) Res_{F/Q}GL2 with F imaginary quadratic: complexified Lie algebra gl2 ⊕ gl2 has rank 4, rank U(2) = 2, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = 0 instead of 1.
(c) Res_{F/Q}PGL2 with F imaginary quadratic, the paper's own Part 1 case: 2 − 1 − 1 = 0, but the paper treats this case as l0 = 1 (Part 1 "l0 equals 1"; §8.3 "n = 2 and l0 = 1").
(d) Remark 5.14 (p. 3xx, "l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) for PGL(2)/H ... equal to the number of complex places of H") has no A term. The literal intro formula would give r2 − 1 there.
With A taken as the Q-split torus in the centre, every value comes out right: GL2/Q gives 0, GL2 over imaginary quadratic F gives 1, PGL2 gives 1 (trivial central torus), and Res GL1 gives r1 + r2 − 1, matching §8.2. So the printed definition is wrong as stated and the fix is the missing "in the centre". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also in the accepted arXiv v2, so it is not a production artifact. On length, the paragraph does say "length l0 + 1" and then "length l0", but each use is correct under its own meaning: number of degrees versus length of the interval. That part is a stylistic inconsistency, not an error. The paper's main convention elsewhere is "range of length l0", including p. 300 below, and Part 2's "degrees of arbitrary length l0" and "range of degrees of length l0".

issues.printed: Thm 1.3 (p. 302): "Assume conjecture A. Let F/Q be an imaginary quadratic field. Let p ≥ 3 be unramified in F. Let ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) be a continuous representation with cyclotomic determinant, and suppose that: (1) If v|p, the representation ρ̄|D_v is either finite flat or ordinary. (2) ρ̄ is modular of level N = N(ρ̄). (3) ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_p)} is absolutely irreducible. (4) If ρ̄ is ramified at x where N_{F/Q}(x) ≡ −1 mod p, then either ρ̄|D_x is reducible or ρ̄|I_x is absolutely irreducible. Let R^min denote the minimal finite flat (respectively, ordinary) deformation ring of ρ̄ with cyclotomic determinant. Let T_m be the algebra of Hecke operators acting on H_1(Y_0(N), O) localized at the maximal ideal corresponding to ρ̄. Then there is an isomorphism: R^min ⥲ T_m, ..." §5.1 (p. 369): "(3) If x ∈ S(ρ̄), then either: (a) ρ̄|I_x is irreducible. (b) ρ̄|I_x is unipotent. (c) ρ̄|D_x is reducible, and ρ|I_x is of the form ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. (d) If ρ̄|D_x is irreducible and ρ̄|I_x is reducible, then N_{F/Q}(x) ≢ −1 mod p." §5.4 (p. 380): "From these remarks we see that Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11."
issues.correction: Add to Theorem 1.3 a hypothesis, and make §5.1(3) exhaustive to match: for each prime x ∤ p at which ρ̄ is ramified, if ρ̄|I_x is reducible then it is either unipotent or semisimple. Equivalently, ρ̄|I_x is never ≅ ψ ⊗ (1 ∗; 0 1) with ∗ ≠ 0 and ψ a non-trivial character. Such a ψ is necessarily quadratic, and this case is the twisted Steinberg type. The analogous twist-minimality assumption "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0)" is imposed in §3.1 (p. 310) for the case over Q. The alternative is to add a fifth local type T: the lift condition ρ|I_x ≅ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊗ unipotent, a matching level K_{Q,x} in §5.2.1(5), and a matching clause in Conjecture A(2). The tangent-space term L_{Q,x} = H^1(G_x/I_x, (ad^0)^{I_x}) and Proposition 5.1 carry over unchanged, because ad^0 does not change under a twist. Both reported corrections are right. Adding the hypothesis is the minimal fix.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 302, 369–371, 374 and 379–380.

1. The case is possible and falls outside the paper's types. Take x ∤ p. Since det ρ̄ = ε, the restriction det ρ̄|I_x is trivial. Suppose ρ̄|I_x is reducible but not semisimple. Then the unique I_x-stable line is D_x-stable, so ρ̄|D_x is reducible, with characters χ1, χ2 and a non-zero class in H^1(I_x, χ1χ2^{-1}). Because ℓ ≠ p, this group is H^1(I_x/P, k(χ1χ2^{-1})^P), and it vanishes unless χ1|I_x = χ2|I_x = ψ. Together with ψ^2 = 1 this gives ρ̄|I_x ≅ ψ ⊗ (1 *; 0 1) with * ≠ 0. If ψ ≠ 1, the image contains −1 times a matrix of the form (1 *; 0 1), so ρ̄|I_x is not unipotent in the paper's sense (image inside the matrices (1 *; 0 1)). It is not semisimple, so it is not (c). It is not irreducible, so it is not (a). Since D_x is reducible, it is not (d)/M in the intended sense. So it is none of the types S, P, M, H. The deformation conditions (5)–(8) impose nothing at x, §5.2.1(5) defines K_{Q,v} only for types S, P, M, H, and Conjecture A(2) has no clause for this type. The proof of Theorem 5.11 therefore never reaches this case: it needs R^min, Y = Y(K_∅), the tangent bound of Prop. 5.1 with L_{Q,x} = H^1(G_x/I_x, (ad^0)^{I_x}), and Conjecture A.

2. Theorem 1.3's hypotheses do not exclude the case. Hypothesis (4) is satisfied because D_x is reducible.

3. An explicit example. Take E = 11a1, which has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with v_11(Δ) = 5 and surjective mod-7 image. Let χ be the quadratic character of Q(√−11), which is ramified only at 11. Take p = 7 and F = Q(i), so 7 and 11 are inert in F, and set ρ̄ = ρ̄_{E^χ,7}|G_F.
- The determinant is cyclotomic, and ρ̄ is finite flat at 7 (E^χ has good reduction there).
- At x = (11), ρ̄|I_x = χ|I_11 ⊗ (non-trivial unipotent), since 7 ∤ 5.
- The image of G_{F(ζ_7)} is a normal subgroup of SL_2(F_7) with abelian quotient, so it is all of SL_2(F_7) (SL_2(F_7) is perfect). Hence (3) holds.
- N(x) = 121 ≡ 2 mod 7, so (4) holds.
- The Artin conductor at x is x^2 (ρ̄^{I_x} = 0), and the base change of the level-121 newform E^χ gives modularity at Γ_0(N(ρ̄)).
So Theorem 1.3 as printed applies to this ρ̄, but §5 does not cover it.

4. Side remarks. Read literally, the conditional in §5.1(3)(d) is vacuously true when D_x is reducible. That reading makes things no better, because the levels and the type assignment ("we say that ρ̄|D_x is of type S, P, M or H") would then be undefined at x. Twisting ρ̄ by a global quadratic character would reduce this case to type S, as v1 did, but the published paper does not carry out that reduction and it does not transfer the Y_0(N) statement. The conclusion may even fail as stated at Γ_0(N) level: when N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, Γ_0(x^2) also sees principal series π(ψη, (ψη)^{-1}) with η of p-power order, and these are not minimal lifts. I did not verify this possible failure, so I classify the problem as a gap rather than an error.

On locators: C-K1-0's p. 379 for the "follows from" sentence should be p. 380. X-K6-15's aside that Y_0(N) in Theorem 1.3 should be read as Y(K_∅) (K_∅ uses Γ_p(v^c) for types P, M, H) is plausible, but I did not assess it separately. The case exists and is excluded nowhere. Take x ∤ p. Because det ρ̄ is cyclotomic, det ρ̄|I_x = 1. If ρ̄|I_x is reducible and not split, the extension class lies in H^1(I_x, ψ1ψ2^{-1}). The wild inertia group is pro-ℓ with ℓ ≠ p, so this group vanishes unless ψ1 = ψ2 = ψ. Then ψ^2 = 1. With ψ = 1 we get type S. With ψ ≠ 1 we get ρ̄|I_x ≅ ψ ⊗ (non-split unipotent). The line fixed by I_x is D_x-stable, so ρ̄|D_x is reducible and hypothesis (4) of Theorem 1.3 says nothing at x.

This ρ̄ matches none of the lift conditions (5) S, (6) P, (7) M or (8) H on p. 369:
- It is not unipotent.
- It is not a direct sum ψ ⊕ ψ^{-1}.
- ρ̄|D_x is reducible, which rules out M.
- It is not irreducible.
Condition (4) covers only x ∉ S(ρ̄). So R^min puts no condition at x, and that does not match the Selmer condition L_{Q,x} = unramified classes used in Proposition 5.1. The level K_{Q,v} in §5.2.1(5) is defined only for types S/P/M/H. Conjecture A(2) speaks only to S and P, so it gives no local-global compatibility at x for R^min → T_m.

Defence tried and failed:
- Read literally, §5.1(3)(d) is an implication. It is then vacuous whenever ρ̄|D_x is reducible, and §5.1(3) becomes logically equivalent to Theorem 1.3(4). On that reading §5 itself admits the case and leaves it untreated.
- On the intended reading, (a)–(d) list the types, so §5.1(3) excludes the case, but Theorem 1.3 does not.
- Either way, "Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11" fails for these ρ̄.
- No nearby statement fills the gap. The §3.1 twist-minimality assumption applies only over Q. The global twist in arXiv v1 was dropped.

Such ρ̄ really occur. Take E = 11a1, which has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with v_11(Δ) = 5, and p = 3 ∤ 5. Twist E by χ_{-11}, which is unramified at 3. Then E^χ has good reduction at 3. Restrict to F = Q(i), where 3 and 11 are inert. At x = (11), ρ̄ = E^χ[3] has cyclotomic determinant and ρ̄|I_x ≅ χ|I_x ⊗ (non-split unipotent) with χ|I_x ≠ 1. It is finite flat at 3, and its image over F(ζ_3) contains SL_2(F_3), so it is absolutely irreducible. N(x) = 121 ≢ −1 mod 3, and ρ̄ is modular via base change of the level-lowered form. So every hypothesis of Theorem 1.3 holds.

Consequences:
- Nothing later in the paper uses Theorem 1.3 except the deduction of Theorem 1.2.
- Theorem 1.2 is unaffected. There ρ is semi-stable, so ρ̄|I_x is unipotent (type S) or trivial.
- Theorem 5.11 is affected only if §5.1(3)(d) is read literally.
- The theorem is expected to hold in the missing case once the right definitions are in place, so this is a gap, not a false statement.

issues.locator: §1, Theorem 1.4, p. 303, versus the standing assumption of §3.1, p. 310 (published version)
issues.printed: p. 303 (PDF p. 7): "Theorem 1.4 Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation of Serre level N. Assume that ρ̄ is unramified at p. Let R^min denote the universal minimal unramified-at-p deformation ring of ρ̄. Then there exists a quotient X_U of X_1(N) and a vector bundle L_σ on X_U such that if T denotes the Hecke algebra of H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ), there is an isomorphism R^min ⥲ T_m where m is the maximal ideal of T corresponding to ρ̄. Moreover, H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m is free as a T_m-module." p. 310 (PDF p. 14), §3.1: "We further assume that if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0). Note that this last condition is always satisfied by a twist of ρ̄ by a character unramified outside of S(ρ̄)." p. 311, Definition 3.1(4): "If x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ^{I_x} is a rank one direct summand of ρ as an R-module." (The candidate's quote leaves out the opening "Suppose that p ≥ 3." but is otherwise accurate.)
issues.correction:
Simplest fix: add the §3.1 hypothesis to Theorem 1.4, namely "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0", so the statement matches what §3 proves. Other fixes also work but take more effort:
- Keep the statement general and define R^min in the Diamond sense, i.e. ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x) at such x, as in Cor. 1.5(1). The Hecke side then needs a new type-cutting bundle at those x, e.g. U_x = K_0(x^{max(a1,a2)}) with the character ψ̃1(a)ψ̃2(d).
- State the Hecke side for the twist ρ̄⊗χ̄, with N, X_U, T and m taken from the twist.
Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 then each need a one-line twisting reduction, which is valid: weight-one modularity, finite image, the minimality in Cor. 1.5(1) and R^min are all unchanged by twisting by the Teichmüller lift of a character unramified at p.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at pp. 303, 310–311, 338, 340 and 342 against the text. The same wording is in arXiv v2.

(1) Theorem 1.4 as printed covers every odd irreducible ρ̄ that is unramified at p. The whole proof runs under the §3.1 standing assumption. §3.8 (p. 340) says "We now deduce Theorem 1.4, under Assumption 3.9 … we take X_U = X = X_1(N)/H". §3.9.2 (p. 342, and p. 354) removes only Assumption 3.9, the vexing primes. The §3.1 assumption is never removed; the only thing said about it is the one-line twisting remark.

(2) For ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2 with both characters ramified, ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. So Definition 3.1(4) already fails for ρ̄ over k, and the functor is empty. The R^min of the introduction then has to mean Diamond-minimal (ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x); compare Corollary 1.5(1)), and the §3 machinery does not apply to it directly.

(3) On the Galois side, twisting by the Teichmüller lift of χ̄ does give R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). The determinant condition and the inertia condition both carry over. On the Hecke side, the Serre level drops at x (from x² to x or 1), and X_U changes with it. The Hecke algebra of ρ̄' = ρ̄⊗χ̄ has no maximal ideal for ρ̄: ρ̄ cannot occur at level N' < N. So the twist does not directly give "X_U a quotient of X_1(N), m corresponding to ρ̄".

(4) Taking the paper's own level structure directly does not work either. For P(ρ̄) (p. 342) the paper uses U_x = {g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order}, which here has c_x = 2. Take x ≡ 1 mod p and θ a nontrivial character of Z_x^× of p-power order and conductor x. The representation π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor 1+1 = 2 and central character ψ̃1ψ̃2, which is trivial on elements d of p-power order. Its newvector is therefore U_x-invariant, it is congruent to ρ̄, and it is non-minimal. Under the §3.1 assumption, by contrast, ψ̄1 is unramified, and such twists raise the conductor to 1+c_x, which excludes them. So the assumption is really used.

Conclusion: the statement of Theorem 1.4 goes beyond what is proved. The theorem is probably still true with a different choice of X_U and L_σ, so this is a gap, not an error. It is minor, and the fix is routine.

Dependencies: Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 are unchanged by twisting, so they survive. §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 351), which implies the §3.1 condition. Only Theorem 1.4's generality is affected. Defences I tried, and why each fails. I checked page images for pp. 303, 310, 311, 340 and 342 and read the text of pp. 325–330 and 350–354.

(1) "R^min refers to §3, so the §3.1 assumption is implicit." Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly: p ≥ 3, odd, irreducible (which gives absolute irreducibility for p odd), and unramified at p. These are all the §3.1 standing assumptions except the twist condition. Under the paper's own Def. 3.1(4), a ρ̄ with ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2, both characters ramified, has ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. No lift then satisfies (4), so the functor is empty and "R^min" means nothing. The intro must therefore intend Diamond-minimality, which is the reading of Cor. 1.5(1): "ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1". The §3 proof never treats that notion.

(2) "By twisting, WLOG." On the Galois side this works. There is a global χ̄ with χ̄|I_x = ψ̄1^{-1}, ramified only at such x, and R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). On the Hecke side it does not. The twist has a smaller Serre level N' (the x-part drops from x^{a1+a2} to x^{cond(ψ̄2/ψ̄1)}), and its m' corresponds to ρ̄⊗χ̄. Theorem 1.4 requires m to correspond to ρ̄ itself, and ρ̄ does not occur at level N'. The paper says nothing beyond the one-line remark on p. 310, which is the only occurrence of "twist" in §3 apart from the remark on p. 334 about twisting a scalar local ρ̄ to trivial.

(3) "The paper's own X_U works anyway." It does not in general. §3.3 (p. 325) takes X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×, and §3.9 (p. 342) takes U_x = {g ≡ (* *; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order} for x ∈ P(ρ̄). Suppose x ≡ 1 mod p and θ is a p-power-order character of Z_x^× of conductor x. Then π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor exponent a1+a2 = c_x, because ψ̃iθ^{±1} is still ramified with the same conductor. Its central character ψ̃1ψ̃2 has prime-to-p order, so it is trivial on p-power d, and the newvector is U_x-invariant. This representation is congruent to ρ̄ but not minimal. So Theorem 3.14 ("follows from the choice of N and H") and the p. 341 claim "all minimal lifts … appear in H^0(X_U, ω)" do not give R^min → T_m. Under the §3.1 assumption, ψ̄1 is unramified and such twists raise the conductor, so the assumption is really used. A concrete case exists: p = 3, x = 13, ρ̄|I_x ≅ χ̄ ⊕ χ̄^{-1} with χ̄ of order 4.

(4) Where the proof ends. §3.8 deduces Theorem 1.4 "under Assumption 3.9", and §3.9.2 removes only that assumption (vexing primes). The §3.1 assumption is never removed.

Consequences:
- Only the generality of Theorem 1.4 is affected. The theorem is very likely true with a type-cutting L_σ built with the paper's own §3.9 formalism, so this is a gap rather than a false statement.
- Cor. 1.5 and 1.6 ("immediately deduce") still hold after a routine twist.
- §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 361), which implies the condition, so it is unaffected.
- The proposed correction (add the hypothesis) is right and minimal.
- A side observation, not part of this candidate: p. 340's "if x^2|N, then U_x = 0" fits the both-ramified case but misses a wildly ramified ψ̄2 under the §3.1 assumption. U_x ∈ T_m still follows from the invariant-line argument in that case.

issues.locator: §1, Corollary 1.5, hypothesis (1), p. 304 (same in arXiv v1 Cor. 1.4 and v2)
issues.printed: We immediately deduce from Theorem 1.4 the following: Corollary 1.5 Suppose that p ≥ 3. Suppose also that ρ : G_Q → GL_2(O) is a continuous representation satisfying the following conditions. (1) For all primes v, either ρ(I_v) ~→ ρ̄(I_v) or dim(ρ^{I_v}) = dim(ρ̄^{I_v}) = 1. (2) ρ̄ is odd and irreducible. (3) ρ is unramified at p. Then ρ is modular of weight one.
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF p.8 = p.304; the printed text matches the transcription. The same statement appears in arXiv v2. I checked the setup the corollary relies on. Def. 3.1(1) (p.307) fixes det ρ = Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and R^min is taken with Q=∅. Theorem 1.4 is proved with X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3). In §3.9, U_x at x ∈ P(ρ̄) requires d to have p-power order. So T_m only sees forms whose nebentypus has order prime to p.

Redoing the counterexample. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1 ⊕ χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1. Frobenius fixes the trivial isotypic line, so ρ̄|G_v is reducible, v ∈ S−T, and dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1. Let ρ|I_v = 1 ⊕ [χ̄]θ with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. Then dim ρ^{I_v} = 1, so (1) holds. Put ψ = det ρ/[det ρ̄], which has p-power order and ψ|I_v = θ. Any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant forces ε = [ε̄]·ψ^{-1/2}, because squaring is bijective on 1+m when p is odd. The standing hypothesis ρ̄^{I_v} ≠ 0 forces ε̄|I_v ∈ {1, χ̄^{-1}}. In both cases (ρ⊗ε)|I_v has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial, so there are no inertia invariants and Def. 3.1(4) fails. So no twist of ρ is a point of any R^min covered by Theorem 1.4. The Hecke side agrees: the twist has conductor v² at v, and the untwisted ρ has non-p'-order nebentypus.

A global example exists. Take p=3, v=13, K=Q(√−14): 13 splits, 3 is unramified, and O_K^× = ±1. Let ψ be a character of order 6 on I_w, unramified at w' and elsewhere. ψ_w(−1) = 1 because 12/6 is even, so ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c at w), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 (order-2 inertia) and at 13. ρ is modular, but only on X_1(728), not on X_U. So the claimed "immediate" deduction fails for part of the hypothesis. The paper itself says non-minimal lifting is hard (p.304 text after Cor. 1.6).

Corollary 1.5 is not cited again in the paper (grep). Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality, so it is unaffected. The candidate's gap is correct. Its correction's "equivalently" and "only at v ≡ 1 mod p" are overstated, as the correction field explains. I checked the Steinberg case only locally and did not construct a global example. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Theorem 1.4 is proved in §3 for R^min as defined in Def. 3.1 with Q = ∅. That ring has a fixed determinant, equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄ (Def. 3.1(1)), and it requires ρ^{I_x} to be a rank-one direct summand at every x ∈ S−T where ρ̄|G_x is reducible (Def. 3.1(4)). T_m lives on X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3, p. 2141 of the text). At x ∈ P(ρ̄), the group U_x forces d to have p-power order (§3.9). So T_m sees only forms of conductor dividing N whose nebentypus has no p-part.
The intended deduction runs: twist by ψ^{-1/2}, get a minimal deformation, conclude modularity, twist back. This only works if hypothesis (1) makes some twist of ρ minimal. Two cases show that it does not.

(i) DETERMINANT CASE. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1⊕χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1, and ρ|I_v = 1⊕[χ̄]θ, with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. The second alternative of (1) holds. Consider any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant. Since squaring is bijective on 1+m, this forces ε = [ε̄]ψ^{-1/2}. On I_v the twist then has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial. So Def. 3.1(4) fails for every such twist.
A global example, which I re-checked: p = 3, K = Q(√−14), in which 13 splits, 3 is unramified and O_K^× = ±1. Take ψ of order 6 on I_w for one prime w | 13; since ψ_w(−1) = 1, ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 and 13. This ρ is modular (it is dihedral), but no twist of it is a point of T_m.

(ii) UNIPOTENT-REDUCTION CASE. Take x ≡ ±1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x unipotent and nontrivial, so ρ̄(I_x) ≅ Z/p. Let ρ|I_x = ζ⊕ζ^{-1} with ζ of order p. This occurs as a non-split lattice; I checked the lattice explicitly. Here ρ(I_x) ⥲ ρ̄(I_x), so the first alternative of (1) holds, and det ρ|I_x = 1. But ρ^{I_x} = 0 and the conductor is x^2. Any p-power twist still has no inertia invariants, and a prime-to-p twist destroys ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0.
In fact, at a Steinberg-type x the first alternative never yields a minimal ρ. Minimal lifts there have infinite inertia image and satisfy the second alternative instead. I expect global examples to exist (for instance p = 3 tetrahedral or octahedral forms with inertia of order 3 at some prime), but I did not construct a specific one.

In both cases ρ is a non-minimal lift. The paper itself says (p. 304–305) that its method cannot handle such lifts. So the word "immediately" is unjustified for part of the range of hypothesis (1). The conclusion is probably true, as predicted by Fontaine–Mazur, and the examples above are modular by classical results. That makes this a gap rather than a false statement.

CONSEQUENCES. Corollary 1.5 is not used later in the paper. Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality outright, and Theorem 1.4 is unaffected. Only the corollary, as a stated result, is not established in the generality stated.
