issues.locator: §3.8, proof of Theorem 3.26, published p. 339 (PDF p. 43), the paragraph just before item (a). The cited Theorem 3.11 is on pp. 326–327 (PDF pp. 30–31). arXiv v2 has the same sentence ("By Theorem 3.11, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}") and the same Theorem 3.11. arXiv v1 has the same sentence citing Theorem 3.8, whose statement has no local condition at x | Q at all.
issues.printed: p. 339: "By Theorem 3.11, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}. Since T_{Q_N,m} acts on H_N, we get an induced action of R_∞ on H_N (via φ̃_N and the map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m})." The only local statement at x in Theorem 3.11 (p. 327) is: "For a prime x|Q, the restriction of ρ'_Q to D_x is conjugate to a direct sum of residually unramified characters ξ ⊕ ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩|_{D_x} ξ^{-1} where ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m, and such that the restriction of ξ to I_x and hence via local class field theory to Z_x^× ⊗ Z_p = Δ_x is compatible in the usual way with the diamond operators in T_m." (§3.2.4, p. 325: "Let T denote the O-algebra generated by these same operators together with U_x for x dividing Q.")
issues.correction: There are two minimal fixes. (i) Replace "surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}" with "homomorphism R_{Q_N} → T_{Q_N,m} whose image contains the diamond operators at Q_N". This is all the proof uses. (ii) Keep surjectivity and add the missing local-global compatibility at x|Q to Theorem 3.11. That statement says the unramified constituent ξη^{-1} of ρ_Q|_{D_x} sends Art_x(x) to U_x. Then U_x lies in the image of R_{Q_N}, which is generated by traces together with the local characters χ_{α_x}. The statement follows from the proof of Theorem 3.11 as given: ρ_{Q,m} is the pushforward of ρ_{n,α} along T_{n,m} → T_m/I_m. That map is equivariant for U_x (x ≠ p), and in weight n ≥ 2 the relation is the classical Carayol/Langlands compatibility. The candidate's correction is right.
issues.reason:
1. The printed page (p. 339) matches the quoted sentence. T_{Q_N} is the full algebra T of §3.2.4, which includes U_x for x | Q_N (p. 325).
2. R_{Q_N} is topologically generated by the traces of the universal deformation, because ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible. So its image in T_{Q_N,m} is the O-subalgebra (a closed submodule of a finite O-module) generated by the traces of ρ'_Q = ρ_Q ⊗ η. By Chebotarev, that is generated by the T_ℓ η(Frob_ℓ) with ℓ ∤ pNQ, together with the diamond operators, since η is diamond-valued. Surjectivity is therefore equivalent to U_x lying in the anaemic subalgebra of T_{Q_N,m}.
3. That can only come from local information at x. On the ramified-at-x part, where Δ_x acts nontrivially, the U_x eigenvalue is the value at Frobenius of the unramified constituent of ρ|D_x. This is Carayol's local–global compatibility, and traces at unramified primes do not recover it.
4. Theorem 3.11 as printed states only the residual congruence ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m (the bar over ξ is confirmed at 300 dpi) and the compatibility of ξ|I_x with the diamond operators. It never relates U_x to ξ. So "By Theorem 3.11 ... surjective" does not follow from what is cited.
5. The authors do handle this explicitly in the analogous place in §5. Conjecture A(3) builds the full T_α-character, including the operator at a uniformiser, into ρ|D_v, and Lemma 5.6 then argues "the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". Nothing like that appears in §3.
6. The claim is still true: local–global compatibility at x holds in higher weight, where x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄|D_x is unramified with distinct eigenvalues. It passes to weight one because the Hasse-invariant map is Hecke-equivariant away from p modulo ϖ^m (Remark 3.12).
7. Surjectivity is never used afterwards. Proposition 2.3 needs only an R_∞ ⊗ S_N-module structure; (5a) uses the diamond compatibility, which is stated; (5b) needs only T^an-equivariance, since the R_Q-action factors through traces, and Lemma 3.5 provides it. The final conclusion uses R^min ↠ T_{∅,m∅}, where Q = 1 and there are no U_x.
So this is a genuine but minor gap: a step asserted with an insufficient citation. The mathematics is right as intended. Defence tried and fails. By §3.2.4, T_{Q_N} = T is generated over O by T_n, the diamond operators ⟨a⟩ and U_x for x|Q_N. So surjectivity needs U_x in the image of R_{Q_N}. From Theorem 3.11 as printed, the image contains the following. (a) Traces: tr ρ′_Q(Frob_ℓ) = T_ℓ·η(Frob_ℓ). (b) The values of ξ on D_x: the universal representation splits at x as χ_α ⊕ χ_β over R_{Q_N}, and ξ is the image of χ_α. (c) Hence the Δ_{Q_N} diamond operators, by the I_x compatibility. (d) Hence η, a p-power-order function of those diamond operators, and so every T_ℓ. U_x is not reached. On forms whose Δ_x-character is nontrivial, ρ_Q is ramified at x, so no trace of a Frobenius lift equals U_x. Theorem 3.11 fixes ξ(Frob_x) only mod m ("ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m"), and the diamond compatibility is only for ξ|I_x. Nothing else in §3 closes the gap. Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6 get U_x from T^an by Hensel only at Γ_0(Q) level, where U_x² − T_xU_x + x⟨x⟩ = 0. A characteristic-0 argument (T^an determines the eigensystem) is not available either, because weight-one H^0 can have torsion that does not lift, which is the point of the paper. Remark 3.12's "the required information is preserved under congruences" covers only what the theorem states. §5 shows the authors knew the step is needed. Conjecture A(3) includes U_x = T_{π_x} in the local character φ, and Lemma 5.6 then argues explicitly "by Hensel's Lemma … the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces" before claiming R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} in Thm 5.11. §3 has no such argument. So this is a step asserted without adequate proof, a gap. Consequences: surjectivity is never used. The R_∞-action on H_N only needs some homomorphism. Condition (5a), first part, needs the S_N (Δ_N-diamond) image inside the image of R_∞, which comes from the I_x compatibility in Thm 3.11. Its second part is argued from χ_{α_x}|I_x and R_{Q_N}/aug = R^min. (5b) and (5c) use Lemmas 3.5/3.7 and Prop. 3.8. The proof of Prop. 2.3 (p. 312) never uses surjectivity onto a Hecke algebra. Theorem 3.26's conclusion needs surjectivity only for Q = 1 (R^min ↠ T_∅,m∅), and T_∅ has no U_x. Theorem 3.30, which repeats this proof, and §4 add no dependence on it. The claim is also true, by standard local-global compatibility transported from weight n.

issues.printed: We claim that U_x ∈ T_{∅,m_∅} for all x|N. This is a consequence of the assumption that N(ρ̄) = N as we now explain. Suppose that x‖N. Then the T^2_m-representation has a unique invariant T_m-line on which Frob_x acts by U_x, and so U_x ∈ T_m. On the other hand, if x^2|N, then U_x = 0 is also in T_m. Since we have also shown that T_p ∈ T_{∅,m_∅}, we may deduce this from the fact that q-expansion is completely determined by the Hecke eigenvalues T_x for all (x, N) = 1 and U_x for all x|N. (§3.8, p. 340 = PDF p. 44, checked on the rendered page. arXiv v2 has the same wording, and the 2022 Correction deals only with the brackets.)
issues.correction: Split the cases by whether ρ̄^{I_x} is zero, not by the exponent of x in N. (1) If ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0, it is a line. This always happens when x‖N. By the standing hypothesis of §3.1 it also happens whenever ρ̄|G_x is reducible, including cases with x²|N, e.g. ρ̄|G_x ≅ μ ⊕ μχ with χ wildly ramified. In this case the paper's own argument works: the minimal representation into GL_2(T_m) has a unique invariant T_m-line (Def. 3.1(4)) on which Frob_x acts by U_x, so U_x ∈ T_m. (2) If ρ̄^{I_x} = 0, which is equivalent to ρ̄|G_x being irreducible and forces x²|N, then U_x = 0. The conclusion U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} for all x|N still holds, and so does the rank-one claim. This correction is right and minimal: it changes only which condition labels the two cases.
issues.reason:
Setup (pp. 310, 325): N = N(ρ̄), and X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×. §3.1 assumes that ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0 whenever ρ̄|G_x is reducible. Minimal deformations have det equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and their I_x-invariants are a rank-one direct summand when ρ̄|G_x is reducible. The conductor exponent at x is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan. So x‖N does imply dim ρ̄^{I_x} = 1, but x^2|N does not imply ρ̄^{I_x} = 0: a 1-dimensional invariant space with a wild complementary character gives exponent ≥ 2. I redid the counterexample. Take p = 3, K = Q(i), and ψ a character of the ray class group mod 7O_K, which is (Z[i]/7)^×/μ_4 = F_49^×/μ_4 ≅ Z/12. Choose ψ faithful of order 12, so ψ̄ = ψ mod 3 has order 4. On F_49^×, ψ̄^c = ψ̄^7 = ψ̄^{-1} ≠ ψ̄, so ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ is irreducible. It is odd (det(c) = χ_{-4}(c) = -1) and unramified at 3. It stays irreducible on G_{Q(ζ_3)}, since the inertia at 7 still separates ψ̄ from ψ̄^c. At 2, ψ̄ is unramified and K_2/Q_2 is totally ramified, so ρ̄|G_2 ≅ μ ⊕ μχ_{-4}: reducible, invariants 1-dimensional, and χ_{-4} is wild with Swan conductor 1, so the exponent is 2. At 7 (inert, and 7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so not vexing), ρ̄|I_7 = ψ̄ ⊕ ψ̄^{-1} with no invariants, exponent 2. Hence N(ρ̄) = 196, T(ρ̄) = ∅, and every standing hypothesis plus Assumption 3.9 holds. The nebentypus of θ_ψ is χ_{-4}·(n ↦ ψ((n))), and the second factor is cubic because F_7^× maps onto a subgroup of order 3 in F_49^×/μ_4. So it is not trivial on H. Twist by a cubic η mod 7 with η^2 = (ψ|_Z)^{-1}: this gives ψ' = ψ·(η∘N), a newform θ_{ψ'} of level 196 with nebentypus χ_{-4} (the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄). It lies on X_1(196)/H and reduces to ρ̄, since η ≡ 1 mod 3. Its a_2 = ψ((1+i))η(2) is a root of unity. So U_2 acts on H^0(X,ω)_{m_∅}, and on the reduction in H^0(X,ω_k(-∞))[m_∅], by a unit, although 4|N. This agrees with Li's theorem: a newform with v_x(N) ≥ 2 has a_x ≠ 0 exactly when v_x(N) = v_x(cond ε), and here both equal 2. So the printed step 'x^2|N ⇒ U_x = 0' is false, not a slip of notation. The repair uses the paper's own invariant-line argument. With N(ρ_f) = N(ρ̄) and Swan conductors unchanged by reduction (wild inertia acts through an x-group, x ≠ p), the lift also has a 1-dimensional inertia-invariant line. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED.
- Setup (pp. 310, 325): N = N(ρ̄) is the prime-to-p Artin conductor, and X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×. The paper defines U_x only for x|Q, so U_x for x|N here must be the standard operator.
- §3.1 standing hypothesis: "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0)". It forces ρ̄^{I_x} to be a line in the reducible case. It does not force x‖N, because the conductor exponent is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan, and Swan is positive when the ramified character is wild. For x = 2 this is possible for every odd p, since χ_{-4} is ±1-valued.
- The paper's split is correct only in the tame case. Nothing nearby, including Assumption 3.9 (T(ρ̄) = ∅), excludes the wild case.

EXPLICIT COUNTEREXAMPLE (the F_49 facts were checked in python).
- Take p = 3, K = Q(i), and ψ' the order-4 character of the ray class group mod 7 of K, i.e. of F_49^×/μ_4 ≅ Z/12.
- Computed facts: ψ' is trivial on the units and on the image of Z, so it gives an order-4 ray class character. ψ'^c = ψ'^7 = ψ'^{-1} ≠ ψ'. ψ'^2 = χ_{-7}∘N. ψ'((1+i)) = −1 (a root of unity for any choice).
- ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ̄' has these properties:
  - It is absolutely irreducible and odd, with det = χ_{-4}.
  - It is unramified at 3.
  - It stays irreducible over Q(ζ_3), since the quadratic fields in Q(i, √−7) do not include Q(√−3).
  - At 7 (7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so not vexing), ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible and ρ̄|I_7 = ψ̄' ⊕ ψ̄'^{-1}, so the exponent is 2.
  - At 2, ρ̄|G_2 ≅ μ ⊕ μχ_{-4}. This is reducible, with a 1-dimensional invariant line, and χ_{-4} is wild, so the exponent is 1 + 1 = 2.
- So N(ρ̄) = 196 and 4|N, and every hypothesis of §3.1, Assumption 3.9 and Theorem 1.4 holds.
- The theta series θ_{ψ'} is a weight-1 newform of level 196 with nebentypus χ_{-4}, which is trivial on H. It therefore lies in H^0(X,ω)_{m∅}. Its U_2-eigenvalue is a_2 = ψ'((1+i)) = −1, which is nonzero mod 3. So "x²|N ⇒ U_x = 0" is false.
- This agrees with Atkin–Lehner–Li: when v_x(N) ≥ 2, a_x ≠ 0 exactly when v_x(N) = v_x(cond ε). In the wild reducible case both equal a(χ).
- Reporter X-K4-0's local example (ρ̄|G_2 ≅ χ_{-4} ⊕ 1, 4‖N) is the same phenomenon. I agree with the earlier verdict on H-part1a-7.

'FINITE CASE' DEFENCE. The passage sits inside "In the finite case", but the step is justified only by N(ρ̄) = N. In a finite case with the same local type the claim still fails:
- Take a U_x-eigenform f in H^0(X,ω_k(−∞))[m∅]. Multiply by the Hasse invariant to get weight p, where H^1 vanishes.
- Lift by Deligne–Serre to a characteristic-0 eigenform g of weight p and level N. It is new, because N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_g) | N.
- Swan conductors are unchanged by reduction, so ρ_g^{I_x} is a line, and a_x(g) = its Frob_x-eigenvalue, which is a unit. So U_x f ≠ 0.

CONSEQUENCES.
- The passage is used only to prove the side claim, made in prose, that H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one over T_{∅,m∅} in the torsion ('finite') case.
- It is not part of any numbered statement. Theorem 1.4 asserts only R^min ≅ T_m and freeness, which come from Theorem 3.26.
- Theorem 4.8 does not use it. The §3.9.2 rank-one remark is only for the characteristic-0 case, via multiplicity one.
- With the corrected split, U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} still holds for every x|N, so the side claim survives. Only the proof step is wrong.

issues.locator: §3.8 (Modularity lifting), the paragraph after the deduction of Theorem 1.4 that proves 'H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one' in the finite case. Published p. 340 (PDF p. 44), checked on the rendered page. arXiv v2 has the same wording on p. 33 (rendered and checked). arXiv v1 (p. 30, §3.8) does not have the sentence: it says only 'Since we have shown that T_p ∈ T_{∅,m∅}, we may deduce this from the fact that q-expansion is completely determined by the Hecke eigenvalues T_x for all x.' So the U_x claim and its one-line justification were added in v2. The 2022 Correction deals only with the brackets.
issues.printed: We claim that U_x ∈ T_{∅,m_∅} for all x|N. This is a consequence of the assumption that N(ρ̄) = N as we now explain. Suppose that x‖N. Then the T^2_m-representation has a unique invariant T_m-line on which Frob_x acts by U_x, and so U_x ∈ T_m. On the other hand, if x^2|N, then U_x = 0 is also in T_m.
issues.correction: Justify local–global compatibility at x‖N for U_x. Let A ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m lift a power of the Hasse invariant. Multiplication by A embeds H^0(X, ω_{O/ϖ^m})_{m∅} injectively into H^0(X, ω^n_O)_{m∅}/ϖ^m. The embedding respects T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ Np), the diamond operators and U_x for x|N, because on q-expansions mod ϖ^m it is the identity and U_x acts by a_j ↦ a_{jx} in every weight. In weight n, every eigenform f in the m∅-part has level N with N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_f) | N, so f is new at x. This is where N(ρ̄) = N is really used. By Carayol, U_x f is the Frob_x-eigenvalue on the line ρ_f^{I_x}. The weight-n Hecke algebra T^an_{n,m∅} is O-flat and becomes a product of fields after inverting p (strong multiplicity one for newforms), and ρ_n^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. So the Frob_x-eigenvalue λ_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅} on that summand equals U_x. Hence U_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅}, and its image gives U_x ∈ T_m. The case m = 1 already gives what the rank-one argument needs. The candidate's correction is this argument and is correct. The one point it should state explicitly is the newness at x of every weight-n form, which gives both the reducedness it invokes and Carayol's formula.
issues.reason:
Defence attempted. Nothing in the paper supplies the Frobenius/U_x identification for x|N.
(1) Theorem 3.11 ('Local–Global Compatibility', p. 323) gives only three things: traces T_x for x ∤ pNQ, minimality outside Q, and the local shape at x|Q. For x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), minimality (Definition 3.1(4)) says only that ρ^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. It says nothing about which element of T acts on it by Frob_x. So existence and uniqueness of the line are supplied, but 'Frob_x acts by U_x' is not.
(2) U_x for x|N is not even in the paper's Hecke algebras. T and T^an_n are generated by T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ NQp), the diamond operators, U_x for x|Q and U_p (pp. 314–315, 327). So Theorem 3.14 ([15, Lemma 5.1.1], Carayol) and the proof in §3.5 transfer only conditions (2) and (4) to weight one, not any U_x-compatibility.
(3) Remark 3.12 describes the Hasse-invariant congruence method only for x|Q. It is the right tool here, but the paper never applies it to x|N.
(4) In the 'finite case' (H_0(X, ω_K)_{m∅} = 0) there are no characteristic-0 weight-one forms, so compatibility must be proved for a torsion, possibly non-reduced T_m. The paper itself stresses that such local–global compatibility for weight-one Katz forms over Z_p-algebras 'is non-trivial, and requires us to prove' it (p. 298). So the one-line assertion is a step without proof or citation, which is a gap under PROTOCOL §18.
The assertion is nevertheless true, by the argument in the correction; I checked each step. One check was that I_x-invariants of the minimal ρ commute with base change here: when x‖N, ρ̄|I_x is either 1 ⊕ ψ with ψ of prime-to-p order or non-trivial unipotent, and in both cases the rank-one summand persists in quotients. So nothing false is asserted.
Consequences: the claim feeds only the unnumbered remark 'We also show that H_0(X,ω)_{m∅} has rank one as a T_{∅,m∅}-module' in the finite case. Theorem 1.4 as stated (R^min ≅ T_m and H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m free, with no rank) does not use it. Corollary 1.5 does not use it, and nothing later cites it. The analogous remarks after Theorem 3.30 and after Theorem 5.11 claim rank one only when there are characteristic-0 forms. The companion sentence 'x^2|N ⇒ U_x = 0' is a separate error, recorded as X-K4-0 / H-part1a-7, and is not judged here.

issues.locator: §3.9, definition of U_x, V_x for x ∈ S(ρ̄) − (T(ρ̄) ∪ P(ρ̄)), p. 342 (same in arXiv v2, p. 34)
issues.printed: p. 341 (PDF p. 45): "Let P(ρ̄) denote the set of x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄) where ρ̄ is ramified and reducible." p. 342 (PDF p. 46): "• If x ∈ P(ρ̄), we let U_x = V_x = { g ∈ GL_2(Z_x) : g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d ∈ (Z/x^{c_x})^× has p − power order }." ... "• If x ∈ S(ρ̄) − (T(ρ̄) ∪ P(ρ̄)), U_x = V_x = { g ∈ GL_2(Z_x) : g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 1) mod x^{c_x} }." p. 340 (PDF p. 44): "In the statement of Theorem 1.4, we take X_U = X = X_1(N)/H". The arXiv v2 wording is identical.
issues.correction: Give every x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄) the group of the P-bullet: U_x = V_x = { g ∈ GL_2(Z_x) : g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d ∈ (Z/x^{c_x})^× of p-power order }. Equivalently, change the third bullet from "0 1" to "0 d, d of p-power order". This changes nothing unless x ≡ 1 mod p, because x ≠ p and |(Z/x^c)^×| = x^{c−1}(x−1). With this U, when T(ρ̄) = ∅ we get X_U = X_1(N)/H, with H the p-part of (Z/N)^× as in §3.3 (p. 325). That agrees with "we take X_U = X = X_1(N)/H" (p. 340) and with the introduction (p. 303): X_1(M) → X_U has p-power degree, and X_U = X_1(N) when ρ̄ is unramified at every prime ≡ 1 mod p. No minimal form is lost. A minimal lift has Teichmüller determinant, so its nebentypus has prime-to-p order and is trivial on the p-power diamonds. Reading "reducible" in the definition of P(ρ̄) as "ρ̄|I_x reducible" does not fix the problem on its own (see the reason).
issues.reason:
I transcribed the text from the page images of pp. 340–342 and p. 318. The candidate's example is valid under the natural reading of P(ρ̄), where 'reducible' means ρ̄|G_x reducible, as in Def. 3.1(4) and §3.1.

The example, redone:
- p = 3, F = Q(i). ψ is a Hecke character mod 7 of order 4, trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on the norm-kernel μ_8 of F_49^×, so ψ^7 = ψ^{-1} ≠ ψ.
- ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄. At 7: ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible, ρ̄|I_7 is reducible, 7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so 7 is not vexing. At 2: ρ̄|G_2 is reducible with ρ̄^{I_2} ≠ 0, as §3.1 requires.
- For a cubic character χ mod 7, the forms θ_{ψ·χ^j∘N} (j = 0, 1, 2) have conductor 7² at 7 (tame twist of an unramified induction). They are newforms of level 196, congruent mod m, with nebentypus changed by χ^{2j}. Their T_ℓ-eigenvalues are distinct: take ℓ split with ψ(λ) = 1 and χ(ℓ) ≠ 1.
- With U_7 = U_1(49), all three occur in T_m. Twisting to fixed determinant uses η = χ^{-j}, so all three give the same point of R^min. Hence φ: R^min → T_m is not surjective. The step "easily seen to be surjective" (p. 339) holds only because H removes p-power nebentypus.
- Theorem 3.30 is the result stated for X_U. For it to fail, T ≠ ∅ is needed, and the candidate's example has T = ∅. Adding a vexing prime fixes this: also ramify ψ at 23 (inert in Q(i), 23 ≡ −1 mod 3) with a tame order-4 character, trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on μ_8. Twisting by χ keeps the type at 23, so all three forms stay σ-isotypic and Theorem 3.30 still fails.

The candidate's remark "contradicting p. 340" is loose. Page 340 simply defines X_U := X_1(N)/H for the case T = ∅. The real inconsistency is with §3.9's U.

Under the I_x reading, the problem persists for odd x ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x irreducible (see the correction). So the printed definition is wrong under either reading, not merely ambiguous. I have classified it as an 'error' rather than a 'gap'. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Defence attempted and failed. The standing assumptions (§3.1, p. 318: p ≥ 3, ρ̄ odd, absolutely irreducible, unramified at p, and ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0 when ρ̄|G_x is reducible) do not stop a prime x in S − (T ∪ P) from satisfying x ≡ 1 mod p.

(a) Natural reading: "reducible" means ρ̄|G_x reducible, as in Def. 3.1(4). Example: p = 3, ρ̄ = Ind_{Q(i)}^Q ψ, where ψ is a character mod 7 with ψ(g) = i on F_49^× = ⟨g⟩. It has order 4, is trivial on μ_4 = ⟨g^12⟩, and ψ(g^6) = −1 on the norm kernel μ_8, so ψ^7 = ψ^{-1} ≠ ψ.
- At 7: ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible and ρ̄|I_7 is reducible. Since 7 ≡ 1 ≢ −1 mod 3, 7 is not vexing and lies in S − (T ∪ P).
- At 2: ρ̄|G_2 = ψ̃ ⊕ ψ̃ε is reducible with ρ̄^{I_2} ≠ 0, so 2 ∈ P. Then N = 196 and the printed X_U is X_1(196), not X_1(196)/H with H ≅ Z/3.
- For a cubic character χ mod 7, the forms θ_{ψ·(χ^j∘N)} (j = 0, 1, 2) are newforms of level 196. The twist stays tame and cannot factor through the norm, so the conductor at 7 stays 2. They are congruent mod m. Their nebentypus changes by χ^{2j}, which has nontrivial 3-part, so they appear on the printed X_U. Their T_ℓ eigenvalues differ: take ℓ split in Q(i), with a_ℓ ≠ 0 and χ(ℓ) ≠ 1.
- The normalising twist of Thm 3.11 has η = χ^{-j}, the unique p-power square root of χ^{-2j}. So all three forms give the same point of R^min, and φ: R^min → T_{∅,m∅} is not surjective.
- To make T ≠ ∅, so that Theorem 3.30 (p. 350) itself fails, also ramify ψ tamely at 23. This prime is inert in Q(i) and 23 ≡ −1 mod 3; use an order-4 character trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on μ_24, so 23 is vexing. χ is unramified at 23, so the twists keep the inertial type there and stay σ-isotypic.

(b) Reading "reducible" as "ρ̄|I_x reducible" does not save the text. For odd x with ρ̄|I_x irreducible (wild dihedral case) the same failure occurs. Example: p = 3, ρ̄ = Ind from Q(√−7) of an order-7 ray class character of conductor 𝔭_7² (the ray class group has a Z/7 quotient). Complex conjugation acts by −1 on (1+𝔭)/(1+𝔭²), so ρ̄|I_7 is irreducible. Here c_7 = 3, (Z/343)^× has 3-part Z/3, and cubic twists keep the conductor at 7^3.

This also refutes H-part1a-8's claim that S − (T ∪ P) would then contain only x = 2.

Why the paper's argument breaks: in §3.8 (p. 339), φ is "easily seen to be surjective" only because X = X_1(N)/H kills the p-power diamond operators. Then η = 1 and T is generated by the images of the traces. Theorem 3.30's proof says it "is the same as the proof of Theorem 3.26", with ρ'_Q := ρ_Q ⊗ η "defined as before" (item (4), p. 353). With the printed U, η is nontrivial and surjectivity fails.

Nothing nearby supplies the missing quotient. The only uses of P(ρ̄) are the U-bullets and the cusp remark ("∏_{T} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{P} Z_x^× acts transitively", p. 351). Enlarging the group there to ∏_{S−T} Z_x^× only helps transitivity, so the correction is compatible with it.

The P/non-P split looks deliberate, so the intended group is not clear from context. It is an error, not a misprint. X-K4-2's correction and the earlier verdict on H-part1a-8 agree with mine, and theirs is the minimal change. H-part1a-8's first fix (the I_x reading) is insufficient, as shown in (b); its alternative fix (p-power d at every x in S − T) is correct.

issues.printed: We have ℒ_σ|_Y = f_*(𝒪_{Y(V)} ⊗_𝒪 W_σ)^G since the inclusion Y → X is flat. Since the map Y(V) → Y is étale, it follows from [43, Sect. issues.correction: Mumford's theorem gives f^*(ℒ_σ|_Y) ≅ 𝒪_{Y(V)} ⊗_𝒪 W_σ as G-equivariant sheaves (G acting diagonally). Hence ℒ_σ|_Y is locally free of rank rk_𝒪 W_σ, étale-locally isomorphic to 𝒪_Y ⊗_𝒪 W_σ. Equivalently, as in v1, ℒ_σ|_Y ≅ 𝒪_Y ⊗_𝒪 F_σ with F_σ the twisted local system.
issues.reason: Mumford III.12 Thm 1(B) is the equivalence F ↦ f^*F between coherent 𝒪_Y-modules and G-equivariant coherent 𝒪_{Y(V)}-modules. Its inverse is E ↦ (f_*E)^G. Under it, ℒ_σ|_Y corresponds to 𝒪_{Y(V)} ⊗ W_σ with the diagonal G-action. The constant sheaf 𝒪_Y ⊗ W_σ corresponds to 𝒪_{Y(V)} ⊗ W_σ with G acting trivially on W_σ. These two G-sheaves differ in general, so the cited theorem does not give the global isomorphism as printed; it gives only local freeness. The candidate says the printed claim is false 'in general'. That holds for arbitrary G-torsors, where the descended bundle is a twisted form of the trivial one. I did not find a concrete counterexample in this modular setting. On the 1-dimensional generic fibre, a determinant argument suggests the bundle may even happen to be free. So I treat the printed claim as a slip that the cited result does not justify, not as a proven-false statement. v1 settles the intended meaning: there the sentence was ℒ_σ|_Y ⥲ 𝒪_Y ⊗_𝒪 F_σ, with F_σ a locally constant étale sheaf. When the definition was rewritten, F_σ became W_σ. Only local freeness on Y is used. The very next sentence says 'To show that ℒ_σ is locally free … it remains to check … X − Y'. The later use on p. 348 relies only on compatibility of Mumford's equivalence with duals.

issues.locator: §3.9.1, proof of Lemma 3.27(1), published p. 346 (PDF p. 50), middle of the page. arXiv v2 has the same text (p. 37 of the preprint). arXiv v1 has the same argument (p. 33) and uses it again in part (3), where it says "each O_{X_V,x′,χ} is free of rank 1 over O_{X,x}".
issues.printed: "To show that L_σ is locally free of finite rank on X, it remains to check that its stalks at points of X − Y are free. Let x be a point of X − Y. We can and do assume that for each point x′ of X(V) lying above x, the natural map on residue fields is an isomorphism. We have  L_{σ,x} = ( ⊕_{x′↦x} O_{X_V,x′} ⊗ W_σ )^G. ... Then W_σ ≅ ⊕_χ W_{σ,χ} and similarly O_{X(V),x′} ≅ ⊕_χ O_{X(V),x′,χ}. Each W_{σ,χ} (resp. O_{X(V),x′,χ}) is free over O (resp. O_{X,x}), being a summand of a free module. (Note that f is finite flat). We now have  L_{σ,x} ⥲ (O_{X(V),x′} ⊗ W_σ)^{I(x′/x)} ⥲ ⊕_χ W_{σ,χ} ⊗_O O_{X(V),x′,χ^{-1}}, which is free over O_{X,x}."
issues.correction: Do the computation after completing (or henselising) at x, not with Zariski stalks. f is finite, so 𝓛_{σ,x} ⊗ Ô_{X,x} = ((f_*𝒪_{X(V)})^∧_x ⊗ W_σ)^G, because G-invariants are a finite kernel and commute with the flat base change 𝒪_{X,x} → Ô_{X,x}. Also (f_*𝒪_{X(V)})^∧_x = ∏_{x′↦x} Ô_{X(V),x′}, and each Ô_{X(V),x′,χ} is a direct summand of a finite free Ô_{X,x}-module, so it is finite free. The rest of the argument then gives 𝓛_{σ,x} ⊗ Ô_{X,x} ≅ ⊕_χ W_{σ,χ} ⊗ Ô_{X(V),x′,χ^{-1}}, which is free. Since 𝓛_{σ,x} is finitely generated and Ô_{X,x} is faithfully flat over 𝒪_{X,x}, 𝓛_{σ,x} is flat and therefore free. The candidate's proposed correction is right and minimal. Using henselisations or étale stalks in place of completions works equally well. Lemma 3.28 itself already works with completions, "as in the proof of Lemma 3.27".
issues.reason:
I transcribed the text from a 200 dpi render of p. 346. The proof speaks of "stalks at points of X − Y", L_{σ,x} and O_{X,x}, so the rings are Zariski local rings; Lemma 3.28 separately says "along the formal completions at x" when it means completions. For a finite map f, the Zariski stalk (f_*O_{X(V)})_x is the semilocal ring of X(V) along the fibre over x. It equals ⊕_{x′↦x} O_{X(V),x′} only when the fibre points lie on different connected components.

Here G = ∏_{x∈T} GL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), and when T ≠ ∅ several fibre points lie on the same component. Let C be the component through x′ and H its stabiliser in G. H contains S = ∏ SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), which acts through det-trivial elements and so fixes each geometric component. H also contains the inertia group I(x′/x). The fibre points on C are H·x′, and under the paper's residue-field assumption the decomposition group equals I. So C contains |H|/|I| of them. That number is greater than 1 because S is nonabelian (SL_2(F_ℓ) is nonabelian for every ℓ, including SL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3) while I is abelian ([42, VI.5]). The semilocal ring of C at these points is a normal domain, so it is not the product of its localisations.

Worse, O_{X(V),x′} is then not finite over O_{X,x}. It contains inverses of functions that vanish at another point x″ over x, so it is not inside the integral closure of O_{X,x} in K(C), which is that semilocal ring. So the claim "O_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over O_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" is false as written. A toy model with the same shape: t = s^2 at t = 1 over a field of characteristic ≠ 2 (a Z/2 cover). Here k[s] localised at (s−1) contains 1/(s+1), which is not integral over k[t]_{(t−1)}, and the semilocal ring at {±1} is a domain, not a product.

Lemma 3.27(1) is still true, and the standard completion/henselisation argument plus faithfully flat descent proves it. So the text asserts the key step with an invalid justification, and the descent step is missing. That is a gap, with no effect on any result. It is unrelated to the 47 bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v1 and v2 and in the published version. Defence attempted: nothing in the paper's conventions rescues the Zariski reading. Lemma 3.28 explicitly writes 𝒪^∧_{X,x} for completions, so 𝒪_{X,x} and 𝒪_{X_V,x′} mean Zariski local rings. The stalk 𝓛_{σ,x} is also a Zariski stalk ("its stalks at points of X − Y are free"). Taken literally, the displayed equality is false. (f_*𝒪_{X(V)})_x = 𝒪(X(V)) ⊗ 𝒪_{X,x} is the semilocal ring of X(V) along f^{-1}(x). Because X(V) is normal, it is a product of normal domains, one for each irreducible component through the fibre. In this setting a component C has several points over x. G acts transitively on the fibre, and the stabiliser of x′ is I(x′/x) (the residue fields agree), which is cyclic of order e prime to p (cusp inertia). The stabiliser of C contains a copy of SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), whose order is much larger than e. So the semilocal ring has a domain factor with at least two maximal ideals, and it is not ⊕_{x′} 𝒪_{X(V),x′}. The claim "𝒪_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over 𝒪_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" also fails. 𝒪_{X(V),x′} is not a summand of the stalk and is not finitely generated. If it were free it would have finite rank, hence be integral over 𝒪_{X,x}. But it contains 1/s for some s in the maximal ideal of another point x″ of C over x, and 1/s is not integral. A one-dimensional analogue: Z[i]_{(2+i)} is not free over Z_{(5)}. For the same reason the intermediate map 𝓛_{σ,x} → (𝒪_{X(V),x′} ⊗ W_σ)^{I(x′/x)} cannot be an isomorphism of Zariski stalks, because the right side is not finitely generated. After completion (or henselisation) every step is correct, and freeness descends, so Lemma 3.27(1) is true. Kind is borderline gap/error: the conclusion is right and the repair is standard, but the argument as printed is not valid. Later uses: the proof of 3.27(2) ("the proof of the previous part shows that (𝓛_σ)_A ≅ (f_*(𝒪_{X(V)_A} ⊗ W_σ))^G"); p. 347 (X(V)_A/G ≅ X_A "by applying the argument of the proof of Lemma 3.27(1)"); and Lemma 3.28, pp. 348–349 ("as in the proof of Lemma 3.27", "(𝓛^sub_{σ*})^∧_x by the proof of Lemma 3.27(1)"). All of these are formal-local statements, and the corrected completed version supports them. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: §3.9.1, proof of Lemma 3.28, published p. 348 (PDF p. 52). arXiv v2 has the same text. Lemma 3.28 is not in v1.
issues.printed: Away from the cusps, all three inclusions ℒ^{sub}_{σ*} ↪ ℒ_{σ*} ↪ ℒ^*_σ and (ℒ^*_σ)(−∞) ↪ ℒ^*_σ are isomorphisms. It therefore suffices to show that at each closed point x of 𝒞, the natural map gives rise to an isomorphism (ℒ^{sub}_{σ*})^∧_x ⥲ (ℒ^*_σ)(−∞)^∧_x along the formal completions at x.
issues.correction: '… at each closed point x of the cuspidal divisor ∞ of X (i.e. at each cusp x of X) …'
issues.reason: The printed symbol is calligraphic 𝒞. Nothing in §3.9 defines 𝒞 before this point. §3.9 names the reduced cuspidal divisor ∞ (p. 343: 'we let ∞ denote the reduced divisor supported on the cusps'). The 𝒞 notations elsewhere are all decorated and defined locally: 𝒞_Δ(Q) ⊂ X_Δ(Q) in §3.2, and 𝒞_{V_Δ(Q)} ⊂ X_{V_Δ(Q)} in §3.9.2(2). The context ('Away from the cusps …') and the next sentence ('all cusps of X and X(V) are defined over 𝒪') show that 𝒞 means the cusps of X. So this is an undefined-symbol slip with a clear meaning, and it has no effect on the proof.

issues.locator: §3.9.2, Theorem 3.30 (published p. 350; PDF p. 54), with the definition of T_∅ just before it, proof steps (3) (p. 351) and (4) (pp. 353–354), and the closing sentence on p. 354. The convention is set on p. 341 (§3.9) and p. 343 (§3.9.1). arXiv v2 has the same text (§3.9.2, Theorem 3.30, pp. 39–43), and so does v1 (§3.10.3, Theorem 3.34).
issues.printed: p. 341: "In this case, minimal modular lifts of ρ̄ will appear in the σ* := Hom(σ, O)-isotypical part of H^0(X_V, ω))." p. 343: "H^0(X_U, ω^{⊗n} ⊗_{O_X} L_σ) ≅ (H^0(X_V, ω^{⊗n}) ⊗_O W_σ)^G = Hom_{O[G]}(W_σ^*, H^0(X_V, ω^{⊗n})) … The sheaf L_σ will thus allow us to extract the W_σ^*-part of the space of modular forms at level V." p. 350: "Let T_∅ denote the ring of Hecke operators acting on H_0(X_U, ω ⊗ L_σ) generated by Hecke operators away from S(ρ̄) ∪ {p}. … Theorem 3.30 The map φ : R^min ↠ T_{∅,m∅} is an isomorphism and T_{∅,m∅} acts freely on H_0(X_U, ω ⊗ L_σ)_{m∅}." p. 351, step (3): "H_i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ L_σ) = H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (ω^{2−n} ⊗ L^sub_{σ*})_{K/O})^∨. We use this to endow the left hand side with a Hecke action." p. 353, step (4): "let T denote the subalgebra of endomorphisms of H^0(X_{U_1(Q)}, (ω ⊗ L_σ)_{K/O}) … Then there is a Galois representation ρ_Q : G_Q → GL_2(T_m) deforming ρ̄ … minimal outside Q." p. 354: "However, this is precisely the point of the representation W_σ: it cuts out the automorphic representations giving rise to minimal deformations of ρ̄ at the primes in T(ρ̄) (see [15, Lemma 5.1.1])." and "Theorem 1.4 follows from the previous result and Verdier duality as in Sect. 3.8."
issues.correction:
Theorem 3.30 should concern the module whose Hecke algebra step (4) controls. The paper's convention (p. 341, p. 343, step (4)) is that minimal lifts lie in the W_σ^*-part H^0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ). Accordingly, state Theorem 3.30 in one of two equivalent forms.
(a) Use H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_{σ^*}) in place of H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ). This is the Pontryagin dual of H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L^sub_σ)_{K/O}), which by step (2) agrees with H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O}) at m_∅. Steps (1)–(3) go through with σ and σ^* swapped, and step (4) then supplies R_Q ↠ T_Q verbatim.
(b) Equivalently, keep L_σ but localise at m_∅^* (T_x ↦ tr ρ̄(Frob_x)/det ρ̄(Frob_x), ⟨a⟩ ↦ det ρ̄(a)^{-1}), with R^min(ρ̄^∨) ≅ R^min(ρ̄).
Theorem 1.4 for H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m then follows from (b). Verdier duality D: H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) ≅ H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) matches T_x and ⟨a⟩ on H^1 with ⟨x^{-1}⟩T_x and ⟨a^{-1}⟩ on H_0 (by T_x^t = ⟨x^{-1}⟩T_x, p. 352), so it carries the m_∅^*-part to the m_∅-part. This twisted duality replaces the w_ζ^*-equivariant isomorphism of Sect. 3.8 cited on p. 354. The closing rank-one remark needs the same change. When det ρ̄|I_x = 1 for every x ∈ T(ρ̄), σ ≅ σ^* and the printed statement is correct. The candidate's correction is right in substance. Its alternative branch (that CDT's σ_x is normalised the other way) does not arise; see reason.
issues.reason:
I checked this from the printed definitions. (i) By the definition of H_i in §3.2.4 and step (3), H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) is the Pontryagin dual of H^0(X_U, (ω⊗L^sub_{σ*})_{K/O}), with the dual Hecke action. By Lemma 3.27(2), that module is (H^0(X_V, ω(−∞))_{K/O} ⊗ W_{σ*})^G = Hom_G(W_σ, ·). So T_∅ in Theorem 3.30 is the Hecke algebra of the W_σ-part. (ii) Pp. 341 and 343 and step (4) say the minimal lifts of ρ̄ live in H^0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) = Hom_G(W_σ^*, ·), and step (4) builds minimal Galois representations only on that algebra. The patching in Thm 3.26 needs R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} for the algebra acting on H_N = H_0(X_{Δ_N}(Q_N), ω⊗L_σ)_m, which is the σ*-coefficient algebra. Step (4) does not supply this map. (iii) The two parts are genuinely different. dim Hom_G(W, π) = dim Hom_G(W*, π^∨), so they carry contragredient inertial types, and W_σ, W_σ* have mutually inverse central characters on the centre of GL_2(F_x). Take ρ̄|I_x = ξ⊕ξ^x. The two parts can both contain lifts of ρ̄ only if ξ^{-1}⊕ξ^{-x} ≅ ξ⊕ξ^x, i.e. ξ^{1+x} = det ρ̄|I_x = 1. (iv) A concrete case. Let p = 3, x = 5, K = Q(√−2): 5 is inert, 3 splits, class number 1. Take a finite-order Hecke character θ of conductor 5·𝔮, where 11 = 𝔮𝔮̄. Let θ_5 have order 8 on F_25^× and θ_𝔮 be quadratic, so θ(−1) = (−1)(−1) = 1. Then ρ = Ind θ is an odd weight-one Artin representation unramified at 3. Its reduction ρ̄ is irreducible, and 5 is a vexing prime with ξ of order 8. A computation over the order-24 cyclic group gives the type exponents {3,15} against the dual {9,21}, and det ρ̄|I_5 of order 4. ρ itself satisfies Definition 3.1, so R^min has an O-point. Under the paper's convention, the W_σ-part has no characteristic-0 eigenforms at m∅. The x-component of the nebentypus even rules them out mod p, since ω_σ ≢ ω_σ^{-1} (order 4). So T_{∅,m∅} is zero or torsion, and 'R^min ≅ T_{∅,m∅}' fails. (v) The reverse normalisation of [15] is the only way out, and it makes the p. 341 statement and the minimality claim of step (4) false instead. So the paper as printed contains a genuine σ/σ* inconsistency either way. I could not obtain [15] to fix which side, so I report the reading under the paper's own stated convention. Theorem 1.4 is existential in L_σ and survives after the repair. 1. What acts on H_0 (defence fails). By the paper's own definition, H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) = H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_{K/O})^∨, with the dual Hecke action (p. 351; §3.2.4). By Lemma 3.27(2), (H^0(X_V,ω(−∞))⊗W_{σ^*})^G = Hom_G(W_σ, S_1(V)). So T_∅ is the Hecke algebra of the W_σ-part. Step (3) says this itself: 'dim H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L_{σ^*})_m'.
2. Where the Galois representations are built. Step (4) builds them only on the Hecke algebra of H^0(X_{U_1(Q)},(ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O}) = Hom_G(W_σ^*, ·), the W_σ^*-part. So the 'same proof as Theorem 3.26' has no map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} for the patched modules H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m, and no φ for T_∅. Nothing nearby bridges the two parts:
- the contragredient in step (3) sends the W_σ^*-part at m to the W_σ-part at m*, not m;
- the 'self-dual up to twist' remark in v1 changes ρ̄ to a twist of ρ̄.
3. Which side is right: I checked [15] (CDT, Taylor's copy).
- In §5.1, σ_{S,p} = Θ(χ_p), with ρ̄|I_p ≅ χ̄_p∘η_{p,2} ⊕ χ̄_p∘Frob∘η_{p,2}.
- Lemma 5.1.1: π ∈ N_S iff Hom_{U_S}(σ_S, π^∞) ≠ 0.
- CDT's Notation fixes η_1 = ε^{-1}, with the arithmetic-Frobenius normalisation.
- Θ(χ) has central character χ|Z_x^×.
Now take a minimal lift f. Then det ρ_f|I_x = χ|Z_x^× ∘ ε^{-1}, so the x-part of the nebentypus of f is (χ|Z_x^×)^{-1}. That character is how scalars of G act under the moduli action α ↦ α∘g. It is the central character of σ_x^*. So under the paper's moduli action, minimal forms lie in the W_σ^*-part: p. 341 and step (4) are right, and the statement of Theorem 3.30 is the slip.
4. The two parts really differ. Hom_G(W_σ, π) ≅ Hom_G(W_σ^*, π^∨), and CDT Lemmas 3.2.1(2) and 4.2.4(3) apply. Together they show the W_σ-part contains only forms of the dual type, whose reduction is ξ^{-1}⊕ξ^{-x}. That is ≇ ξ⊕ξ^x unless det ρ̄|I_x = ξ^{1+x} = 1.
- Example: p = 3, x = 5, ξ of order 8 on F_25^×; then ξ^5 ≠ ξ and ξ^6 ≠ 1.
- A dihedral ρ̄ = Ind_K ψ is one realisation.
In such a case H_0(X_U, ω_K⊗L_σ)_{m_∅} = 0 (in fact T_{∅,m_∅} = 0, by step (4)'s Hasse-invariant argument). But R^min ≠ 0, and it has a characteristic-zero point when there is a minimal weight-one lift. So Theorem 3.30 as printed is false.
5. What uses it. Theorem 3.30 is used only to deduce Theorem 1.4 (p. 354), and Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 come from Theorem 1.4. Theorem 1.4 is existential in the bundle and still holds for L_σ via form (b). So the stated result that fails is Theorem 3.30 (and the rank-one remark); Theorem 1.4 and its corollaries are unaffected.
Confidence: the σ/σ^* mismatch is certain. The direction (the statement is wrong, not step (4)) rests on the normalisation check in point 3.

issues.printed: (3) (Proposition 3.8): We need to show that the 𝒪[Δ]-module M = H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω⊗ ℒ_σ)_𝔪 is balanced. First of all note that Ω^1_{X_Δ(Q)/𝒪} ⊗ ℒ^*_σ = ω^2(−∞) ⊗ ℒ^*_σ = ω^2 ⊗ ℒ^{sub}_{σ*} by Lemma 3.28, and hence H_i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ ℒ_σ) = H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (ω^{2−n} ⊗ ℒ^{sub}_{σ*})_{K/𝒪})^∨.
issues.reason: X_Δ(Q) is the §3.2 curve: the quotient of X_1(NQ) by H with Δ-structure at Q. ℒ_σ is defined only on the §3.9 curves X_U, X_{U_i(Q)} and, implicitly, X_{U_Δ(Q)}; it does not exist on X_Δ(Q). The identity ω^2(−∞) ⊗ ℒ^*_σ = ω^2 ⊗ ℒ^{sub}_{σ*} comes from Lemma 3.28, which is about the §3.9 curves. Step (2), the displayed consequence in the same sentence, and the definition of Φ all work on X_{U_Δ(Q)}. The notation X_Δ(Q) was carried over from Proposition 3.8. The meaning is clear.

issues.locator: §3.9.2, proof of Theorem 3.30, step (3), after the definition of Φ, published p. 351 (PDF p. 55). arXiv v2 has the same text. The §3.2.4 analogue (published p. 322 region; v2 line ~993) states the relation with no explicit range.
issues.printed: Φ ∘ T_x = x^{1−n} T_x^{t,∨} ∘ Φ,  for all x prime to NQ, and the same relation holds for the operators U_y with y|Q.
issues.correction: '… for all primes x ∤ pNQ (i.e. x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {p}), and the same relation holds for the operators U_y with y|Q.'
issues.reason: On the groups H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, …), T_x is defined only for x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {p} (summary on p. 345). Likewise, T^univ in §3.2.3 has T_x only for x ∤ pNQ. Here N = N(ρ̄) (§3.3). Its prime divisors form S(ρ̄), and ρ̄ is unramified at p (§3.1). So 'x prime to NQ' includes x = p, and no T_p is defined on these coherent cohomology groups. Remark 3.4 uses the correct range 'x prime to pNQ'. The factor p was dropped. Since there is no T_p, this is only an imprecise quantifier range with no effect on the argument.

issues.locator: §3.9.2, proof of Theorem 3.30, item (2), p. 351 (published version)
issues.printed: (2) (Proposition 3.7 (2)): The corresponding statement holds: namely, the natural map H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (ω ⊗ L^sub_σ)_{K/O})_m → H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (ω ⊗ L_σ)_{K/O})_m is an isomorphism for i = 0, 1 whenever m is non-Eisenstein.
issues.correction: "(2) (Lemma 3.7 (2))": the result being adapted is Lemma 3.7(2). Lemma 3.7 begins at the foot of p. 321 and its part (2) is on p. 322.
issues.reason: I rendered PDF page 55 (p. 351), in §3.9.2 in the proof of Theorem 3.30. It reads "(2) (Proposition 3.7 (2)): The corresponding statement holds". Section 3 numbers all environments in one sequence. The text and page images show Remark 3.4, Lemma 3.5, Lemma 3.6, Lemma 3.7, Proposition 3.8, Assumption 3.9 and Remark 3.10, so no Proposition 3.7 exists. PDF pages 25–26 (pp. 321–322) print "Lemma 3.7 Let Δ be a quotient of Δ_Q. Then: … (2) For i = 0, 1, we have an isomorphism H^i(X_Δ(Q), ω(−∞)_{K/O})_m → H^i(X_Δ(Q), ω_{K/O})_m". Item (2) of the proof of Theorem 3.30 is the version of this statement with L^sub_σ ⊂ L_σ. Its argument is the same: take the exact sequence through the cusps and use the Eisenstein property from Remark 3.4. So the number 3.7(2) is correct and only the label "Proposition" is wrong. The other items in the same list are labelled correctly: item (1) cites "Lemma 3.5" and item (3) cites "Proposition 3.8", so the mislabel stands out. The arXiv v2 has the same wording (cg-v2.txt line 2104: "(2) (Proposition 3.7 (2))") while also printing "Lemma 3.7." (line 949). This is a wrong environment label and has nothing to do with the 47 known bracket errors. It does not affect the mathematics, because a reader can find the result from the number alone and nothing later depends on the label.

issues.printed: We also have Φ ∘ ⟨a⟩ = ⟨a^{−1}⟩ ∘ Φ for x|NQ because D switches ⟨a⟩^* with ⟨a⟩^∨_* = ⟨a^{−1}⟩^{*,∨}.
issues.correction: "We also have Φ ∘ ⟨a⟩ = ⟨a^{−1}⟩ ∘ Φ for all a prime to NQ (a coprime to the elements of S(ρ̄) ∪ Q) …". The candidate's extra change of ⟨a^{−1}⟩ to ⟨a^{−1}⟩^∨ is optional and not part of the misprint. The paper routinely leaves the ∨ off diamond operators acting on a dual; §3.2.4 (p. 323) writes Φ ∘ ⟨x⟩ = ⟨x⟩ ∘ Φ.
issues.reason: Here the quantified variable is a, not x, and diamond operators exist only for a coprime to the level. On p. 345 the paper defines ⟨a⟩ 'for a coprime to the elements of S(ρ̄) ∪ Q'. So 'for x|NQ' is a slip. It uses the wrong letter and states the divisibility condition backwards: the preceding clause reads 'for all x prime to NQ'. The relation itself holds. This Φ has no Atkin–Lehner factor w^*, unlike the one in §3.2.4, so Verdier duality swaps ⟨a⟩ and ⟨a^{−1}⟩. The dual relation Ψ ∘ ⟨a^{−1}⟩ = ⟨a⟩ ∘ Ψ displayed on p. 352 matches. The intended meaning is clear.

issues.locator: §3.9.2 (the proof of Theorem 1.4 with vexing primes), proof of Theorem 3.30, item (2) (the analogue of Lemma 3.7(2), which the paper labels "Proposition 3.7 (2)"), published p. 351 (PDF p. 55). The claim rests on Remark 3.4, p. 316 (PDF p. 20), which makes the same kind of transitivity claim for (Z/NQZ)^× on C_Δ(Q). The text is identical in arXiv v2 (p. 40 for §3.9.2; Remark 3.4 at v2 line 732). arXiv v1 has neither transitivity claim: its Lemma 3.7(2) proof just says "the action of Hecke on H^0(X, I) is Eisenstein".
issues.printed: (2) (Proposition 3.7 (2)): ... and it suffices to show that the cohomology of the last term (which is concentrated in degree 0) is Eisenstein. However, the argument of Remark 3.4 (noting that the group ∏_{x∈T(ρ̄)} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{x∈P(ρ̄)} Z_x^× acts transitively on the set of cusps in X_{V_Δ(Q)}) shows that H^0(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (f_*((ω ⊗ W_σ)|_{C_{V_Δ(Q)}}))^G) = (H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) ⊗_O W_σ)^G is Eisenstein, which gives the desired result.   [Remark 3.4, p. 316, which this relies on: "... but note that the group (Z/NQZ)^× acts transitively on the set of cusps in C_Δ(Q). In particular, suppose f ∈ H^0(C_Δ(Q), ω_k^{⊗n}) is a non-zero mod p eigenform ... Then f cannot vanish at any cusp and the formula [28, (3.5)] implies that ... T_x(f) = (1 + χ(x)x^{n−1})f."]
issues.correction: Delete the parenthetical transitivity claim, because it is false. Justify the Eisenstein property type by type. The cusps of X_{V_Δ(Q)} have local "types" at each prime x of Q, of P(ρ̄), of S(ρ̄)−(T∪P) and at the auxiliary Γ_1(q) prime. These are the N(Z_x)\GL_2(Z_x)/U_0-type double cosets, i.e. the analogues of '∞' and '0'. The listed group, even with all the diamond operators added, preserves every type; within a type it permutes the cusps. On H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω^n), each T_x (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}) acts as B_x + x^{n−1}A_x. Here A_x and B_x come from left translation by diag(x^{-1},1) and diag(1,x^{-1}) away from x. They permute the cusps and rescale by roots of unity, they commute, and they are multiplicative in x. So every simultaneous eigenvalue has the form ψ_1(x)+x^{n−1}ψ_2(x) with ψ_i finite-order characters, and the associated semisimple Galois representation ψ_1 ⊕ ψ_2ε^{n−1} is reducible. T_x commutes with G and acts trivially on W_σ, so the submodule (H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) ⊗ W_σ)^G is also Eisenstein. The conclusion of item (2) is therefore correct. The candidate's first proposed fix is right and is the minimal one. Its Atkin–Lehner alternative is only a sketch: at P and S−(T∪P) the Atkin–Lehner element conjugates V_x to a different group, so it needs more care.
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 351 and p. 316 and transcribed the text. The claim is refuted by an equivariant projection. Here V_Δ(Q) = ∏_{x∉Q} V_x × ∏_{x∈Q} (a group between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}), and patching needs Q ≠ ∅. Fix x ∈ Q and let W' = ∏_{y≠x} GL_2(Z_y) × U_{0,x}. Then W' contains V_Δ(Q), and it also contains the group K' = ∏_{T} GL_2(Z_y) × ∏_{P} Z_y^×, whose components all lie at primes other than x. The projection X_{V_Δ(Q)} → X_{W'} = X_0(x) is therefore K'-equivariant. K' acts trivially on X_0(x) because it lies inside W': on cusps, [h]_V ↦ [hg]_V maps to [hg]_{W'} = [h]_{W'}. The projection is surjective on cusps, and X_0(x) has two cusps, 0 and ∞. So K' has at least two orbits on the cusps of X_{V_Δ(Q)}. Equivalently, the local Bruhat type in B(Q_x)\GL_2(Q_x)/U_{0,x}, which has 2 elements, is an invariant that K' preserves. The same happens even when Q = ∅, at primes in S − (T∪P) with U_1(x^{c_x}) level.

Remark 3.4 fails in the same way. The diamond operators commute with X_Δ(Q) → X_0(NQ), which has at least 2 cusps when NQ > 1. Its consequence is also false: a Hecke eigenvector can vanish at the ∞-type cusps and have eigenvalue ψ_1(x) + ψ_2(x)x^{n−1} ≠ 1 + χ(x)x^{n−1}. An example is the constant-term vector of E_n^{χ,1} for n ≥ 3 and nontrivial χ.

The target conclusion (the boundary term is Eisenstein) is still true by the standard constant-term argument. So a false assertion is used as a proof step, while the result survives. arXiv v1 simply asserted the Eisenstein property without this faulty justification. Defence attempts. (a) Could "cusps in X_{V_Δ(Q)}" mean only the cusps over a fixed cusp of X_{U_Δ(Q)}? G acts transitively on those fibres, but then the factor ∏_P Z_x^× would be pointless, and the text says "the set of cusps". Also the argument of Remark 3.4 needs a global statement: an eigenvector is non-zero at '∞', and its eigenvalue is read off there. (b) Could "cusps" mean Galois orbits? Galois acts through det, i.e. by upper-triangular matrices, which preserve the types. Neither reading rescues the claim.

Why it is false. Adelically, cusps = B(Q)\GL_2(A^∞)/V = ({±1}^2·N(Ẑ))\∏_x GL_2(Z_x)/V_x. The listed group acts only on the T- and P-components on the right. At x ∈ Q, where V_x lies between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}, the invariant N(Z_x)\GL_2(Z_x)/U_{0,x} = N\P^1(F_x) has two values. Neither the global ±1 nor the group can change it. At x ∈ P, the Z_x^× action is by elements of U_0(x^{c_x}), which preserve the c_x+1 ≥ 2 valuation types.

Brute-force check (script work/agents/vK4-9B/cusps57.py): p=3, vexing t=5 (5≡−1 mod 3, V_t=Γ(5)), Q={7} (7≡1 mod 3) with U_{1,7}-level. There are 288 cusps. GL_2(Z/5) has 6 orbits on them, and adding the diamonds at 7 still leaves 2 orbits.

So the claim fails whenever Q≠∅, P≠∅, S≠T, or the auxiliary Γ_1(q) level is used. It holds only in the degenerate case S=T, Q=∅ with no auxiliary level, which footnote 4 says needs that level anyway. Patching uses #Q_N = q ≥ 1, so the claim is false exactly where it is used.

Nuance on the candidate's reason: its example has T=∅, but §3.9.2 assumes T≠∅. The failure persists with T≠∅, as above.

Consequences. Item (2) is used in item (3): "which in turn, by point (2) above, is equal to". Through that it feeds the analogue of Prop 3.8 and the patching proof of Thm 3.30, and hence Thm 1.4. The conclusion of item (2) is true by the standard type-by-type computation, so no stated result changes. Only the given justification fails, so 'affects' is 'the proof'.

Specifically, let α : T → T/m = k be the reduction map. Then m* is the kernel of the map β : R → k defined by: β(T_x) = α(⟨x⟩T_x), β(U_y^t) = α(U_y), and β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a^{−1}⟩)." arXiv v2 (p. 41) has the same text.
issues.correction: β(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x), that is α(T_x)·α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}. β(U_y^t) = α(U_y) and β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a^{−1}⟩) are correct as printed. This is the minimal fix: ⟨x⟩ becomes ⟨x^{−1}⟩, and it matches v1's m* (T_x − d_x^{−1}a_x).

I redid the computation with n = 1, the case in use here: the left-hand side is ω ⊗ L_σ. Write c(r) = ΨrΨ^{−1} for an operator r on H^0. The printed relations then give c(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x) = T_x and c(⟨a⟩) = ⟨a^{−1}⟩. It follows that c(T_x) = c(⟨x⟩)c(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x) = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x on H_1. So Ψ(H^0_{m*}) = H_{1,m} exactly when β(r) = α(c(r)), which gives β(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x). The printed β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a^{−1}⟩) and β(U_y^t) = α(U_y) agree with this computation. Only β(T_x) has the wrong sign in the exponent.

The paper's own final step gives an independent check that does not depend on how ⟨a⟩ is normalised. The proof says that taking contragredients swaps H^0(ω⊗L_σ)_{m*} and H^0(ω⊗L_{σ*})_m, so m* has to be the contragredient of m. Item (4) on p. 353 uses the Hecke polynomial X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. With that convention, the contragredient of an eigensystem (t_x, d(a)) is (t_x·d(x)^{−1}, d(a)^{−1}). That again gives β(T_x) = α(T_x)α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}. With the printed β, the contragredient of m* would have T_x-eigenvalue α(⟨x⟩)^2α(T_x), which is not m.

The discrepancy is real in general. α(⟨x⟩) is the reduction of the nebentypus, which is det ρ̄(Frob_x) in weight 1, and it has order > 2 in general. So α(⟨x⟩)^2 is not identically 1, and read literally, the printed m* makes both the step "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" and the contragredient step false.

The error is in β, not in T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x: the Ψ relations and the contragredient check both force the corrected β. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it.

Scope: m* and β appear only in this item, and nothing later uses the formula. With the obvious fix, the argument goes through exactly as the authors intend, so no stated result is affected. As the candidate noted, I did not check the scalar normalisation of T_x^t from [31]. It would only change x-power factors, which are trivial when n = 1.

A separate small slip that is not part of this item: the display at the foot of p. 352 has "ω^n ⊗ L_σ" where n = 1 is meant. Defence attempted and it fails. Two independent checks both force the corrected β.

(1) The paper's own relations with n = 1, the case in use. Take v in H^0(ω⊗L_σ) with T_x v = τv and ⟨x⟩v = δv, and put w = Ψ(v). Then T_x w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x v) = δ^{−1}τ w and ⟨x⟩w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩v) = δ^{−1}w. For w to lie in the m-part we need δ^{−1} ≡ α(⟨x⟩) and δ^{−1}τ ≡ α(T_x). So τ ≡ α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}α(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x). The same computation gives β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a⟩)^{−1} and β(U_y^t) = α(U_y), exactly as printed. So only β(T_x) is off, by a factor α(⟨x⟩)^2.

The printed β cannot be rescued by reading T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x differently. That formula follows from the paper's own isogeny argument (φ^t : (E,α) → (E', x∘α')) with the moduli convention ⟨a⟩f(E,α) = f(E,aα). It also agrees with v1, which has D(T_x c) = ⟨x⟩^{−1}T_x D(c).

(2) The paper's final step, which does not depend on Ψ. The proof says that taking contragredients swaps H^0(ω⊗L_σ)_{m*}⊗C and H^0(ω⊗L_{σ*})_m⊗C, so m* must be the contragredient eigensystem of m. The paper's convention (p. 326) is that m_∅ is generated by ϖ, T_x − tr ρ̄(Frob_x) and ⟨x⟩ − det ρ̄(Frob_x); item (4) likewise uses X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. Since ρ̄^∨ ≅ ρ̄ ⊗ det^{−1}, the contragredient has T_x ↦ t_x/d_x and ⟨a⟩ ↦ d_a^{−1}, where d = det ρ̄(Frob). This is again the corrected β. The printed m* would instead need a residual representation with trace d_x t_x and determinant d_x^{−1}. Its trace is that of ρ̄⊗det ρ̄, whose determinant is d^3, so this is impossible unless (det ρ̄)^4 = 1. The printed and corrected ideals differ as soon as d_x^2 ≠ 1 and t_x ≠ 0 for some x, which happens in general, since det ρ̄ can have order > 2. Read literally, then, the claim "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" is false and the contragredient step fails.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. It is a single inverted exponent. The correct value follows at once from the displayed relations just above it. The earlier version (v1) states the correct ideal, and the argument goes through verbatim with it.

Consequences. m* and β occur only in this item; the other m* on pp. 417 ff. and in §9 are unrelated. The item proves that H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω⊗L_σ)_m is balanced, which is then used in patching for Theorem 3.30, i.e. Theorem 1.4 with vexing primes. With the fix, that conclusion stands, so no stated result is affected. The mathematics is right as intended, so under PROTOCOL §18 'affects' is 'nothing'. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it. A separate cosmetic slip: the display "dim_K H^0(X_{U_0(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ L_σ)_{m*}" has ω^n where n = 1 is meant.

On the other hand, ramification at Q is exactly what "minimal outside Q" allows. T_m is built from H^0(X_{U_1(Q)}, ...), on which the diamond operators at x ∈ Q act, and these give the ramification at Q used in patching.
(iii) The trace condition is ill-posed at Q. p. 345 (PDF p. 49) says that on X_{U_i(Q)} the operators are T_x for x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {p}, and U_y for y ∈ Q. Item (4) itself defines T using "T_x, U_y and ⟨a⟩" and m using U_x − α_x for x ∈ Q. So "trace T_x for all x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ {p}" refers to operators T_x (x ∈ Q) that are not defined in T, and to Frob_x at primes where ρ_Q may ramify.
The proof that follows establishes the corrected statement: it constructs ρ_Q so that ρ'_Q satisfies the conditions of Definition 3.1, using Sections 3.3–3.7, the unramified-at-p argument. The error is a slip in writing the analogue's statement, not a mathematical gap. The proposed correction is right.

issues.locator: §4.1, Lemma 4.2 ('Moreover…') and its proof, p. 355 (same in arXiv v2, §4.1)
issues.printed: p. 355 (PDF p. 59), §4.1: "Lemma 4.2 If B is a complete local Cohen–Macaulay O-algebra and admits a dualizing module ω_B with μ generators, then the same is true for the power series ring A = B[T1, . . . , Tn]. Moreover, the same is also true for B⊗̂_O C, for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection. Proof For power series rings this is a special case of the discussion above. Consider now the case of B⊗̂_O C. By assumption, C is a quotient of O[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence. Hence B⊗̂_O C is a quotient of B[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence, and the result follows from the discussion above applied to the maps B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B and B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B⊗̂_O C respectively." The single brackets are among the 47 known bracket errors and should read ⟦T1,…,Tn⟧; arXiv v2 prints B[[T1,…,Tn]] and O[[T1,…,Tn]].
issues.correction:
Add a Tor-independence hypothesis, for example: "…for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection, provided that B or C is flat over O." Over the DVR O, this is equivalent to Tor_1^O(B,C) = 0, which is exactly the condition the proof needs.

If B is O-flat: (ϖ, T1, …, Tn) is a regular sequence on B⟦T⟧, so Tor_1^{O⟦T⟧}(k, B⟦T⟧) = 0. By the local flatness criterion, B⟦T⟧ is then flat over O⟦T⟧.

If C is O-flat: write B = O⟦S⟧/I. Then Tor_i^{O⟦S,T⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B⟦T⟧) = Tor_i^{O⟦S⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B). This is 0 for i > 0, because C⟦S⟧ is O⟦S⟧-flat by the same criterion.

In either case, a regular sequence f in O⟦T⟧ with C = O⟦T⟧/(f) stays regular on B⟦T⟧, and B⟦T⟧/(f) = B⊗̂_O C, so the printed proof then works. "B or C" is better than "B O-flat" alone, because it also covers the remark after the lemma (B⟦Δ⟧ for arbitrary B, where C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat).
issues.reason:
I checked the counterexample independently. The paper's conventions allow it: C_O is "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k" and nothing requires flatness. The proof also defines "complete intersection" only as "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence".

Take B = k = O/ϖ. It is complete local, Cohen–Macaulay of dimension 0, with ω_B = k, so μ = 1. Take C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ).
- In the regular local ring O⟦x,y,z⟧ with maximal ideal (ϖ,x,y,z), xy−ϖ lies in m but not in m². So R = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is regular of dimension 3, hence a domain.
- In R, xz−ϖ = x(z−y). Both factors are nonzero, as their images in k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy) show. So xz−ϖ is a nonzerodivisor, and C is a complete intersection of dimension 2.
- B⊗̂_O C = C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) = k⟦x,y,z⟧/((x)∩(y,z)). Its associated primes are (x) and (y,z), with dim R/(y,z) = 1. Since depth ≤ dim R/p for every associated prime p, the depth is 1 while the dimension is 2. So the ring is not Cohen–Macaulay.
- The proof breaks exactly at "quotient of B⟦T⟧ by a regular sequence": in k⟦x,y,z⟧, xz times y lies in (xy), but y does not. So xz is a zero-divisor mod xy.
- Necessarily C here is not O-flat: ϖ = xy lies in the minimal prime (x) of C.

The second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is therefore false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint.

Downstream effect: Lemma 4.2 is cited only in §4.1 (pp. 363–364).
- For R_loc⟦x1,…,xn⟧, B = R̃†, which the proof of Thm 4.3 states is O-flat.
- For T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧, B = T_{1,m} is O-flat and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The B⟦Δ⟧ remark holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat. The candidate's line that "every application has B O-flat" is slightly wrong for this remark, where B is arbitrary. The remark is still true through the C-flat variant.

The paper also says §4.1 is "not needed for our main results". Beyond what the candidate addressed, the R_loc application also needs C = ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a complete intersection. That implicitly uses the R_v being O-flat, which I did not check further. So the flaw is in a stated result, Lemma 4.2, and the paper's conclusions stay intact. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.
(a) No flatness convention. The Notation section (p. 305) defines C_O as "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k", with no flatness. §4.1 adds none. B = k and B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx) are allowed.
(b) "Complete intersection" cannot be read as "O-flat relative CI". The paper uses the term in the absolute sense for non-flat rings: Thm 1.3 (p. 302) and p. 380 say "If dim(T_m)=0, then T_m is a complete intersection", and there T_m is Artinian. The proof's own gloss, "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence", is satisfied by the counterexamples below.
(c) No nearby statement supplies the missing Tor-vanishing.

COUNTEREXAMPLES (checked by hand).
1. X-K4-14: B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx).
- B is a hypersurface of dimension 1, hence CM and Gorenstein (ω_B = B, μ = 1). It is CM because ϖ+x lies in neither associated prime (ϖ), (x).
- C = O⟦y⟧/(ϖy) is a CI.
- B⊗̂_O C = O⟦x,y⟧/(ϖx,ϖy) = O⟦x,y⟧/((ϖ)∩(x,y)). Its minimal primes have coheights 2 and 1, so it is not equidimensional and not CM.
- The step that fails: ϖy·x = 0 in B⟦y⟧ with x ≠ 0.
2. H-part1b-1 / X-K5-0: B = k (CM, ω = k, μ = 1) and C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ), or (xy−ϖ, xz).
- xy−ϖ ∉ m², so O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is a regular domain, and x(z−y) and xz are nonzero in it. So C is a CI of dimension 2.
- C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) has associated primes (x) and (y,z).
- It has depth 1: y+x is regular, and modulo it x ≠ 0 is killed by m. Its dimension is 2, so it is not CM.
In all of these, neither B nor C is O-flat. As shown in the correction, flatness of either one is enough.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 4.2 is cited only on pp. 365–366.
- (i) R_loc⟦x⟧ = R̃† ⊗̂ (⊗̂_v R_v)⟦x⟧, with B = R̃†. The proof of Thm 4.3 (p. 356) says it is O-flat.
- (ii) T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧. Here B = T_{1,m} is O-flat because the forms are ϖ-torsion free, and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The remark after the lemma, "B⟦Δ⟧ for any B", holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat.
So the multiplicity-two conclusion survives with the corrected lemma. Also, §4.1 is "not needed for our main results" (p. 355).

A side point that is independent of this candidate: application (i) also needs ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a CI, which implicitly uses O-flatness of the R_v. The R_v are O⟦Δ⟧-power-series rings or O⟦x1..x4⟧/(r) with r = C(T)−T; I did not check further whether ϖ ∤ r.

Verdict: the second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint, and the 2022 Correction does not fix it. v1 and v2 have the same text.

issues.locator: §4.1, Lemma 4.4 (first sentence), p. 357 (published version)
issues.printed: Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. We have  H_{R/x}(t)/(1 − t) ≥ H_R(t) · (1 − t^d)/(1 − t),  and equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. Moreover, if there is an isomorphism  R ≃ gr(R) = ⊕ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1},  and x is pure of degree d, then equality holds if and only if x is a regular element.   [Remark after the proof, pp. 357–358: "Note that, in the non-graded case, the converse is not true, namely, x may be regular of degree one and yet the equality H_{R/x}(t) = H_R(t)(1−t) fails; as an example one may take R = k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] and x = φ^6. Then x is regular, but (1+2t+2t^2+t^3)/(1−t) > (1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5)/(1−t) = H_R(t)." Here k[...] is one of the known bracket errors and should be k⟦φ^6, φ^7, φ^15⟧.]
issues.correction: Minimal fix: in the first sentence, replace "equality holds if and only if x is a regular element" with "equality holds only if x is a regular element" (equivalently: if x is a zero-divisor, the inequality is strict). Keep "if and only if" only in the 'Moreover' clause, where R ≃ gr(R), meaning R is the completion of its associated graded ring, and x is pure of degree d. A true 'iff' also holds in the ungraded case if "x is regular" is replaced by "the degree-d initial form of x is a regular element of gr(R)". That is not what the paper intends, though: its remark uses "regular" to mean regular in R.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered PDF pages 61–62 (pp. 357–358). The first sentence of the statement really does say "equality holds if and only if x is a regular element", with no graded hypothesis. The setup on p. 356 is just "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k". The authors' remark right after the proof ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true") gives a counterexample to that first sentence.

I redid the computation myself with a Python script over the semigroup ⟨6,7,15⟩, using the m-adic order of φ^s = the maximal number of generators summing to s.
- H_R = 1+3t+4t^2+5t^3+5t^4+6t^5+6t^6+…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.
- The Apéry set of the semigroup with respect to 6 is {0,7,14,15,22,29}, with orders 0,1,2,2,3,3. So H_{R/φ^6} = 1+2t+2t^2+t^3 and H_{R/x}/(1−t) = 1+3t+5t^2+6t^3+6t^4+….
- This is strictly larger than H_R at t^2, t^3 and t^4, and equal at t^0, t^1 and from t^5 on.
- R is a domain and x = φ^6 ≠ 0 lies in 𝔪 (d = 1), so x is regular while the inequality is strict. That breaks the 'if' direction of the first sentence.
- The script also shows that the initial form of φ^6 is not regular in gr(R): the order jumps by 2 at s = 15, 22, 29. This matches the authors' explanation.

The proof establishes only two things: (a) if x is not regular, the inequality is strict (Krull intersection argument); (b) if x is regular and R ≃ gr(R), equality holds. The 'Moreover' clause would be redundant if the first sentence were meant as 'iff', which confirms the intended reading is 'only if'. arXiv v2 (line 2332) has the same wording.

Downstream: the lemma is used only in Lemma 4.6 (p. 358–359). There it is applied (i) explicitly "in the graded case" to get H_{B/I} = H_B(1−t)^3 for a regular sequence of pure degree-one elements in B ≃ gr(B), and (ii) for "H_{B/I} = 1+3t ⇒ regular sequence", which is the direction that is true in general. Neither use relies on the false ungraded 'if' direction. So the misstatement affects Lemma 4.4 as stated, but not the proof or any later result. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the only bracket error nearby is k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] in the remark, which is already known. Defence attempted and failed. The setup on p. 356 is only "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k", with no grading. "Regular element" gets no special definition. The remark after the proof uses it in the usual sense: x = φ^6 is regular because R is a domain. Read this way, the first sentence claims regular ⇒ equality for every such R. The paper's own remark refutes exactly that ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true").

Independent check with python3 on the semigroup ⟨6,7,15⟩. For a monomial, ord_𝔪(φ^s) is the largest number of generators summing to s.
- H_R has coefficients 1,3,4,5,5,6,6,…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.
- The Apéry set with respect to 6 is {0,7,14,15,22,29}, with orders 0,1,2,1,2,3. So H_{R/x} = 1+2t+2t^2+t^3, and H_{R/x}/(1−t) has coefficients 1,3,5,6,6,….
- This is strictly larger than H_R at t^2, t^3 and t^4, although x ∈ 𝔪 (d = 1) is regular.
- The initial form of x is a zero-divisor in gr(R): ord(s+6) ≠ ord(s)+1 at s = 15, 22, 29.
These values match the paper's printed series. A small side note: the earlier verdict gave the Apéry orders as 0,1,2,2,3,3, which is wrong because 15 has order 1. Its Hilbert series was still right.

The proof gives only two things: (a) x not regular ⇒ strict inequality (Krull intersection argument), which is the 'only if' direction and holds in general; and (b) x regular and R ≃ gr(R) ⇒ equality. The 'Moreover' clause would add nothing if the first sentence were a true 'iff'. So the intended statement is clear, but the printed one is false.

Consequences: Lemma 4.4 is cited only in the proof of Lemma 4.6 (p. 360). There it is used in two ways:
- (i) Explicitly "in the graded case", to get H_{B/I} = H_B(1−t)^3 for a pure degree-one regular sequence in B ≃ gr(B). This is the valid 'Moreover' direction.
- (ii) To deduce, from H_{B/I} = 1+3t, that three pure degree-one generators form a regular sequence. This uses the chain H_{B/I}/(1−t)^3 ≥ H_{B/(x1,x2)}/(1−t)^2 ≥ H_{B/x1}/(1−t) ≥ H_B = (1+3t)/(1−t)^3, which forces equality at each step. Then equality ⇒ regular, the direction that is true in general.
Neither use needs the false ungraded 'if' direction, so Lemmas 4.6 and 4.7 and Theorem 4.3 are unaffected. The damage is confined to the statement of Lemma 4.4. That is why affects = 'a stated result': the lemma as stated is false, but no later proof or result is.

Kind: this is a false mathematical claim (an overstated 'iff'), not a slip of notation, so I classify it as an error, even though the intended weaker statement can be recovered from the remark. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors; the only bracket error nearby is k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] in the remark, which is already known.

issues.printed: Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. We have H_{R/x}(t)/(1 − t) ≥ H_R(t) · (1 − t^d)/(1 − t), and equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. Moreover, if there is an isomorphism  R ≃ gr(R) = ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1},  and x is pure of degree d, then equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. [proof:] "Finally, assume that x is a regular element, and that R ≃ gr(R)." [p. 358:] "All the relations in B are pure of degree two, and hence there is an isomorphism B ≃ gr(B)."
issues.correction: Read the hypothesis as: R is isomorphic to the 𝔪-adic completion ∏_n 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} of gr(R). In other words, R ≅ k⟦x_1,…,x_r⟧/I with I generated by homogeneous polynomials, and 'pure of degree d' refers to that grading. The same reading applies to 'B ≃ gr(B)' on p. 358.
issues.reason:
The setup on p. 356 makes R a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪). The ring B that the lemma is applied to is a quotient of the power series ring k⟦a,b,c,φ1,φ2,φ3⟧ (printed with single brackets, which is one of the known bracket errors). By Lemma 4.6/4.7, B has Krull dimension 3.

The displayed ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} = k[a,…,φ3]/(homogeneous quadrics) is a finitely generated k-algebra of positive dimension. It therefore has infinitely many maximal ideals, so it is not local and not 𝔪-adically complete, and no ring isomorphism B ≃ ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} exists. As printed, the hypothesis can only hold for Artinian R, and the claim 'B ≃ gr(B)' is literally false.

The intended meaning is clear, and the paper uses it elsewhere: the proof of Lemma 4.6 begins 'Let R be a complete local Cohen–Macaulay Noetherian graded k-algebra' and then invokes 'Lemma 4.4 (in the graded case)'.

With the completed reading, the proof works. Take R = Ĝ with G standard graded and x ∈ G_d regular. Then R/𝔪^{m+d} = ⨁_{j<m+d} G_j, and x·y ∈ 𝔪^{m+d} forces the components y_j with j < m to vanish. So the kernel is exactly 𝔪^m/𝔪^{m+d}, as the proof claims. B satisfies this reading because its defining relations are homogeneous quadrics. The induction in Lemma 4.6 keeps the reading, since quotients by homogeneous elements stay completions of graded rings.

This is an abuse of notation, not a wrong idea, so it is a misprint that affects nothing. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also separate from the 'if and only if' problem in the first sentence of Lemma 4.4 (candidates X-K5-1 / H-part1b-0). Confidence is medium only because some readers treat 'R ≃ gr(R)' for complete local rings as standard shorthand. The explicit '= ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}' makes the printed statement literally wrong.

issues.locator: §4.1, last sentence of the proof of Lemma 4.7, published p. 361 (PDF p. 65), top of the page. arXiv v2 has the same wording ('the Hilbert polynomial of C is 1 + 3t', v2 text line 2485). arXiv v1 does not contain Lemma 4.7.
issues.printed: On the other hand, since all the relations are trivial in 𝔪^2, we have dim(𝔪/𝔪^2) = 3. Hence the Hilbert polynomial of C is 1+3t, and the sequence is regular in A.
issues.correction: "Hence the Hilbert series H_C(t) of C is 1 + 3t"
issues.reason:
The only notion the paper defines is the Hilbert series H_R(t) = Σ dim_k(𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}) t^n (p. 356). Lemma 4.6 is stated in terms of H_{B/I}(t) = 1+3t, and the proof of Lemma 4.7 itself opens with 'it suffices to show that the Hilbert series of B/I … is 1+3t'.

C = B/I is a quotient of k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz) with dim 𝔪/𝔪^2 = 3, so C ≅ k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x,y,z)^2. It is Artinian with Hilbert function 1, 3, 0, 0, …. Its Hilbert series is therefore 1+3t, while its Hilbert polynomial in the standard sense (the polynomial agreeing with the Hilbert function for n ≫ 0) is 0.

The word 'polynomial' is a terminology slip for 'series' (the series happens to be a polynomial here). The computation and the comparison with Lemma 4.6 are correct under the intended reading. I also rechecked the relations of C from those of B (a = 0, φ3 = −φ2, φ1 = −(b+c)): they match the printed list, and they give xz = yz = xy = x^2 = y^2 = z^2 = 0. This is not a bracket error.

issues.locator: §4.1, p. 361 (setup before Theorem 4.8) (published version)
issues.printed: p. 361 (PDF p. 65): "One knows that ρ̄ occurs as the mod-p reduction of a modular form of weight 2 and level N*, where N* = N if k = 2 and Np otherwise." p. 362 (PDF p. 66): "For φ ∈ Φ̂, and let χ_φ denote the character ε · ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩φ of G_Q." p. 363 (PDF p. 67): "Let ψ denote the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×, which we may regard as a character of G_Q. After twisting ρ by ψ^{−1/2}, we obtain a Galois representation G_Q → GL_2(T^an_{φ,m}) with determinant χ_φ = ε · ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩φ which is classified by R = R_φ." (The same text is in arXiv v2, pp. 47–49.)
issues.correction: Replace ⟨ρ̄ε^{−1}⟩ with ⟨det(ρ̄)·ε̄^{−1}⟩ in both places, on p. 362 and p. 363. This gives χ_φ = ε·⟨det ρ̄·ε̄^{−1}⟩·φ = ε·ω^{−1}·⟨det ρ̄⟩·φ. There are also two minor fixes. On p. 361, "N* = N if k(ρ̄) = 2" is meant: k is the residue field, and the Serre weight is k(ρ̄). On p. 363, the product should be ∏_{x|N, x∤M}. The factor at x = p is irrelevant because Z_p ⊗ (Z/pZ)^× = 0.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at 250 dpi, and the printed text is as quoted. The main point is a real misprint. The Notation section on p. 305 defines ⟨χ⟩: G → O^× only for a character χ: G → k^×. But ρ̄ε^{−1} is a 2-dimensional representation, not a character. Elsewhere the authors write the determinant explicitly: "ν := ⟨det ρ̄⟩ det(ρ_{Q,m})^{−1}" on p. 332, and ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩ in §3.4 of arXiv v2. So here the word "det" has been dropped, and it is dropped in both occurrences.

I redid the bookkeeping. For weight-2 forms with nebentypus χ, det ρ = ε·χ, so ε^{−1} det ρ = χ, as the paper says. Reducing, χ ≡ det ρ̄·ε̄^{−1} mod m. So χ = ⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·χ_p, where χ_p is the p-power-order part, a character of Z_p⊗(Z/NpZ)^×. Since p ∤ N, this group is Z_p⊗(Z/NZ)^× = Φ × Z_p⊗∏_{x|N, x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×. On Φ, χ_p = φ; on the other factor, χ_p = ψ. After twisting by ψ^{−1/2}, det = εχψ^{−1} = ε·⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·φ. This reduces to det ρ̄, and on G_p it equals εω^{−1} times an unramified character, as the ordinary ring R† of §3.7 needs. So the proposed correction is right.

The other two parts of the candidate are much weaker. "k = 2" is a notation clash with the residue field k, but the meaning k(ρ̄) = 2 is clear: the text later says "Thus N* = pN (since p is odd)", which uses k(ρ̄) = p. "∏_{x∤M}" is shorthand, since χ is a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, so x | Np is implicit. Neither needs its own entry.

Nothing depends on the misprint. The intended meaning is clear from the notation convention and the computation. Neither the statement of Theorem 4.8 nor the proof that follows (Lemma 4.11 uses χ_φ only as the fixed determinant) is affected.

issues.locator: §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, published p. 362 (display defining Φ) and p. 363 (definition of ψ) (PDF pp. 66–67). arXiv v2 and v1 have the identical formulas.
issues.printed: p. 362 (display): "Φ := Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x|M} (Z/xZ)^×"; p. 363: "Let ψ denote the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×, which we may regard as a character of G_Q."
issues.correction: Φ := Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x | M, x prime} (Z/xZ)^× (= Z_p ⊗ (Z/MZ)^×). ψ is the restriction of χ to Z_p ⊗ ∏_{x | N, x prime, x ∤ M} (Z/xZ)^×, the p-part of (Z/NpZ)^× at the non-harmless primes.
issues.reason: The candidate's premise holds. At a harmless prime v, ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible, so ρ̄^{I_v} = 0 and the conductor exponent is at least 2. Hence v^2 | N and M is never squarefree when M > 1. Read with x ranging over all divisors of M, the first product is the wrong group: for M = v^2 it gives two copies of the p-part of (Z/vZ)^×. The usual convention that the index x is prime fixes the first formula. Under that convention it equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/MZ)^×, since for x ≠ p the tensor Z_p ⊗ (Z/x^eZ)^× equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/xZ)^×. The second product is genuinely wrong as printed even with x prime. It runs over all primes not dividing M, so it is infinite. It must be cut down to primes x | N (x = p adds nothing because p is odd). Only then is 'the restriction of χ', a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, meaningful. The intended meaning is clear from context, so this is a misprint that affects nothing. Confidence is medium only because the Φ half could be defended as an abuse of notation. The ψ half cannot.
