issues.printed: p. 363 (PDF p. 67), first paragraph, read from the page image: "The reason for dealing with the harmless primes in this manner is as follows. For all non-harmless v ≠ p, the conductor-minimal deformation ring of ρ̄|G_v (which classifies deformations which appear at level Γ_1(N)) is isomorphic to the ring R_{v,φ} (up to unramified twists). Equivalently, for non-harmless primes, any characteristic zero lift ρ of ρ̄ is uniquely twist equivalent to a lift of minimal conductor. The only time this is not true is when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v. Since we are assuming that ρ̄|_{G_v} is minimally ramified amongst all its twists, this only happens when ρ̄|_{G_v} is absolutely irreducible and v ≡ 1 mod p." The next paragraph, which depends on it, reads: "Kisin's improvement of the Taylor–Wiles method yields an isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p]." On p. 362: "(2) When v ≠ p, R_v = R_{v,φ} is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with determinant χ_φ|G_v."
issues.correction: The exceptional set is wrong. Uniqueness of the minimal-conductor twist, and the claimed isomorphism with R_{v,φ} up to unramified twist, also fail at the non-harmless primes of Lemma 4.11 case (3): v ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄^{I_v} one-dimensional and ρ̄^{ss}|G_v unramified. Take a lift in R_{v,φ} with ρ|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{-1}, where ψ ≠ 1 has p-power order (one of the (q−1)/2 non-Steinberg components in footnote 5). It has two minimal-conductor twists by characters ≡ 1 mod ϖ, namely ρ⊗ψ (ψ² ⊕ 1 on I_v) and ρ⊗ψ^{-1} (1 ⊕ ψ^{-2} on I_v). These two twists are not related by an unramified twist. The correct statement is: uniqueness holds except when v ≡ 1 mod p and either ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible (harmless) or ρ̄|G_v is, up to unramified twist, a ramified non-split extension of 1 by 1 (case (3)). The candidate's correction of the claim is right and minimal. Its assessment of the consequences is not. The proof also needs the twisting map (eigenforms in S_φ) → (points of R_φ) to be injective, and at case-(3) primes it is not. Primes of type (3) therefore need a separate treatment in the proof of Theorem 4.8. For example, one could use at v the ring of lifts with conductor exponent ≤ 1 and p-power inertial determinant, taken over O[Δ_v], instead of R_{v,φ}, or handle these primes differently from the ψ^{-1/2} twist.
issues.reason:
I checked this from scratch using the page images (PDF pp. 65–70).

**Setup.** R_{v,φ} is the full fixed-determinant ring. For non-harmless v, χ_φ|I_v is trivial (φ is ramified only at harmless primes). In case (3), after an unramified twist, ρ̄|G_v = (1 *; 0 1) with * ramified.

**The non-Steinberg lifts exist.** Take ρ(σ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}) with ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order dividing v−1, and ρ(Frob) = a·I. Then ρ(σ)^v = ρ(σ). The lift reduces to (1 1; 0 1), and its determinant is unramified and adjustable through a. For example p=3, v=7, ζ a cube root of 1. The paper itself describes these points on p. 365 ("χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order") and in footnote 5 (the (q−1)/2 components).

**Twists of such a lift.** Let η ≡ 1 mod ϖ, so ρ⊗η still lifts ρ̄. Then ρ⊗η has conductor exponent 1 = a(ρ̄) exactly when η|I_v ∈ {ψ, ψ^{-1}}. That gives two minimal twists. They differ by ψ², which is ramified and nontrivial because p is odd. So neither "uniquely twist equivalent" nor the claimed ring isomorphism holds. The ring statement fails under either reading:
- If "conductor-minimal" fixes the determinant up to unramified twist, it gives only the Steinberg component, one of (q+1)/2.
- If the determinant is free, it gives q components mapping 2:1 onto the non-Steinberg ones.

**Impact on the proof.** This is more than motivation. Take a newform f ∈ S_{φ,m} with ρ_f|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ η, η ≠ 1 (the paper needs such forms: every component of R_{v,φ} must be in the support of S_φ). Let Θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order with Θ|I_v = η^{-1}, and let g = f⊗Θ. Then:
- g has the same level N*, is still ordinary, and lies in the same m.
- χ_g|Φ = χ_f|Φ = φ, because Θ is trivial on the harmless part.
- ψ_g = ψ_f Θ², so ρ_g⊗ψ_g^{-1/2} = ρ_f⊗ψ_f^{-1/2}.
- ρ_g ≇ ρ_f, since the inertial types 1⊕η^{-1} and 1⊕η differ, so g and f have different T_l eigenvalues for some l.

So two points of Spec T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] map to one point of Spec R_φ[1/p]. Hence R_φ → T^an_{φ,m} is not surjective, and the asserted R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is false whenever such a prime occurs. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365): U_p eigenvalues also agree after the twist. The 2:1 fibres are exactly what the "uniqueness" claim was meant to rule out.

**Status of Theorem 4.8.** The theorem is probably still true via a double-cover local ring, which is still a complete intersection. So only the proof is affected. I did not build an explicit global ρ̄ satisfying the scalar hypothesis with a case-(3) prime. I disagree with the reader's "affects: nothing". 1. The claim is false.

Case (3) primes are non-harmless because ρ̄|G_v is reducible. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|G_v ≅ (unramified) ⊗ (1 *; 0 1), * ramified. p. 365 (Lemma 4.11) itself says the generic fibre of R_{v,φ} contains lifts 'χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order'. Footnote 5 says it has (q+1)/2 components.

- A twist ρ⊗θ with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ has conductor exponent 1 (minimal) exactly when θ|I_v = ψ or θ|I_v = ψ^{-1}.
- These two twists differ by ψ², which is ramified. Since p is odd and ψ ≠ 1, ψ² ≠ 1 and ψ² ≠ ψ^{-2}. So the minimal twist is not unique, not even up to unramified twist.
- The rings do not match either. The conductor-minimal ring with free determinant has 1 + (q−1) = q generic components (Steinberg, and θ ⊕ 1 for each θ ≠ 1). With determinant fixed to χ_φ|G_v, which is unramified here, it has only the Steinberg component. R_{v,φ} has (q+1)/2. So no reading of 'isomorphic up to unramified twists' works.
- Cross-check of the other v ≡ 1 mod p cases: in case (1), ρ̄|I_v ≅ χ̄ ⊕ 1, the other twist would be by a character ≡ χ̄^{-1} ≠ 1 mod ϖ, so uniqueness holds. The paper's exception list is therefore incomplete exactly by case (3).

2. Defence attempted.

Read 'conductor-minimal deformation ring' charitably, as 'lifts with determinant χ_φ that are twists of level-Γ_1(N) lifts'. Then sentence 1 is tautologically R_{v,φ}. But the 'Equivalently ... uniquely' sentence cannot be saved: uniqueness is exactly the property the authors use to separate harmless primes, where every twist has conductor 2.

3. Consequences: the passage is load-bearing.

- Uniqueness is what makes f ↦ ρ_f ⊗ ψ_f^{-1/2} injective from eigenforms in S_φ to points of R_φ. Given two such forms f, f', the twisted representations coincide iff ρ_{f'} = ρ_f⊗θ, with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ ramified only at non-harmless primes. Uniqueness at each such prime forces θ to be unramified everywhere, so θ = 1.
- Case (3) breaks this. Let θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order, and let f1 ∈ S_φ be ordinary with ρ_{f1}|I_v ≅ θ ⊕ 1. Such f1 exists by the paper's own claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ. Set f2 = f1⊗θ^{-1}. Then ρ_{f2}|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ θ^{-1}, which still has conductor exponent 1. The nebentypus of f2 is χ1θ^{-2}, and its restriction to Φ is still φ. So f2 ∈ S_φ, it is ordinary, and it lies in the m-part.
- Computation: ψ2 = ψ1θ^{-2}. Since the square root is unique in a p-group with p odd, ψ2^{-1/2} = ψ1^{-1/2}θ. Hence ρ_{f2}⊗ψ2^{-1/2} = ρ_{f1}⊗ψ1^{-1/2}. The twisted U_p-eigenvalues also agree.
- So f1 and f2 have distinct Hecke eigensystems: a_l(f2) = θ^{-1}(l)·a_l(f1), and the nebentypus at v is θ versus θ^{-1}. Yet they give the same Q̄_p-point of R_φ, and of R̃.
- Therefore R_φ[1/p] → T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is not surjective, and the asserted isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] (p. 363) is false whenever N has a case-(3) prime. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365).
- The conclusions drawn from it are then unproven in that case: T_{φ,m} Cohen–Macaulay with dim ω/m = 3, hence the same for T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ], hence dim J_1(N*)[m] = 2.
- Lemma 4.11 treats case (3) explicitly, and Theorem 4.8 does not exclude it.

The statement of Theorem 4.8 is not shown false. The repair looks plausible: use a conductor-≤1 local ring over O[Δ_v] that should be Cohen–Macaulay. So I rate affects as 'the proof', not 'nothing' as the candidate proposed. Confidence is high that the passage is wrong, and medium-high on the exact extent of the damage to the proof.

issues.reason:
I transcribed the text from 220-dpi renders of PDF pp. 68–69 (pp. 364–365). Setup: v ≠ p, p odd, and R_v is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with fixed determinant. By the local Euler characteristic, dim Z^1 = 3 + h^2(ad^0ρ̄). So R_v is not smooth exactly when H^0(G_v, ad^0ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Redoing the classification for ρ̄ minimal among twists gives four cases, not three:
- v≡1, split, χ ramified.
- v≡−1, induced from the unramified quadratic extension.
- v≡1, ramified unipotent.
- v≡−1, ρ̄ ≅ μ⊗(ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified.
The fourth case is missing. It is minimal: the conductor exponent is 1 and no twist lowers it. In this case e = (0 1; 0 0) spans H^0(ad^0ρ̄(1)), because G_v acts on it by ω̄^2 and ω̄(Frob_v) = −1. Also H^0(ad^0ρ̄) = 0: e is inertia-fixed, but Frobenius acts on it by −1. So h^2 = 1 and dim Z^1 = 4. That exceeds the relative dimension 3, so R_v is not formally smooth.

I checked the extra lifts. Take ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{−1}) with ζ ≠ 1, ζ^{v+1} = 1, of p-power order, and S = (d1, (d2−d1)/δ; d1δ, −d1) with δ = ζ^{−1}−ζ. Then S ρ(τ) S^{−1} = ρ(τ)^v; I verified this numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19). Taking d1 ≡ −1 and d2−d1 ∈ δO, the lift reduces to ρ̄. Hensel's lemma lets det S hit the fixed determinant.

Lemma 4.11 itself still holds. At Steinberg points H^0(ad^0ρ(1)) = 0, since Frobenius acts on e by v^{±2} ≠ 1. At the induced points, ad^0ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)⊗ε. Frobenius acts on ηε by −v^{±1}, and the second summand has no inertia invariants because ζ^2 ≠ 1.

I believe such ρ̄ exist within the §4.1 scope: unramified at p with scalar Frob_p (Thm 4.8). One route is an S4-quartic construction with p=3, v=2. I have not verified an explicit example. The submitter's elliptic-curve example is only local, since det ρ̄_{E,3} is ramified at 3.

The submitter says the case-(3) argument covers this "verbatim". That is not quite right: the description of the generic points has to change.

Lemma 4.11 is used only in the proof of Thm 4.8 (p. 363); grep finds no other citations. There is a related, more serious flaw that should be a separate item. On p. 363 the paper claims that for non-harmless v every lift is twist-equivalent to a conductor-minimal one, and that the only exception is v≡1 with ρ̄ having trivial I_v-invariants. The induced lifts above have conductor v^2 and cannot be twisted down to conductor v. So the claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*)) fails at such v. The likely repair is to use the smooth Steinberg quotient at such v. So I rate this as affecting the proof, not the stated results.

Minor side point: in footnote 5, "primitive q-th root of unity" should be "q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1". Otherwise the count (q−1)/2 is wrong when q = p^2. Setting. By p. 365 of the paper, p ≥ 3 and v ≠ p. R_v is the unrestricted framed ring with fixed determinant. Here χ_φ|G_v is unramified at every v that is not harmless. The only condition the paper imposes at v | N is that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists, and the mod-p Steinberg type (conductor exponent 1) satisfies it. The local Euler characteristic gives dim Z¹(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h²(ad⁰ρ̄) − h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) + h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)). R_v has relative dimension 3, so it fails to be formally smooth exactly when H⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Missing case. Take v ≡ −1 mod p and ρ̄ = (ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified. Such an extension exists and is unique: h¹(G_v, ω̄) = h⁰(ω̄) + h⁰(ω̄^{-1}·ω̄) = 0 + 1, and the unramified part is ω̄/(Frob−1) = 0. Conjugating by the unipotent ρ̄(τ) shows H⁰(I_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = k·e with e = (0 1; 0 0), since p is odd. Frobenius acts on e by ω̄(Frob) = −1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 0. On e⊗ω̄ it acts by (−1)(−1) = 1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄(1)) = k·e. Hence h² = 1, dim Z¹ = 4 > 3, and R_v is not smooth. This case is none of (1)–(3): v ≢ 1, and ρ̄|G_v is reducible.

Checks. I brute-forced H⁰ over F_p. It has dimension 1 for (p,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (5,19), (7,13). It has dimension 0 for v ≢ ±1, e.g. (5,7) and (7,5). Redoing the classification (irreducible, split, and non-split types) gives exactly four non-smooth twist-minimal cases, so only this one is missing.

Lemma 4.11 survives. The lifts are of two kinds.
- Steinberg twists. H⁰(ad⁰ρ(1)) = 0 because Frobenius acts on e by v² ≠ 1.
- The extra points, with ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}), ζ^{v+1} = 1, ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order, and ρ(σ) = S swapping the eigenlines. I checked S·T = T^v·S numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19), (3,8), (9,26). These lifts reduce to ρ̄. Here ad⁰ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)ε. Frobenius acts on the first summand by −v ≠ 1. The second has no inertia invariants, since ζ^{±2} ≠ 1.

So the error is in the proof only. The submitted corrections are right. H-part1b-2 says the argument covers the new case "verbatim", which is slightly off: the generic-point description must change. X-K5-8's correction states it correctly.

Could the case be excluded? Nothing in §4.1 rules it out. Examples plausibly exist: take the mod-3 reduction of an odd octahedral Artin representation (projective image S4 ≅ PGL2(F3)) that is tamely ramified of index 3 at some v ≡ 2 mod 3, with 3 split completely. Projectively, D_v = S3 is the Borel subgroup, and this forces ρ̄|G_v to be of the missing type. I have not verified an explicit example.

Consequences. Lemma 4.11 is cited only in the proof of Thm 4.8, on p. 363, and it is used implicitly on p. 365 through Lemma 4.2. The consequence is serious but separate, and it deserves its own item, distinct from C-K5-0. For this local type, p ∤ v−1, so no nebentypus twist is available at v. The Ind components have conductor v² and cannot be twisted down. So the p. 363 claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*), v ∥ N*) fails at such v. The natural repair is to use the minimally ramified (Steinberg) quotient there, which is formally smooth (CHT §2.4). The stated results are unaffected.

issues.locator: §4.1, footnote 5, p. 365 (published version)
issues.printed: Footnote 5, p. 365 (PDF p. 69), checked on a 300 dpi render: "One may take r to be C(T) − T, where C is the Chebyshev-type polynomial determined by the relation C(t + t^{−1}) = t^v + t^{−v}, and T is the trace of a generator of tame inertia (note that T − 2 ∈ m_{R_v}). The generic fibre of R_v has (q + 1)/2 geometric components, where q is the largest power of p dividing v − 1 (see also Theorem 1.0.1(A2.2) of [55]). One component corresponds to lifts of ρ̄ on which inertia is nilpotent, and in particular has trace T = 2. The remaining (q − 1)/2 components correspond to representations which are finitely ramified of order dividing q, on which T = ζ + ζ^{−1} for some primitive q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1." The arXiv v2 footnote 5 (cg-v2.txt l. 2716–2721) has the same wording, "primitive" included.
issues.correction: Replace "for some primitive q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1" with "for some q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1", i.e. ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1}, taken up to ζ ↔ ζ^{−1}. The candidate's second change, "inertia is nilpotent" → "inertia is unipotent" (or "acts unipotently"), is fine as a wording fix. The paper says "unipotent" elsewhere (e.g. p. 297 text line 205, and §5 conditions), but "nilpotent" here can also be read loosely as "σ − 1 is nilpotent / N is nilpotent", so on its own it is not a mathematical error.
issues.reason:
I redid the computation. Set t^v + t^{−v} − t − t^{−1} = (t^v − t)(1 − t^{−v−1}). So C(T) = T at T = t + t^{−1} exactly when t^{v−1} = 1 or t^{v+1} = 1. C(T) − T is separable of degree v in T: its roots are ±2, (v−3)/2 values from t^{v−1} = 1 and (v−1)/2 values from t^{v+1} = 1. The condition T − 2 ∈ m forces t ≡ 1, so t is a 1-unit root of unity of p-power order. Since v ≡ 1 mod p and p is odd, p does not divide v + 1, so t^{v+1} = 1 gives only t = 1, and t^{v−1} = 1 gives t ∈ μ_q.

The T-values in the residue disc are therefore T = 2 plus ζ + ζ^{−1} for ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1} modulo inversion. That is 1 + (q−1)/2 = (q+1)/2 values, matching the footnote's count. Each ζ ≠ 1 gives one geometric component: σ is regular semisimple with eigenvalues ζ^{±1}, Frobenius lies in its centralizer torus with fixed determinant, and the result is irreducible of dimension 3.

If only primitive ζ were allowed there would be φ(q)/2 = p^{s−1}(p−1)/2 such components, fewer than (q−1)/2 once q = p^s with s ≥ 2. Concrete check: p = 3, v = 19, so q = 9. ζ_3 + ζ_3^{−1} = −1 satisfies T − 2 = −3 ∈ m and is a genuine root, giving 4 = (9−1)/2 non-trivial values against 3 primitive ones.

The sentence itself points the same way. It says "finitely ramified of order dividing q", and "ζ ≠ 1" would be redundant for a primitive q-th root, since q ≥ p > 1. So "primitive" is a slip. The counts (q+1)/2 and (q−1)/2 are correct; only this adjective is wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. (That known defect does appear on the same page in "R_v ≅ O[x1,…,x4]/(r)", which should read O⟦x1,…,x4⟧/(r), but that is separate.)

issues.locator: §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, p. 366 (published version)
issues.printed: (p. 366, PDF p. 70, checked on the page image) "If T_m is the Hecke ring at full level Γ_1(N*), then the restriction map induces an inclusion map T_m ↪ ⊕ T_{φ^2,m} ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕ O(φ). Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Because the map above is an isomorphism after tensoring with K, and since all the relevant spaces of modular forms are ϖ-torsion free, we have an isomorphism T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O[Φ]. Hence, applying Lemma 4.2 once more, we deduce that T_m is Cohen–Macaulay and dim ω_{T_m}/m = 3"
issues.correction:
The isomorphism T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O[Φ] is true, but the proof should use generators.

Embed T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] in ⊕_φ T_{1,m} by t⊗[g] ↦ (φ(g)t)_φ. Identify S_{φ²,m} with S_{1,m} by twisting by φ, where φ is viewed as a Dirichlet character mod M through the projection (Z/N*Z)^× → Φ, g ↦ ḡ. Then:
- T_l, and U_l, U_p for l ∤ M, map to (φ(l)T_l)_φ = T_l ⊗ [l̄].
- U_l for l | M is 0 on the m-part, since every lift is supercuspidal at harmless l.
- ⟨d⟩ maps to ⟨d⟩ ⊗ [d̄]².

So the image lies in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. This replaces "since T_m is local".

For d in Φ ⊂ (Z/N*Z)^×, ⟨d⟩ acts trivially on S_1, so ⟨d⟩ maps to 1 ⊗ [d]². Since |Φ| is odd, squaring is a bijection of Φ, so every 1 ⊗ [g] is in the image. Then T_l ⊗ 1 = (T_l ⊗ [l̄])(1 ⊗ [l̄]⁻¹) is in the image. Together with the surjection T_m → T_{1,m}, this shows the map is onto. This replaces "isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free", which gives only injectivity.

Two smaller points:
1. The argument needs ⟨d⟩ ∈ T_m. This is not automatic, because T is generated by the T_l for primes l. It holds for p odd because det = (tr² − tr(g²))/2 for the pseudo-character.
2. T_m, a Z_p-algebra, should be read as T_m ⊗_{W(k_m)} O.

The fix proposed in X-K5-11 is right with the + signs (its ± is harmless), and it is minimal. H-part1b-5 gives the same argument.
issues.reason:
This is confirmed on the page image, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. O[Φ] is the group ring of a finite group, so it is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Both justifications given in the paper fail:
(1) Being local does not force the image into T_{1,m}⊗O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m}=O, Φ=Z/p and O=Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A={(a_φ)∈⊕O : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ[g], which is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p)=p−1≥2.
(2) An injection of ϖ-torsion-free lattices that becomes an isomorphism after ⊗K need not be onto. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself an example. Torsion-freeness gives only injectivity.
So the printed reasons prove at most an inclusion of finite index. I checked the candidate's replacement argument myself, including the twisting convention, the images T_l ↦ T_l⊗[l] and ⟨d⟩ ↦ 1⊗[d]^2 for d∈Φ, and that squaring is bijective on Φ. It is correct, apart from the small base-change caveat noted in the correction.
On 'affects', I disagree with the candidate's "nothing". The proof of Theorem 4.8 as printed does not establish the isomorphism, and a different argument is needed, so it affects the proof. Theorem 4.8 still holds, because the intermediate isomorphism is true. Only the multiplicity-two statement of Thm 4.8 uses this step, together with Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument"), and neither is changed. I tried to defend the printed argument and could not.

(1) "Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]" does not follow. A local subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕_φ O need not lie in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m} = O, Φ = Z/p, O = Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A = {(a_φ) : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ_g[g], and this is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p) = p−1 ≥ 2. The containment is true only because of the explicit images of the generators, and the paper never states them.

(2) "Isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free" gives only an injection of lattices of the same rank. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself such an injection, and it is not onto.

I looked for other readings:
- a Nakayama argument would need surjectivity onto target/m_{T_m}·target, not just onto the residue field;
- an integral module isomorphism S_2(Γ_1(N*),O)_m ≅ S_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] would still leave the same generator argument to be made;
- nothing elsewhere in the paper supplies the step (I searched every twisting passage and the 2022 Correction).

The step cannot be skipped. Lemma 4.2 (p. 334) gives CM-ness and the number of generators of ω only for an actual B ⊗_O C, and a finite-index subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] inherits neither. Without the equality, the proof of dim ω_{T_m}/m = 3, and so of multiplicity two, is incomplete.

I checked the repair myself, including the twisting direction (on S_{φ²}, ⟨d⟩ for d ∈ Φ acts by φ²(d), so it matches 1⊗[d²]) and that U_l = 0 for l | M. The repair is sound, so the stated result is correct.

Consequences: Theorem 4.8 is used nowhere else. §4.1 opens with "Although this is not needed for our main results". Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument shows…") inherits the same step. So the proof of the multiplicity-two case of Thm 4.8 is affected, but no stated result is.

issues.locator: §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8 (final display), p. 366 (published version)
issues.printed: dim J_1(N^*)[m] = (1/2) dim G[m] = (1/2)(dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m]) = (3+1)/2 = 2.  [displayed, end of proof of Thm 4.8, p. 366 (PDF p. 70), preceded by "and it follows that dim G^0[m] = dim T_pG^e/m = 3, and hence"]
issues.correction: Change the middle "=" to "≤" and add a closing step. From 0 → G^0 → G → G^e → 0, taking m-torsion is only left exact, so 0 → G^0[m] → G[m] → G^e[m] is exact. This gives 3 = dim G^0[m] ≤ dim_k G[m] ≤ dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] = 3 + 1 = 4. Also J_1(N*)[m] = G[m] ≅ ρ̄^{⊕d}: this is Boston–Lenstra–Ribet, which the theorem's formulation already takes for granted. Even without it, every Jordan–Hölder factor is ρ̄, by Eichler–Shimura, Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt. So dim_k G[m] = 2d is even, hence dim G[m] = 4 and d = 2. Equivalently, G[m] ≠ G^0[m] because 3 is odd, so the map from G[m] to the 1-dimensional G^e[m] is onto. Another route: Wiese's bound d ≥ 2, quoted in Remark 4.9, together with the upper bound. Minor notation point: "dim J_1(N*)[m]" on the left means the multiplicity d, not the k-dimension. The proposed corrections in X-K5-12 and H-part1b-6 are correct and minimal.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image (PDF p. 70 = p. 366); the display is exactly as quoted, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. I recomputed the parts. G^0 = T_pG^0 ⊗ Q_p/Z_p has Pontryagin dual Hom(T_pG^0, Z_p) = T_pG^e ≅ ω, so dim G^0[m] = dim ω/m = 3. G^e has dual Hom(T_pG^e, Z_p) = T_pG^0 ≅ T_m (free of rank 1), so dim G^e[m] = 1. Both values are correct. The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] needs G[m] → G^e[m] to be onto. The obstruction lives in Ext^1_T(k, G^0), which is Pontryagin dual to Tor_1^T(k, ω). That group is nonzero because ω needs 3 generators (T_m is not Gorenstein), so additivity is not automatic, and the proof gives no argument for it. The paper only cites the Tate-module exact sequence from Gross 12.9/12.10. In Gross's multiplicity-one setting only the upper bound is needed, and here the "=" is simply asserted. The equality is true after the fact: the image of G[m] in the 1-dimensional G^e[m] is either 0 or everything, and 0 would force dim G[m] = 3, which is odd and contradicts BLR. So Theorem 4.8 is unaffected. The candidate's correction and its two side remarks are right. I disagree only on 'affects': the printed proof has an unjustified step that is false in general and needs a one-line repair (parity via BLR, or Wiese's d ≥ 2 from Remark 4.9), so I rate it 'the proof', not 'nothing'. No stated result changes. Theorem 4.8 is a standalone application and nothing later depends on it (grep finds only the introduction and Remarks 4.9/4.12). Remark 4.12's "similar argument" would need the same repair. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The page image confirms the display. The two dimensions are right. Pontryagin duality gives G^0[m]^∨ = Hom(T_pG^0,Z_p)/m = T_pG^e/m ≅ ω_{T_m}/m, which has dimension 3. Likewise G^e[m]^∨ = T_pG^0/m ≅ T_m/m, which has dimension 1.

The additivity dim G[m] = dim G^0[m] + dim G^e[m] is the step in question. It holds only if G[m] → G^e[m] is surjective. Dually, T_m/m → T_pG^∨/m must be injective in 0 → T_m → T_pG^∨ → ω → 0, where the obstruction is the connecting map Tor_1^{T_m}(ω,k) → k. That group is nonzero because T_m is not Gorenstein (ω needs 3 generators). So the equality is not formal, and the proof gives no argument for it. Its only input is the Tate-module sequence of Gross, Prop. 12.9/12.10. In Gross's Gorenstein case only the upper bound is needed.

Defence attempts:
(a) Gross's exact sequence is for Tate modules, and those sequences do not stay exact after taking [m].
(b) Nothing in §4.1 splits the sequence of T_m-modules. Ext^1_T(ω, T) can be nonzero, and the Galois structure is not used.
(c) The strongest charitable reading is Remark 4.9, just before the proof. It says Wiese proved multiplicity ≥ 2 and that "our contribution … is to show that the multiplicity is exactly two". With that bound only "≤" is needed. But the proof never invokes it; it asserts "=" and concludes "= 2" from the display alone.
So the printed proof has an unjustified step. It is not an error: the equality is true here by parity or by Wiese's bound, so the stated result is unaffected.

issues.correction: (i) Replace "Hence R[1/p] is a Noetherian semi-local ring, which therefore decomposes as a direct sum of its localizations over all finite ideals 𝔭" with "Hence R[1/p] is a Noetherian ring with finitely many prime ideals, all of them maximal (zero-dimensional, i.e. Artinian), so it is the product of its localizations at its finitely many prime ideals 𝔭". (ii) Replace "a Z_p-extension which is unramified outside primes outside those above S" with "a Z_p^r-extension of L (the image of G_L is 1+εX for X in a compact subgroup of M_2(E), so ≅ Z_p^r) unramified outside the primes above S". (iii) Replace "because G_{L,S} has finite image in G_{F,S} ... because the inflation map is injective" with "because G_{L,S} has finite index in G_{F,S} (take L the fixed field of ker V, so L ⊂ F_S and L/F is Galois), the extension also splits over G_{F,S}, because the restriction map H^1(G_{F,S}, ad V) → H^1(G_{L,S}, ad V) is injective: its kernel is the inflation of H^1(Gal(L/F), ad V), which is 0 because Gal(L/F) is finite and ad V is a Q_p-vector space".

I rendered PDF pp. 71–72 (pp. 367–368) and the text is exactly as quoted. arXiv v2 (p. 52–53) has the same wording. Each point in the candidate holds.
(a) A Noetherian semi-local ring is not in general the product of its localizations. For example, Z_(p) is not Q × Z_(p). What makes it work is dimension 0. The paper has that one sentence earlier: Spec R[1/p] is in bijection with Spec of a finite product of fields, so every prime is maximal. So "semi-local" names the wrong property, and "finite ideals" is a misprint for "(finitely many) prime ideals". "Direct sum" is harmless because there are finitely many factors.
(b) "G_{L,S} has finite image in G_{F,S}" is literally false: the image is an open subgroup of finite index and is infinite in general. It should say "finite index".
(c) The step needs the restriction H^1(G_{F,S}, ad V) → H^1(G_{L,S}, ad V) to be injective. By inflation–restriction its kernel is H^1(Gal(L/F), (ad V)^{G_L}), which is 0 because the group is finite and the coefficients are in characteristic zero. That is exactly what the paper's parenthetical describes. Inflation is always injective on H^1 and is not the relevant map. Even on a generous reading with an arbitrary L, where G_{L,S} → G_{F,S} factors as a surjection onto a finite-index subgroup, the kernel of H^1 of a finite group comes from restriction.
(d) "unramified outside primes outside those above S" has a doubled "outside". Read literally it contradicts the next clause, "unramified at all primes v|p", because S has no primes above p. Also, the image is Z_p^r, not necessarily Z_p. The step itself is fine: in a torsion-free abelian pro-p extension, inertia at v∤p has finite image and is therefore trivial. So an extension unramified at p is unramified everywhere, hence finite, hence trivial.
I re-checked the rest of the proof and it is correct: R[1/p] → A/m² is surjective since 𝔭 is maximal, and the traces argument goes through. Lemma 4.14 is cited only in the introduction (p. 298, comparison with Buzzard–Taylor) and in the remark right after it. No later theorem uses it. So these are wording slips in a correct proof of a correct lemma, and none of them is one of the 47 known bracket errors.

Write ρ(t) = s·u, where u ≡ 1 lies in the centraliser R[s] = R⊗W(k'). The determinant condition only gives N(u) = uσ(u) = 1, which does not force u = 1. Frobenius adds u^{N+1} = 1 if it swaps the eigenlines, or u^{N−1} = 1 if it fixes them.

- Non-swap case: N = 13 or 169 (≡ 1 mod 12), ρ(Frob) = 1.
In all four cases F t F^{−1} = t^N holds (also with N^{−1}), and det ρ = ε on D_x. Yet |ρ(I_x)| = 12 while |ρ̄(I_x)| = 4, so H fails.

The swap case is allowed by (3)(a) as printed. It is not caught by (3)(d), which asks ρ̄|I_x to be reducible. Here ρ̄|D_x is dihedral of order 8, hence absolutely irreducible, so x is a genuine vexing prime. A global example is E[3] of y^2 = x^3 + 11x at 11 over F = Q(√−2). This is exactly the case that v1 and Theorem 1.3(4) exclude.

4. Effect on the proof. Conjecture A(2) gives only types S and P. So "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply ... ϕ: R^min → T_{m∅}" (p. 379), and likewise Lemma 5.6, rely on H being automatic, and that is unjustified in this case. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected: its hypothesis (4) excludes the N ≡ −1 case, and the N ≡ +1 case is repaired by extending scalars. DEFENCE: with the absolute reading the parenthetical is correct. Let J = ker(ρ̄|I_x). Then ρ(J) is pro-p, so it factors through tame inertia. It is procyclic, generated by some u ≡ 1, and u is central in ρ(I_x): it commutes with t, and [P_x,u] ⊂ ρ(P_x)∩⟨u⟩ = 1. When ρ̄|I_x is absolutely irreducible, Nakayama gives R·ρ(I_x) = M_2(R), so u is scalar. Then det u = ε|I_x = 1 gives u² = 1, hence u = 1 since p is odd, and ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x).

LITERAL READING FAILS: suppose ρ̄|I_x is irreducible over k but not absolutely. Then the centraliser of the prime-to-p part s̃ of ρ(t) is R' = R⊗W(k'), and det gives u·σ(u) = 1. Two cases break the claim.

(B) Frobenius swaps the eigenlines. Then σ(u) = u^{N(x)}, and N ≡ −1 allows u ≠ 1. This is the candidate's case. Checked explicitly: p = 5, N(x) = 29, ρ̄(t) = [[0,−1],[1,−1]] (order 3, char. poly x²+x+1 irreducible mod 5), ρ̄(Frob) = [[1,−1],[0,−1]], image S_3, absolutely irreducible on D_x. Over F_5[ε] take ρ(t) = ρ̄(t)(1+εX) with X = [[1,−2],[2,−1]]. Then the relation Frob·t·Frob^{-1} = t^{29} holds, det ρ(t) = 1 and det ρ(Frob) = 29 mod 5, but ρ(t) has order 15. This x satisfies (3)(a) literally, and (3)(d) is vacuous for it over k.

(A) Not noted by the candidate: Frobenius centralises and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. Then u^{N−1} = 1 and u·σ(u) = 1 again allow u ≠ 1. Checked explicitly: p = 3, N = 13, ρ̄(t) = [[0,−1],[1,0]], ρ̄(Frob) = 1, ρ(t) = ρ̄(t)(1+ε·ρ̄(t)) of order 12. This is realised locally, e.g. by y² = x³+13x+13² at 13, mod 3. Thm 1.3's hypotheses do not exclude case A. Under the absolute reading it is type P, covered by Conj A(2)(b).

WHY THIS IS A MISPRINT, NOT AN ERROR: the intended meaning is clear from context.
(i) Thm 1.3(4) says 'absolutely irreducible'.
(ii) The sentence right after (8) says the N ≡ −1 vexing primes 'have been eliminated'. That is true only if (3)(d)'s 'reducible' means 'over k̄'.
(iii) §3.9 defines vexing primes by 'ρ̄|I_x ≃ ξ⊕ξ^c is reducible', which is reducibility over k̄.
(iv) v1 states the hypothesis with 'absolutely'.
Under the absolute reading, case B with N ≡ −1 is excluded by (d), case B with N ≢ −1 is type M (automatic: u^{N+1} = 1), case A is type P, and H is automatic. So Conj A (1)–(4) do give ϕ on p. 379, and Thm 5.11 and Thm 1.3 stand as intended.

issues.correction: ... denote the open compact subgroups of G(A^∞) such that:
issues.reason: On p. 371 Y(K) := G(Q)\G(A)/K^0_∞ K is defined only for compact open K ⊂ G(A^∞). issues.locator: §5.2.1 (Arithmetic quotients), item (5)(b) in the definition of K_Q and L_Q, published p. 373 (PDF p. 77). It is read with the definition of Γ_p(v^c) (p. 372), deformation condition (6) P (p. 369), standing hypothesis (3)(c) (p. 369) and Conjecture A(2)(b) (p. 374). arXiv v2 §5.2.1 has the identical text. arXiv v1 §4.2.1 has the same item (5)(b), but with GL_2 in place of PGL_2 and an extra type Sc.
issues.printed:
(5) If v ∈ S(ρ̄), K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} is defined as follows:
(a) If ρ̄ is of type S at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
(b) If ρ̄ is of type P, M or H at v, then K_{Q,v} = Γ_p(v^c), where c is the conductor of ρ̄|D_v.
[p. 372: Γ_0(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 *) mod π_v^c}, Γ_p(v^c) = {g ∈ PGL_2(O_v) | g ≡ (1 *; 0 d) mod π_v^c, d has p− power order}. p. 369, condition (6): "P : If x ∈ S(ρ̄), and ρ̄|I_x ≃ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_x ≃ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}." p. 374, Conjecture A(2)(b): "If ρ̄|D_v is of type P, so that ρ̄|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, then ρ|I_v ≅ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}."]
issues.correction: At a type-P prime the level has to cut out the minimal inertial type ⟨ψ⟩ ⊕ ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}. With c equal to the Artin conductor 2a(ψ) of ρ̄|D_v, it does not. Γ_p(v^c) ⊂ Γ_0(v^c), and Γ_0(v^c) fixes the newvector of every π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with a(χ'') ≤ a(ψ). This includes the non-minimal case χ''|O_v^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, with ξ ≠ 1 of p-power order, which occurs exactly when p | N(v) − 1. When ψ² = 1, the level also contains the ⟨ψ⟩-twisted Steinberg lifts, and (when N(v) ≡ −1 mod p) depth-zero supercuspidal lifts; these are non-minimal and are congruent to ρ̄ under a level-raising condition on ρ̄(Frob_v). Proposed fix for ψ² ≠ 1: take c = a(ψ), the conductor of ψ, which is half the conductor of ρ̄|D_v at type-P primes. Then Γ_p(v^{a(ψ)}) sees π(χ, χ^{−1}) only with a(χ) ≤ a(ψ) and χ|O_v^× of prime-to-p order, so χ|O_v^× = ⟨ψ⟩^{±1}; this is the analogue of v1's level. For multiplicity one, also take the ⟨ψ⟩-isotypic part under Γ_0/Γ_1. The candidate's suggested fix is right in substance for ψ² ≠ 1. It does not cover ψ² = 1; there a twisted-spherical level is needed, namely the ⟨ψ⟩∘det-isotypic part of the PGL_2(O_v)-invariants. Theorem 1.3's Y_0(N) must change in the same way. Types M and H are fine as printed.
issues.reason:
1. The printed text matches the rendered page. Γ_p(v^c) ⊂ Γ_0(v^c), and Γ_0(v^c) is the image of K_0(π^c) in PGL_2.

2. For v ∤ p, a p-power-order character ξ of O_v^× factors through (O_v/π_v)^×, so a nontrivial one exists iff p | N(v) − 1. Put χ″|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ.
- If a(ψ) ≥ 2, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ agrees with ⟨ψ⟩ on 1 + π^{a−1}.
- If a(ψ) = 1, then ⟨ψ⟩ξ is still nontrivial, because the orders of ⟨ψ⟩ and ξ are coprime.
Either way a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = a(ψ). So π″ = π(χ″, χ″^{−1}) is irreducible with trivial central character and conductor 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman its newvector is K_0(π^c)-fixed, hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed.

3. Mackey check (script at work/agents/K6-1-A/mackey.py). Take N(v) = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic, so c = 2. Double cosets B(O)\GL_2(O)/K_0(7^n) have representatives (1 0; 7^i 1), and the character condition becomes a(χ) ≤ min(i, n − i). For both the minimal χ = ⟨ψ⟩ (order 2) and the non-minimal χ″ = ⟨ψ⟩ξ (order 6):
- n = 1: no coset contributes.
- n = 2: only i = 1 contributes.
So each has exactly a 1-dimensional space of K_0(v²)-fixed vectors.

4. π″ reduces to ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1} on I_v, and T_∅ has no operators at v, so π″ lies in the m∅-part. Moreover ⟨ψ⟩ξ ∉ {⟨ψ⟩, ⟨ψ⟩^{−1}}, because ξ ≠ 1 has p-power order while ⟨ψ⟩ has prime-to-p order. So π″ is excluded by condition (6).

5. Existence of such forms. Take r̄ over Q with trivial character and weight 2, ℓ ≡ 1 mod p split in F, and r̄|I_ℓ = ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. Lifts of prescribed type exist (Diamond–Taylor 1994; Gee 2011); take a newform f with type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1} at ℓ and minimal elsewhere. Then BC_F(f) is a cohomological cuspidal π″ at level K_∅. At the Q̄_p-point of T_{∅,m∅} it defines, the specialisation of ρ_m has the traces of r_f|G_F. So it is r_f|G_F, and by Carayol r_f|I_v has the non-minimal type, contradicting A(2)(b). In that case R^min ≅ T_m (Theorem 1.3) fails too, and the theorem survives only because its hypothesis, Conjecture A, is false.

6. §3 avoids this by twisting (p. 310: ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0) together with X_H / U_x at level x^{c_x}, c_x = a(ψ). That route is unavailable in §5, where det = ε is fixed on PGL_2.

7. Types M and H are fine: with fixed determinant ε, a non-minimal lift at a type-M prime needs p | N(v) + 1, which is excluded. A separate case, not checked in detail: when ψ is quadratic, a twisted Steinberg St⊗χ (conductor c) also sits at Γ_0(v^c) whatever N(v) is.

I classify this as an error rather than the candidate's "gap": Conjecture A as formulated at this level is false in cases where π″ occurs. Defence attempts, none of which works:
(1) Γ_p(v^c) is contained in Γ_0(v^c) by definition. Take π'' = π(χ'', χ''^{−1}) with χ''|O^× = ⟨ψ⟩ξ, where ξ ≠ 1 is tame of p-power order. Then π'' has trivial central character and conductor 2a(⟨ψ⟩ξ) = 2a(ψ) = c. By Casselman newform theory, K_0(ϖ^c) acts on the newvector through ω(d) = 1, so the newvector is Γ_0(v^c)-fixed and hence Γ_p(v^c)-fixed. The restriction "d has p-power order" therefore removes nothing here.
(2) Explicit check in the induced model: at PGL-level {a ≡ d, c ≡ 0 mod ϖ^n}, π(χ, χ^{−1}) has vectors on which K_0 acts by χ^{±1}(a/d), and only when a(χ) ≤ n. The p-power restriction does separate ⟨ψ⟩ from ⟨ψ⟩ξ at n = a(ψ), but not at n = 2a(ψ), where both have Γ_0-fixed newvectors. The paper's own §5.5 (p. 380) says the level was chosen as the X_H(N) analogue to exclude such twists. v1's GL_2 version (type 1 ⊕ ψ, c = a(ψ)) does exclude them. Nothing in the hypotheses rules out p | N(v) − 1 at type-P primes: (3)(c) and Theorem 1.3(4) only exclude N ≡ −1 for vexing primes.
(3) Consequence. π'' has I_v-type ⟨ψ⟩ξ ⊕ (⟨ψ⟩ξ)^{−1}, which fails condition (6). If π'' is cohomological at level K_∅ with residual representation ρ̄, it contributes to T_{∅,m} ⊗ Q̄_p. Then Conjecture A(2)(b) for Q = ∅ contradicts local–global compatibility at v, even up to semisimplification.
Such π'' exist. Take the base change to F, with ℓ split, of a classical weight-2 form on Γ_0(ℓ²) with ℓ ≡ 1 mod p and local type ⟨ψ⟩ξ that is congruent to a minimal form of type ⟨ψ⟩; Carayol and Diamond–Taylor give such congruences. So Conjecture A as stated is false for such ρ̄, and Theorems 5.11 and 1.3 are vacuous for them.
Theorem 1.2 is unaffected: semistable minimal ρ has only type-S primes. The proofs of 5.11 and 1.3 use the level only through Conjecture A, so the patching argument survives once the level is corrected. However, the conclusion of Theorem 1.3 as stated, R^min ≅ T_m on H_1(Y_0(N)), is false in these cases.
On kind: I classify this as an error (a wrong definition that makes a stated conjecture false), not a gap.

issues.locator: §5.2.1, item (4) of the definition of K_Q, L_Q, p. 373 (published version)
issues.printed: (4) If v|p, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = GL_2(𝒪_v) if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
issues.correction: (4) If v|p, then K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = PGL_2(𝒪_v) (equivalently, the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v)) if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} = Γ_0(v).
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered image of p. 373 (PDF p. 77). Item (4) of §5.2.1 does print "GL_2(𝒪_v)". On p. 372, §5.2 sets G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(2), and K_Q = ∏_v K_{Q,v} is described as an open compact subgroup of G(A) (the text says G(A); it should be G(A^∞)). So each K_{Q,v} has to be a compact open subgroup of PGL_2(F_v), and GL_2(𝒪_v) is literally not one. The rest of the definition is written for PGL_2 throughout:
- Item (3) on the same page uses PGL_2(𝒪_v).
- Γ_0(v^c), Γ_1(v^c) and Γ_p(v^c) on p. 372 are all defined as subsets of PGL_2(𝒪_v), and item (5) uses them.
- §5.5 ("The distinction between GL and PGL") explains why the paper deliberately works with PGL rather than GL.
- In the PGL(n) analogue in §9.1, the authors write "the image in PGL(𝒪_v) of {g ∈ GL_n(𝒪_v) | …}", which shows they distinguish the two groups when they mean the image.

The intended meaning is still clear. 𝒪_v is local, so Pic(𝒪_v) = 0 and PGL_2(𝒪_v) = GL_2(𝒪_v)/𝒪_v^×. That is the image of GL_2(𝒪_v) in PGL_2(F_v), the maximal compact subgroup that stabilises the lattice class [𝒪_v^2]. So the proposed correction to PGL_2(𝒪_v) is right, and it agrees with the finite-flat (unramified, maximal level at p) intent and with item (3) of §9.1 (PGL_n(𝒪_v) for v ∉ S ∪ Q, which includes v|p). The arXiv v2 text (§5.2.1) has the identical wording "GL2 (Ov)", so the slip was never corrected. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Downstream: I searched the rest of the paper for K_{Q,v}, "maximal compact" and "hyperspecial", and found nothing that relies on the literal GL_2(𝒪_v). All later arguments use Y(K_Q) and Y(L_Q) with the evident maximal level at p. This is a purely notational slip with no mathematical consequence.

issues.locator: §5.3, Lemma 5.6 (statement and proof), published p. 375 (PDF p. 79); Conjecture A(3) runs from p. 374 to p. 375. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §5.3, p. 58) has word-for-word the same text for Conjecture A(3) and Lemma 5.6. arXiv v1 does not contain this section.
issues.printed: Lemma 5.6 Assume Conjecture A. Assume that there exists a maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. Suppose that Q consists entirely of Taylor–Wiles primes. Then there exists a representation: ρ_Q : G_F → GL_2(T_{Q,m}) whose traces generate T_{Q,m} and such that ρ_Q is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ outside Q with cyclotomic determinant. Proof By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m to T_{Q,m} is such a representation. Moreover, assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces. [Conjecture A(3), same page: "... and so φ(Frob_v) mod m is well defined; assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. Then ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}."]
issues.correction: Lemma 5.6 needs one more hypothesis: for each v ∈ Q, U_v = T_{π_v} ≢ ±1 mod m, which is the same as φ_v(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m. One way to guarantee this is to take m ⊇ (m_∅, U_v − α_v) with α_v a root of X² − T_vX + 1 mod m_∅, as in Lemma 5.8 and Theorem 5.11. The proposed correction is right and minimal for the Hensel step. Conjecture A(3) also takes "the image of φ mod m is unramified" "by assumption". If that phrase is read as a hypothesis too, the lemma also needs the diamond operators at v to be trivial mod m. That holds in Theorem 5.11, where the diamond operators act through the p-group Δ_N. The rest of the lemma does not use (3): the minimality and cyclotomic-determinant parts need no change.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 374–375 and read them. Conjecture A(3) is conditional: it gives ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1} only after "assume that φ(Frob_v) ≢ ±1 mod m". Nothing else in Conjecture A mentions v ∈ Q: (1) covers λ outside S ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}, (2) covers S(ρ̄) and (4) covers v|p. Lemma 5.6 allows any maximal ideal m of T_Q associated to ρ̄. By Definition 5.5, "associated to ρ̄" only constrains T_λ for λ outside S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. "Taylor–Wiles primes" (§5.1 and Prop. 5.2) only means N(x) ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues, which is a condition on ρ̄ and not on m. So nothing ensures U_v mod m ≠ ±1. The proof uses the conclusion of (3) without checking its hypothesis. Without that conclusion, the operators T_α at Q are not linked to ρ_m at all, so "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not justified. Hensel's lemma alone splits ρ|D_x into two characters, but it cannot identify either character with the Hecke character φ.

I also checked whether the paper excludes such m elsewhere. It does not. Lemma 5.8, like Lemma 3.5 (pp. 305–307), treats only the m containing U_x − α_x. The step showing V[m] = 0 gives x·U_x² = ⟨x⟩, i.e. γ² ≡ α_xβ_x ≡ 1 for the eigenvalue γ of U_x on V. That contradicts γ = α_x (since α_x ≠ β_x), but it is consistent with γ = ±1. So "new at x" torsion with U_x ≡ ±1 (Steinberg type) is not ruled out without local–global compatibility at x, which Conjecture A deliberately leaves out.

The minimality part of the conclusion and the cyclotomic determinant (from (1) plus Chebotarev) do not use (3). Lemma 5.6 is never cited later. Theorem 5.11 repeats the argument itself for m ∋ U_x − α_x, where α_x ≢ ±1, and its step (a) invokes (3) correctly. So the main results are unaffected, and only Lemma 5.6 as stated overreaches. A charitable reading ("there exists m" meaning a suitably chosen m) does not help, because the conclusion is about T_{Q,m} for the given m and no choice of U_x-eigenvalue is specified. Defence tried and failed. (i) The "Taylor–Wiles primes" hypothesis (Prop. 5.2: N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄ unramified at v, ρ̄(Frob_v) has distinct eigenvalues) is a condition on ρ̄, not on U_v mod m. It would give U_v ≢ ±1 mod m only through the conclusion ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}. Then the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) are φ̄(Frob_v)^{±1}, which are distinct iff φ̄(Frob_v) ≠ ±1, because ε(Frob_v) = N(v) ≡ 1. But that conclusion is exactly what (3) withholds when φ(Frob_v) ≡ ±1, so the argument is circular. (ii) "Associated to ρ̄" (Def. before Conj. A) constrains only T_λ for λ ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {v|p}. (iii) Nothing else in Conjecture A controls U_v mod m. (1) gives ρ_m mod m ≅ ρ̄, but no statement ties φ(Frob_v) to the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v) in the ±1 case. (iv) No nearby result supplies the step. Lemma 5.8 and the Ihara argument in the proof of Lemma 9.6 deal only with m ∋ U_x − α_x where U_x² − 1 is invertible. They do not show that H_1(Y_1(Q))_m = 0 when U_x ≡ ±1. For torsion classes, nothing rules out "new at x" classes with U_x ≡ ±1. Such classes would be excluded under full local–global compatibility (Steinberg at v would force equal eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_v)), but Conjecture A does not assume that. (v) T_{Q,m} is generated by the T_λ, which are traces by (1), together with U_v and the diamond operators at v ∈ Q. The only route to putting U_v in the trace subalgebra is Hensel applied to ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}, using the fact that the roots φε(σ) and φ^{-1}(σ) are distinct mod m. So for an m with U_v ≡ ±1 mod m, "traces generate T_{Q,m}" is not proved. The rest of the lemma does not use (3). Minimality outside Q holds because R_Q (§5.1) puts no condition at x ∈ Q, and L_{Q,x} is the full H^1. The determinant is cyclotomic by (1) and Chebotarev. Consequences: the paper never cites Lemma 5.6 by number (grep finds only its own statement). Its content is re-derived in the proof of Theorem 5.11 ("Applying Conjecture A to T_{Q_N,m}, we deduce the existence of a surjective homomorphism R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}", together with step (5a) using part (3)). There m ⊇ (m_∅, U_x − α_x), and by Lemma 5.8, which step (b) invokes, α_x is a root of X² − T_xX + 1 whose two roots are distinct mod m_∅. Since α_xβ_x ≡ 1 and α_x ≢ β_x, we get α_x ≢ ±1, so (3) applies. Theorem 5.11, Theorem 1.3 and §9 (Conjecture B, with m = (m, U_x − α_x) stated explicitly) are therefore unaffected. Only Lemma 5.6, as stated for an arbitrary m, overreaches.

issues.locator: §5.3, Conjecture A(4), p. 375 (published version)
issues.printed: (4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary.
issues.correction: (4) If v|p and ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, then ρ|D_v is finite flat (that is, (ρ ⊗ T_{Q,m}/m^n)|D_v is finite flat for all n ≥ 1, as in §5.1 condition (3)); and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary. An equivalent phrasing is "If v|p, then ρ|D_v is finite flat if ρ̄|D_v is". Deleting the first bar alone would not fix it. An unconditional "ρ|D_v is finite flat" would force ρ̄|D_v to be finite flat, because finite flat representations are closed under quotients when e = 1 < p − 1 (Raynaud). That contradicts the allowed case where ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at 110 and 250 dpi. Conjecture A starts on p. 374 (PDF p. 78), and part (4) is at the top of p. 375 (PDF p. 79). It reads exactly: "(4) If v|p, then ρ̄|D_v is finite flat, and if ρ̄|D_v is ordinary, then ρ|D_v is ordinary." The first two ρ's have bars and the last one does not. arXiv v2 (p. 58, image checked) has the same text.

As printed, the first clause says something about the residual representation ρ̄ and nothing about ρ = ρ_m. Taken literally, it contradicts the paper's own setup:
- §5.1 hypothesis (2), p. 369: "ρ̄ is either ordinary or finite flat at v|p".
- Theorem 1.3(1): ρ̄ is "either finite flat or ordinary" at v|p.
- §5.2 level condition (4), p. 373: K_{Q,v} = GL2(O_v) "if ρ̄|D_v is finite flat. Otherwise … Γ0(v)".

So the printed conjecture would be false whenever ρ̄ is ordinary but not finite flat. When ρ̄|D_v is finite flat and not ordinary, it says nothing about ρ|D_v.

The conclusion that is missing is exactly what the proofs need. §5.1 deformation conditions (2) and (3), p. 369, require the reductions mod m^n to be finite flat or ordinary, and finite flat whenever ρ̄|G_v is finite flat. These conditions define R_Q and R^min. They are used in three places:
- Lemma 5.6, p. 375: "By Conjecture A, the representation ρ_Q := ρ_m … is such a representation", i.e. a minimal deformation.
- §5.4, p. 378: "Properties (1)–(4) of Conjecture A then imply that ρ_{m∅} gives rise to a homomorphism ϕ : R^min → T_{m∅}".
- §5.4, p. 379: the surjection R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m}, which the proof of Theorem 5.11 uses. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are deduced from that result.

Under the printed wording, ρ_m need not satisfy condition (3), so ϕ is not justified. The intended meaning is clear, and the proofs work once (4) is corrected. So this is a misprint in the statement of an assumed conjecture that the proofs depend on. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

A side note on a separate issue: the pdftotext layer drops the ε in part (3). The image shows "ρ|D_v ∼ φε ⊕ φ^{-1}", which is correct as printed.

issues.locator: §5.3.1, proof of Lemma 5.9(1) (and hence (2)), p. 377 (published version)
issues.printed: Proof Consider part (1). By Nakayama’s Lemma, we reduce to the case when μ = k. Yet H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0 and the action of Hecke operators on H_0(Y_0(Q), k) (which preserve the connected components) is via the degree map, and this action is Eisenstein (in the sense that the only m in the support of H_0 are Eisenstein).  [§5.3, proof of Lemma 5.9, p. 377 = PDF p. 81; identical wording in arXiv v2, line ~3114 of cg-v2.txt]
issues.correction:
Replace "H_3(Y_0(Q), k) = 0" by the localized statement "H_3(Y_0(Q), k)_m = 0". That is all the Nakayama/dévissage step needs.

For p ≥ 5 the step holds as intended. A finite-order element of PGL_2(F) has order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6, since ζ+ζ^{-1} ∈ F ∩ R = Q. So the lattices have no p-torsion, the orbifold homology with k-coefficients is the homology of a non-compact 3-dimensional quotient, and H_3 = 0 even before localizing.

For p = 3 the paper gives no argument, although §5.1 and Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 allow p = 3. Two fixes are possible:
(a) add the hypothesis p ≥ 5 to §5 and to Theorems 1.2 and 1.3; or
(b) prove that the 3-primary Farrell classes vanish after localizing at m. These classes are carried by order-3 subgroups, whose centralizers are rank-one tori coming from F(√−3). My unproved assessment is that their Hecke eigensystems are induced from F(ζ_3). The standing hypothesis that ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_3)} is absolutely irreducible would then exclude them.

Two corrections proposed earlier are not quite right:

issues.correction:
Multiplicity one only gives μ = dim π_f^{K_∅} = ∏_{v of type P,M,H} dim π_v^{Γ_p(v^c)}. This value is the same for every contributing π, because a minimal lift fixes the inertial type. It is at least ∏_v (N(v)−1)_{p'}, so μ ≥ 2 whenever S(ρ̄) contains a P/M/H prime with v ∤ 2. The remark and Theorem 1.3's clause "then μ = 1" are therefore correct only when every prime of S(ρ̄) has type S. (Theorem 1.2 only has type S primes and does not claim μ = 1 anyway.) Two ways to repair it:
(a) Add that restriction.
(b) Replace H by its Δ-invariants, where Δ = ∏_v Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c), which is equivalent to working at the literal Γ_0(v^c) level. Δ has prime-to-p order and commutes with T_∅, so H^Δ is a T_m-direct summand of the free module H, hence itself free. Its rank in characteristic 0 is ∏ dim π_v^{Γ_0(v^c)} = 1, and it is nonzero once H⊗Q ≠ 0. This restores "μ = 1" for the space Y_0(N) of literal Γ_0(N) level.
Theorem 5.11 itself (R^min ≅ T and freeness) is not affected, and neither is the complete-intersection clause.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered PDF pages 84, 76, 77 and 6.

The group. In PGL_2, "g ≡ (1 *; 0 d)" only makes sense up to scalars. So Γ_p(v^c) is the set of g that are upper triangular mod π^c with d/a of p-power order. The map g ↦ d/a gives Γ_0(v^c)/Γ_p(v^c) ≅ (O_v/π^c)^×/Syl_p. Since π_v has trivial central character, π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(K_0(v^c), η(d/a))}, where η runs over the characters of (O_v/π^c)^× of order prime to p.

The η-summand. Let η̃ be any extension of η to F_v^×. If v ∈ π_v transforms under K_0 by η(d/a), then as a vector of π_v⊗η̃ (central character η̃²) it transforms by η(d)². So the η-summand equals (π_v⊗η̃)^{K_1(v^c)}. By Casselman this has dimension max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃) + 1).

Tame η contribute. Let η be tame, of prime-to-p order. There are (N(v)−1)_{p'} such η.
- Types M/H: π_v is supercuspidal and a tame twist keeps the conductor, since the Swan conductor is unchanged and there are no inertia invariants. So a(π_v⊗η̃) = c.
- Type P: π_v = π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψ̃, and a(ψη) + a(ψ^{-1}η) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c.
Either way each such η contributes at least 1.

Brute-force check. I computed dim π^{K'} by Mackey double cosets on GL_2(Z/ℓ²) (script work/agents/k6v/ps.py).
- ℓ = 7, p = 3, ψ quadratic (a valid type P): dimension 4, as the formula predicts.
- ℓ = 7, p = 5, ψ of order 3: dimension 8, as predicted.
- The unramified test case also matches.

Global step. Localized at the non-Eisenstein m∅, H ⊗ Q̄ is the direct sum of the spaces π_f^{K_∅} ⊗ H^1(g,K;π_∞) over the π that contribute. Here m(π) = 1 and the (g,K) cohomology has dimension 1. Definition 5.4 builds T_∅ only from T_α with α trivial at S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p}, so T_∅ acts on each π_f^K by a scalar. By strong multiplicity one, different π have different eigensystems. So T⊗Q̄ is a product of copies of Q̄, and freeness of rank μ forces μ = dim π_f^K ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}. For v ∤ 2 this is at least 2, because N(v)−1 is even and p is odd.

The extra vectors lie in the same π and have the same Hecke eigenvalues. Classically they correspond to the twists f⊗η: same level, nebentypus η². In §3 (GL(2)/Q, U_x with d of p-power order) and in v1 (GL(2)/F), the nebentypus is pinned instead, so no extra vectors arise there.

Hence the printed claim is false whenever S(ρ̄) has a P/M/H prime v ∤ 2 and H⊗Q ≠ 0. Theorem 1.3 inherits the error if "Y_0(N)" means the paper's Y, as the deduction "Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11" requires. If Y_0(N) is read literally as Γ_0(N) level, the μ = 1 clause can be rescued via the prime-to-p invariants, but that is not the argument the paper gives. (The separate issue that non-minimal type-P forms also appear at this level is candidate C-K6-1, not this one.) The defence fails.
(1) T_∅ is generated only by T_α with α trivial at Q ∪ S(ρ̄) ∪ {v|p} (Def. 5.4), and m_∅ involves only T_λ for λ ∉ S∪{v|p} (§5.4). T_α then acts on π_f^{K} = ⊗_w π_w^{K_w} by the characteristic function of K_λ g K_λ, which is a scalar on the whole space. So the T_∅-eigenspace of π in H_1(Y,K)_{m∅} has dimension dim π_f^{K_∅} · dim H^1(g,K;π_∞) = dim π_f^{K_∅}, and μ = dim π_f^{K_∅} (strong multiplicity one rules out any other π with the same eigenvalues).
(2) In PGL2, Γ_p(v^c) = {d/a ∈ Syl_p((O_v/π^c)^×)}, and Γ_0/Γ_p has prime-to-p order. Hence π_v^{Γ_p} = ⊕_η π_v^{(Γ_0, η(d/a))}, summed over characters η of prime-to-p order. Twisting by η̃ and conjugating by Atkin–Lehner, Casselman's theory gives dim of the η-summand = max(0, c − a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) + 1). With trivial central character, nothing forces η = 1. That is exactly what v1 had (GL2, central character in T) and v2 lost.
(3) For a minimal π_v, a(π_v) = c. For every tame η, a(π_v⊗η̃^{-1}) ≤ c:
- type P: a(χη̃^{-1}) + a(χ^{-1}η̃^{-1}) ≤ 2a(ψ) = c;
- types M and H: σ⊗η stays without inertia invariants and keeps its Swan conductor.
So each such η contributes at least 1, giving dim ≥ (N(v)−1)_{p'}, which is ≥ 2 for N(v) odd since p ≥ 3.
(4) I checked this numerically (principal series, computed as dim of K-invariants of Ind_{B(O)}^{GL2(O)}(ψ(a)ψ^{-1}(d)) by the character formula; script work/agents/K6-B/ps.py). Results:
- q=5, c=2, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_0-invariants 1, Γ_p-invariants 6;
- q=7, p=3, ψ quadratic: 1 and 4;
- q=13, p=3, ψ of order 4: Γ_p-invariants 6.
All three match the formula exactly.
(5) If H⊗Q ≠ 0, then under Theorem 5.11 every contributing π is a minimal lift, so μ ≥ 2 whenever there is a P/M/H prime with v ∤ 2. For H/M primes (not vexing), minimality is automatic, so Conjecture A is not contradicted and such cases can really occur.
Consequences: the remark is used only to deduce Theorem 1.3 ("From these remarks we see that Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11"). That deduction identifies H_1(Y_0(N),O)_m with H = H_1(Y,O)_{m∅} at Γ_p level, so the μ = 1 clause of Theorem 1.3 is false as the paper intends it. Nothing else in the paper uses μ = 1. The candidate's correction is right. Fix (b) above is a minimal alternative that keeps μ = 1.
Separate issue, not verified here and not part of this finding: at type P primes with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, the level Γ_p(v^c) already contains Γ_0(v^c)-newforms π(χ,χ^{-1}) with χ|O^× = ψε, ε of p-power order. These are non-minimal, which puts pressure on Conjecture A(2)(b) at this level.

issues.locator: §5.5 (informal sketch for GL), p. 381 (published version)
issues.printed: (§5.5 "The distinction between GL and PGL", p. 381, last paragraph) "splits. This imposes a further Chebotarev condition on the Taylor–Wiles primes x ∈ Q which corresponds to x splitting completely in a metabelian extension of F. Explicitly, if 𝔞 ∈ Cl_p(𝒪_F) has p-power order h, let 𝔞^h = (α). The necessary condition on x is that (assuming p is prime to the order of the unit group of F) that α^{(N(x)−1)/p} ≡ 1 mod x, or equivalently that x splits completely in F(α^{1/p}, ζ_p)." (displayed formula checked on the page image; the text is identical in arXiv v2, p. 63)
issues.correction: Replace p by h in both places: "α^{(N(x)−1)/h} ≡ 1 mod x, or equivalently that x splits completely in F(α^{1/h}, ζ_h)". This is needed for every 𝔞 ∈ Cl_p(𝒪_F), or equivalently for the generators 𝔞_i (of orders h_i) of a cyclic decomposition. In that case x splits completely in the metabelian compositum of the fields F(α_i^{1/h_i}, ζ_{h_i}). The formula needs h | N(x)−1. This holds for Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p^N and p^N ≥ h. With no divisibility assumption the condition is α^{(N(x)−1)/gcd(h, N(x)−1)} ≡ 1 mod x. The printed p-th-power condition is necessary but not sufficient when h > p. It gives the right answer only when Cl_p(𝒪_F) has exponent p, for example the Z/pZ case discussed earlier in the paragraph.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85 = p. 381). I redid the computation. Assume p ∤ |O_F^×|, as the paper does. Then tensoring O_F^× → (O/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(O_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(O_F) → 0, where G = ((O/x)^×)_p is cyclic of order p^v, v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Take the lift ã = [𝔞] of 𝔞. Every lift has the form ãu with u ∈ G, and (ãu)^h = [α]·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff the image of α lies in G^h. In a cyclic group of order N(x)−1 this is the same as α being an h-th power, i.e. α^{(N(x)−1)/h} ≡ 1 when h | N(x)−1. It is not p-th power residuosity.

Explicit counterexample to sufficiency: Cl_p = Z/p^2, v ≥ 2, and α ≡ g^p for a generator g of G. Then the printed condition holds, but E ≅ (Z × Z/p^v)/⟨(p^2, −p)⟩. The Smith normal form of [[p^2, −p], [0, p^v]] gives E ≅ Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p^2 × Z/p^v. So the map does not split. Applying the printed condition to every element of Cl_p does not help: an element b with b^p = 𝔞 gives the same α.

Interpretive caveat: read literally, "The necessary condition" is true as a necessary condition, and the stated equivalence with splitting in F(α^{1/p}, ζ_p) (given N(x) ≡ 1 mod p) is correct. But the sentence is introduced by "Explicitly" as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition equivalent to splitting ("corresponds to x splitting completely in a metabelian extension"). As that, it is wrong for h > p. It looks like a slip from generalising the Z/pZ example: h is introduced but only used to define α.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It sits in an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of an alternative GL approach that the authors explicitly do not pursue ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma or proof uses it. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (PDF p. 85).

Setup. Assume p ∤ |𝒪_F^×|, as the paper does. Tensoring 𝒪_F^× → (𝒪/x)^× → RCl(x) → Cl(𝒪_F) → 0 with Z_p gives 0 → G → RCl_p(x) → Cl_p(𝒪_F) → 0, where G = (𝒪/x)^× ⊗ Z_p is cyclic of order p^v, with v = v_p(N(x)−1).

Why h, not p. The class ã = [𝔞] lifts 𝔞, and every lift of 𝔞 has the form ãu with u ∈ G. Then (ãu)^h = ι(α)·u^h. So a lift of order h exists iff α ∈ G^h. For a set Q of primes the kernel is ∏G_x, so the condition is imposed prime by prime. Because Cl_p is a direct sum of cyclic groups, the map splits iff this holds for the generators. So the correct condition is that α is an h-th power mod x, not a p-th power.

Group-theoretic counterexample. Take Cl_p = Z/p², v ≥ 2 and α = g^p, with g a generator of G. Then RCl_p ≅ Z²/⟨(p², −p), (0, p^v)⟩. Its Smith normal form is Z/p × Z/p^{v+1}, which is not Z/p² × Z/p^v, so the map does not split.

Concrete counterexample (python, ex.py in my work dir).
- F = Q(√−199), 𝒪_F = Z[ω] with ω² − ω + 50 = 0, and Cl ≅ Z/9. Take p = 3, which is prime to |𝒪^×| = 2.
- 𝔭' = (2, ω−1) has order exactly 9, and 𝔭'^9 = (21+ω), since the norm of 21+ω is 512. So h = 9 and α = 21+ω.
- Take x | 487 with ω ≡ 185, so N(x)−1 = 2·3^5.
- Then α^{162} ≡ 1 mod x, so the printed condition holds and x splits completely in F(α^{1/3}, ζ_3).
- But α^{54} ≢ 1 mod x, so α is not a 9th power. Hence RCl_3(x) ≅ Z/3 × Z/3^6 does not split over Z/9.
- Primes over 829 and 1009 behave the same way.

Defence attempts.
(i) Read literally, "necessary condition" is true. But the sentence opens with "Explicitly", continues "or equivalently", and is presented as the explicit form of the Chebotarev condition that "corresponds to" splitting. As that it is wrong for h > p. If the authors had meant only a necessary condition, h would still be introduced solely to define α, so the context does not show which reading was intended.
(ii) The printed condition is exactly the splitting condition for the pushout extension by G/G^p. That corresponds to Taylor–Wiles data Δ_N with N = 1. The text, however, speaks of RCl_p(Q) = RCl(Q) ⊗ Z_p, and Taylor–Wiles needs N → ∞. For the pushout to G/G^{p^N} the condition is α ∈ G^{p^{min(k,N)}} (where h = p^k), which is the h-th-power condition once p^N ≥ h. So neither reading saves the printed claim.
(iii) Because p appears consistently twice, this looks like a generalisation of the Z/pZ example rather than a one-character typo, and the intended meaning is not clear from context. That makes it an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The passage is an informal, hedged sketch ("It seems that…") of a GL approach that the authors explicitly abandon ("We ultimately decided, however, to impose the simplifying assumption that det(ρ) is cyclotomic"). No theorem, lemma, remark or proof cites it. §8.2 uses RCl(Q)/p^n, but not this splitting condition. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: Part 2, Theorem 5.16, hypothesis (6), p. 383 (PDF p. 87). arXiv v2 (p. 64) has identical text. arXiv v1 does not contain Part 2.
issues.printed: (6) If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent. Moreover, if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x, then N(x) ≡ 1 mod p.
issues.correction: (6) If r is ramified at a prime x ∤ p, then r|I_x is unipotent. Moreover, if r̄ is unramified at x, then N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. (Dropping the redundant "if, furthermore" is only stylistic.)
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF p. 87 at 130 and 250 dpi. The text matches word for word, and no restriction to x ∤ p appears. The paper's Notation section has no convention that x denotes a prime away from p.

Read literally, (6) contradicts (1) and (2) when n ≥ 2. By (1) and (2), r|G_v is crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0, …, n−1 at each v | p, so r is ramified at v (an unramified representation has all HT weights 0). (6) would then force r|I_v to be unipotent. That makes r^ss|I_v trivial, so r^ss|G_v is unramified and all its Hodge–Tate weights are 0. Sen weights are additive in extensions, so this contradicts weights 0, …, n−1. The theorem would therefore be vacuous for n ≥ 2.

The context shows that x ∤ p is intended:
(i) The remark right after the theorem (p. 384) says "If conditions 1, 2, and 3 are satisfied, then conditions 5 and 6 are satisfied after a solvable extension which is unramified at p". That is impossible at primes above p under the literal reading.
(ii) The setting of §8.5 (p. 406), from which Theorem 5.16 is deduced, says "For each v ∤ p, r̄|G_v has at worst unipotent ramification…".
(iii) The definition of semi-stable before Theorem 1.2 (p. 301) asks for unipotence only "for all finite v not dividing p".
(iv) In §10 the theorem is applied to crystalline r with distinct weights.

Rendered PDF p. 87 at 250 dpi. The text is exactly as printed above. [3] = CHT, whose Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness for a subgroup H ⊂ GL_n(k). The paper never defines "r̄ is big" (grep finds 'big' only at pp. 383, 410, 422, 425). The natural literal reading, r̄(G_F) big, is not the hypothesis the proof uses.

The theorem is said to "follow immediately from Theorem 9.19" (p. 384). §9.5 (p. 425) says "Theorem 5.16 follows from it immediately as a corollary". Theorem 9.19 is proved under the standing assumption "We assume also that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big" (p. 425). It uses Proposition 8.5 (p. 410), "Assume that r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big", which follows CHT Prop. 2.5.9 and needs bigness over F(ζ_p).

Bigness of r̄(G_F) does not formally pass to the normal subgroup r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) of prime-to-p cyclic index, and the paper gives no argument that it does. The CHT conditions are not inherited in general: no p-power quotient; H^1(H, ad^0) = 0 (restriction only controls the H/H'-invariants); and condition (c) on irreducible submodules. Hypothesis (3) only says F(ad^0 r̄) ⊉ F(ζ_p); it does not make the intersection F(ad^0 r̄) ∩ F(ζ_p) trivial, so it does not close the gap.

The intended hypothesis is clear from §9.5 and Prop. 8.5, so this is a misprint or loose statement rather than a false theorem. The printed hypothesis must still be read with bigness over F(ζ_p). I give an abstract argument, not an explicit counterexample satisfying (1)–(8). Partly overlaps with X-K10-10.

issues.reason: I rendered PDF p. 87 (published p. 383) at 130 and 250 dpi. The printed text matches the candidate word for word: condition (8)(a) introduces π_0 but then writes r_p(π) and r̄_p(π) (plain π, no subscript). Nothing named π is defined in the statement before this point. On p. 384 (PDF p. 88) the conclusion reads "Then r is modular, that is, there exists a regular algebraic cusp form π for GL_n(A_F) with trivial infinitesimal character such that L(r,s) = L(π,s)." So π is the form whose existence is being proved. Hypothesis (8)(a) must refer to the given lift π_0: it is the only automorphic representation in the hypothesis, and the discussion after the theorem ("if r̄ admits an automorphic lift with trivial infinitesimal character and good reduction at p, then condition 8a is also satisfied after a solvable extension...") confirms that 8a is about a residually modular characteristic-zero lift π_0. Read literally, the printed hypothesis puts a condition on the unknown π from the conclusion, which is circular. So this is a genuine notational slip, not a convention. It is also in the arXiv version 1207.4224v2 (cg-v2.txt lines 3349-3352: "rp(π) ... rp(π) = r"). It has nothing to do with the 47 known bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction only deals with brackets. Knock-on effects: the proof of Theorem 9.19 in §9.5 (Theorem 5.16 is a corollary of it) never mentions π_0 or r_p(π). It only assumes a maximal ideal m of T_{∅,1} with r̄_m ≅ r̄. §10 applies Theorem 5.16 by saying its hypotheses hold "with the possible exception of residual modularity", which does not depend on this notation. The intended meaning is clear and the theorem's content is unchanged, so 'affects: nothing' is right. The slip sits inside the statement of Theorem 5.16, but it changes no mathematics.

issues.locator: §6 (opening of Part 2, before §6.1 Patching), Lemma 6.1 and its proof, published p. 385 (PDF p. 89). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) has word-for-word the same statement and proof (Lemma 6.1, citing [Mat86] Thm 17.2). The lemma is not in arXiv v1. Its only use is in the proof of Lemma 6.2 on the same page ("the central inequality is Lemma 6.1").
issues.printed: Lemma 6.1 Let S be a Noetherian local ring. If N is an S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n. Proof Let 𝔭 be an associated prime of M (and hence of N). Then 𝔭 is the annihilator of some 0 ≠ m ∈ M, and it suffices to prove the result for M replaced by mS ⊂ M. On the other hand, for a Noetherian local ring, one has the inequality (see [69], Theorem 17.2) n = depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass(N)} dim S/𝔭 ≤ dim(M).
issues.correction: Assume N is finitely generated: "If N is a finitely generated (finite) S-module with depth n, and 0 ≠ M ⊆ N, then dim(M) ≥ n." Nothing else needs to change. This is the minimal fix, and it is exactly the hypothesis of the cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/p for p ∈ Ass M, where M is a finite module over a Noetherian local ring). With it the proof is complete as printed.
issues.reason:
I rendered PDF page 89 and the printed text is as quoted. The Notation section adds no convention that modules are finitely generated, and elsewhere the paper states that hypothesis explicitly (for example Lemma 5.9, "Let μ be a finitely generated O[Δ]-module"). The cited result, Matsumura Thm 17.2 (depth M ≤ dim A/𝔭 for 𝔭 ∈ Ass M), is stated for finite modules, and its proof needs Nakayama on Hom(A/𝔭, M).

Without finite generation the lemma is false under every standard definition of depth (Ext, Koszul, or regular sequence). My counterexample: S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 and x acts invertibly on k((x)).
(1) (x, y) is an N-regular sequence. x is injective on both summands. N/xN = k⟦y⟧ ⊕ 0, and y is regular on it. N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
(2) Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly. So Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is nonzero first at i = 2. Hence depth N = 2 under either definition.
(3) Take M = S·(0,1) ≅ S/(y) ≅ k⟦x⟧, a nonzero cyclic submodule of N. Then dim M = 1 < 2 = depth N, which contradicts the lemma.

The reader's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x))) gives depth ∞ only under the Ext definition. Under the regular-sequence definition its depth is 0, so the example above is the sturdier one. Note that here M is even finitely generated, so the finiteness is needed on N specifically.

I class this as an error (the statement as printed is false) rather than a gap. The intended fix is clear from the citation, and one could argue the hypothesis is implicit, since Matsumura defines depth only for finite modules. That is why I rate confidence medium, not high. No stated result is affected: the lemma is used only in Lemma 6.2, with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}), a cokernel in a perfect complex and hence finitely generated. This is not one of the 47 bracket defects. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. (a) The paper sets no convention that modules are finitely generated. The Notation (p. 306) only defines a perfect complex as a bounded complex of finitely generated projective modules. Elsewhere, whenever finiteness matters the paper says "finitely generated" explicitly, e.g. Thm 6.3's P∞ "of finitely generated S∞-modules". (b) The paper never defines depth. The strongest defence is that the textbook definitions (Matsumura §16; Bruns–Herzog 1.2) define depth only for finite modules. On that reading "an S-module with depth n" tacitly means a finite one, and the lemma holds. So the intended meaning is clear. But the printed hypothesis says only "an S-module", and depth is routinely used for arbitrary modules (via Ext, local cohomology or regular sequences). Under those definitions the literal statement is false.

ROBUST COUNTEREXAMPLE, which works under every standard definition of depth, including the regular-sequence definition with no ∞ convention. Take S = k⟦x,y⟧ and N = S ⊕ k((x)), where y acts as 0 on k((x)). Take M = 0 ⊕ k⟦x⟧, which is finitely generated, or M = 0 ⊕ k((x)).
- dim M = dim S/(y) = 1.
- depth N = 2. x, y is an N-regular sequence: x is injective on S and invertible on k((x)); N/xN = k⟦y⟧, on which y is regular; and N/(x,y)N = k ≠ 0.
- Ext check: Ext^i_S(k, k((x))) = 0 for all i, because x acts on it both as 0 (through k) and invertibly (through k((x))). Hence Ext^i_S(k, N) = Ext^i_S(k, S), which is first nonzero at i = 2.
So depth N = 2 > 1 = dim M. The reporter's own example (S = k⟦x⟧, N = M = k((x)), depth ∞ via Ext) also works, but it depends on the convention for depth; the example above does not. The proof's step "depth(N) ≤ min_{Ass N} dim S/p" is exactly where it fails, because Matsumura 17.2 needs N finite.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 6.1 is cited only once, in the proof of Lemma 6.2 (p. 385: "where the central inequality is Lemma 6.1"). There it is applied with N = K^m = P^m/Im(δ^{m−1}) and M = H^m(P) ≠ 0. K^m is a quotient of the finitely generated projective module P^m, since P is perfect, so it is finitely generated. Lemma 6.2 is then used in the proof of Thm 6.3 (p. 389) with the perfect complex P∞. All uses therefore satisfy the added hypothesis, and no stated result beyond the literal Lemma 6.1 is affected.

CLASSIFICATION. It is "error" rather than "gap": with N finite the proof is complete, and without it the statement is false. It could also be seen as a misprint-level omitted word, since the intended meaning is clear. Either way it affects nothing.
