issues.locator: §9.4 "An approach to Conjecture B part 5", first paragraph, published p. 419 (PDF p. 123). arXiv v2 has the same text in §9.2 (v2 PDF p. 90). arXiv v1 does not contain this section.
issues.printed: In this section, we present an informal approach to proving part 5 of Conjecture B under a stronger assumption that r̄ has enormous image, at least in the analogous case of GL(n) (from which it should be easy to deduce the corresponding claim for PGL, since manifolds for the former are circle bundles over manifolds for the latter, and so have highly related Hecke actions).
issues.correction: Replace "circle bundles" with "torus bundles". Each fibre of a GL(n) space over the corresponding PGL(n) space is a quotient of the GL(1) arithmetic manifold of §8.2, so up to finitely many components it is (S^1)^{r1+r2−1}, or (S^1)^{r1+r2−1} × R if the identity component A_∞^0 of the split central torus is not divided out. With A_∞^0 divided out, the fibres are circles only when r1+r2 = 2. For F = Q or F imaginary quadratic the fibres are finite: the two spaces agree up to components, as §5.5 already says. Without the A_∞^0 quotient the fibres are never circles. The point the authors need still holds: the fibres come from the centre, so the Hecke actions are closely related.
issues.reason:
Rendered p. 419; the printed text matches the quote. §9 treats an arbitrary number field F (G = Res_{F/Q}PGL(n), G_∞ = PGL_n(R)^{r1} × PGL_n(C)^{r2}). The GL(n) spaces are never defined in the paper, so the natural reading takes the paper's own GL(1) conventions from §8.2, p. 403: Y = F^×\A_F^×/UK_∞, with K_∞ the identity component of the maximal compact of (F⊗R)^×, and X_Q the further quotient by A_∞^0.

Compute the fibre of Y_GL → Y_PGL. It is F^×\A_F^× modulo (the level ∩ centre) and (K_∞^0 ∩ centre). At a real place, SO(n) ∩ scalars ⊂ {±1}. At a complex place, U(n) ∩ scalars = S^1. So the archimedean part is (R_{>0})^{r1+r2} up to finite index. Dividing by the diagonal R_{>0} gives R^{r1+r2-1}. Dirichlet's unit theorem (units of rank r1+r2-1) then turns this into a compact torus T^{r1+r2-1}, times a finite set. Without the R_{>0} quotient there is an extra R factor.

The paper's own §8.2 (p. 403) gets exactly this for GL(1): "the cokernel of the map O_F^× → R^{×r1} × C^{×r2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r1+r2-1} × R … the components of X_Q consist simply of a product of circles".

Test cases:
- F = Q or F imaginary quadratic (r1+r2 = 1): the fibres are finite, so the GL spaces are finite covers (times R), not circle bundles.
- F totally real cubic: the fibres are 2-tori.
- The statement is literally true only when r1+r2 = 2.

A non-standard choice such as K_∞ = SU(n) at complex places changes the count, but it still does not give circles in general.

The intended point is correct: the GL spaces fibre over the PGL spaces with fibres that are compact abelian orbits of the centre, so their Hecke actions are closely related. The authors plainly know the right fibre (p. 403), so this is loose wording in an explicitly informal heuristic remark. One could also file it as a misprint whose intended meaning ("products of circles") is clear from §8.2. Nothing in the proofs or results depends on it. Printed text checked on the rendered page (PDF p. 123). The paper never defines GL(n) spaces in §9: Y(K) there is only for G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n). With any standard choice, GL_n(F)\GL_n(A_F)/K K_∞^0 (optionally also divided by A_∞^0) maps onto the PGL(n) space. The fibres are orbits of the centre Z(A) = A_F^×, i.e. quotients of F^×\A_F^×/U K_∞ (A_∞^0). The paper computes these itself in §8.2, p. 403. The fibres of Y_Q are "the connected components of the cokernel of O_F^× → R^{×r1} × C^{×r2}/K_∞, which is (S^1)^{r1+r2−1} × R. Passing to X_Q excises the factor of R." This follows from Dirichlet's unit theorem: Z(R)/(Z(R) ∩ K_∞^0 · R_{>0}) ≅ R^{r1+r2−1}, and the unit lattice has full rank there.

So the fibre dimension is r1+r2−1 (or r1+r2 without the R_{>0} quotient). It is 1 only for r1+r2 = 2, e.g. a real quadratic field or a cubic field with one complex place. The paper contradicts itself here. §5.5, p. 380, says: "When F = Q or an imaginary quadratic field, the associated locally symmetric spaces are very similar (the same up to components)". That is fibre dimension 0, not circle bundles, and imaginary quadratic F is the paper's main case.

Defence tried: §8.2 speaks of "a product of circles". Read loosely as "torus bundle", including the zero-dimensional case, the remark would be right for every F under the A_∞^0 convention. But "circle bundle" means S^1 fibres, and as printed the claim is false outside r1+r2 = 2. The intended meaning (torus fibres coming from the centre) can be recovered from §§5.5 and 8.2, so one could argue for "misprint". I kept "error" because a precise geometric claim is false as stated.

Consequences: the remark is a parenthetical in a section the authors call "informal". It only motivates working with GL(n) instead of PGL(n). Nothing later cites it. §9.4.2 is an informal sketch, and Theorem 9.19 and the other results assume Conjecture B outright. The Correction (Invent. Math. 227, 2022) only fixes brackets and does not mention this.

issues.reason: This is a genuine notation clash, confirmed on the page images (PDF pp. 123–128 = pp. 419–424). The Notation section fixes k = 𝒪/ϖ, and elsewhere the paper writes k_v for the residue field of F_v (§7; §9.1, "(k_v^×)^n"). Section 9.4.1 itself writes GL_n(𝒪_x/ϖ_x) for the local residue ring. Even so, from Cor. 9.13 on, §9.4 uses the bare letter k for 𝒪_x/ϖ_x, whose characteristic is ℓ ≠ p, while still using k for 𝒪/ϖ, whose characteristic is p. The two meanings sit in one phrase: "universal deformation over k of D(k) to k[k^×/k^{×q}]" and "k[G(k)]". Read with the paper's own convention k = 𝒪/ϖ, the statements are wrong. First, |k^×| = |k| − 1 is prime to p, so k^× ⊗ Z_p = 0 and q = 1. Cor. 9.13 and the display before it would then lose the tame p-part. I recomputed the local group: F_x^× ≅ Z × k_x^× × (1+ϖ_x𝒪_x), and the last factor is pro-ℓ, so the pro-p completion is Z_p ⊕ (k_x^× ⊗ Z_p). This group is cyclic of order the p-part of N(x) − 1, which is at least p. Second, GL_n(𝒪_x)/U(x) ≅ GL_n(𝒪_x/ϖ_x), not GL_n(𝒪/ϖ); the two residue fields have different characteristics. The intended meaning can be recovered, so this is a misprint and not a mathematical error. 'affects' = nothing is right. §9.4 is explicitly an "informal approach" to Conjecture B part 5. Definition 9.11 through Remark 9.18 are cited only inside §9.4 (9.4.2 uses Thm 9.16), and the main results assume Conjecture B rather than depending on §9.4. The candidate's correction is right in principle, but it lists only some of the affected places. Its suggested exponent m is itself already in use.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.12, p. 421 (arXiv v2, p. 91)
issues.printed: (§9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.12, p. 421 = PDF p. 125; identical wording in arXiv v2 p. 91) "There is a natural map M → n-ind^G_B res^B_G(M) = ⊕_W n-ind^G_B M^w_B → n-ind^G_B M_B. Note that M and n-ind^G_B M_B are elements of 𝒞 of the same length, and all the irreducible constituents of n-ind^G_B M^w_B for w ≠ id are distinct from π. Thus, by comparing lengths, to prove that the composite of these maps is an isomorphism it suffices to prove that the first map is injective. If K denotes the kernel, then res^B_G(K) = 0. Yet this contradicts the assumption that M (and hence K) lies in 𝒞, since res^B_G(π) ≠ 0. □"
issues.correction: Delete the clause "and all the irreducible constituents of n-ind^G_B M^w_B for w ≠ id are distinct from π". It is false: for every w, each constituent of n-ind^G_B M^w_B is n-ind^G_B(χ^w) ≅ π. Then run the kernel argument on the composite g: M → n-ind^G_B M_B, not on the first map. By Frobenius reciprocity (res^B_G left adjoint to n-ind^G_B), g is adjoint to the projection res^B_G(M) → M^{id}_B = M_B. Let K' = ker g. By naturality, res(K') → res(M) → M_B is zero. res is exact and the decomposition into χ^w-parts is functorial, so res(K')^{id} ↪ M^{id}_B. Hence res(K')^{id} = 0. But K' ∈ 𝒞 has finite length. If K' ≠ 0 it contains a copy of π, and res(π)^{id} = χ ≠ 0, a contradiction. So K' = 0. Equivalently, g is nonzero on every irreducible subrepresentation π' ⊂ M, so ker g contains no irreducible and is 0. Since g is an injection between modules of the same length, it is an isomorphism. The minimal textual fix is to replace "the first map" by "the composite", "res^B_G(K) = 0" by "res^B_G(K)^{id} = 0" and "res^B_G(π) ≠ 0" by "res^B_G(π)^{id} ≠ 0", and to drop the false clause. Both candidates' repairs (C-K10-0 and H-part2-22) are correct. The statement of Lemma 9.12 is unchanged.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 220 dpi and the quoted text is exact; v2 has the same wording. The premise fails because each χ^w is χ with its entries permuted, and n-ind^G_B(χ^w) ≅ n-ind^G_B(χ) = π for every w ∈ W. I checked this in two ways. (a) By the paper's own Lemma 9.9: π is fixed by ρ̄ and equals n-ind(χ) for χ sending the uniformizers to the distinct eigenvalues, with no ordering specified. So every ordering χ^w gives the same π. (b) Directly: the Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w) has constituents {χ^v : v ∈ W}, each exactly once. The χ^v are distinct on the uniformizers because the α_i are distinct, so the Jacquet module splits into generalized eigenspaces for D. Hence χ is a D-quotient, and Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero, hence surjective, map n-ind(χ^w) → π, with π irreducible by Lemma 9.9. Both Jacquet modules have dimension n!, so the kernel has zero Jacquet module. A nonzero subrepresentation of an induced representation cannot have zero Jacquet module, so the kernel is 0. By exactness of n-ind, every constituent of n-ind M^w_B is ≅ π. The inference the paper wants is: M has only π-constituents, so its projections to the w ≠ id summands vanish, so injectivity into ⊕ gives injectivity into the id factor. That inference needs the false premise, so the step is invalid as written. The repair above is just the paper's own kernel argument applied to the id-eigenspace, and I checked it step by step. One small point in the candidate's reasoning: what makes Frobenius reciprocity work is that χ (not χ^w) occurs as a direct-summand quotient of the Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w). The conclusion is still correct. The lemma's statement is unaffected. Its later uses are Cor. 9.13 (the equivalence with R-modules) and the proof of Thm. 9.16 ("we may assume that M = n-ind^G_B M_B"), and both rely only on the true statement. §9.4 is also explicitly presented as an informal approach. This is not a bracket-typesetting issue. Defence attempted and it fails. Here χ^w is χ with its components permuted, so it sends the uniformizers to the same distinct eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_x).

(1) The paper's own Lemma 9.9 says rec(π) = ρ̄ iff π is "the irreducible unramified principal series n-ind(χ)" with χ sending each uniformizer to a distinct eigenvalue. No ordering is specified, so n-ind(χ^w) is that same π. Lemma 9.10 and Definition 9.11 also treat 𝒞 as a block with the single irreducible π.

(2) Directly: the normalized Jacquet module of n-ind(χ^w) has constituents χ^v (v ∈ W), each once. These are pairwise distinct on the uniformizers, so Ext^i vanishes between them (the paper says this itself) and the Jacquet module is a direct sum. So χ is a quotient, and Frobenius reciprocity gives a nonzero map n-ind(χ^w) → n-ind(χ). Both sides are irreducible (Lemma 9.9; with q ≡ 1 mod p the reducibility condition χ_i/χ_j = ν^{±1} reduces to χ_i = χ_j, which does not occur). So the map is an isomorphism. By exactness of n-ind, every constituent of n-ind M^w_B is ≅ π, for every w.

The inference the paper needs is this: M has only π-constituents, so its projections to the w ≠ id summands are zero, so injectivity into ⊕_W gives injectivity into the id-summand. That inference rests entirely on the false clause. Injectivity of M → ⊕_W n-ind M^w_B does not rule out a kernel of the id-projection. I found no charitable reading: "distinct from π" can only mean non-isomorphic, and no nearby statement supplies the missing step.

The paper's own tools repair the step: the same adjunction and kernel argument, restricted to the id-eigenspace. Length equality holds as the paper says: length_A(M_B) = length_G(M), and n-ind(χ) = π is irreducible. So the lemma is true.

Downstream uses: Lemma 9.12 is not cited by number. It is used implicitly in Cor. 9.13 (n-ind gives an equivalence with R-modules), in Lemma 9.14 ("Using this description of 𝒞"), and in the proof of Thm. 9.16 ("we may assume that M = n-ind^G_B M_B"). All of these need only the true statement, so no stated result is affected. §9.4 is also explicitly labelled an "informal approach". This is not one of the 47 bracket defects.

Side note: Def. 9.11's "associated to π" should read "associated to ρ̄". That is a separate slip and does not bear on this item.

issues.printed: p. 421 (PDF p. 125), checked on the page image. Display: "(lim_← F^×/F^{×p^m})^n ≃ (Z_p ⊕ lim_← k^×/k^{×p^m})." It is followed by "The universal deformation of this group can be given quite explicitly:" and then "Corollary 9.13 Let q = |k^× ⊗ Z_p|. Then n-ind_B^G induces an equivalence of categories between the category of direct limits of finite length modules over the ring R below and and 𝒞: R := ⨂_{i=1}^n A[T]/(T^q − 1) ⊗_𝒪 A[X]." The published A[X] is one of the known bracket errors; arXiv v2 p. 91 prints A[[X]] and is otherwise the same, including the missing exponent on the right and the doubled 'and'. The sentence before the display also has a stray capital: "Since χ is trivial on D(O_x), Any finite deformation ...".
issues.correction: In the display, the right-hand side should be (Z_p ⊕ lim_← k^×/k^{×p^m})^n, which is ≅ (Z_p × k^×⊗Z_p)^n ≅ (Z_p × Z/q)^n. In Cor. 9.13, 'below and and 𝒞' should read 'below and 𝒞'. For R, the only needed change is the known bracket fix A[X] → A⟦X⟧. Writing R = ⨂_{i=1}^n (A[T_i]/(T_i^q − 1) ⊗ A⟦X_i⟧), completed, i.e. A⟦(Z_p × Z/q)^n⟧, only makes the intended reading explicit. It does not fix an error. The printed R is correct if the big ⊗ is read as covering both factors, with each variable implicitly indexed by i. Using ⊗_A instead of ⊗_𝒪 changes nothing, because A = 𝒪/ϖ^k is a quotient of 𝒪. A[T]/(T^q − 1) is correctly a polynomial quotient, since it is the group ring A[Z/q].
issues.reason: I checked this against the setup at the start of §9.4.1 (p. 420). There, x is a prime with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so x ∤ p, and D ≅ (F_x^×)^n. For one factor, F_x^× ≅ Z × k_x^× × (1+m_x), and 1+m_x is pro-ℓ with ℓ ≠ p. So lim_m F_x^×/F_x^{×p^m} ≅ Z_p × (k_x^× ⊗ Z_p) ≅ Z_p × Z/q. The left side of the display explicitly carries the exponent n, so it is (Z_p × Z/q)^n, of Z_p-rank n. The right side as printed has rank 1, so the isomorphism is false as written. The large parentheses around the right side, with nothing after them, also point to a dropped exponent n. The doubled 'and' in the statement of Cor. 9.13 is a plain typo. Both slips appear identically in arXiv v2 p. 91. The part of the claim about R is weaker than stated. The candidate says the printed R has only one X, but the natural reading of ⨂_{i=1}^n A[T]/(T^q−1) ⊗_𝒪 A⟦X⟧ is the n-fold tensor product of the whole factor. That reading gives the completed group ring of (Z_p × Z/q)^n, which is correct. At most this is ambiguous notation, and it is not counted here as an error. The proof of Lemma 9.14 drops the n in the same way ('A[T]/(T^q−1)-modules', 'k[k^×/k^{×q}]'), consistent with loose notation rather than a mathematical mistake. None of the three slips is one of the 47 known bracket errors.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, proof of Lemma 9.14, p. 422 (PDF p. 126). arXiv v2 p. 92 has the same text.
issues.printed: p. 422 (PDF p. 126), proof of Lemma 9.14: "Since finitely generated injective A[T]/(T^q − 1)-modules are free, it follows that the image of an injective module has a filtration whose pieces are isomorphic to Φ := Ind_{B(k)}^{G(k)}(ψ), where ψ is the universal deformation over k of D(k) to k[k^×/k^{×q}]. Yet Φ is a direct summand of Ind_{B(k)}^{G(k)} k[D(k)] and thus of k[G(k)]; hence it is injective and acyclic."
issues.correction: ψ is the universal deformation, over k, of the trivial character of D(k_x) = (k_x^×)^n. It takes values in k[(k_x^×/k_x^{×q})^n] = k[D(k_x)/D(k_x)^q], which is the direct factor of k[D(k_x)] belonging to the p-part of D(k_x). Here k_x = O_x/ϖ_x and q = |k_x^× ⊗ Z_p|.
issues.reason: D(k) = (k^×)^n (printed in the same proof: "(k^×)^n = D(k) ⊂ B(k)"). The universal deformation ring of its trivial character over k is the group algebra of its maximal p-quotient, k[(k^×/k^{×q})^n], which is n-fold and matches R = ⊗_{i=1}^n A[T]/(T^q−1) ⊗ … of Cor. 9.13. The single factor matters for the proof. For a quotient D → D/H, the module k[D/H] = Ind_H^D k is projective (equivalently injective) over k[D] only when p ∤ |H|. With one factor k[k^×/k^{×q}] and n ≥ 2, H has order divisible by q^{n−1}. So Φ would not be a direct summand of Ind k[D(k)], and the conclusion 'hence it is injective' would fail. With the n-fold group algebra the argument works. The meaning is clear from Cor. 9.13 and from the parallel dropped exponent on p. 421 (H-part2-23 / X-K10-1). The H-part2-23 verdict called the dropped n in this proof 'loose notation'. I count it as a misprint because, read literally, it would break the injectivity step. The overload of k (residue field at x versus k = O/ϖ) is recorded separately in H-part2-24.

issues.locator: §9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422 (published version)
issues.printed: Remark 9.15 Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes. Hence, for any subgroup U(x) ⊂ Γ ⊂ G(O_x), by Hochschild–Serre there are identifications H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}).  [published p. 422 = PDF p. 126, §9.4.1; arXiv v2 p. 92 has the identical wording "Since the group U(x) is pro-p, the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes."]
issues.correction: Replace "pro-p" with "pro-ℓ, where ℓ ≠ p is the residue characteristic of x (so U(x) is pro-prime-to-p)". The phrase "the higher cohomology of U(x) vanishes" should say "with coefficients in any M ∈ 𝒞" (these are smooth, p-power-torsion A = O/ϖ^k-modules). Nothing else in the remark needs to change. Both candidates propose this correction. It is correct and minimal.
issues.reason:
Checked on the rendered page images (published PDF p. 126 = p. 422, and v2 p. 92): "pro-p" is printed as quoted, with no lost prime such as p′. Setup (§9.4.1, p. 421): x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and U(x) ⊂ G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x. Let ℓ be the residue characteristic of x, so N(x) = ℓ^f. If ℓ = p, then N(x) ≡ 0 mod p, which contradicts N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so ℓ ≠ p. U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x) has successive quotients (1+ϖ^i M_n)/(1+ϖ^{i+1} M_n) ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups. So U(x) is pro-ℓ and not pro-p. The coefficient modules M lie in C, which consists of smooth modules over A = O/ϖ^k, so they are p-power torsion and ℓ acts invertibly. For a pro-ℓ group, H^i(U(x), M) = lim H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) is then 0 for i ≥ 1, which is the vanishing the remark needs. The stated reason would give the opposite: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0, and U(x) is infinite. So the sentence as printed is false, but the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is clear from context and from the correct conclusion. That makes it a slip rather than a failed argument, so I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18; "error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is a false statement. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, which the 2022 Correction lists and which concern only ⟦ ⟧. Only the stated reason is wrong. The conclusion (U(x)-cohomology vanishes, so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ,M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)})) is correct. So the later use of the remark still holds: identifying R^kF ≃ H^k(G(O_x),M) and R^kG ≃ e_α H^k(U_0(x),M) on p. 422, and hence Theorem 9.16 and §9.4.2. Two small comments on the candidate: its locator (§9.4.1, Remark 9.15, p. 422; same in v2) is correct. Its correction is right, though the letter ℓ is also used for the invariant l_0 elsewhere in the paper, so "pro-prime-to-p" may be clearer. Defence attempted and failed. In §9.4.1 (p. 421), p is the paper's fixed global prime: x is a prime of F with N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, π is a mod-p representation, and 𝒞 is the category of locally admissible G-modules over A := O/ϖ^k. There is no local convention under which p could mean the residue characteristic of x. U(x) is the full congruence subgroup of level x in G(O_x) = GL_n(O_x), so U(x) = 1 + ϖ_x M_n(O_x). Its successive quotients are ≅ M_n(O_x/x), which are elementary abelian ℓ-groups, where ℓ is the residue characteristic of x. Since N(x) = ℓ^f ≡ 1 mod p, we get ℓ ≠ p. So U(x) is infinite and pro-ℓ, and not pro-p. The stated reason would in fact give the opposite conclusion: a nontrivial pro-p group U has H^1(U, F_p) = Hom(U, F_p) ≠ 0.

The conclusion is nonetheless true for the right reason. Take M ∈ 𝒞, which is smooth and p-power torsion. Then H^i(U(x), M) = colim_V H^i(U(x)/V, M^V) over open normal V. Each U(x)/V is a finite ℓ-group, and |U(x)/V| acts invertibly on M, so this is 0 for i ≥ 1. U(x) is normal in G(O_x), hence in every Γ between U(x) and G(O_x), so Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Γ, M) ≃ H^i(Γ/U(x), M^{U(x)}) as printed.

The slip may have come from the paragraph on p. 421, where "pro-p image" is correctly said of the deformation χ̃ restricted to D(O_x). Only the justifying adjective is wrong, and the intended meaning (pro-prime-to-p) is forced by the correct conclusion. So I class it as a misprint under PROTOCOL §18. "Error" is also defensible, since "U(x) is pro-p" is literally false; the candidates chose that label.

issues.correction: State in Theorem 5.16 the hypotheses under which Theorem 9.19 is proved. (6) should read "If r is ramified at a prime x, then r|I_x is unipotent and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p", i.e. delete the proviso "if, furthermore, r̄ is unramified at x". (4) should read "r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big (in the sense of [3, Definition 2.5.1])". This is exactly what §8.5 (p. 406 bullet; R ⊇ ramification primes of r̄ with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p), Proposition 8.5 and §9.5 assume. issues.reason:
Checked from the page images. Theorem 9.19 is proved inside the §8.5/§9.5 setup. That setup explicitly assumes N(v) ≡ 1 mod p at every v ∤ p where r̄ ramifies. It also needs a set R that contains all primes where r̄ ramifies and has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p for each v ∈ R.

This congruence is actually used. Lemma 8.2, whose conclusion "Spec R^χ_loc is irreducible" is needed for Theorem 6.4, rests on [76, Lemma 3.3] and Taylor's [11, Prop. 3.1]. Those are Ihara-avoidance local computations in the setting q_v ≡ 1 mod p. The characters χ_{v,i} of p-power order that the rings R_v^χ need must also be nontrivial.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. Where r̄ is ramified, it asks nothing. Such cases exist. Take n=2 and E an elliptic curve with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ_E) and N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. By Tate-curve theory, r̄ = E[p] is ramified at x and r|I_x is unipotent, so (6) holds, but no R as in §8.5 can exist. So Theorem 9.19 does not apply, and the claim that Theorem 5.16 is "immediate" fails in this case.

This is not just a formality for n ≥ 3. Take n = 3, q = N(x) ≢ 1 mod p, and r̄|I_x unipotent of Jordan type (2,1), with Frobenius eigenvalues a, aq on the block and b ≡ aq² on the rest. Then there are unipotent lifts of type (2,1) and of type (3), so R_x^1[1/p] can have more than one component. Without the nontrivial χ_{x,i}, Ihara avoidance is not available, and nothing in the paper handles this. Hypothesis 8b does not exclude it, since r may still be non-minimally ramified at primes where r̄ ramifies.

Secondary point: (4) says only "r̄ is big" (CHT Def. 2.5.1 applies to subgroups), while Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 assume r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) is big. Bigness does not obviously pass to the normal subgroup of prime-to-p index: H^1(H, ad^0) = H^1(H', ad^0)^{H/H'} does not force H^1(H', ad^0) = 0. This part could be read as loose wording, and I did not build an explicit counterexample.

Theorem 1.1 is likely unaffected. In §10, Theorem 5.16 is applied over fields L chosen by Moret–Bailly, and there these extra conditions can be arranged. What is affected is Theorem 5.16 in the generality stated. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(a) Congruence condition. The whole proof of Theorem 9.19 lives in the §8.5 setting. There R must contain every prime where r̄ ramifies and have N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. The Hecke side (§9.1) uses Iwahori level at v ∈ R with characters ψ_v of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) = (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× → 1+m_O, and these are trivial unless p | N(v)−1. Lemma 8.2, which gives irreducibility of Spec R^χ_loc for Taylor's trick, is proved via [11, Prop. 3.1], which assumes q_v ≡ 1 mod p.

Theorem 5.16(6) imposes the congruence only where r is ramified and r̄ is not. So it admits r̄ that is unipotently ramified at x with N(x) ≢ 1 mod p. Example: n = 2, E semistable with multiplicative reduction at x, p ∤ ord_x(Δ). Case (8b) makes this especially clear: r is then ramified only where r̄ is, so (6) imposes no congruence at all. Such x cannot lie in R, so Theorem 9.19 does not apply.

Putting x in R with trivial χ_x does not repair the argument when n ≥ 3. Example: n = 3, q̄ = N(x) mod p with q̄, q̄² ≠ 1, r̄|G_x with Frobenius eigenvalues ᾱ, q̄ᾱ, q̄²ᾱ and rank-1 monodromy. Unipotent lifts then lie on two distinct components of R^1_x[1/p], one with regular N and one with rank-1 N. Without Ihara avoidance, r and r_p(π_0) may lie on different components.

The condition in (6) mirrors the n = 2 condition of Part I, which is harmless there because the unipotent ring at a ramified r̄ is just the Steinberg component. For general n it is not.

(b) Bigness. CHT Definition 2.5.1 defines bigness of a subgroup of GL_n(k), so "r̄ is big" literally means r̄(G_F) is big. Prop. 8.5 and §9.5 need r̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) to be big, and (3) does not bridge the gap. Computation (script h1.py in my scratch dir): take p = 7, n = 3, r̄ = Sym² ρ̄ with ρ̄(G_F) = GL_2(F_7), det ρ̄ = ε̄, and F linearly disjoint from Q(ζ_7).
- H^1(GL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) = 0, so r̄(G_F) is big (the other conditions are easily checked).
- H^1(SL_2(F_7), ad^0 Sym²) has dimension 1, so r̄(G_{F(ζ_7)}) is not big.
- (3) still holds.
- r = Sym² of an elliptic curve's 7-adic representation satisfies (1), (2), (5) and (7).
Taken alone, (4) could be read charitably as a slip for the standard hypothesis. Together with (a), though, the claimed "immediate" deduction does not cover the stated generality.

Consequences: only Theorem 5.16 as stated is affected. Its only later use is the sketch in §10 (proof of Theorem 1.1, potential modularity and Sato–Tate). There the stronger hypotheses can be arranged: take p large and L linearly disjoint, so the image of G_{L(ζ_p)} contains Sym^{2n−1} SL_2(F_p), which is big. Then a further solvable base change, unramified at p, makes N(x) ≡ 1 mod p at the finitely many ramified primes, and the paper notes this preserves 8a. So Theorem 1.1 is unaffected, but Theorem 5.16 is proved only under the corrected hypotheses.

Checked on the page images at PDF pp. 116, 129, 130 and 131, and at arXiv v2 p. 95.

1. The paper's definition (§9.1, p. 412) is H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q), O) := H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Here a section of O(ψ) is an f on π^{-1}(U) with f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So "H_{∗,χ}" means homology with coefficients in O(χ) itself, not in its dual.

2. Recomputation. Let A = O/ϖ^n, which is self-injective. Let C = C_*(Ỹ), a finite free Z[Γ]-complex (via Borel–Serre), and M the monodromy module. Then Hom_A(Hom_{Z[Γ]}(C, M), A) ≅ C ⊗_{Z[Γ]} Hom_A(M, A), and Hom_A(−, A) is exact. So H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨) canonically. The transpose of T(g) is T(g^{−1}), which gives 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Sections g with g(γu) = χ(γ)^{−1}g(u) pair with O(χ) into O, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{−1}). This gives H^*_χ(..)^∨_𝔪 ≅ H_{∗,χ^{−1}}(..)_{𝔪^∗}. Equivalently, the printed right-hand side H_{∗,χ}(..)_{𝔪^∗} is (H^*_{χ^{−1}}(..)_𝔪)^∨.

3. The cited Conjecture B part (4) only covers vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and vanishing of boundary cohomology. It cannot turn χ^{−1} into χ.

4. Is the printed isomorphism accidentally true? For n = 2, yes, though not for the reason given. Then χ_{v,2} = χ_{v,1}^{−1}, so χ^{−1} is the Weyl swap of χ. The Iwahori normaliser [[0,1],[ϖ_v,0]] identifies O(χ) with O(wχ) compatibly with Hecke operators away from R. For n ≥ 3 this fails in general. The normaliser only gives cyclic rotations, and a generic tuple of distinct p-power-order characters with trivial product has {χ_i^{−1}} ≠ {χ_i}. So the two sides involve different Bernstein components and inertial types at v: ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) versus ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{−1}).

5. Where it is used. The proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427, first bullet) says the cohomology of D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N computes H^*_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_𝔪, and makes this an R_{S_χ}-module. As printed, D̃^χ_N computes instead the dual of H^*_{χ^{−1}}, which is naturally an R_{S_{χ^{−1}}}-module. So one step of the proof is wrong as printed. The fix is a pure relabelling.

6. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is fine. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

On 'affects': I choose "the proof" rather than the candidate's "nothing", because a step of the proof of Theorem 9.19 literally depends on this false identification. No stated result changes: Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, the χ-side is auxiliary, and the argument survives the relabelling. I tried to defend the printed text, then checked the page images of PDF pp. 116, 117, 129, 130 and 131, and v2 p. 95.

(1) Definitions (p. 412). H_{i,ψ}(Y_i(Q),O) is defined as H_i(Y_i(Q), O(ψ)). Sections of O(ψ) satisfy f(γu) = ψ(γ)f(u). So the subscript χ on H_{∗,χ} means coefficients in O(χ) itself; no convention hides a dual. The pointwise product of an O(ψ)-section and an O(ψ')-section is constant on fibres exactly when ψψ' = 1, so O(χ)^∨ = O(χ^{-1}).

(2) Universal coefficients. A = O/ϖ^n is self-injective, and Hom_A(C_*(Ỹ) ⊗_Γ M, A) = Hom_Γ(C_*(Ỹ), Hom_A(M, A)). This gives H^i(Y, L)^∨ ≅ H_i(Y, L^∨), with T(g) dual to T(g^{-1}), which accounts for 𝔪 ↦ 𝔪^∗. Using Poincaré duality, as in Remark 9.5, still leaves the dual local system. Conjecture B(4) is about vanishing outside degrees [q0, q0+l0] and about the boundary. It cannot change χ^{-1} into χ.

(3) Strongest defence, which works only partly. H^*_χ ≅ H^*_{wχ} holds Hecke-equivariantly away from R for every Weyl permutation w, not just cyclic rotations. The reason is that the Iwahori intertwiners T_s satisfy T_s' T_s = ±q_v, which is a unit because v ∤ p; I checked this numerically for GL_2(F_5). So the printed identity is true whenever {χ_{v,i}^{-1}} = {χ_{v,i}} for every v ∈ R, and in particular always when n = 2, since χ_{v,1}χ_{v,2} = 1. This is not the reason the paper gives. In §8.5.1, however, χ_v is an arbitrary tuple of distinct characters with trivial product. For n ≥ 3 that generally fails the condition. For example, take n = 3, χ_v = (a, a^2, a^{-3}) with a of order p ≥ 5; then {a^{-1}, a^{-2}, a^3} ≠ {a, a^2, a^{-3}}.

(4) Why the printed identity fails in that case. The two sides are Hecke modules of different inertial types, ∏(X−χ_{v,i}) and ∏(X−χ_{v,i}^{-1}) (Conjecture B(3)), and strong multiplicity one separates their rational eigensystems. The printed right-hand side is really (H^*_{χ^{-1}})^∨_𝔪, which is naturally an R_{S^{χ^{-1}}}-module. There is also a semilinear isomorphism through an automorphism σ of O with σχ = χ^{-1}, but it is not O-linear, so it does not rescue the O-linear R^2_∞-structure that patching needs.

(5) Consequences. The only place the paper uses this passage is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (p. 427). There, D^2_N = D̃^χ_N/ϖ^N is said to compute H^*_χ(…)^∨_𝔪, and that identification is used to transport the R_{S^χ_{Q_N}}-action (and hence the R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc[[x]]-action). As printed, that step fails for general χ when n ≥ 3. After relabelling χ to χ^{-1} in the homology, everything goes through: the degree bounds, the minimal complex, and the mod-ϖ identification H^{l0} ≅ H^{l0}_χ, since χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. Theorem 9.19 concerns H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_𝔪 with trivial coefficients, so no stated result changes.

(6) This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The trivial-coefficient analogue on p. 425 is correct.

On classification, I keep 'error' rather than 'misprint'. The subscript χ appears consistently in two displays (the D̃^χ_N definition and the note), and it comes with a justification that does not address the coefficients. So the intended meaning cannot be read off from context; the reader has to redo the duality. I choose 'the proof' rather than the candidate's 'nothing', because a step of the proof as written fails, even though the fix is a relabelling.

issues.correction: Add a condition to the choice. For each N, choose the surjections R^1_∞ = R^1_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} and R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}} so that their reductions mod ϖ agree. They must agree under the fixed N-independent isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ (Lemma 8.2(2) with x_i ↦ x_i) and the isomorphism R^□_{S_{Q_N}}/ϖ ≅ R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}/ϖ (the global rings agree mod ϖ, and the representatives agree mod ϖ). Such a choice exists. Take any surjection on side 1 as in Prop. 8.5(4); it is an R^1_loc-algebra map. On side 2, use the natural map R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_{Q_N}}, which reduces mod ϖ to the side-1 map. Send each x_i to any lift of the image of x_i mod ϖ. The resulting map is surjective mod ϖ, so it is surjective by complete Nakayama, since it is surjective on reduced cotangent spaces. Strictly, only equality of the induced actions on H^{l_0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),O/ϖ)^□ is needed, and this choice is a sufficient way to get it. (Separately, the actions on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M),…) should come from R_{S_{Q_M}} and R^i_∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_M}}; the printed index is Q_N, which is an index misprint.)
issues.reason:
Proposition 6.6 (p. 390) needs, for each M ≥ N, an isomorphism H^{l0}(D^1_M⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l0}(D^2_M⊗S_N/ϖ) that becomes an isomorphism of R^1_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ-modules. The ring identification is the fixed one from the first bullet, and it must work at every level for the patching to go through.

In the proof of Theorem 9.19, the R^i_∞-actions come from the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□. The paper makes the framings agree mod ϖ but puts no condition on these surjections: it just says "we can and do choose". It then states without argument that the isomorphisms are compatible with the R^i_∞-actions.

That statement fails for some choices the text allows. Take g ≥ 1, which is the usual case since q can be taken large. Let f^1, f^2 be a compatible pair, and change f^2 to x_1 ↦ f^2(x_1) + z_1^2. Since z_1^2 lies in m^2, the new map still hits generators of the cotangent space, so it is still a surjection as Proposition 8.5 provides. Here j = n^2|T|−1 ≥ 1. On H^{l0}(...)^□ ⊗ k = H⊗k[[z_1,…,z_j]], a nonzero free k[[z]]-module, the element z_1^2 acts injectively. So x_1 acts differently on the two sides by the nonzero operator z_1^2, and the required equivariance fails.

The other ingredients do match mod ϖ. The maps R^1_loc → R^□_{S_Q} and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ_Q} both come from restricting the same mod-ϖ framed deformation. The Hecke/Galois actions on H(O/ϖ) ≅ H_χ(O/ϖ) agree by Carayol/Chebotarev. So the only missing condition is compatibility of the images of the x_i. The authors took this care for the framings ("agree modulo ϖ") but not for the surjections.

This is an omitted but necessary condition behind an asserted step, so it is a gap. It is easily repaired by the Nakayama argument above, and Theorem 9.19 stays true. Prop. 6.6 (p. 390) takes as input one fixed isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ. It also needs, for each M ≥ N, isomorphisms H^{l_0}((D^1_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) ⥲ H^{l_0}((D^2_M)^□⊗S_N/ϖ) "of R^1_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ ⥲ R^2_∞⊗S^□_N/ϖ-modules". In the proof of Thm 9.19, R^i_∞ acts on these groups only through the chosen surjections R^i_∞ ↠ R^□ followed by Conjecture B. The paper fixes the representatives so that they agree mod ϖ, but it puts no condition on the surjections: it says only "By Proposition 8.5, we can and do choose surjections". Prop. 8.5(4) says only that R^□ is a quotient of R_loc⟦x_1,…,x_g⟧, a non-canonical choice made separately on each side and for each N.

The R_loc part is compatible automatically, because the natural maps R^1_loc → R^□_S and R^χ_loc → R^□_{S^χ} agree mod ϖ. The images of the x_i are free. For example, swap the images of x_1 and x_2 on side 2 only, or add to one of them a non-zero element mod ϖ of the maximal ideal. Both give valid surjections, but then x_1 acts differently on the two sides, and the Hecke/z-module H^{l_0}(…)^□ does not generally make the two actions agree. So the claim "These isomorphisms are compatible with the actions of R^i_∞" does not follow from the choices as stated.

Defences tried:
- The "natural" isomorphism R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ cannot be adjusted per N to absorb the mismatch, because Prop. 6.6 fixes it independently of N.
- Nothing nearby in the paper supplies the condition. A search for "compatib" finds no such statement, and the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) is only about brackets.
- A charitable reader would read "we can and do choose" as meaning a compatible choice, and that choice is easy to make (see correction). So this is a small omitted condition plus an unjustified compatibility claim, not a false result.

The step matters. The compatibility is exactly what gives the R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ-module isomorphism H^{l_0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ on p. 428. That isomorphism, with [11, Lemma 2.2] and Lemma 8.2, gives near-faithfulness over R^1_∞, and then over R_S by Prop. 6.3(iv). Theorem 9.19 in turn gives Theorem 5.16 ("This theorem will follow immediately from Theorem 9.19") and hence Theorem 1.1. With the compatible choice described above, the proof goes through, so no stated result is affected.

On the candidate's correction: it is right and essentially minimal, except that "Only with this choice" overstates it. Agreement of the maps mod ϖ is sufficient, while what is necessary is only agreement of the induced actions.

So the reindexing has to send homological degree q0+l0−i to cohomological degree i. Top cohomological degree l0 is then the lowest homological degree q0: H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_N/ϖ) = e H_{q0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)_𝔪 = e H^{q0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ)^∨_𝔪.

issues.reason: I rendered PDF pp. 132–133 and confirmed the text. The mismatch is real: the bullet assumes N_2 > n, while the next paragraph and condition (4) use N_2 > n + 1. The deeper problem is that "N_2 > n + 1" is copied from [76] = BLGHT II without changing its n. I checked a local copy of BLGHT II (cy2fin.pdf). Its Theorem 6.4 reads: "n is an even positive integer ... l + 1 = N_1N_2 ... Suppose that N_2 > n + 1" with "r : Gal(F̄/F) → GSp_n(Z_l)". So n there is the dimension of r. The proof then says "apply the results of section 4 with N = N_2". Section 4 starts: "Let N > n + 1 denote positive integers with n even and N odd", and by Lemma 4.1 the piece V_λ has rank n. In CG §10, r = Sym^{2n−1}ρ takes values in GL_{2n}, and M/Q has degree 2n, which CG did adjust. So the n of BLGHT equals 2n here, and the hypothesis needed is N_2 > 2n + 1. Neither N_2 > n nor N_2 > n + 1 gives this. For example, with n = 3 (dimension 6), N_2 = 5 satisfies N_2 > n + 1, but the degree-5 Dwork family has no rank-6 piece. So the candidate is right that the text is inconsistent, but wrong that the fix is N_2 > n + 1 and that nothing is affected. The repair is routine: N_2 can be taken as large as needed, since p, or A and p in the general case, are chosen freely via Moret–Bailly/Chebotarev. It is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. A side note: BLGHT also needs N_2 odd and prime to S, where S contains 2. CG only says "prime to the conductor of A", which is another imprecision in this sketch.

issues.correction:
The minimal repair is to the reduction sentence. Replace "it suffices ... to prove that for each n, there exists a p such that r is potentially modular" by: "it suffices to show that for each n there is a finite Galois extension L/K such that ρ and Sym^{2n−1}ρ are both modular over every L′ with K ⊂ L′ ⊂ L and L/L′ soluble."
- The simultaneous statement for {ρ, Sym^{2n−1}ρ} comes from the same argument, applying Moret–Bailly (Prop. 6.2 of [76]) to the product of the two moduli schemes. This is the device of HSBT Thm 3.2/4.1 with a finite set N, and of the remark after BLGHT II Thm 8.1.
- Modularity over soluble subfields follows from Arthur–Clozel cyclic descent (AC Thm 4.2, which holds over any number field). The right twist is fixed by the Galois representations attached to regular algebraic cuspidal π over arbitrary number fields ([7], [8]).
- HSBT's Brauer + Rankin–Selberg computation (Jacquet–Shalika, Shahidi, Gelbart–Jacquet) then works unchanged over any K.

Item (5) should also refer to the p-adic representations: r|G_L and the λ′-adic V_{λ′,t}, whose reductions are r̄|G_L and r̄′|G_L. The candidate's proposed correction is broadly right but is a to-do list rather than a minimal fix. It misses the need for simultaneity, and its point about the CM case is not an error.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images for PDF pp. 132–133 and pp. 87–88 (Theorem 5.16). I also downloaded HSBT (Annals 171) and BLGHT (Taylor's cy2fin.pdf) and read the cited proofs.

(1) What the cited argument actually uses. HSBT Theorem 4.2's proof says: "Apply Theorem 4.1 with N = {2, m+1}. Let F′/F be as in the conclusion ... Then (A,i) × F_j is automorphic arising from ... π_j of GL_2(A_{F_j}), and Symm^m(A,i) × F_j is automorphic arising from ... Π_j of GL_{m+1}(A_{F_j})". It then uses the Rankin–Selberg product π_j × Π_j to get L(Sym^{m+1})L(Sym^{m−1}, s−1). HSBT Theorem 4.1 gives automorphy of all n ∈ N simultaneously over one Galois F′, and over "any intermediate field F′ ⊃ F″ ⊃ F with F′/F″ soluble", via CHT Lemma 4.3.2, which is for totally real fields. This is how HSBT get the even symmetric powers from odd-dimensional-rep (odd-m) potential automorphy.

(2) What CG reduce to. CG reduce only to "for each n, there exists a p such that r [= Sym^{2n−1}] is potentially modular". That is individual potential modularity, with p and the field depending on n. It says nothing about a common field for Sym^1 and Sym^{2n−1}, and nothing about soluble intermediate fields. Remark 10.1 confirms that even symmetric powers are not handled directly.

(3) The reduction is not just unexplained; the stated input is too weak for the cited route. Suppose each odd Sym^a is automorphic over its own field. Brauer induction plus Rankin–Selberg of Π_a with itself then gives only two kinds of fact: every odd Sym^a, and the products L(Sym^2)L(Sym^4)⋯L(Sym^{2a}). The measure (1 + c(χ_4 − χ_6))·μ_ST with c = 0.05 is positive (minimum density 0.9) and is not μ_ST, where χ_k = tr Sym^k. Yet I checked numerically that it gives mean 0 to every χ_odd, to χ_2, and to every sum Σ_{k≤a} χ_{2k} with a odd. So those facts cannot force Sato–Tate. The simultaneous version is needed, and the paper neither states nor proves it. Over an arbitrary K, the soluble descent HSBT rely on is also not available off the shelf. Neither point is addressed.

(4) Both points can be filled by standard means. BLGHT remark after Thm 8.1: "one simply chooses F′ so that the schemes ... simultaneously have F′ rational points". Descent works via Arthur–Clozel plus the Galois representations from Conjecture B. So the stated result is not in doubt, but the proof as written has a gap.

The candidate's reason overstates some things. The representations are stated. Item (5)'s r̄ notation is a slip. Theorem 5.16(6) asks for N(x) ≡ 1 mod p only where r ramifies and r̄ does not, which can be arranged. The CM dismissal is standard. Its core point about the Brauer/Sato–Tate reduction over arbitrary K is right, and (1)–(3) sharpen it. Potential modularity, part (1), is the n = 1 case and is not affected. Defence first.

**Points where the paper is standard practice, not wrong**
- **CM case.** "If A has CM, then the result is well known" copies BLGHT II Cor. 8.8 word for word ("If E is CM then the result is well known. If E is not CM it follows from the previous theorem as in the proof of 4.2 of [HSBT]"). CM Sato–Tate goes back to Hecke and Deuring. The separate cuspidality issue is candidate C-K10-4.
- **Arbitrary K.** "[81] is totally real" is not fatal. HSBT's descent step (CHT Lemma 4.3.2, BLGHT Lemma 1.3) is AC Thm 4.2 descent plus a twist fixed by attached Galois representations, and both exist over any number field.
- **Moret–Bailly.** BLGHT Prop. 6.2 is stated for an arbitrary number field and yields a Galois F′/F.
- **Construction details.** These can be carried out routinely:
  - put l′ in S2 using t ≡ 0, so that V_{λ′,t} is crystalline and l′ is unramified in L, as Thm 5.16 needs where BLGHT used the ordinary Thm 2.3;
  - choose M cyclic, so automorphic induction over L exists;
  - kill the auxiliary ramification at q locally while staying linearly disjoint, so bigness survives;
  - get condition (6) and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p by a soluble base change unramified at p (the remark after Thm 5.16).
- **Item (5).** It loosely names residual representations, but the next sentence makes clear that the λ′-adic V and the λ-adic Sym^{2n−1}(A) are meant.

**What is genuinely missing**
I checked HSBT (Annals text, Thms 4.1–4.2). Thm 4.1: "There is a Galois totally real field F′/F such that for any n ∈ N and any intermediate field F′ ⊃ F′′ ⊃ F with F′/F′′ soluble, Symm^{n−1} A is automorphic over F′′." The proof of Thm 4.2 then says "Apply Theorem 4.1 with N = {2, m+1}". So it needs Sym^1 and Sym^m modular over one common Galois field, and over all its soluble subfields, for the Rankin–Selberg identity L(Sym^{m+1})L(Sym^{m−1}) = ∏ L(σ_j×π_j⊗χ_j)^{a_j}.

CG's reduction, "for each n ... r is potentially modular", treats each n separately. On that route, separate information does not suffice:
- Using only Sym^{2n−1} over its own field, Rankin–Selberg π_j×π_j^∨ controls only sums of consecutive even powers: χ_2, then χ_4+χ_6, then χ_8+χ_10, and so on.
- The measure μ(1+ε(χ_4−χ_6)) satisfies every one of those constraints, so they do not pin down the Sato–Tate measure.

So the step "it suffices" is asserted with a citation whose proof uses a stronger input that CG never states. The candidate's own descent point is real but routine.

**Consequences**
§10 is the last section, and nothing later uses it (Remark 10.1 only). Theorem 1.1 (conditional on Conjecture B) is not in doubt, since every repair is standard. Hence affects = the proof. Related slips in the same sketch are recorded separately: the N_2 bound (H-part2-32) and the p/q swap (H-part2-31).

issues.printed: p. 429 (PDF p. 133), §10, proof of Theorem 1.1: "For a general elliptic curve E, we reduce to the previous case as follows. It suffices to find a second elliptic curve A, a number field L/K, and primes p and q such that: (1) The mod-p representation r̄ = (Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_E)|_{G_L} satisfies all the hypotheses of Theorem 5.16 with the possible exception of residual modularity. (2) A and E are semistable over L and have good reduction at all primes dividing p and q. (3) p and q split completely in L. (4) p + 1 is divisible by an integer N_2 > n + 1 which is prime to the conductor of A. (5) E[q] ≃ A[q] as G_L-modules, and the corresponding mod-p representation is surjective. (6) The mod-p representation ρ̄_A : G_L → GL_2(F_p) associated to A is surjective, and ρ̄_A|_{G_{Q_p}} ≃ Ind_{Q_{p^2}}^{Q_p} ω_2. This lemma also follows easily from Proposition 6.2 of [76], now applied to twists of a modular curve. We deduce as above (using the mod-q representation) that Sym^{2n−1}(A) is potentially modular over some extension which is unramified at p, and then use Theorem 5.16 once more now at the prime at p to deduce that Sym^{2n−1}(E) is modular." (Identical in arXiv v2, pp. 97–98.)
issues.correction: The roles of the primes p and q need to be made consistent. The most economical fix, and the likely origin of the slip, is this: items (4) and (6) were copied from the 'extra hypothesis' bullet on p. 428, which is stated at p. Keep (1), (2), (3), the words 'mod-p' in (5) and the final sentence, and change the rest as follows. (4): 'q+1 is divisible by an integer N_2 > n+1 which is prime to the conductor of A'. (5): 'E[p] ≃ A[p] as G_L-modules, and the corresponding mod-p representation is surjective'. (6): 'The mod-q representation ρ̄_{A,q} : G_L → GL_2(F_q) associated to A is surjective, and ρ̄_{A,q}|_{G_{Q_q}} ≃ Ind_{Q_{q^2}}^{Q_q} ω_2'. An equally valid alternative (X-K10-14's primary fix) keeps (4), (6) and E[q] ≃ A[q], changes 'mod-p' to 'mod-q' in (1) and in (5), and interchanges p and q throughout the final sentence ('using the mod-p representation … unramified at q … at the prime q'). X-K10-14's 'equivalently, interchange p and q in (4)–(6)' is slightly off: interchanging within (5) would make its 'corresponding mod-q representation' no longer match E[p]. In the final sentence 'Sym^{2n−1}(E) is modular' means modular over the extension L′, i.e. potentially modular. That is harmless shorthand, used in the same way in the special case ('the modularity of r follows'), and needs no correction.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 250 dpi. The printed text is as quoted, and it is identical in arXiv v2. As printed, A satisfies the special-case hypothesis at p: items (4) and (6) mirror the bullet hypothesis on p. 428. But A is tied to E only through E[q] ≃ A[q], in item (5). The last step applies Theorem 5.16 at p to Sym^{2n−1}ρ_{E,p}, with hypotheses coming from (1). Its residual-modularity condition (8)(a) (p. 383) needs an automorphic lift of Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_{E,p}. Nothing in (1)–(6) provides one, because A[p] has no stated link to E[p]. There are also internal clashes. "(using the mod-q representation)" for A contradicts (4) and (6), which are stated at p. Item (5) says "E[q] ≃ A[q] ... the corresponding mod-p representation". And "unramified at p" only makes sense if p is the prime of the final congruence, since Theorem 5.16 needs p unramified in the base field. The rest of the text (1, 5's "mod-p", and the final sentence) consistently points to one reading: A is special at q, and E ≡ A mod p. This is also the standard BLGHT-style argument. So the error is a p/q role swap in (4)–(6). It is a relabelling slip rather than a mathematical error, which is why I use kind=misprint (the candidate said error). Theorem 1.1, which is conditional on Conjecture B, is still true once the labels are fixed. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. I checked the page image at 250 dpi. The printed text is exactly as quoted: (4) says 'p+1', (5) says 'E[q] ≃ A[q] … mod-p', (6) says 'mod-p … F_p … G_{Q_p} … Ind_{Q_{p^2}}^{Q_p}', and the final sentence says 'mod-q … unramified at p … at the prime at p'.

Defence attempted, and it fails.
(a) Reading 1: take (4) and (6) literally, so A is 'special' at p like the bullet on p. 428. The special-case argument for A then runs at p, with the auxiliary prime l, and never uses a 'mod-q representation' of A. The final step applies Theorem 5.16 at p to r = Sym^{2n−1}ρ_{E,p} over L′, as its hypotheses in (1) indicate. Its hypothesis (8)(a) (p. 383) needs an automorphic π_0 with good reduction at p whose p-adic representation reduces to Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_{E,p}. Nothing supplies one, because A is tied to E only mod q.
(b) Reading 2: transfer through E[q] ≃ A[q] and apply 5.16 at q. Then (1) is at the wrong prime, and so are 'unramified at p' and 'at the prime at p'. Theorem 5.16 needs the prime to be unramified in the base field (p. 382), and nothing makes L′ unramified at q.
(c) q is not a power of p: (2) and (3) treat q as a second prime.
So no faithful reading makes the printed hypotheses support the printed final step.

Why it is a misprint. The intended argument is clear and standard (as in BLGHT II §6), and either relabelling makes every step work. Take the minimal fix. By Proposition 6.2 of [76] applied to the twisted modular curve X_{E[p]} ('twists of a modular curve'), pick A with A[p] ≅ E[p] which is special at q. The special case then gives Sym^{2n−1}(A) automorphic over some L′ unramified at p. Moret–Bailly can impose splitting at p. So Sym^{2n−1}ρ_{A,p}|_{G_{L′}} is an automorphic lift of Sym^{2n−1}ρ̄_{E,p}|_{G_{L′}} with good reduction at p, since A has good reduction at p by (2). That is (8)(a) for Theorem 5.16 at p, and the other hypotheses come from (1) and are preserved over L′. X-K10-14's side remark is also right: if A were special at p and E[p] ≅ A[p], then E would already be special at p over L and A would be pointless. That confirms the congruence prime and the special prime must differ.

Consequences. The passage is the last step of the paper's final proof. Nothing later uses it (Remark 10.1 and the references follow). The statement of Theorem 1.1, which is conditional on Conjecture B, is unaffected. The printed proof fails as written: its final application of Theorem 5.16 lacks its residual-modularity input. It is restored by relabelling alone, so kind = misprint (H-part2-31 said error) and affects = the proof (X-K10-14 said nothing). 'Nothing' is arguable, since the mathematics as intended is right. I chose 'the proof' because the slip swaps the logical roles of the two primes across three hypotheses, rather than being a local typo in one symbol.

issues.locator: §1, the paragraph before Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.2 itself, pp. 802–803. Compare Theorem 9.1, pp. 878–879; the Koecher principle in §5.2, p. 821; Definition 5.13, pp. 834–835; Definition 6.15, p. 844; the sentence after the definition of e_{α,β}, p. 845; Lemma 7.10, p. 852. arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text: intro p. 2–3, Definition 6.15 and the sentence "The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is non-zero after localization at m".
issues.printed: p. 2–3: "Let Y_1(N) denote the (open) Siegel modular variety of level N = N(r̄) over Spec(O), ... and let ω(j,2) denote the coherent sheaf on Y_1(N) whose complex sections define Siegel modular forms of weight (j,2) ... Let T denote the subring of endomorphisms of eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O) ≃ lim_→ eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ O/ϖ^n) (where e = e_{α,β} is a certain ordinary projection; see Section 6.4) generated by Hecke operators at primes not dividing Np." Theorem 1.2: "... Then there is an isomorphism R^min ~→ T_m, and moreover, the T_m-module eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O)^∨_m is free as a T_m-module." Compare p. 79 (Theorem 9.1): "Furthermore, the space H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} is a free T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅}-module." And p. 21: "The Koecher principle states that there is an isomorphism H^0(Y, ω(a,b)_M) ≃ H^0(X, ω(a,b)_M)." And p. 45: "The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is nonzero after localization at m."
issues.correction: There are two ways to fix it. (a) Minimal fix: state Theorem 1.2 for cusp forms, as Theorem 9.1 does (with Q = ∅). Let T be the image of the prime-to-Np Hecke operators in End_O(e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(N), ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})), where ω(j,2)(−∞) = ω(j,2)^sub. Take m to be a maximal ideal of this T, and conclude R^min ≅ T_m with H^0(X_1(N), ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_m free over T_m. (b) Keep the printed statement and add a lemma: for m non-Eisenstein, the inclusion e H^0(X, ω(j,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m ⊂ e H^0(X, ω(j,2)_{K/O})_m is an equality. Then the two localised Hecke algebras agree too. The standard argument: the quotient embeds, through the Siegel Φ-operator/constant terms, Hecke-equivariantly mod ϖ^n into elliptic modular forms and constants on the boundary strata. Its Hecke eigensystems are therefore Klingen/Siegel-Eisenstein, and their Galois representations are reducible. Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt rule this out when r̄_m is absolutely irreducible. The same lemma, or at least its non-vanishing half, is needed for the claim on p. 845 that Katz modularity (η in the full space, Definition 6.15) makes the cuspidal space nonzero at m. That is the related candidate X-K4-17.
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 802, 803, 821, 844, 845, 846, 852, 878 and 879 and checked each point.
(1) Theorem 1.2 is stated for H^0 over the open variety Y_1(N) with K/O coefficients. By the paper's own Koecher statement (p. 821, for any O-module M), this equals H^0(X, ω(j,2)_{K/O}): all forms, not only cusp forms.
(2) Every Hecke algebra in the body is defined on the cuspidal space: Definition 5.13 uses End_O H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}); §6.4 defines T_σ(Q)^{α,β} on e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O}). Theorem 9.1, which p. 878 calls "the main result of this paper", asserts R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅} and freeness only for H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅}. Its proof (p. 879) takes H to be that cuspidal module.
(3) The only comparison of the canonical and subcanonical sheaves is Lemma 7.10 (pp. 852–853), and only after ⊗K, via Harris–Zucker boundary cohomology over C. That says nothing about torsion. A grep of the text for canonical/boundary/cusp/Eisenstein turns up no torsion-coefficient comparison anywhere.
(4) Definition 6.15 puts the Katz eigenform η in H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O})[m_∅], the full space. Yet p. 845 asserts without argument that Katz modularity makes the cuspidal e_{α,β}H^0(...(−∞)_{K/O}) nonzero at m.
So Theorem 1.2 as printed is not what the paper proves. Getting from Theorem 9.1 to it needs the fact that the boundary (non-cuspidal) part vanishes after localizing at a non-Eisenstein m with ϖ-torsion coefficients, and the paper never states or proves this.
I believe the missing step is true and standard (q-expansion principle plus the classical Hecke-equivariance of Φ, and reducibility of Klingen/Siegel-type boundary eigensystems). So Theorem 1.2 is almost certainly correct, and this is a minor gap, not an error. It is not a misreading: the intro deliberately works on the open Y_1(N), "whose complex sections define Siegel modular forms", which by Koecher means all forms. The intro is informal in other ways too (level Y_1(N) versus the level K of §6.3), which is why my confidence is only medium that this counts as a register-worthy gap rather than a harmless informal restatement. I looked for a defence and found none.

1. **The space is the full one.** On the open variety, the Koecher principle (p. 821: "H^0(Y, ω(a,b)_M) ≃ H^0(X, ω(a,b)_M)" for any O-module M) makes H^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O) the space of all forms on X_1(N), cuspidal or not. p. 822 makes this the paper's convention: "We may therefore pass freely between the open variety Y and the (any) smooth projective toroidal compactification X ... when dealing with H^0". The paper sometimes drops (−∞) elsewhere (Lemma 6.2, §8), but that cannot rescue the reading here: on Y there is no (−∞) to drop, and the text stresses "(open)".

2. **The body proves only the cuspidal statement.**
   - Definition 5.13 (p. 834) defines T_σ on H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}).
   - p. 845 defines T_σ(Q)^{α,β} on e_{α,β}H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O}).
   - Theorem 9.1 ("the main result of this paper") concludes only that H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m∅} is free over T^{α,β}_{σ,m∅}. Its proof (pp. 879–880) and the balancedness input (Theorem 7.11, H^2 vanishing for ω(−∞) via Theorem 5.1/Assumption 7.7, Serre duality with ω^3(−∞)) are intrinsically subcanonical. The proof does not transfer to the canonical sheaf.

3. **Nothing in the paper bridges the two.** The only comparison is Lemma 7.10 (p. 852), and it holds only after ⊗K. Its proof uses boundary cohomology over C, which says nothing about ϖ-torsion. From Lemma 7.10 one gets only that cusp_m has finite index in full_m over O. Torsion in H^1 of either sheaf could still separate e·full_{K/O,m} from e·cusp_{K/O,m}. The paper also defines no Hecke action on H^0(∂X, ·) with torsion coefficients, and Lemma 8.8 constructs T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} on the full space but proves nothing about boundary support.

4. **The printed statement is almost certainly true.** The Φ-operator argument in the correction is standard folklore (also used implicitly in [16] in weight 1). So this is an omitted step, not a false claim. That is why I call it a gap rather than an error.

5. **Not a misprint.** The difference between full and cuspidal spaces with K/O coefficients is mathematical content, not a notational slip. The hypothesis is also stated for the full-space algebra ("maximal ideal m of T"), which matches the full-space Katz-modularity condition of Definition 6.15, not a cuspidal one.

6. **What uses the passage.**
   - Nothing later uses the full-space form of Theorem 1.2.
   - Theorem 1.1 needs only a cuspidal eigenform, which Theorem 9.1 supplies directly. Its deduction is not written out anyway (H-h1-1).
   - The appendix's "Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above" (p. 889) reuses the method, not the full-space statement.

So the damage is confined to Theorem 1.2 as printed. That statement is not established by the paper, although the minimal restatement (a) is exactly Theorem 9.1 and the lemma in (b) restores it verbatim. The candidate's correction is right and minimal.

issues.printed: THEOREM 1.1 Let r : G_Q → GSp_4(Q̄_p) be a continuous irreducible representation satisfying the following conditions: (1) The restriction r | G_{Q_p} is ordinary with Hodge–Tate weights [0, 0, j − 1, j − 1] for some integer j satisfying p − 1 > j ≥ 4. (2) If α and β are the unit root eigenvalues of Frobenius on D_cris(V), then (α² − 1)(β² − 1)(α − β)(α²β² − 1) ≢ 0 mod p. (3) The image of r̄ | G_{Q(ζ_p)} contains Sp_4(F_p). (4) For a prime x ≠ p, the image of inertia at x is unipotent, and the image of any generator of tame inertia has the same number of Jordan blocks mod p as it does in characteristic 0. (5) The representation r̄ is modular of level N(r̄) and weight (j, 2). Then r is modular, that is, there exists a cuspidal Siegel modular Hecke eigenform F of weight (j, 2) such that L(r, s) = L(F, s), where L(F, s) is the spinor L-function of F. [next paragraph] We deduce Theorem 1.1 from our main result, which we now state.
issues.correction:
The deduction should be written out, and Theorem 1.1 should be stated in the form the paper can actually prove.

Hypothesis (5) should become: r̄ is Katz modular of weight (j,2) in the sense of Def. 6.15, with α, β as in (2), at the level K of §6.3. N(r̄) is never defined, and K includes the auxiliary prime q. Crystallinity of r|G_{Q_p} should be stated; (2) already presupposes it through D_cris(V).

The conclusion should be "there is a cuspidal eigenform F of weight (j,2) and level K with r_F ≅ r". Equivalently, L_x(r,s) = L_x(F,s) for every prime x ∉ S(r̄) ∪ {p}.

Routine steps of the deduction:
(a) Crystallinity with (1), (2) and (4) gives ν(r) = ε^{1−j}, since Q has no everywhere-unramified extension. The same hypotheses give Def. 4.6(1)–(3) and (6), so r is minimal. Hypothesis (4) makes r̄ of type U1, U2 or U3 at each x ∈ S(r̄) (Assumption 4.3), because p ≥ 7 gives u = exp(log u).
(b) Hypothesis (3) implies Assumption 4.1. Example 4.11(2) covers only the case where the image is GSp_4(F_p).
(c) Hypothesis (3) implies neatness (Assumption 4.2). The remark after Assumption 4.2 covers only surjective r̄. Use instead g0·Sp_4(F_p), which contains diag(a, b, ν0/b, ν0/a).
(d) Oddness is forced by (5), which in turn forces j to be even (Remark 8.2).
(e) Hypothesis (6) of Theorem 9.1 holds by Theorem 5.1.
(f) R^min ≅ T and the freeness of H turn the point of R^min given by r into a characteristic-0 eigenform F.
(g) At q: Mok [55, Thm 4.14] gives local–global compatibility up to semisimplification. The choice of q makes π_q spherical with N = 0, so the Euler factors agree there.

Complete equality L(r,s) = L(F,s) at x ∈ S(r̄) and at p needs full local–global compatibility, including N, in nonregular weight. The paper does not supply this, so either that input must be added or the conclusion weakened as above.
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 802, 803 and 878 and transcribed them; the printed text matches the candidate.

The deduction is missing:
- "Theorem 1.1" occurs only on p. 802 and p. 804 (a remark about a weight-(2,2) analogue).
- In arXiv v1 it appears only in the statement, the "We deduce" sentence, and §1.2.
- Theorem 9.1 concludes only that R^min → T^{α,β}_{σ,m∅} is an isomorphism and that H is free. Its proof ends on p. 880 with no passage to r.
- Nothing later uses Theorem 1.1. Appendix Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2" (p. 889).

I checked which steps of the deduction are routine.
- Theorem 1.1(4) forces r to be unramified wherever r̄ is: 4 Jordan blocks means the identity. It also makes r̄ of type U1, U2 or U3 at x ∈ S(r̄), since p ≥ 7 means u = exp(log u), and Def. 4.6(3) holds.
- H1–H3 hold whenever r̄(G_{Q(ζ_p)}) ⊇ Sp_4(F_p). The adjoint image lies in PGSp_4(F_p), and PSp_4(F_p) has index ≤ 2 there, which is less than p−1. PSp_4(F_p) is simple and perfect. A regular torus element gives H2.
- For neatness I checked the diagonal-element argument by brute force for p = 7, 11, 13 and 17. For every ν0 and every q ≠ 1 there is some diag(a, b, ν0/b, ν0/a) with no eigenvalue ratio equal to q.
- A Q̄_p-point of T ≅ R^min gives a characteristic-0 cusp form F by the divisible-part argument.

What is not routine or not in the paper:
- Local–global compatibility for weight (j,2) forms. Prop. 6.8 assumes b ≥ 3, and §6.4 handles low weight only by passing to high weight. So nothing identifies the Euler factors of F at x ∈ S(r̄), at p, or at q with those of r. At a type-U prime the up-to-semisimplification data plus the level K_x does not fix N.
- The ordinary Hecke eigenvalue condition at p in Def. 6.15, which Theorem 1.1(5) does not state.
- The definitions of N(r̄) (§5 defines no N) and of "odd".

The literal conclusion, equality of complete L-functions, is therefore not proved in the paper. Confidence is medium for two reasons. First, "L(r,s) = L(F,s)" is often used as shorthand for r ≅ r_F; on that reading this is an omitted deduction plus imprecise hypotheses. Second, I could not check whether Mok [55, Thm 3.5] gives full compatibility in weight (k,2); the paper cites it only for b ≥ 3. Defence attempted, and it fails. First, the deduction is really missing. I rendered p. 802, 813, 815, 816, 818 and 878–880 and searched the whole text. "Theorem 1.1" occurs only on p. 802 and in a remark on p. 804. Theorem 9.1 ends with "the conclusions of Theorem 9.1 follow immediately" (p. 880) and never passes back to r. The appendix's Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2" (p. 889). So nothing later in the paper uses Theorem 1.1, and nothing proves it.

Second, the best charitable reading. Theorem 1.1 is offered as "an example of what we can prove". Read "modular" in (5) as Katz modularity at level K, and "L(r,s) = L(F,s)" as shorthand for r ≅ r_F. On that reading the deduction is standard R = T bookkeeping, and every hypothesis of Theorem 9.1 can be checked:
- ν(r) and minimality follow from (1), (2), (4) plus crystallinity. A unipotent image of finite-order wild inertia is trivial in characteristic 0. Equal Jordan-block counts give Def. 4.6(2)–(3).
- Hypothesis (3) gives big image by standard group theory.
- Neatness is not covered by the paper. Its remark on p. 813 assumes r̄ surjective onto GSp_4(F_p). Under (3) that can fail: for p = 7, j = 4 the similitudes lie in (F_7^×)^3 = {±1}, and there is no scalar λ ≠ ±1 in the image. I brute-forced the diagonal argument (work/agents/vB-K1-12/neat.py). For p = 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, every ν0 and every q ≠ 1 admit some diag(a, b, ν0/b, ν0/a) with no eigenvalue ratio equal to q. The argument fails at p = 5, which p − 1 > j ≥ 4 excludes.
- Oddness is not in Theorem 1.1. Galois representations of holomorphic Siegel forms have ν(c) = −1, so (5) forces j to be even; for odd j the theorem is vacuous.
So on this reading the result is true and only its proof is missing.

Third, the literal conclusion cannot be reached. L(r,s) = L(F,s) for complete L-functions needs Euler factors to match at x ∈ S(r̄), where r has N ≠ 0 of rank 1, 2 or 3, and at p.
- The paper states local–global compatibility only for b ≥ 3 (Prop. 6.8(5), citing Mok [55, Thm 3.5]).
- I checked arXiv:1109.5392. Mok's Thm 3.5 covers cohomological Π only. For holomorphic limits of discrete series, which is weight (j,2), Mok's Thms 4.11 and 4.14 give compatibility only "up to semi-simplification".
- The level K_x does not determine N_aut. At Iwahori, Klingen or paramodular level, constituents with the same semisimple parameter but smaller N also have fixed vectors. So the Euler factors at S(r̄) are not determined.
- At p, the relation between D_cris and the Satake parameters of F in weight (j,2) is not proved in the paper either.

Checks on the proposed corrections:
- X-K1-12's list of checks is right, but its last step ("F with L(r,s) = L(F,s)") is not routine as printed.
- H-h1-1's weakened statement ("x ∉ S(r̄) ∪ {p}") is correct, but at q it needs Mok's semisimple compatibility together with the choice of q. Theorem 6.13(2) only covers x ∉ S(r̄) ∪ {q, p}.

Theorems 1.2, 9.1 and A.1 are not affected.

Affects is set to "a stated result": Theorem 1.1 has no proof, and as printed its conclusion and hypothesis (5) must be corrected. On the loose shorthand reading it would drop to "the proof". This is why confidence is medium; that the gap exists is certain.

issues.locator: §1, the paragraph stating the main result (p. 802) and Theorem 1.2 (p. 803). Compare the opening of §4 (p. 812), Remark 4.4 (p. 814), Definition 4.6(1) (p. 815), the level K at the start of §6.3 (pp. 840–841) and Theorem 9.1 (pp. 878–879). 802–803, 812, 814–815, 840–841, 878–879). arXiv 1907.08691v1 has the same text, pp. 2–3.
issues.printed: p. 2 (checked on the page image): "We deduce Theorem 1.1 from our main result, which we now state. (We refer to Sections 4 and 6.4 for precise details concerning ramification behavior, level subgroups, and the exact definition of minimal deformations.) Let ε denote the p-adic cyclotomic character. Let O be the ring of integers of a finite extension K of Q_p. Let r̄ : G_Q → GSp_4(k) be a continuous irreducible representation whose similitude character ν(r̄) on inertia at p is the mod-p reduction of ε^{1−j}. Suppose that r̄ | G_{Q_p} contains an unramified subspace of dimension 2 on which Frob_p acts by the scalars α and β, respectively, where (α²−1)(β²−1)(α−β)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0. Suppose further that r̄ has big image (explicitly, satisfies Assumption 4.1) and that r̄ | G_{Q_x} for a prime x ≠ p is either unramified or is one of the types listed in Assumption 4.3. Let Y_1(N) denote the (open) Siegel modular variety of level N = N(r̄) over Spec(O), where N is determined by r̄ as in Section 5, and let ω(j,2) denote the coherent sheaf on Y_1(N) whose complex sections define Siegel modular forms of weight (j,2) for some integer p−1 > j ≥ 4. Let T denote the subring of endomorphisms of eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O) ≃ lim→ eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ O/ϖ^n)". p. 3: "(where e = e_{α,β} is a certain ordinary projection; see Section 6.4) generated by Hecke operators at primes not dividing Np. Let R^min denote the universal minimal deformation ring of r̄ (see Definition 4.6 for more details). THEOREM 1.2 Suppose that there exist both a maximal ideal m of T and a corresponding representation r̄_m : G_Q → GSp_4(k) which is isomorphic to r̄. Let R^min denote the universal minimal ordinary deformation ring of r̄. Suppose that p−1 > j ≥ 4. Then there is an isomorphism R^min ⥲ T_m, and moreover, the T_m-module eH^0(Y_1(N), ω(j,2) ⊗ K/O)^∨_m is free as a T_m-module." For comparison, Theorem 9.1, p. 78: "Let r̄ : G_Q → GSp_4(k) be a continuous, odd, absolutely irreducible Galois representation. Suppose that ν(r̄) = ε^{−(a−1)}, where p−1 > a ≥ 2. … (5) (Neatness) The representation r̄ satisfies Assumption 4.2. … let K ⊂ GSp_4(A^∞) be the compact open subgroup defined as in the beginning of Section 6.3." Remark 4.4, p. 14: "Since we are assuming that the similitude character of r̄ is a power of the cyclotomic character, it turns out that r̄ | I_x can never be of type P. We expect that our arguments can also be adapted to deal with representations r̄ with more general (odd) similitude characters, but we made this assumption to simplify …". arXiv 1907.08691v1 has the same text with small wording changes ("We shall refer to § 4 and § 6.4", "behaviour", "as in § 5", "Suppose that there exists a maximal ideal m of T", with no "both"). Its Remark 4.4 and Theorem 9.1 are also the same.
issues.correction:
Add two hypotheses to Theorem 1.2.
(i) ν(r̄) = ε̄^{1−j} on all of G_Q, not only on inertia at p. Given the condition at p, this is the same as asking that ν(r̄) be unramified at every x ≠ p. It rules out type P (Remark 4.4) and type-H primes where ν is ramified.
(ii) "absolutely irreducible" in place of "irreducible".
Adding "odd" costs nothing.
Do NOT add Assumption 4.2 (neatness), which both candidates ask for: it already follows from Assumption 4.1(H1), which Theorem 1.2 assumes. The level pointer is a cosmetic fix, since the disclaimer covers level details: the level is fixed in §6.3, including the auxiliary prime q, not in "Section 5" or "6.4". When (i) fails, R^min is not defined, because Definition 4.6(1) fails even for r̄. So "zero ring" is the wrong description.
issues.reason:
I transcribed p. 802, 803, 814, 815, 840, 841, 878 and 879 from the page images. The candidate's quotes are accurate.
(1) The intro theorem is broader than Theorem 9.1. It fixes ν(r̄) only on inertia at p, and it allows every type in Assumption 4.3, including P. Theorem 9.1 and all of §4 assume ν(r̄) = ε̄^{−(a−1)} on all of G_Q (p. 812), and Definition 4.6(1) requires ν(r) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
(2) Type P really does force a ramified similitude. I redid the computation. The I_x-invariant plane V_1 and the χ_x-plane V_2 are complementary isotropic planes, so the symplectic form pairs them. For g ∈ I_x this gives ν(g)⟨v,w⟩ = ⟨gv,gw⟩ = χ_x(g)⟨v,w⟩, so ν(r̄)|I_x = χ_x ≠ 1, while ε̄ is unramified at x. Type H can also have ramified ν: for r̄|G_x induced from a tame ψ, ν|I_x = ψ^{1+x²}, which can be a nontrivial character of order dividing x−1.
(3) Such an r̄ can have an m in T. §6.3 gives type-P primes level Π(x)^+, and §5.1 gives Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^×, so nebentypus is allowed there. Theorem 6.13(1) only gives ν = ψ_{λ,0}ε^{−w}. The step "ψ_{λ,0} trivial mod m", used in the proof of Theorem 6.17, needs the global similitude condition. Remark 4.4 says the authors only expect the general case. So Theorem 1.2 claims something the paper does not prove.
(4) Neatness (Theorem 9.1(5)) is left out of Theorem 1.2. It is not implied by Assumption 4.1: H2 only gives elements of G_{Q(ζ_{p^m})}, where ε ≡ 1. The pointer "Section 5" is wrong: the level is chosen from r̄ only in §6.3.
Defence tried. The parenthetical on p. 802 sends the reader to §§4 and 6.4 for "precise details". It does not save the statement: the intro states a strictly weaker similitude hypothesis and lists type P outright, and neatness is not a matter of detail. The same defence was rejected for the parallel item PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18/E6, where an intro theorem dropped a standing hypothesis of §3.1.
Effects are limited. Theorem 9.1 is correct as stated. Theorem 1.1 is unaffected on (i): unipotent inertia at x ≠ p and HT weights at p make ν(r)ε^{j−1} unramified everywhere, hence trivial. Theorem A.1 ("follows as in Theorem 1.2") concerns semistable abelian surfaces with End = Z. There ν = ε^{−1} (Weil pairing), inertia is unipotent, and the image is surjective for large p, which gives neatness by the remark after Assumption 4.2. So A.1 lies within Theorem 9.1.
The only thing affected is the stated generality of Theorem 1.2. The fix is routine: add the hypotheses. I checked p. 802, 803, 812–815, 840–842, 846 and 878–880 against the page images.

GENUINE PART: the similitude.
- All of §4 and Theorem 9.1 assume ν(r̄) = ε̄^{−(a−1)} on G_Q, and Definition 4.6(1) requires ν(r) = ε^{−(a−1)}.
- The intro fixes ν only on I_p, and it allows every type in Assumption 4.3.
- Type P: the I_x-invariant plane and the χ_x plane are complementary isotropic planes, so they pair nondegenerately. For g in I_x, ⟨gv,gw⟩ = ν(g)⟨v,w⟩ then gives ν|I_x = χ_x ≠ 1.
- Type H can also have ramified ν. Take x = 3 and ψ of order 20 in F_81^×. Its Frobenius orbit {1,3,9,7} has size 4, and ν|I_x = ψ^{1+9} = ψ^{10} has order 2.
- In such cases no lift, r̄ included, satisfies Definition 4.6(1).
- The proof needs the global condition in two places. Theorem 6.13(1), p. 842, says χ_{μ,0} is "trivial modulo m". The proof of Theorem 6.17, p. 846, says "χ_Q is ... of p-power order", then twists by its square root.
- Remark 4.4 only "expect[s]" that the general case works.

DEFENCE TRIED.
- (a) The p. 802 disclaimer ("precise details concerning ramification behavior"), and the fact that R^min presupposes ν(r̄) = ε̄^{1−j}. Under that reading the theorem is true, but it states a strictly weaker similitude hypothesis and lists type P outright, which can then never occur. That is how the parallel CG18/E6 item was treated: confirmed as a gap in a stated result.
- (b) Could the existence of m force the global condition? No. §6.3 uses full level at type-H primes and Π(x)^+ at type-P primes, so a nebentypus is allowed there.

REFUTED PART: neatness.
- H1 says ζ_p ∉ Q(ad^0 r̄). So some σ is trivial on ad^0 r̄ but has ε̄(σ) = q ≢ 1.
- The centralizer of sp4 in M4 consists of the scalars. I checked this by computer for p = 3, 5, 7: the centralizer has dimension 1, and dimension is stable under field extension.
- So r̄(σ) is scalar and every ratio of its eigenvalues is 1 ≢ q, which is exactly Assumption 4.2. Chebotarev then gives the q of §6.3.
- The earlier verdict's "H2 only gives elements where ε ≡ 1" overlooked H1.

"irreducible": nothing in the hypotheses forces absolute irreducibility. The proof needs it: Assumption 6.12(1), the non-Eisenstein condition of Definition 6.11, and the representability of R^min all use it. This is minor.

CONSEQUENCES: Theorem 9.1 and its proof are unaffected.
- Theorem 1.1 is deduced from 1.2 and is unaffected. Unipotent inertia at x ≠ p together with the HT weights forces ν(r) = ε^{1−j} globally, and an image containing Sp4(F_p) forces absolute irreducibility.
- Theorem A.1 ("follows as in Theorem 1.2", p. 889) is unaffected: semistable abelian surfaces have ν = ε^{−1}.
- Only the stated generality of Theorem 1.2 is affected.
