issues.correction:
**What survives.** The displayed map φ is a well-defined isomorphism of holomorphic vector bundles on G(C)/Q^−. It is equivariant only for ker ν = Sp4(C). For general h it satisfies φ(h·x) = ν(h)^{−1}·h·φ(x).

**What is false.** The claimed target, "𝒱_σ^∨ ≅ 𝒱_τ^∨ as G(Q)-equivariant bundles", cannot be proved by this or any other map, because no such isomorphism exists.

**Correct argument.** On X × G(A^∞)/U, put f(x,h) = sgn ν(x) · |ν(h)|_f^{−1}.
- sgn ν(x) is well defined on X = G(R)/K^h, since the centralizer of h(i) = J has ν > 0.
- By the product formula, f(γx, γh) = ν(γ)·f(x,h) for γ ∈ G(Q).
- f(x, hu) = f(x,h) for u ∈ U.

Therefore (x, v, h) ↦ (x, f(x,h)·φ(v), h) is G(Q)-equivariant and descends to an isomorphism 𝒱_σ ≅ 𝒱_τ on Y(C). Right translation by g ∈ G(A^∞) multiplies f by |ν(g)|_f^{−1}. That factor is exactly the Hecke twist by a power of ν that the paper notes.

**Alternatives.**
- Work componentwise. Write Y(C) = ⊔ Γ_i\X^+ with Γ_i = G(Q)^+ ∩ g_iUg_i^{−1}. Then ν(Γ_i) ⊂ Q_{>0} ∩ Ẑ^× = {1}, so the Sp4-equivariant map φ already descends on each component.
- Use the paper's own Lemma 5.4. It gives 𝒱_τ = 𝒱_σ ⊗ 𝒱_(0,0;2), and 𝒱_(0,0;2) = O_Y(1) ≅ O_Y as a bare bundle.

**On the two candidates' corrections.**
- X-K3-8 calls φ "an isomorphism of G(C)-bundles". That is inaccurate, since φ is not G(C)-equivariant.
- X-K3-8's factor "|ν(h^∞)|^{±1}" must have exponent −1. It also only handles γ with ν(γ) > 0, and G(Q) contains γ with ν(γ) < 0, such as diag(1,1,−1,−1). So either the sgn ν(x) factor is needed, or one must restrict to G(Q)^+ acting on X^+.
- H-h1-15's correction, f = sgn ν(x)·|ν(h)|_f^{−1}, is right and minimal.
issues.reason:
I transcribed the text from renders of p. 826 and p. 20 of arXiv v1. The two are identical.

I redid the computation with ν(q) = ν of the Levi part and ν trivial on P^−. Well-definedness holds: (gq, w) ↦ (gq, ν(g)^{−1}ν(q)^{−1}w), which is equivalent to (g, τ(q)ν(g)^{−1}ν(q)^{−1}w) = (g, ν(g)^{−1}σ(q)w), the image of (g, σ(q)w). Equivariance fails: h·(g,w) = (hg,w) ↦ (hg, ν(h)^{−1}ν(g)^{−1}w) = ν(h)^{−1}·h·φ(g,w). The candidate's example is valid: J is antidiagonal, pairing e1 with e4 and e2 with e3, so diag(1,1,2,2)^t J diag(1,1,2,2) = 2J. A scalar also works: ν(2I_4) = 4, and 2I_4 acts on V_σ by 2^c, since the (0,0;c) part of the weight gives zI ↦ z^c, and on V_τ by 2^{c+2}.

So the printed claim that the map "gives the required isomorphism … as G(Q)-equivariant bundles" is false, and no such isomorphism exists. The unnumbered observation it supports ("the bundle 𝒱_σ does not depend on c", with Hecke action twisted by a power of ν) is true, via the trivialization f above.

Effect on the rest of the paper: I found no later use of the observation. Lemma 5.4 (W_(a,b;c) ≅ V_(b,a;a+b+2c), compatibly with Hecke actions) is proved independently, from W_(0,0;1) = V_(0,0;2) = O_Y(1) and W_(1,0;0) = V_(0,1;1) via [52], [54]. Theorems 5.5 and 5.6 use Lemma 5.4. A grep for "depend on c", "value of c" and "power of the similitude" finds only this remark, its parallel on p. 824 for W_μ, and the Serre-duality twist note. The item is the flawed proof of a true, unnumbered remark, so 'affects: nothing' holds. One could argue for 'error' instead of 'gap', since an intermediate claim is false, but the conclusion stands. **Printed text and conventions.**
- The passage is identical in the Duke text (p. 826) and in arXiv v1 (p. 20).
- ν has weight (0,0;2): p. 811 says so explicitly, and it follows from the p. 809 identification (a,b;c) ↔ a·t1·i + b·t2·i + c·z, since ν(e^z) = e^{2z}. Hence τ = σ⊗ν has highest weight (a,b;c+2), as printed.
- 𝒱_σ on Y(C) = G(Q)\(G(R)/K^h × G(A^∞)/U) (p. 824) is defined by quotienting 𝒱_σ^∨|_X × G(A^∞)/U by G(Q). So the reduction to a G(Q)-equivariant isomorphism is the relevant one.

**Well-definedness holds.** ν is a character of G and is trivial on the unipotent radical, so τ|_{Q^−} = σ⊗ν. Then (gq, w) ↦ (gq, ν(g)^{−1}ν(q)^{−1}w) ~ (g, ν(g)^{−1}σ(q)w), which is the image of (g, σ(q)w).

**Equivariance fails.** h·(g,w) = (hg, w) ↦ (hg, ν(h)^{−1}ν(g)^{−1}w) = ν(h)^{−1}·h·φ(g,w). I checked with python that diag(1,1,2,2) ∈ GSp4 with ν = 2, and that 2I_4 has ν = 4.

**No G(Q)-equivariant isomorphism exists at all.**
- The central element z = 2I_4 ∈ G(Q) lies in K^h_C ⊂ Q^−.
- It acts trivially on G(C)/Q^−.
- On fibres it acts by the scalar σ(z) = 2^c on 𝒱_σ^∨ and by τ(z) = 2^{c+2} on 𝒱_τ^∨, because z·[g,w] = [gz,w] = [g, σ(z)w].
- Any equivariant bundle map F therefore satisfies 2^c·F_p = 2^{c+2}·F_p on each fibre, so F = 0.

**No charitable reading rescues it.**
- It is not a slip for Sp4(Q). With Sp4(Q) the "by the definition of 𝒱_σ it suffices" step would need the componentwise argument, which the paper does not give.
- The paper defines 𝒱^∨ = G(C)×_{Q^−}V with its natural G(C)-action, so no normalization in [9] could change the central-scalar obstruction.

The unnumbered conclusion is true (see the correction). So the printed step is false, but the observation it supports is correct. By PROTOCOL §18 ("a step that fails") this is an error rather than a gap.

**Downstream uses.** I checked every later use, and none relies on this argument.
- Lemma 5.4 (p. 827) proves W_(a,b;c) ≅ 𝒱_(−b,−a;a+b+2c), compatibly with Hecke actions, independently. It uses W_(0,0;1) = 𝒱_(0,0;2) = O_Y(1), W_(1,0;0) = 𝒱_(0,−1;1) and tensor compatibility.
- Theorem 5.5 (p. 828) applies Lemma 5.4 at the given c. Theorem 5.6 (p. 829) cites Lemma 5.4 and the proof of Theorem 5.5.
- Remark 5.10 (pp. 833–834) passes from c = −a−b to μ = (a,b;3−a−b), σ = (−b,−a;6−a−b). That is Lemma 5.4 applied with c = 3−a−b, plus the W-side fact from the proof of Theorem 5.1. Remark 5.12 is likewise direct.
- A grep for "depend on c", "value of c" and "power of the similitude" finds only this remark, the parallel W_μ remark on p. 826, and the Serre-duality twist note on p. 888.

**Scope.** The proof of this unnumbered observation needs repair, but no stated result is affected. I set affects = "the proof" because the given argument fails, not merely through a slip. "nothing" (H-h1-15's choice) is defensible, since no downstream statement or proof depends on it.

issues.correction: Replace "μ = (a − 1, b − 2; c) ∉ C_i" with "(a − 1, b − 2; c) ∉ C_i". This is equivalent to "μ − w0(ρ) ∉ C_i", where w0(a,b;c) = (b,a;c) as in §2.1 (this map is s_{α1}) and ρ = (2,1;−3/2). Then μ − w0(ρ) = (a−1, b−2; c+3/2), and the chambers C_i (p. 828) put no condition on the third coordinate, so the third entry does not matter. This is the reading Definition 5.7 (p. 830) uses.
issues.reason: The page image confirms the printed text. The first line of the same statement fixes μ = (a,b;c), so the chain "μ = (a−1, b−2; c)" is false as written. The proof (pp. 828–829) shows the intended condition. There, σ = (−b,−a; a+b+2c), λ = ((σ+ρ)|Sp4(R); −a−b−2c) = (2−b, 1−a; −a−b−2c), and w0 swaps the first two coordinates (p. 808). So −w0(λ) = (a−1, b−2; a+b+2c) ∈ C_i, and the proof says this "is equivalent to the condition in the statement". I redid this computation and it agrees. The reading "μ ∉ C_i" gives a different and false criterion. Take μ = (a,2;c) with a ≥ 2. The intended point (a−1, 0) lies in C0 ∩ C1 but not in C2 or C3, so H^i vanishes for i = 2,3. That is exactly what p. 830 deduces: "H^i(X(C), ω(a,2))_{(2),temp} = 0 for i = 2,3". Under the literal reading, μ = (a,2) lies only in C0, which would also make H^1 vanish. That contradicts the l0 = 1 setting of the paper, where weight (2,2) has cohomology in degrees 0 and 1. For μ = (a,3−a), the point (a−1, 1−a) lies in C1 ∩ C2 only, so H^i vanishes for i = 0,3, again matching p. 830. Theorem 5.6(3) ("established in the proof of Theorem 5.5") and Definition 5.7 also use (a−1, b−2; ·), and nothing later uses the misprinted form. So the mathematics is correct and only the printed statement is garbled. Minor points: the candidate's gloss "w0 = s_{α1}" is my own check, not text from Definition 5.7, but it is correct: the paper's w0 acts as (a,b;c) ↦ (b,a;c), which is s_{α1}. There is also an unrelated slip on p. 828, "C0, …, C4", which should read C0, …, C3.

A_6 is simple, so it has no subgroup of index 3, and every S_5 ⊂ S_6 therefore meets A_6 in A_5. Its order-4 elements are then odd permutations, while (1,2,3,4)(5,6) is even. The outer automorphism of S_6 preserves parity, so it also fixes both 90-element classes (4,1,1) and (4,2).

(2) Direct check. f ≡ (x−2)^4(x−4) mod 5 (the coefficient vectors agree). f(x+2) = x^5 + 8x^4 + 30x^3 + 60x^2 + 60x + 20, with 5-adic valuations 1,1,1,1,0,0 from the constant term up. The Newton polygon therefore has a slope-1/4 segment of length 4, so four roots generate a totally and tamely ramified quartic extension of Q_5. Because μ_4 ⊂ Q_5, this extension is cyclic Galois. The fifth root is simple mod 5, so it lies in Q_5. Inertia therefore acts on {roots, ∞} as a 4-cycle fixing two points.

(3) The image is indeed S_5. disc f = 1824000 = 2^8·3·5^3·19. Mod 17, f is irreducible (a 5-cycle). Mod 7 it factors with pattern [2,3], whose cube is a transposition. So Gal(f) = S_5, and the phrase 'image S_5' is correct.

(4) Consequence. On V = (even subsets)/⟨all⟩, both (1234) and (1234)(56) have rank(σ−1)^k = 3, 2, 1, 0 for k = 1..4, so both are regular unipotent (U3). The Iwahori conclusion is unaffected.

The authors do call this example 'a slight variation of this argument', which points to the 4-cycle as the intended class. Even so, the class as printed is false. A side remark: the preceding sentence says the unipotent σ with (σ−1)^2 ≠ 0 'has conjugacy class (1,2,3,4)(5,6)'. That is also incomplete, since 4-cycles satisfy it too, but it is not part of this candidate. 1. The printed text contradicts itself. A_6 has no subgroup of index 3, so no S_5 ⊂ S_6 lies inside A_6. Hence S_5 ∩ A_6 = A_5 for every copy of S_5 in S_6. The order-4 elements of S_5 are odd, so in S_6 they have cycle type (4,1,1). The class of (1,2,3,4)(5,6) is even, so it meets no S_5 ⊂ S_6. This holds for both the point-stabiliser S_5 and the transitive PGL_2(F_5), where x ↦ 2x fixes 0 and ∞.

2. Direct check, done in python (work/agents/X-K3-15-B/f5.py). Mod 5, f ≡ (x−2)^4(x−4). f(x+2) = x^5 + 8x^4 + 30x^3 + 60x^2 + 60x + 20, with 5-adic valuations 0,0,1,1,1,1 from the leading coefficient down. The Newton polygon has a segment of slope 1/4 of length 4 and a segment of slope 0 of length 1. So over Q_5, f is a totally and tamely ramified irreducible quartic times a linear factor. The linear factor is the simple root ≡ 4, which is in Z_5 by Hensel. Since μ_4 ⊂ Q_5, the quartic field is cyclic Kummer, and inertia permutes its four roots as a 4-cycle. The point ∞ is rational. disc(f) = 2^8·3·5^3·19, and v_5 = 3 = e − 1 fits this. Mod p factorisation patterns are [2,3] at p = 7 and [5] at p = 17, and the discriminant is not a square, so Gal = S_5 on the roots, as printed. A[2] is the even subsets of the six Weierstrass points modulo the whole set, so the image of inertia is ⟨(1,2,3,4)⟩, not ⟨(1,2,3,4)(5,6)⟩. The isomorphism S_6 ≅ GSp_4(F_2) may be taken via either of the two 6-sets. This does not help the printed text: automorphisms preserve sign, so the outer automorphism fixes both the (4) class and the (4,2) class.

3. Defence attempted and failed. The phrase "slight variation of this argument" can explain why the example has 5 = 𝔭^4𝔮 in the quintic field rather than 𝔭^4𝔮^2 in a sextic. It cannot save the explicit assertion about the class. The assertion follows from the earlier claim that the unique class with (σ−1)^2 ≠ 0 is (4,2). That claim is itself inaccurate. On F_2^4, the ranks of (σ−1)^k for k = 1..4 are [3,2,1,0] for both (1,2,3,4) and (1,2,3,4)(5,6) (jordan.py). Both are single Jordan blocks. Since σ^2 ≠ 1, every order-4 element has (σ−1)^2 = σ^2 − 1 ≠ 0. This matches the count 720/4 = 180 = 90 + 90 of regular unipotents. The authors intended (4,2); this is not a typo whose meaning is clear from context, so it is an error rather than a misprint.

4. Consequences. The 4-cycle is also regular unipotent: by the paper's own test (σ−1)^2 ≠ 0 it is U3-like. The literal U3 definition via exp(N_3) is not defined mod 2. So Iwahori level at 5 and paramodular level at 3 and 19 are unchanged. The conductor exponent 3 at 5 is also consistent: inertia eigenvalues 1, −1, i, −i give 4 − 1 = 3. §5.4 is a speculative remark. Nothing later cites the example (grep finds no other mention), and Theorem 5.9 is independent of it.

issues.printed: THEOREM 5.9 If π is a cuspidal automorphic representation associated to a Siegel modular form of weight (2, 2), then π_x is not the Steinberg representation for any p.
issues.correction: ... then π_x is not the Steinberg representation for any prime x.
issues.reason: The local component is indexed by x, and p is the fixed residue characteristic of the whole paper. 'For any p' binds nothing in the statement. The proof works at an arbitrary prime x: the Steinberg Frobenius eigenvalues are x^{(w±3)/2}, x^{(w±1)/2} with w = j + k − 3, and the U_{x,1}-eigenvalue is x^{(w−3)/2}. I rendered p. 810, 825, 828, 829, 833, 834, 854 and 855 and zoomed in on the relevant lines. All the quoted text is confirmed.

(1) There is no Proposition 5.6. The numbered statements in §5 are Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Definition 5.3, Lemma 5.4, Theorem 5.5, Theorem 5.6, Definition 5.7, Corollary 5.8, Theorem 5.9, Remarks 5.10–5.12 and Definitions 5.13–5.14. No "PROPOSITION 5.x" appears anywhere in the paper. Theorem 5.6(2) is the statement giving the infinitesimal character of the transfer to GL4(R), so it is the intended reference.

I redid the check myself. With c = 3−a−b (Remark 5.11), Theorem 5.6 gives w = −(a+b+2c) = a+b−6 and σ = (−b,−a;−w) = (−b,−a;6−a−b), which agree with Remarks 5.10 and 5.12. Putting w = a+b−6 into Theorem 5.6(2) gives τ = (3/2, 7/2−b, 5/2−a, 9/2−a−b). This equals (0, −(b−2), −(a−1), −(a+b−3)) + 3/2(1,1,1,1), so the formula in Remark 5.12 is right and only the label is wrong.

(2) On p. 810, P^− is defined as the unipotent radical of Q^− = K^h_C P^−, so Lie P^− = p^−. The objects H^i_{∗,σ} that Theorem 5.2 is about are defined on p. 825 with (Lie Q^−, K^h). The paper never defines (Lie P^−, K^h)-cohomology, and (p^−, K^h) is not a pair in the usual sense, since Lie K^h is not contained in p^−. The proof of Theorem 5.5 obtains its display directly "by Theorem 5.2", so the intended object is the Lie Q^− one. The slip probably comes from the fraktur-P notation 𝔓 = k ⊕ p^− used in Harris [37] and in [9].

The mathematics is unaffected. p^− is an ideal of Lie Q^− = k^h_C ⊕ p^−, and K^h is compact. So if one reads the misprinted object as K^h-invariants of p^−-cohomology, it is isomorphic to (Lie Q^−, K^h)-cohomology. This makes the error purely notational.

The candidate's locator is incomplete. The same "Lie P^−" also appears three times in the proof of Theorem 7.11 on pp. 854–855, and the correction applies there too.

The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 has identical text: "Furthermore, by Proposition 5.6," on p. 26, with the same statement numbering, and "H^i(Lie P^−, K^h; π∞ ⊗ V_σ)) ≠ 0" with the doubled parenthesis on p. 822. It also has "Lie P^−" on p. 823, 840 and 841, and defines H with "Lie Q^−" on p. 819.

"Affects nothing" is correct. Later results cite Remark 5.12 (p. 854, proof of Theorem 7.11), but the content of Remark 5.12 is correct.

A separate, unrelated misprint turned up while checking: on p. 854 the subscript "χ_{(0,0−(a−1),−(a−1))+3/2(1,1,1,1)}" is missing a comma. It should read (0,0,−(a−1),−(a−1)), which is Remark 5.12 with b = 2.

issues.correction:
In §5.5 the "key property" should read as follows. For the weights in question (k ≥ 3 for the first operator, j ≥ 4 for the second), T_{p,1} ≡ U_{p,1} mod p and p^{3−k}T_{p,2} (= T_{p,2}/p^{k−3}) ≡ U_{p,2} mod p. The division by p^{k+j−6} is wrong. U_{p,2} here is Tilouine's ordinary operator from [68, Lemme 8.5], which is the operator used in the proof of Lemma 6.2. In the notation of Lemma 8.4 it is Z_2 (= UZ), not U_2. The two agree mod p on q-expansions, since p^{3−k}T_2 = p^{j−3}U_2 + Z_2 + p^{j+k−3}V_2 ≡ Z_2 when j ≥ 4.

Correspondingly, §8.3 should not identify U_{p,2} with U_2. The U_2 = −1 + pX_2 of Lemma 8.4 and Definition 8.5 is the Gauss-sum term from the A = pI cosets, and it is ≡ −1 mod p. It is not a U_p-type operator. The minimal fix is:
- on p. 833, replace "T_{p,2}/p^{k+j−6} act by" with "p^{3−k}T_{p,2} act (mod p) by";
- on p. 858, drop "and U_{p,2}" / "and U_2", or say that U_{p,2} corresponds to Z_2.

This fix makes the proof of Lemma 6.2 consistent with §5.5 and §8. The corrected normalisation still holds on (j,k) + m(p−1)(1,1) for m ≥ 1, because then j' ≥ p+1 ≥ 4 and k' ≥ p+1 ≥ 3.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 833, 836, 858, 859, 860, 863 and 864, and the quoted text matches the page images.

**How the weights line up.** Section 8 writes weights as σ = (j,k) with j ≥ k ≥ 2 (Lemma 8.12). The paper's Q_2 = (pT_2 + (p+p^3)S)p^{2−k} matches Q_{p,2} = (pT_{p,2} + (p+p^3)S_p)p^{2−b} on p. 833. So (j,k) = (a,b).

**The computation, redone.** Lemma 8.4 gives T_2 = p^{k+j−6}U_2 + p^{k−3}Z_2 + p^{2k+j−6}V_2.
- Multiplying by p^{3−k} gives p^{3−b}T_{p,2} = p^{a−3}U_2 + Z_2 + p^{a+b−3}V_2. This is ≡ Z_2 mod p when a ≥ 4.
- By Definition 8.5, U_2 = −1 + pX_2 ≡ −1 mod p. Since Z_2 has unit eigenvalue αβ on ordinary forms (Lemma 8.12), p^{3−b}T_{p,2} is not ≡ U_2.
- Dividing by p^{k+j−6} instead gives T_2/p^{k+j−6} = U_2 + p^{3−j}Z_2 + p^kV_2. For j ≥ 4 this is not integral, so the "key property" stated in §5.5 is false. It gets worse as the weight grows, not better.
- Lemma 8.12 (p. 864) repeats this calculation and concludes Q_2 ≡ Z_2 (for (j,k) ≠ (2,2)), with the eigenvalue of Z_2 being αβ mod p. §8.5 (p. 863) likewise puts the ordinary eigenvalue on p^{3−k}T_2, not on T_2/p^{k+j−6}.

**Consequence.** Under the paper's own cross-references (§5.5 says the explicit definition is in Lemma 8.4; §8.3 identifies U_{p,2} with U_2), "p^{3−b}T_{p,2} ≡ U_{p,2}" on p. 836 is false. It is true only for Tilouine's operator, which the proof cites. So the symbol U_{p,2} is overloaded, and §5.5 misstates the normalisation. That is a genuine notational and misstatement slip, not a mathematical error.

**Tilouine's paper.** I downloaded Tilouine, Ann. Inst. Fourier 62 (2012), pp. 1417 and 1419. Lemme 8.5 is exactly as the proof cites it, and Lemme 8.7 says multiplication by H commutes with U_{p,2}.

**Scope of "affects: nothing".** The statement and proof of Lemma 6.2 are unaffected when U_{p,2} is read as Tilouine's operator, which the citation forces. That statement is used later in Remark 6.5 and in the proof of Theorem 6.13. Section 8 uses U_2 only in Lemma 8.4, Definition 8.5 and Lemma 8.12, consistently with its own definition. The sentence in §5.5 is not used in any proof.

**A separate edge case, not part of this claim** (low confidence): at (a,b) = (3,3), Lemma 8.4 gives T_{p,2} ≡ Z_2 − 1. Also, the S-term of Q_{p,2} is ≡ 1 in weight (3,3) but ≡ 0 in weight (p+2,p+2). So the claim is right to restrict the Z_2 identification to a ≥ 4.

**arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1) has the same text:** §5.5 (the only difference is "Their explicit definition in given" instead of "is given"), the proof of Lemma 6.2 citing [Til12, Lemme 8.5], and §8.3, Lemma 8.4 and Definition 8.5. I looked for a defence and found none that works. I checked the page images of p. 833, 836, 858, 859, 863 and 864.

**The first half of the sentence is fine.** Lemma 8.3 gives T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V, so T_{p,1} ≡ U_{p,1} = U mod p once k ≥ 3.

**The second half is false in every reading I tried.** Lemma 8.4 gives T_2/p^{k+j−6} = U_2 + p^{3−j}Z_2 + p^kV_2.
- For j ≥ 4 the Z_2 term has a negative power of p. Z_2 has the unit eigenvalue αβ on ordinary forms (Lemma 8.12), so the operator is not even p-integral.
- For j = 3 the operator is ≡ U_2 + Z_2, not U_2.
- The congruence holds only in weight (2,2), where p^2T_2 ≡ U_2. That is the opposite of "large enough weights", and adding (p−1)(1,1) makes the exponent 3−j−m(p−1) worse.

**Could Lemma 8.4 be the misprinted statement instead?** No. Three independent checks agree with Lemma 8.4 and disagree with p. 833.
1. **The paper's own Frobenius polynomial (p. 863).** The X^2 coefficient is pμ + (p^3+p)p^{k+j−6} = αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}), so v_p(μ) = k−3 for ordinary forms. For j = k this matches the classical identity T(p)^2 − T(p^2) − p^{2k−4} = pT_1(p^2) + (p^3+p)p^{2k−6}. Example: for a Saito–Kurokawa lift of an ordinary f, the Frobenius roots are β_1, p^{k−2}, p^{k−1}, β_2, so e_2 has valuation k−2 and μ has valuation k−3 < 2k−6 when k ≥ 4.
2. **Lemma 8.12 (p. 864).** It computes p^{3−k}T_2 = p^{j−3}U_2 + Z_2 + p^{j+k−3}V_2 and concludes Q_2 ≡ Z_2.
3. **Tilouine.** Lemme 8.5 of [68], which I read in the downloaded copy (Ann. Inst. Fourier 62 (2012), p. 1417), says "Pour k ⩾ j ⩾ 3 … T_{p,1}|_V ≡ U_{p,1}, p^{3−j}T_{p,2}|_V ≡ U_{p,2} (mod p)". Tilouine's smaller weight j is the paper's k, and his U_{p,2} = p^{−3−j}Ũ_{p,P} is integral (his Lemme 8.4).

So the correct normalisation is p^{3−k}, and p^{k+j−6} is just the U_2 coefficient read off Lemma 8.4. Together with the §8.3 naming (U_{p,2} → U_2), this shows a substantive confusion between the Gauss-sum term U_2 ≡ −1 and the U_p-type term Z_2, not a one-symbol slip. That is why I classify it as an error rather than a misprint.

**Is Remark 5.10's ν^{-3} twist a way out?** No. The proof of Lemma 6.2 uses Tilouine's correct normalisation p^{3−b}T_{p,2}, so the paper uses U_{p,2} for two different operators. Also, §5.5's Q_{p,2} = (pT_{p,2} + (p+p^3)S_p)p^{2−b} is literally §8's Q_2, so T_{p,2} and T_2 carry the same normalisation.

**What uses the passage.** Only three places mention U_{p,1} and U_{p,2}: p. 833, 836 and 858.
- Lemma 6.2(2) (used later in Remark 6.5 and Theorem 6.13) is proved by citing Tilouine directly, with the correct normalisation.
- The Hecke algebras (Definition 5.13, p. 835) and the ordinary idempotent use T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. So do p. 843 and Lemma 8.8.
- Section 8 (Lemma 8.6, Lemma 8.12, Theorem 8.13 and its proof, pp. 864–874) works with Lemma 8.4's own U_2, X_2, Z_2 and Q_2, and uses them consistently with their definitions there.

No proof relies on the false normalisation, so the error affects nothing. All five candidate corrections are right in substance. One small fix to H-h3-14: [68] is Tilouine, not Pilloni ([57]). The identification with Z_2 needs j ≥ 4.

**A separate edge case, not part of this finding.** At (a,b) = (3,3), Lemma 8.4 gives T_2 ≡ Z_2 − 1, whereas Q_2 ≡ Z_2 by Lemma 8.12. So the claim "Tilouine U_{p,2} = Z_2" should carry the qualifier j ≥ 4.

issues.correction: No change is needed for a ≥ 4. There (1+p^2)p^{3−b}S_p = (1+p^2)p^{a−3} is ≡ 0 mod p in both weights, so the printed argument works. For (a,b) = (3,3), replace the argument with a q-expansion argument. Lemma 8.3 gives T_{p,1} ≡ U mod p once b ≥ 3. The formal computation in the proof of Lemma 8.12 (Lemma 8.4 plus U_2 = −1 + pX_2) gives Q_{p,2} ≡ Z_2 mod p in weight (3,3) and in weight (p+2,p+2). This computation is a formal identity and also holds at (3,3), even though Remark 8.2's standing assumption formally leaves out j = 3. U and Z_2 act on q-expansions by formulas that depend only on a−b, and h has q-expansion 1, so Theorem 8.1 gives the commutation. The proof should also stop citing the congruence p^{3−b}T_{p,2} ≡ U_{p,2} at b = 3, because it is false at (3,3): there p^0·T_{p,2} ≡ Z_2 − 1, and the unit S_p term cancels the −1. An alternative with no downstream cost is to exclude (3,3) from Lemma 6.2(2), from the b ≥ 3 map in Remark 6.5, and from Theorem 6.13. The statement of Lemma 6.2(2) is true as printed.
issues.reason: I redid the computation using the paper's own formulas, checked on the page images. Q_{p,2} = p^{3−b}T_{p,2} + (1+p^2)p^{3−b}S_p (Def. 5.13, §8.4). In weight (p+2,p+2) it is (1+p^2)p^{p−1} ≡ 0. If U_{p,2} commutes with h and p^{3−b}T_{p,2} ≡ U_{p,2} in both weights, as the proof claims, then Q^{(p+2,p+2)}∘h − h∘Q^{(3,3)} ≡ −(1+p^2)h ≠ 0. So "It follows" is a non sequitur at a = b = 3. In fact the premise itself fails there. Lemma 8.4 gives T_2 = p^{k+j−6}U_2 + p^{k−3}Z_2 + p^{2k+j−6}V_2, and Definition 8.5 gives U_2 = −1 + p·X_2. Together they give p^{3−k}T_2 ≡ Z_2 − p^{j−3} mod p, which at (3,3) is Z_2 − 1. The §8.5 Hecke polynomial agrees: at (3,3), pμ = p(αβ + αβ^{-1}p + 2p^2 + ...) − (p^3+p), so μ ≡ αβ − 1. The ordinary operator that commutes with h has eigenvalue αβ. Tilouine's Lemme 8.5 (read from a copy in the scratch dir) is stated "Pour k ⩾ j ⩾ 3", so it includes (3,3). Its proof treats only two kernel types. The two errors cancel, and the conclusion is true by Lemma 8.12, as shown in the correction. For a ≥ 4 the printed proof is fine. Two small inaccuracies in the candidate: Remark 5.12 has no ⟨p⟩, and Lemma 8.12 already covers (3,3) despite Remark 8.2. Downstream effect: the proof of Theorem 6.13 uses Lemma 6.2(2) at its own weight a ≥ b ≥ 3, which includes (3,3). But Theorem 6.13 is only applied in Theorem 6.17, at μ' = (a+t, 2+t) with t = rp^{m−1}(p−1), so b' ≥ p+1. Lemma 7.4 uses only part (1). So at (3,3) the words "It follows" are a non sequitur, and one of the premises must be false. (iii) The false premise is the cited congruence. Lemma 8.4 gives T_2 = p^{k+j−6}U_2 + p^{k−3}Z_2 + p^{2k+j−6}V_2, and Definition 8.5 gives U_2 = −1+pX_2. Together they give p^{3−k}T_2 ≡ Z_2 − p^{j−3}. That is Z_2 − 1 at (3,3) and Z_2 for j ≥ 4. The eigenvalue of p^{3−k}T_2 is ≡ αβ−1 at (3,3) and ≡ αβ at (4,4), (7,7) and (9,9). The S-term is ≡ 1 at (3,3) and 0 otherwise. The eigenvalue of Q_2 is ≡ αβ in every case. The sum of these contributions over the rank-1 symmetric S is p(D/p)−1, which matches the paper's formula a(U_2F,Q) = (−1+p(D/p))a(Q). issues.printed: (4) Suppose that f is ordinary in the sense that it is an eigenform for T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} with eigenvalues being p-adic units. Then Q_p(X) has distinct eigenvalues α_p, β_p, γ_p, δ_p with p-adic valuations 0, b − 2, a − 1, w, respectively.
issues.correction: Then λ_f(Q_p(X)) (the characteristic polynomial of Φ on D_cris(r_f | G_{Q_p}), by (3)) has distinct roots α_p, β_p, γ_p, δ_p with p-adic valuations 0, b − 2, a − 1, w, respectively.
issues.reason: By Definition 6.7, Q_p(X) is a polynomial whose coefficients are Hecke operators. A polynomial has roots, not eigenvalues, and a p-adic valuation only makes sense for the roots of its specialisation λ_f(Q_p(X)) ∈ K'[X]. Item (3) uses exactly this notation: 'the characteristic polynomial of Φ … is λ_f(Q_p(X))'. With that reading everything checks. The ordinary crystalline Frobenius roots have valuations equal to the Hodge–Tate weights 0, b−2, a−1, w from (3). Since a ≥ b ≥ 3, these satisfy 0 < b−2 < a−1 < w, which gives distinctness. Their sum is 2a+2b−6 = v(p^6 λ_f(S_p)^2) with v(λ_f(S_p)) = w = a+b−6, as Prop. 6.6(1) requires. The diagonal matrix entries λ(α_p), ε^{−(b−2)}λ(p^{−(b−2)}β_p), … also agree. This is an abuse of wording whose meaning is clear: a misprint, not an error.

issues.locator: §6.2 (Preliminaries on Galois representations), proof of Proposition 6.8, second paragraph, p. 839
issues.printed: "We take r_f : G_Q → GL_4(\overline{K}) to be the representation R_p of [55, Theorem 3.5] associated to π. When π is simple, generic in the terminology of [55], the representation can be conjugated to take values in GSp_4(\overline{K}), by the main theorem of [6]." (checked against the rendered image of PDF page 39)
issues.correction: "by the main theorem of [7]", i.e. [7, Theorem 1.2] (Bellaïche–Chenevier, "The sign of Galois representations attached to automorphic forms for unitary groups", Compos. Math. 2011), applied through the GL_4 transfer and descent to a unitary group as in the proof of Lemma 6.9 on p. 840. [6] (Astérisque 324) only states this result, as Theorem 9.5.1, and explicitly leaves the proof for even dimension to [7].
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 839 and the printed text matches. Reference [6] is BELLAÏCHE–CHENEVIER, Families of Galois representations and Selmer groups, Astérisque 324 (2009); its back-reference "(39)" shows it is cited only here. Reference [7] is their sign paper, Compos. Math. 147 (2011), back-reference "(40)". On p. 840 (proof of Lemma 6.9) the paper uses "[7, Theorem 1.2]" to show that r_f is symplectic, which is the same fact.

I checked both cited works myself:
(a) The arXiv version of [7] (0804.2860, v1 only) states its main result as "Theorem 1.2. For every finite prime λ of E(Π), every irreducible factor of ρ_{Π,λ} that satisfies (1) has sign +1." It also says this theorem "appears, without its proof, in the concluding remarks of our book [BCh] (see [BCh, theorem 9.5.1])".
(b) The Numdam copy of [6]: its introduction places the "main results" in chapters 8–9, which are about lower bounds for Selmer groups. There, "sign conjecture" means the root-number/Selmer-group conjecture, not the symplectic/orthogonal question. §9.5.1 (a "Remarks, questions, and complements" section) states Theorem 9.5.1 (^tQ = Q) and then says: "If m is odd, then it is clear that e = 1. We postpone the proof that this result also holds for an even m to a subsequent work", with a footnote to the sign paper, i.e. [7]. The case needed here is m = 4, which is even, so [6] does not prove the claim, and it is not [6]'s main theorem in any case. The only reading that makes "the main theorem of" accurate is [7].

The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 (p. 29–30) has the same text, "by the main theorem of [BC09]". Its next lemma cites "[BC11, Theorem 1.2]". So the slip was the authors' (BC09 written for BC11), not an error introduced by typesetting the numbered labels.

On the effect: the mathematics is unchanged, because the claim holds with the correct reference, applied as in Lemma 6.9. The conclusion r_f : G_Q → GSp_4(K′) is used later (Lemma 6.9, Prop. 6.8(5) in §6.3), but it does not depend on which reference is cited.

A side point, outside this candidate: [7] only gives sign +1 for irreducible polarized factors. The case "simple generic but R_p reducible" is not addressed explicitly in this proof, and that would be a separate question.

issues.locator: §6.3, choice of the auxiliary prime q and item (7) defining K_q, pp. 840–841; cf. §5.2, p. 821 and Assumption 4.2, p. 813
issues.printed: p. 40, §6.3 (checked on the rendered page): "By Assumption 4.2 and Chebotarev, there exist infinitely many primes q such that no pair of eigenvalues of r̄(Frob_q) have ratio q mod p and q ≢ 1 mod p. Choose any such q which is disjoint to p and all primes of bad reduction of r̄. We take S = S(r̄) ∪ {q} and Q a possibly empty set of primes disjoint from S ∪ {p}. We define a compact open subgroup K = ∏_x K_x of GSp4(A^∞) as follows: (1) If x = p or r̄ is unramified at x and x ≠ q, then K_x = GSp4(Z_x). ..." p. 41: "(7) If x = q, then K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x. We then let X = X_K and X_i(Q) = X_{K_i(Q)} as in Section 5.2." The sources for the neatness requirement, also checked on the page images: p. 21, §5.2: "We assume that the subgroup K is neat. (This will be the case if S contains a prime x ≥ 3 where K_x is the full congruence subgroup of level x.)" p. 13, Assumption 4.2 (Neatness): "This condition is imposed to avoid dealing with stacks."
issues.correction: Change it to "Choose any such q ≠ 2 (that is, q ≥ 3) which is disjoint to p and all primes of bad reduction of r̄." This is always possible because the printed conditions allow infinitely many q. With q ≥ 3, K_q = Γ(q) is neat, so K is neat by the §5.2 criterion. This is the smallest fix that works. Nothing else in §§6–9 has to change.
issues.reason:
1. The purpose of q. The only role of adding q with full level is to make K neat. §5.2 assumes "K is neat" so that Y_K is a fine moduli scheme with a universal abelian variety A. Assumption 4.2 is titled "Neatness" and is "imposed to avoid dealing with stacks". The paper's own sufficient condition (§5.2, p. 821) needs a prime x ≥ 3 with full congruence level.

2. The printed conditions do not exclude q = 2.
- The condition q ≢ 1 mod p holds automatically for q = 2.
- q = 2 is excluded only when r̄ is ramified at 2.
- The ratio condition can hold at 2. Concrete case: take r̄ = A[p] for an abelian surface A with good reduction at 2, for example the conductor-277 surface in the BCGP setting. The Frobenius eigenvalues λ_i at 2 have |λ_i| = √2 under every complex embedding. So every ratio λ_i/λ_j has absolute value 1, never 2. Hence ∏_{i,j}(λ_i − 2λ_j) is a nonzero integer. For every p not dividing it, no two eigenvalues of r̄(Frob_2) have ratio 2 mod p.
- So q = 2 meets every printed requirement for all but finitely many p. 803. Full level 2 is not neat. The kernel of GSp4(Z_2) → GSp4(Z/2) contains −1, and −1 also lies in GSp4(Z_x), I(x), Π(x), P(x) and K(x). So if every x ∈ S(r̄) is of type U1, U2 or U3, then −1 ∈ K. Its eigenvalue −1 at every place violates Pink neatness. Also, −1 is an automorphism of every principally polarised abelian surface that preserves any K-level structure, so Y_K is not a fine moduli scheme. If S(r̄) contains a type P prime x, then diag(1,−1,−1,1) (in the Klingen Levi with λ = 1, A = −I) lies in Π(x)^+, in Γ(2) and in all the other K_y, so K is again not neat. Only a type H prime x ≥ 3 would save neatness, and nothing guarantees one exists. For q ≥ 3 the argument works: g ≡ 1 mod q has eigenvalues in 1 + qO, and for q ≥ 3 this group contains no nontrivial roots of unity, because v(ζ_q − 1) = 1/(q−1) < 1.

4. The gap is genuine but trivial. The authors clearly intended q ≥ 3, since their own §5.2 criterion says so. The text "Choose any such q" omits the condition, and nothing elsewhere in the paper excludes q = 2 (searched: no "q ≠ 2", "q ≥ 3" or "q odd").

5. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text: "Choose any such q which is disjoint to p and all primes of bad reduction of r." Its (7) and its §5.2 parenthetical ("x ≥ 3") are also identical.

6. On 'affects'. The claim says "nothing"; I would say "the proof". The level K from §6.3 is used in Theorems 6.13 and 6.17 and in the main Theorem 9.1. Theorem 9.1's statement itself says "let K ⊂ GSp4(A^∞) be the compact open subgroup defined as in the beginning of Section 6.3. Let X = X_K". For q = 2 this set-up breaks the standing neatness assumption of §5.2 that all of §§5–9 rely on. No conclusion changes: q is an auxiliary choice, and the ratio condition makes all lifts unramified at q. So after the one-word repair no stated result is false. The gap is in the argument's set-up, not in any conclusion. Defence attempts, all of which fail:
(1) Do the printed conditions exclude q = 2? No. Theorem 9.1 assumes p − 1 > a ≥ 2, so p ≥ 5, and then 2 ≢ 1 mod p holds automatically. q = 2 is excluded only when r̄ is ramified at 2. The ratio condition can hold at 2. For example, if r̄ = A[p] with A an abelian surface with good reduction at 2, the Frobenius eigenvalues λ_i have |λ_i| = √2. So λ_i − 2λ_j ≠ 0, and the condition holds for every p not dividing the nonzero integer ∏(λ_i − 2λ_j). "Such q" is defined by the property itself, not by membership in a Chebotarev class, so q = 2 is allowed whenever the property holds.
(2) Could another K_x make K neat? Only a type H prime x ≥ 3 could, and nothing guarantees one exists. −I lies in Γ(2), because −I ≡ I mod 2. It also lies in GSp4(Z_x), I(x), Π(x) and K(x), and in Π(x)^+ because λ(−I) = 1. So if S(r̄) has no type H prime x ≥ 3, then −1 ∈ K. That makes K not neat: its eigenvalue −1 is torsion, and −1 is an automorphism of every object preserving the level structure. Then Y_K is not a fine moduli scheme and has no universal abelian variety 𝒜, which §5.2 requires.
(3) Is the §5.2 standing hypothesis "K is neat" meant to cover this? Read charitably, §6.3's "as in Section 5.2" does assume neatness. But then the choice "any such q" does not deliver that hypothesis, and the only tool the paper offers, the §5.2 parenthetical, needs x ≥ 3. I searched the whole paper and found no "q ≠ 2", "q ≥ 3" or "q odd".
(4) Does q = 2 break anything else? No. The proof of Theorem 6.13 (p. 844) uses q only to show that H^2(Q_q, ad^0 r̄) ≅ H^0(Q_q, ad^0 r̄(1))^∨ = 0, so that all lifts are unramified at q. That still works for q = 2 when p ≥ 5. Neatness is the only thing that fails.
Consequences: the K of §6.3 is the level used in Theorems 6.13 and 6.17, in §§7–8 (both set up "as in Section 5.2": Siegel 3-folds, the universal 𝒜, Hasse invariants), and in the main Theorem 9.1. That theorem's statement says "let K ⊂ GSp4(A^∞) be the compact open subgroup defined as in the beginning of Section 6.3. Let X = X_K". For q = 2 the proof as printed runs on a non-neat K, where its own set-up is undefined (a stack rather than the scheme of §5.2). No conclusion becomes false: q is an auxiliary choice, the theorem's hypotheses do not involve q, and a reader free to choose q ≥ 3 gets everything. So this is a genuine but trivially repairable gap in the proof's set-up. Affects is "the proof", not "nothing": the text lists the conditions on q explicitly and omits a needed one. It is not "a stated result" either, since after choosing q ≥ 3 no stated result changes.

p. 41 (§6.3, before Theorem 6.13): "H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_M)^β to be the subspace of H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_M) given by the image of the idempotent e_β = lim_{→n}((T_{p,1} − β̃)(Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃))^{n!}, where α̃ and β̃ are lifts of α and β to O;"

The assumption that r̄ is Katz modular implies that this space is nonzero after localization at m."
Both checked on page images rendered at 110 and 250 dpi. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text: v1 p. 31 "e_β = lim_{→n}((T_{p,1} − β̃)(Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃))^{n!}" and v1 p. 33 "Let e_{α,β} be the idempotent lim_{→n}((T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)(Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃))^{n!}".
issues.correction:
Define each idempotent as the projector onto the summand where the shifted operators are topologically nilpotent:
- e_β := (1 − lim_n (T_{p,1} − β̃)^{n!})·(1 − lim_n (Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃)^{n!}). Swap α and β to get e_α.
- e_{α,β} := (1 − lim_n (T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)^{n!})·(1 − lim_n (Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃)^{n!}).
In words, this is the summand on which T_{p,1} − β̃ (resp. T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃) and Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃ are topologically nilpotent. The two factors commute. This is exactly π_β of Theorem 8.13 (p. 865) and the meaning used on p. 843, 846 and 867. The candidates' correction (the same in all six entries) is right and minimal. It is minimal because neither the printed e nor 1 − e works. Printed e_β keeps the part where T ≢ β AND Q ≢ αβ. 1 − e_β keeps the part where T ≡ β OR Q ≡ αβ, which after localising at m still contains the α-part. The intended summand is the intersection, where T ≡ β AND Q ≡ αβ.
issues.reason:
I redid the computation. Take a finite O-algebra, or a finite-length module over the commutative algebra generated by T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. On each local factor, x^{n!} → 1 if x is a unit and x^{n!} → 0 if x lies in the maximal ideal. So lim((T−c)(Q−d))^{n!} is 1 exactly on the factors where both T−c and Q−d are units. The printed e_β therefore keeps the part where T_{p,1} ≢ β and Q_{p,2} ≢ αβ. The printed e_{α,β} keeps the part where T_{p,1} ≢ α+β and Q_{p,2} ≢ αβ.

The paper itself uses the standard convention elsewhere, so there is no other reading:
- p. 835: the ordinary projector is e = lim(T_{p,1}Q_{p,2})^{n!}.
- p. 847: m contains xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x, and pr_x = lim(R'_x)^{n!}, where R_x is the product of the factors for the other eigenvalues (the ones to avoid).
- p. 866, proof of Lemma 8.14: "π_β : N_α ⊕ N_β → N_β is given by π_β = (U − α)^m".

The paper's own uses contradict the printed formulas:
(i) p. 843, proof of Theorem 6.13: "We also have T_{p,1} ≡ β mod m and Q_{p,2} ≡ αβ mod m in T_{μ'}(Q)^β_m (by definition of the idempotent e_β)". The printed e_β gives the opposite.
(ii) p. 865, Theorem 8.13: "π_β denotes the projection onto the summand where U − β and Q_2 − αβ (equivalently, Z_2 − αβ) are nilpotent".
(iii) p. 867, proof of Lemma 8.15, for M = H^0(...)^{α,β}_m: "by assumption we know that Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent".
(iv) Definition 6.15 gives a Katz-modular eigenform η with T_{p,1}η = (α+β)η and Q_{p,2}η = αβη. So (T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)(Q_{p,2} − α̃β̃) kills η, and the printed e_{α,β} sends η to 0. Yet p. 845 says Katz modularity "implies that this space is nonzero after localization at m". Read literally, that claim fails.

This is a real error in the definitions, not a quirk of notation. The intent is clear from the uses above, and all the proofs work with the intended summand. Defence attempted; it fails.

(1) The paper's own convention. lim_{→n} x^{n!} is the idempotent onto the local factors where x is a unit, and 0 where x lies in the maximal ideal. Three places in the paper use it that way:
- p. 835: the ordinary idempotent is e = lim_{→n}(T_{p,1}Q_{p,2})^{n!}.
- p. 847: pr_x = lim(R'_x)^{n!}, where R_x is the product of the factors for the three eigenvalues to be avoided, and m contains xU_{x,2} − α'β'.
- p. 866, proof of Lemma 8.14: on N_α ⊕ N_β, "π_β = (U − α)^m". Here the factor for the unwanted eigenvalue appears, not (U − β).
No other reading of the notation is available.

(2) What the printed formula gives. The printed e_β keeps exactly the factors where T_{p,1} ≢ β and Q_{p,2} ≢ αβ. The printed e_{α,β} keeps the factors where T_{p,1} ≢ α+β and Q_{p,2} ≢ αβ. Either way, the kept part is disjoint from the intended summand. It is not the complement, as some candidate texts say.

Toy check (python, p = 7, α = 2, β = 3, working mod 7^6 with n = 40). I used three pieces:
- a Jordan β-block with (T, Q) = (β + N, αβ);
- an α-line with (α, αβ);
- a non-ordinary line with (7, 0).
The printed e_β has diagonal (0, 0, 0, 1): it kills the β-part and the α-part and keeps only the non-ordinary line. The corrected e_β is diag(1, 1, 0, 0).

(3) The paper intends the opposite, in several places:
- p. 843: "We also have T_{p,1} ≡ β mod m and Q_{p,2} ≡ αβ mod m in T_{μ'}(Q)^β_m (by definition of the idempotent e_β)". The proof there also needs the d_{p,i} to be units, i.e. ordinarity. The printed e_β keeps the non-ordinary part, where T ≡ Q ≡ 0.
- p. 865, Theorem 8.13: "π_β denotes the projection onto the summand where U − β and Q_2 − αβ … are nilpotent". This π_β is the e_β used in the maps e_β∘A^s on p. 846.
- p. 867, Lemma 8.15: "by assumption we know that Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent".
- p. 803: e = e_{α,β} is "a certain ordinary projection". The printed e_{α,β} is not ordinary, since it keeps T ≡ Q ≡ 0 whenever α+β ≠ 0.
- Definition 6.15: η satisfies T_{p,1}η = (α+β)η and Q_{p,2}η = αβη, and η is killed by ϖ ∈ m_∅. So the printed e_{α,β} sends η to 0. The next sentence ("Katz modular implies … nonzero after localization at m") therefore does not follow.
- At m, in the weights used (b' − 2 ≡ 0 mod p − 1 on p. 846), ordinary forms have Q_{p,2} ≡ d_{p,1}d_{p,2} ≡ αβ. So the printed ^β and ^{α,β} parts localised at m contain no ordinary forms at all.

No cited source or nearby statement rescues the printed formulas. It is a genuine error in the two definitions (same text in arXiv v1). The intended object is clear from context, which is why a reader could take it for a misprint. But the printed definition makes a sentence on p. 845 and the "by definition" step on p. 843 fail, and it enters the statements of the main theorems. So I class it as an error, not a misprint. X-K6-21's "misprint / nothing" is too weak.

Downstream uses:
- Theorem 6.13: statement (T_μ(Q)^β_m, d_{p,1} ≡ β) and proof. The α-analogue likewise.
- Theorem 6.17: statement (T_σ(Q)^{α,β}_m), and its proof on pp. 845–846 (e_β∘A^s, e_α∘A^s, Theorem 8.13).
- Theorem 8.13 and Lemma 8.15: the source and target superscripts.
- Theorem 9.1 (pp. 878–880): R^min → T^{α,β}_{σ,m∅} is an isomorphism, and H^0(…)^{α,β,∨}_{m∅} is free. Read literally this fails whenever the printed summand at m∅ is zero, because R^min ≠ 0.
- Theorem 1.2 (e = e_{α,β}), hence Theorem 1.1. Appendix Theorem A.1 depends on it indirectly (p. 889: it "follows as in Theorem 1.2").
With the corrected idempotents, every one of these proofs goes through exactly as written, because they already use the intended summand.

issues.printed: p. 42, proof of Theorem 6.13: "We thus fix an m > 0. Choose an integer s > 0 as in Lemma 6.4, and let t = rs(p−1). By Lemma 6.4 and Lemma 6.2(2), multiplication by A^s restricts to a map: H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{O/ϖ^m})^β_𝔪 ↪ H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a+t,b+t)(−∞)_{O/ϖ^m})^β_𝔪." p. 43: "This in turns gives rise to a surjective map T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}. Thus it suffices to prove the result in weight μ' := (a',b') := (a+t,b+t)." Later on p. 43: "For part (3), note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 factors as (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) for units d_{p,i} ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪." Statement (3), p. 42: "There are units d_{p,1},…,d_{p,4} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪 satisfying Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪[X]". The arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 has the same text and numbering (Theorem 6.13, p. 32 there).
issues.correction:
Replace plain multiplication by A^s with the composite e'_β∘A^s, where e'_β is the β-idempotent in weight μ'. The paper itself does this in Theorem 6.17 (p. 846, "e_β∘A^s") and Theorem 8.13 (π_β∘A).

Why the composite works:
- It is T_μ(Q)-equivariant. A^s commutes with the operators away from p (Lemma 6.4), and e'_β commutes with T_{μ'}(Q).
- It is injective on the β-part. Suppose x ≠ 0 and e'_β(A^s x) = 0, and let y = ϖ^{j−1}x ≠ 0 with ϖy = 0. Then y lies in H^0(…_{O/ϖ^m})[ϖ] = H^0(…_k) (Remark 6.5), in its β-part.
- On that ϖ-torsion, A^s acts as h^{rs}. By Lemma 6.2(2), iterated (every intermediate weight has b ≥ 3), h^{rs} commutes with T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2}. So A^s y is in the β-part of weight μ'.
- Hence 0 = ϖ^{j−1}e'_β(A^s x) = e'_β(A^s y) = h^{rs}y, which is nonzero by Lemma 6.2(1). This is a contradiction.

This gives the surjection T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪/I_{μ,m}. Parts (1), (2), (4), (3)(a) and (3)(b) then transfer from weight μ' to weight μ; for (3)(b), ε^t ≡ 1 mod p^m because (p−1)p^{m−1} | t.

What still needs an argument or a weaker statement: the part of (3) claiming the identity Q_p(X) = ∏(X − p^{n_i}d_{p,i}) with coefficients in T_μ(Q)^β_𝔪, in weight μ. The surjection does not see operators at p. The image of the weight-μ' polynomial is ≡ (X−d_{p,1})X^3 mod ϖ^m, not the weight-μ Q_p(X). Separately, "Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪" is only asserted; a priori T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} lie in T̃, not in T. Either weaken (3) to the existence of units d_{p,i} with (a) and (b), or add an argument.

Remarks on the two proposed corrections:
- Both are right. H-h2-3's phrase "only the shape (3b) transfers" should be "(3)(a) and (3)(b)".
- Its alternative, restricting to m ≤ b−2, also suffices for the only application (Theorem 6.17, where b'−2 = t ≥ m), but it weakens Theorem 6.13. The e'_β∘A^s fix is the minimal one.
issues.reason:
I confirmed the printed text from the page images; the arXiv text is identical.

1. The cited lemmas do not cover the step. Lemma 6.2(2) (p. 836) is only about h: H^0(ω(a,b)_k) → H^0(ω(a+p−1,b+p−1)_k), with coefficients in k. Lemma 6.4(2) (p. 837) gives equivariance for A^s mod ϖ^m only for T_{x,i} with x ∉ S∪Q∪{p} and U_{x,i} with x ∈ Q. Remark 6.5 (p. 837) itself extends the map to the tilde algebras only mod Ĩ_{μ,1}, i.e. for m = 1.

2. I redid the commutator computation. By Lemma 8.3 (p. 858), in weight (j,k) we have T = U + p^{k−2}Z + p^{k+j−3}V, where U and Z are given by formulas whose ρ depends only on j−k. The q-expansion of A^s is ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m, since p^{m−1} | s. Since t ≥ m, T^{(μ')}(A^sF) − A^sT^{(μ)}F ≡ −p^{b−2}ZF − p^{a+b−3}VF mod ϖ^m. This is nonzero in general once m > e(b−2); the candidate's "m > b−2" is the unramified case.

3. The step is not just unjustified; it fails in the GL2 analogue. Take f of level N prime to p and weight k ≥ 2 with a_p = α+β', α a unit and αβ' = p^{k−1}. Take E ≡ 1 mod p^m of weight k'−k. In weight k', T' ≡ U mod p^m. Put g = p^{k−1}Vf. Then T'f ≡ (α+β')f − g and T'g ≡ αβ'f, so (T'−α)(T'−β') = 0 on the span of f and g. Hence e_α f − f = β'(f − αVf)/(α−β'). Comparing q^1-coefficients shows this is nonzero mod p^m for m ≥ k. So Ef is not in the α-part of weight k'.

4. The reduction "it suffices to prove the result in weight μ'" does not handle (3). The coefficients of Q_p(X) (Definition 6.7) involve T_{p,1} and p^{b−2}Q_{p,2}, which lie in T̃ rather than T (Definition 5.13(3)). The candidate's list "T_{p,2}, S_p" is imprecise: S_p acts by the scalar p^{j+k−6} (proof of Lemma 8.12). The surjection sees no operators at p. The image of the weight-μ' polynomial is ≡ (X−d_1)X^3 mod ϖ^m, not the weight-μ polynomial. The proof also only asserts ("note that") that Q_p(X) lies in T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪.

5. Downstream effect. Theorem 6.13 is used only in Theorem 6.17, applied in weight μ' = (a+t, 2+t). That proof uses only (1), (2), (4), (3)(a) and (3)(b). Those survive the e_β∘A^s fix, so no stated downstream result is affected.

Side issues I noticed but did not report as findings:
- On p. 843, "p^{a−1}d_{p,1}" should read d_{p,3}.
- As printed, e_β = lim((T_{p,1}−β̃)(Q_{p,2}−α̃β̃))^{n!} projects onto the part where these operators are units. The text uses it for the part where they are nilpotent (compare Theorem 8.13). I checked the printed text on the page images of pp. 834–847, 857–858 and 864–866. The arXiv v1 text is identical.

Defence attempts, and why each fails:
(i) Cited lemmas. Lemma 6.4(2) (p. 837) gives equivariance of A^s mod ϖ^m only for T_{x,i} with x ∉ S∪Q∪{p} and U_{x,i} with x ∈ Q. Lemma 6.2(2) (p. 836) concerns h on mod-p forms. Remark 6.5 (p. 837) itself extends the map to the tilde algebras only mod Ĩ_{μ,1}, that is, for m = 1. So the paper's own lemmas cover the p-operators only mod ϖ.
(ii) Lemma 8.3 (p. 858). In weight (a,b), T_{p,1} = U + p^{b−2}Z + p^{a+b−3}V, and U, Z, V depend on the weight only through a−b. The q-expansion of A^s is ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m, and T' ≡ U mod ϖ^m in weight μ' because b+t−2 ≥ m. So T'A^s − A^sT ≡ −p^{b−2}Z − p^{a+b−3}V, which does not vanish mod ϖ^m once m > e(b−2).
(iii) The step genuinely fails; it is not merely unjustified. The β-part sits inside the part where T' is a unit, where T'^{n!} acts as the identity for n large. So A^s F ∈ β-part would force U^{n!}F ≡ F mod ϖ^m on q-expansions.
 - GL2 check (script in work/agents/lensB-h23/gl2_check.py). Take f = 11a, p = 3, a_3 = −1 (a unit), and E = E_4^3 ≡ 1 mod 9, weight 12. The q^1-coefficient of lim U^{n!}f is a_{3^{n!}} ≡ 4 mod 9. That is ≡ 1 mod 3 but ≠ 1 mod 9. So Ef is not in the ordinary part of weight 14 mod 9.
 - GSp4 analogue. If the claim held for all m, then P_1(U)F = F, i.e. UF = α_pF for a spherical eigenform F. For generic π_p this contradicts the nonvanishing of the spherical vector's components on the non-ordinary Siegel-parahoric U-eigenlines. This part rests on standard facts that I did not re-derive here.
(iv) Reading e_β literally does not rescue the step. As printed, e_β projects onto the part where the operators are units. Under that reading, (3)(a) and p. 843 ("T_{p,1} ≡ β mod 𝔪 … by definition of e_β") would contradict the definition. The intended meaning is the generalized eigenspace, as in Theorem 8.13. That is a separate misprint.

Consequences. Theorem 6.13 is used only in the proof of Theorem 6.17 (p. 846), in weight (a+t, 2+t); p. 863 cites it only as background. That proof uses (1), (2), (4) and (3)(a)/(b): the unramified rank-1 submodules with Frobenius lifting β, and the α-version. All of these survive the e'_β∘A^s fix. The membership of d_{p,i} in T rather than T̃ is also unargued, but in the application it can plausibly be supplied: under Section 4's hypotheses, r̄|G_{Q_p} is a sum of four distinct characters. Theorem 6.17 then feeds R = T on pp. 878–879, which is unaffected.

Only the unused identity clause of (3), in general weight μ, is left unproven. It is not shown to be false.

Side notes: on p. 843, "p^{a−1}d_{p,1}" should read d_{p,3}; S_p is a scalar, so H-h2-3's listing of S_p among the operators outside T is slightly imprecise.

issues.printed: Statement (p. 42): "(3) There are units d_{p,1}, …, d_{p,4} ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m satisfying Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) ∈ T_μ(Q)^β_m[X], and such that: (a) we have d_{p,1} mod m = β and d_{p,2} mod m = α; (b) r | G_{Q_p} is conjugate in GSp_4 to a representation of the form: [upper triangular, diagonal λ(d_{p,1}), ε^{−(b−2)}·λ(d_{p,2}), ε^{−(a−1)}·λ(d_{p,3}), ε^{−𝐰}·λ(d_{p,4})]." Proof (pp. 42–43): "This in turns gives rise to a surjective map T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}. Thus it suffices to prove the result in weight μ′ := (a′, b′) := (a + t, b + t). … For part (3), note that Q_p(X) ∈ T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m factors as (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,1})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}) for units d_{p,i} ∈ T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m."
issues.correction:
Three repairs are needed.
(i) Weight μ′. Here T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ⊂ ∏ O_{K_i} is reduced. Show that the d_{p,i} and the triangular form (b) are defined over T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m itself. Take a Frobenius lift φ ∈ G_{Q_p} with ε(φ) = 1. By §4, r̄(φ) is upper triangular with eigenvalues α, β, β^{−1}, α^{−1}, and these are pairwise distinct because (α²−1)(β²−1)(α²β²−1)(α−β) ≠ 0. So Hensel's lemma factors the characteristic polynomial of r(φ) over T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m. The ordinary flag of each r_{f_i} is a sum of the matching spectral lines, so it is cut out by projectors in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m[r(φ)], and d_{p,j} = ψ_j(φ) lies in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m. Then T_{p,1} = Σ p^{k_j} d_{p,j} and Q_{p,2} also lie in T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m, which gives the displayed identity in weight μ′.
(ii) Transport to weight μ. Carry only (3)(a) and (3)(b) down, using the images of the weight-μ′ units in T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}. This works because t = rs(p−1) with p^{m−1} | s, so ε^{t} ≡ 1 mod p^m. The d's are fixed by r, so they agree as m varies.

3. By p. 821, Π(x)/Π(x)^+ ≅ (Z/x)^× via λ mod x, where λ is the top-left entry of the Klingen Levi diag(λ, A, λ^{-1}det A). A scalar zI has λ = z, so Π(x) = Z_x^×·Π(x)^+. Hence Π(x)/Π(x)^+ acts on π_x^{Π(x)^+} through the central character on Z_x^×. By local Langlands, that character corresponds to ν(r_{f_i})|I_x. The proof itself says the same in the type-P case: "By [64, Corollary 3] all such characters have to lift the character ν∘r̄|I_x".

4. So in the "remaining case", where that character is nontrivial, ν(r_{f_i})|I_x = χ_{μ,0}|I_x ≠ 1. By step 1, r_{f_i} then does not satisfy Definition 4.6(5), and neither does the untwisted r. Such x ∈ Q really occur, because x ≡ 1 mod p and χ_{μ,0} is a character of p-power order. The theorem's statement includes the twist for exactly this reason.

5. A local model gives the same answer. Take the Klingen induction χ ⋊ τ with χ tamely ramified and τ unramified. Its L-parameter is φ_τ ⊕ χφ_τ, so inertia acts as 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ χ ⊕ χ. The two characters are mutually inverse only after twisting by ψ^{-1}, where ψ² = χ.

The fix is short and routine: the twist keeps (2)–(4), as in the correction. Theorem 6.13(4) as stated is therefore correct; only its proof is incomplete as printed. Defence tried and failed. Definition 4.6(5) (p. 815) forces ν|I_x = 1 for x ∈ Q. The reason: R^4 = V_1⊕V_2 with V_1, V_2 isotropic, so the pairing V_1×V_2 is perfect, and ⟨gv,gw⟩ = ξ(g)ξ(g)^{-1}⟨v,w⟩ gives ν(g) = 1. The proof's "remaining case" is exactly the case where this fails for the untwisted r_{f_i}.

What [64, Cor. 3] says: I read it in Sorensen's arXiv 0806.4967v1, and the wording there is: "ρ_{π,ι}|I_{F_v} = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ χ ⊕ χ … one can arrange for the two eigenspaces, for 1 and χ, to be totally isotropic." The case is not vacuous: Taylor–Wiles forms with nontrivial diamond character are exactly the ones treated here.

The twist announced in (4) never appears in the proof. With the twist, every check works (see correction), so (4) is true and the gap is routine. The twist must be by ψ^{-1}: tensoring with ψ gives inertial characters χ^{1/2} and χ^{3/2}, which are not inverse because χ has odd order greater than 1.

By Definition 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) is generated over T^an_μ(Q) by the U_{x,i} (x ∈ Q) and the ⟨u⟩. T_μ(Q)^β is its image in End(H^0(…)^β) (p. 841). The only justification the proof gives for the embedding is "Thus", following faithfulness on H^0(…) and H^0(…)_K.

The prime-to-level T_{x,i} are normal for the Petersson product and the ⟨u⟩ have finite order, so both are fine. Nothing in the paper addresses the U_{x,i} at Klingen-type level Π(x)^+. A search of the text for semisimplicity, reducedness, Petersson and diagonalization finds nothing relevant. Remark 6.14 only discusses torsion-freeness. The cited [20, Prop. 3.4.4] (Clozel–Harris–Taylor) is an argument for an anemic Hecke algebra, which is reduced for free.

Semisimplicity of U-operators at ramified level is not automatic in general (compare semisimplicity of U_p on old forms). The step also carries weight: the descent of ∏ r_{f_i} to T via [29, Lemma 7.1.1], and "it suffices to show that each r_{f_i} does so", both use the embedding.

I believe the claim is nevertheless true. By local–global compatibility, each π_x (x ∈ Q) is a principal series with parameter lifting four distinct characters, so the parameter is regular.
- Unramified case: π_x^{Π(x)^+} = π_x^{Π(x)}. Casselman's map gives an isomorphism onto the M(Z_x)-invariants of the Klingen Jacquet module. That module is a direct sum of 4 principal series with distinct cuspidal supports, each with a 1-dimensional spherical line. Both U_{x,1} (β_{x,1} is P-positive) and U_{x,2} (β_{x,2} is central in the Klingen Levi) act diagonally there.
- Tamely ramified case (Π(x) acting through ξ ≠ 1): the ξ-isotypic space is 1-dimensional.

So this is a fillable omission, not a false statement. It affects the proof, not the stated result. Checked on the rendered p. 843, with Def. 5.13 (pp. 834–835) and §5.1–5.2 (pp. 820–822).

(1) What the step needs. By Def. 5.13(2), T_μ(Q) is generated by the T_{x,i} (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}), the U_{x,i} = [K_1(Q)β_{x,i}K_1(Q)] for x ∈ Q, where K_{x,1} = Π(x)^+ is Klingen-type, and the ⟨u⟩. Faithful action on the finite free O-module H^0(…) shows only that T is O-torsion-free, so T ↪ T⊗K ⊂ End_K(H^0_K). Landing in a product of the O_{K_i} additionally needs T⊗K to be reduced, i.e. every generator acting semisimply. The text gives no argument for this. The cited [20, Prop. 3.4.4] (CHT) works with an anemic Hecke algebra, where reducedness is automatic, so it does not fill the gap. No other passage does either: a search of the paper for "reduced" and "semisimpl" finds nothing relevant.

(2) Defence: the claim is true, so this is a gap, not an error. By Thm 5.2 the Hecke action on H^0_C factors through ⊕_π π_f^{K_1(Q)}. At x ∈ S and at p the algebra has no operators, so only x ∈ Q matters. For π in the m-part, local-global compatibility (Prop. 6.8(5), since r̄ is absolutely irreducible) and Assumption 6.12(2) give four characters whose Frobenius values are residually distinct. π_x has I(1)-invariants, because I(1) ⊂ Π(x)^+, so π_x is a subquotient of a tamely ramified principal series Ind χ′ with χ′ regular. Because x ≡ 1 mod p, no ratio equals x^{±1}, so π_x = Ind χ′ is irreducible. The Borel–Casselman-type isomorphism π_x^{Π^+} ≅ r_P(π_x)^{M∩Π^+} intertwines U_{x,2} (central in the Klingen Levi M) and U_{x,1} (the GL_2-factor operator diag(1,1,x,x), which is weakly positive) with M-Hecke operators. The four constituents Ind_{B_M}^M(wχ′) of r_P(π_x) are irreducible and have distinct cuspidal supports, since χ′ is regular. So r_P(π_x) is their direct sum. Each constituent has at most a one-dimensional (M∩Π^+, χ)-part, so U_{x,1}, U_{x,2} and ⟨u⟩ are simultaneously diagonalisable. U_{x,2} alone can have a repeated eigenvalue: with α=−γ and β=−δ the relation αδ=βγ holds and αβ=γδ. U_{x,1} still separates those lines, since α+β ≠ γ+δ. The paper has all these ingredients (§6.3 final paragraph, [31, Prop. 3.2.3], [64, Cors. 1, 3]) but never states or proves reducedness. It is not an obvious consequence of torsion-freeness: this is exactly where the Taylor–Wiles conditions enter.

The proof pushes r forward along the surjection T_{μ′}(Q)^β_m ↠ T_μ(Q)^β_m/I_{μ,m}, whose target may be non-reduced; this is the whole point of passing to high weight (Remark 6.14). That identity is only accessible through the embedding T ↪ ∏ O_{K_i}, with ⟨u⟩ and U_{x,i} included, together with [64, Cor. 3]. So the gap sits in the proof chain of the main theorem. However, the missing statement is true and follows by the standard local argument above, so no stated result is affected.

Read strictly, the exponents there should be b'−2, a'−1 and 𝐰' = a'+b'−3, and the next sentence should read "Q_p(X) = X^4 − T_{p,1}X^3 + p^{b'−2}Q_{p,2}X^2 − ⋯". For an eigenform of weight μ', Proposition 6.8(4) gives root valuations 0, b'−2, a'−1, 𝐰'. The unprimed letters are a notational abuse that runs through the whole paragraph. issues.reason:
Page images show the misprint is real.
- **Theorem 6.13(3) (p. 842)** prints Q_p(X) = (X − d_{p,1})(X − p^{b−2}d_{p,2})(X − p^{a−1}d_{p,3})(X − p^𝐰 d_{p,4}), with d_{p,3} also appearing in the matrix of (3)(b).
- **Proposition 6.8(4) (p. 839)** gives four distinct eigenvalues α_p, β_p, γ_p, δ_p with valuations 0, b−2, a−1, 𝐰.
- **The proof (p. 843)** prints d_{p,1} in the third factor and never mentions d_{p,3}, even though it says "for units d_{p,i}". Read literally, it claims the third root equals p^{a−1} times the first. Proposition 6.8(4) does not give this, and it is false in general.

**Redoing the deduction.** Let (A,B) be the working weight, with B ≥ 3 and A ≥ B, and 𝐖 = A+B−3. Take roots d_1, p^{B−2}d_2, p^{A−1}d_3, p^𝐖 d_4.
- From the X^3 coefficient: T_{p,1} = d_1 + p^{B−2}(…) ≡ d_1 mod p.
- From the X^2 coefficient, dividing by p^{B−2}: Q_{p,2} = d_1d_2 + p^{A−B+1}d_1d_3 + p^{A−1}d_1d_4 + p^{A−1}d_2d_3 + … ≡ d_1d_2 mod p. Division is allowed because T_{μ'}(Q)^β_𝔪 embeds into ∏O_{K_i}.
- So d_{p,1} ≡ β and d_{p,2} ≡ α, as the paper says.
- The argument uses only these two coefficients mod 𝔪. It gives the same answer with the misprinted d_{p,1} in the third slot, so the proof is not affected.

**Downstream.** Nothing later uses this displayed line. Theorem 6.17 (pp. 845–846) calls on Theorem 6.13 only through its statement, which is correct, and through the reduction to high weight.

The misprint is in the Duke version and in arXiv v1. The candidate's correction is right, including its secondary remark about primed exponents.

issues.locator: §6.4: Definition 6.15(2), p. 844, and the sentence after the definition of e_{α,β}, p. 845. Compare Definition 5.13, p. 834, Lemma 7.10, pp. 852–853, Theorem 7.2, p. 847, and the proof of Theorem 9.1, pp. 878–880. arXiv 1907.08691v1 (§6.4, pp. 33–34) has the same text.
issues.printed: p. 44, Definition 6.15: "We say that r̄ is Katz modular of weight σ if there exists a maximal ideal m_∅ of T_σ such that (1) we have r̄_{m_∅} ≅ r̄, and (2) there exists a form η ∈ H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O})[m_∅] such that T_{p,1}(η) = (α+β)η, Q_{p,2}(η) = (αβ)η." p. 45, after Assumption 6.16: "We let m be any maximal ideal of T_σ(Q) containing m_∅. For comparison, p. 34, Definition 5.13(1)–(2): "The anemic Hecke algebra T^an_μ(Q) ⊂ End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})) is the O-algebra generated by the operators T_{x,i} for x ∉ S ∪ Q ∪ {p}. … When Q = ∅, we have T^an_μ(∅) = T_μ(∅) and we denote this algebra by T_μ."
issues.correction:
(i) Either take η cuspidal in Definition 6.15(2), i.e. η ∈ H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})[m_∅], or add a lemma. The lemma: since r̄ is absolutely irreducible, m_∅ is non-Eisenstein, so the m_∅-part of the boundary vanishes mod p and H^0(X, ω(a,2)_k)[m_∅] = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)[m_∅]. One route is the Siegel Φ-operator: it is Hecke-equivariant and carries non-cuspidal eigenforms to eigensystems with reducible Galois representations. Lemma 7.10 does not supply this, because it holds only after ⊗K.
(ii) Restrict "any maximal ideal m of T_σ(Q) containing m_∅" to the ideals of Theorem 7.2, one for each isotropic labelling at each x ∈ Q. Those are the only ones used later. If "any" is kept, the argument must be added. The candidate's suggestion (Theorem 7.2 for each labelling) handles only these old-type ideals at level X_0(Q). Two more facts are needed. First, the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q acts trivially on the m-part, which follows from local-global compatibility at x, since r̄ is unramified at x. Second, every maximal ideal above m_∅ is old-type, which is the no-newforms consequence of Assumption 7.1.
(iii) Separately, read e_{α,β} as the projector onto the generalized (α+β, αβ)-eigenspace. As printed it kills η. This is filed as H-h2-0 / X-K4-1.
issues.reason:
I transcribed p. 834, 844, 845 and 846 from the page images; the text matches the candidate.

(1) Cuspidality. T_σ acts on cusp forms: Definition 5.13 embeds it in End_O(H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})). So does T_σ(Q), and the space made nonzero on p. 845 is cuspidal. Definition 6.15(2) only asks for η in the full space H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O}). "[m_∅]" there makes sense only through the abstract Hecke algebra; the paper spells out this abuse for H^2 in Assumption 7.7 but not here. If η were not cuspidal, m_∅ could lie in the cuspidal support only with other T_{p,1}/Q_{p,2}-eigenvalues. Then H = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} would be 0.

The paper proves the boundary is Eisenstein only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10, via Harris–Zucker). It never proves this with torsion coefficients. The statement is true: r̄ is absolutely irreducible, and boundary eigensystems give reducible representations, e.g. via Φ-operator/q-expansion compatibility. It can also be derived from A^s, H^1-vanishing in high weight and Lemma 7.10. So this is a gap, not an error.

(2) Arbitrary m. Katz modularity is a level-K condition. Getting from it to a nonzero (α,β)-part at every m ⊇ m_∅ of T_σ(Q) is a level-raising statement. Pulling back η gives support at only some m, not all. The paper gives no argument at this point. Theorem 7.2, proved later, covers only the m attached to the fixed labelling (U_{x,1} ≡ α_x+β_x, xU_{x,2} ≡ α_xβ_x). Other m need relabelling, plus a Δ_Q-invariants argument that every m is of one of these types.

(3) As printed, the e_{α,β} kills η: η is ϖ-torsion and (T_{p,1} − α̃ − β̃)η = 0. So the sentence can only be read with the corrected idempotent (separate candidates X-K4-1, H-h2-0).

Reach. The proof of Theorem 6.17 does not use the nonvanishing. But the Q = ∅ case, H ≠ 0, is needed in Theorem 9.1: if H = 0, Proposition 3.3 gives only "0 is free", and R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅} fails. Its only justification in the paper is this sentence. §9 uses only the m_N of Theorem 7.2, so part (2) matters only for the remark as stated. I think the claims are true, so the gap can be filled.

Side note, not checked in detail: for an m whose U_{x,1}-eigenvalue is α_x+γ_x, local–global compatibility would seem to make inertia act by scalars on lifts of {α_x,γ_x} ⊕ {β_x,δ_x}, not the {α_x,β_x} ⊕ {γ_x,δ_x} that Definition 4.6(5) requires. That would also make "any m" questionable in Theorems 6.13 and 6.17. Both texts are confirmed from the page images (pp. 844–845, and v1 p. 33).

(1) Cuspidality. T_σ = T_σ(∅) is defined (Definition 5.13, p. 834) as a subalgebra of End_O(H^0(X_1(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})), i.e. through the cusp forms. The idempotent e_{α,β}, and hence T_σ(Q)^{α,β}, is also defined on the cuspidal space. Definition 6.15(2) instead puts η in the full space H^0(X, ω(a,2)_{K/O}). This looks deliberate rather than a dropped "(−∞)": Lemma 8.8 (p. 860) defines T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} on the full space H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,k)_{K/O}), and §1 also uses the full space via the Koecher principle.

For Q = ∅ we have m = m_∅, and the sentence claims e_{α,β}H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_{m_∅} ≠ 0. That follows from η only if η is cuspidal. The only comparison of the two sheaves in the paper is Lemma 7.10 (pp. 852–853), which is proved after ⊗K via boundary cohomology over C and says nothing about torsion. The missing fact is standard and I believe it is true: η is ϖ-torsion, and its image under restriction to the boundary would be killed by the non-Eisenstein m_∅. But the paper does not state or prove it.

(2) Arbitrary m ⊇ m_∅ for Q ≠ ∅. T_σ(Q) acts faithfully, so H_m ≠ 0 automatically. But T_{p,1} and Q_{p,2} are not in T_σ(Q), so the (α,β)-part at m is not automatic. Different m above m_∅ differ in their U_{x,i} and ⟨u⟩ eigenvalues. The claim is plausibly true: Theorem 7.2 for each of the four isotropic labellings gives the old-type ideals at level X_0(Q), and local-global compatibility together with Assumption 7.1 rules out the others. But none of this appears at p. 845, and Theorem 7.2 is stated only for one labelling.

Defence attempts. §6.3 makes no such claim, and Theorem 6.13 has the same degenerate form at an m where the β-part vanishes (see C-K4-4). So the "any m" part is at worst an unjustified remark, and Theorem 6.17's proof never uses it.

What uses the passage. §9 (p. 879) applies Theorem 6.17 only with Q = ∅ (m = m_∅) and with Q = Q_N and m = m_N, the ideal of Theorem 7.2. For m_N, nonvanishing follows from (H_N)_Δ ≅ H (Theorem 7.2 and item (b), p. 879), so the "any m" part affects nothing. The Q = ∅ case is different. The proof of Theorem 9.1 concludes from Proposition 3.3 (p. 812; its hypotheses do not force H ≠ 0) that H = H^0(X, ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})^{α,β,∨}_{m_∅} is free, and hence that R^min ≅ T^{α,β}_{σ,m_∅}. That step needs H ≠ 0: otherwise T = 0, while R^min, an object of C_O, is not. The only justification of H ≠ 0 in the paper is this sentence with Q = ∅. For a non-cuspidal η, as Definition 6.15 allows, that sentence depends on the missing cuspidality step.

So the candidate's "affects nothing" is too weak. The gap sits in the proof of Theorem 9.1. The result stands once (i) is supplied.

issues.printed: Assumption 7.1 (p. 46): "For each x ∈ Q, we have x ≡ 1 mod p, and r̄_{𝔪∅} | G_x is a direct sum of four pairwise distinct characters with Frobenius eigenvalues α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x. We assume that the eigenvalues have been labeled so that the plane λ(α_x) ⊕ λ(β_x) is isotropic, and hence α_xδ_x = β_xγ_x." Theorem 7.2 (p. 47): "Let μ and 𝔪∅ be as above, and suppose that Assumption 7.1 holds. Let 𝔪 denote the ideal of T_μ(Q) containing 𝔪∅ together with the elements xU_{x,2} − α'_xβ'_x and U_{x,1} − α'_x − β'_x for each x ∈ Q. Then 𝔪 is maximal and there is an isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i : H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_{𝔪∅} ⥲ H^0(X_0(Q), ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O})_𝔪 ... Here i is the natural inclusion and pr_Q is defined as follows. For x ∈ Q, let R_x denote the Hecke operator R_x = (xU_{x,2} − α'_xγ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − β'_xδ'_x)(xU_{x,2} − γ'_xδ'_x) ∈ T_μ(Q), and let pr_x denote the idempotent pr_x = lim_{n→∞} (R'_x)^{n!}. Then the pr_x's commute with one another and pr_Q denotes their product." Theorem 7.3 (p. 47) states the same isomorphism pr_Q ∘ i for W^sub_{μ,K/O} under a vanishing hypothesis.
issues.correction:
Assumption 7.1 needs a further condition on the labelling: α_xβ_x ≠ γ_xδ_x in k. Since ν(r̄)(Frob_x) = 1 for x ≡ 1 mod p, this is the same as (α_xβ_x)² ≠ 1, and also the same as α_x ≠ −γ_x or β_x ≠ −δ_x. Genestier–Tilouine (the paper's [31], §5.1, p. 212) state this very condition in their definition of Taylor–Wiles primes, as "(ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1".

A good labelling always exists when the four eigenvalues are pairwise distinct:
- the split {α,β}|{γ,δ} clashes exactly when α = −γ;
- the split {α,γ}|{β,δ} clashes exactly when α = −β;
- if both clashed we would get β = γ, which is excluded.

So swapping β_x and γ_x cures a clash. For the application, the labellings chosen in §4 (p. 815) for the primes Q_N of Prop. 4.10 must satisfy the condition, since §6.3–6.4 and §9 reuse them. Assumptions 6.12(2) and 6.16(2) should say the same.

Another fix is to replace the third factor of R_x by (U_{x,1} − γ'_x − δ'_x). U_{x,1} separates {α,β} from {γ,δ}: in the clash case the difference of the sums is 2(α+β) ≠ 0.

Separately, R'_x in the formula for pr_x is undefined and should read R_x. This is a misprint, and arXiv v1 has it too.
issues.reason:
I checked this on the rendered p. 846 and p. 847 images and on arXiv v1 p. 35. The text is identical in both, including the undefined R'_x. I redid the computation.

(1) Why R_x can lie in 𝔪. The third factor of R_x can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term is in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra and needs no knowledge of U_{x,2}-eigenvalues.

(2) When αβ = γδ is allowed. Using αδ = βγ = ν, we get γδ = ν²/(αβ). So αβ = γδ iff αβ = ±ν. The case αβ = ν would force α = γ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −ν is equivalent to α = −γ, and also to β = −δ. Assumption 7.1 and Prop. 4.10(3) (which only asks for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues") do not exclude it. Concrete check in F_7 with ν = 1: (α,β,γ,δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4), which is (2, −1/2, −2, 1/2). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = −1 ≠ ν, so the plane is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6. Then R_x mod 𝔪 = (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0. Since x ≡ 1 mod p and ν(r̄) is a power of the cyclotomic character, ν(Frob_x) = 1. For r̄ with image containing Sp4(F_p), Chebotarev gives such primes x.

(3) Why the theorem then fails. On the 𝔪-part, every element of the finite ϖ^n-torsion is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x^{n!} → 0 there, pr_x acts as 0 on the 𝔪-part, and pr_Q ∘ i = 0. But the source H^0(X, ·)_{𝔪∅} is nonzero: T_μ acts faithfully (Def. 5.13) and 𝔪∅ is a maximal ideal. So the claimed isomorphism fails. Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6 fail the same way.

(4) The candidate's other claims hold. The first two factors reduce to (αβ−αγ) and (αβ−βδ), which are nonzero since β ≠ γ and α ≠ δ. The swap argument is also right: a clash for the new labelling needs α = −β, and together with α = −γ this gives β = γ, which is excluded.

(5) Where this matters. Theorem 7.2 is used in the patching step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10, and nothing there fixes the labelling. So a stated result is false as printed in an edge case its hypotheses allow. The main theorems survive once the labelling is chosen correctly, which is always possible. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) R_x lies in 𝔪 in the clash case. The third factor can be written as xU_{x,2} − γ'δ' = (xU_{x,2} − α'β') + (α'β' − γ'δ'). The first term is in 𝔪 by definition. If αβ = γδ in k, the second term lies in ϖO ⊂ 𝔪∅. So R_x ∈ 𝔪. This is pure algebra: it needs no facts about U_{x,2}-eigenvalues and no reading of the undefined R'_x.

(2) The theorem then fails. The target is ϖ-power torsion, and each element is killed by a power of 𝔪. So R_x is topologically nilpotent on H^0(X_0(Q), ·)_𝔪, and lim R_x^{n!} = 0 there. Hence pr_Q∘i = 0 into the 𝔪-part. If 𝔪 were not proper the target would be 0, which also fails.

The source is nonzero. By Def. 5.13 (with Q = ∅), T_μ acts faithfully on H^0(X, ω(a,b)(−∞)_{K/O}). T_μ is finite over O and so semilocal, and 𝔪∅ is one of its maximal ideals, so the 𝔪∅-part is nonzero. Therefore Theorem 7.2 fails. So do Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.4–7.6, which assert that pr_Q∘i is an isomorphism with inverse d_Q^{-1}tr.

(3) Assumption 7.1 allows the clash. Here ν = 1, so γ = 1/β and δ = 1/α, and αβ = γδ ⇔ (αβ)² = 1. The case αβ = 1 would force β = δ, which is excluded. The case αβ = −1 means α = −γ, which is not excluded.

Example in F_7: (α, β, γ, δ) = (2, 3, 5, 4). These are distinct, αδ = βγ = 1, and αβ = 6 ≠ 1, so {α,β} is isotropic. Also αβ = γδ = 6, and R_x ≡ (6−3)(6−5)(6−6) = 0.

A script over p ≤ 23 checked that:
- R_x ≡ 0 mod 𝔪 exactly in the clash case, since the first two factors are always units;
- the two Lagrangian splittings never both clash.

This kind of Frobenius occurs in the paper itself. Example 4.11 (p. 819) builds the element c·(g,h), with eigenvalues ±(xy)^{1/2}, ±(xy)^{−1/2}. That is {s, −s, 1/s, −1/s}, and its labelling (s, −1/s, −s, 1/s) clashes. Prop. 4.10(3) and the §4 labelling rule (p. 815) ask only for "four pairwise distinct eigenvalues" and isotropic planes.

(4) The cited source has the missing hypothesis. The proof of Thm 7.3 rests on [31, Prop. 11.1.2]. Genestier–Tilouine define Taylor–Wiles primes (§5.1, p. 212) by: "P_{π,q} a quatre racines distinctes ᾱ_q, β̄_q, γ̄_q = β̄_q^{-1} et δ̄_q = ᾱ_q^{-1} dans k, telles que (ᾱ_qβ̄_q)² ≠ 1". Their injectivity proof (p. 282) inverts (α_qβ_q − α_qγ_q)(α_qβ_q − β_qδ_q)(α_qβ_q − γ_qδ_q), which needs exactly this condition. Calegari–Geraghty dropped it, so the citation does not rescue the statement.

(5) Where it is used. Theorem 7.2 feeds step (b) of the proof of Thm 9.1 (p. 879), with Q = Q_N from Prop. 4.10 and 𝔪_N as in Thm 7.2. Nothing in that proof fixes the labelling. Since a non-clashing labelling always exists, the fix is to add the condition and choose labellings accordingly. Only an abstract Hecke-equivariant isomorphism is used in (b), so Thm 9.1 and the main theorems survive.

Both candidates' arguments and corrections check out:
- X-K5-5: "β≠−δ ⇔ αβ≠−ν", "the alternative split fails iff α=−β", and "both ⇒ α=δ" are all right.
- H-h2-1: "α≠−γ" and the swap argument are right.

It is a p-adic limit of spherical Hecke operators at the primes of Q, since tr∘[Π g Π]∘i is K-spherical. So v_Q lies in (the completion of) T_{m_∅} and commutes with h, h̃, i, tr, restriction to S and S_0(Q), and the connecting maps.

Under Assumption 7.1 (x ≡ 1 mod p, and α_x, β_x, γ_x, δ_x distinct, so the parameter is regular mod ϖ), the value mod m_∅ is d_x·c_x ≡ 4·(1/4) = 1. So v_Q ≡ 1 mod m_∅, and v_Q is a unit.

The correct inverse is v_Q^{−1}∘tr = (tr∘pr_Q∘i)^{−1}∘tr, restricted to the m-summand, which is defined over O. In the statements of Theorem 7.3 and Lemmas 7.5 and 7.6, replace d_Q^{−1}tr by this.
