issues.locator: §9, proof of Theorem 9.1, step (c), p. 880. The root of the problem is the hypothesis of Theorem 7.11 (p. 853), which is Assumption 7.7 (p. 851): "The space H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m is trivial." arXiv v1 has the same text: Assumption 7.7 on p. 38, Theorem 7.11 and its proof on pp. 39–40, hypothesis (6) on p. 56 and step (c) on p. 57.
issues.printed: (c) Finally, H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11.
issues.correction: In the proof of Theorem 7.11, Assumption 7.7 is needed only for Δ trivial, i.e. H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m = 0. It enters through Lemma 7.9, which is applied to H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m. The stated hypothesis for X_Δ(Q) is never used. So Theorem 7.11's hypothesis should read "Assumption 7.7 holds for X_0(Q)", and step (c) should add that this is given by hypothesis (6) with i = 0 for Q = Q_N. This works for three reasons. Q_N satisfies Assumption 6.12(2) by Proposition 4.10(2),(3). m_N ⊂ T_σ(Q_N) is maximal, contains m_∅, and contracts to the maximal ideal m_∅ of T^an_σ(Q_N). So localizing the finite-dimensional k-space H^2 at m_N gives a direct summand of its localization at m_∅. Another fix would be to require x ≢ 1 mod p^{N+1} in Proposition 4.10. Then p does not divide deg(X_1(Q_N) → X_Δ(Q_N)), and a trace argument gives the vanishing on X_Δ from (6) with i = 1. The first fix is the smaller one.
issues.reason:
Pages 51–53 and 78–80 checked as images.

(1) Step (c) cites Theorem 7.11. That theorem assumes Assumption 7.7 for the fixed Δ, i.e. vanishing of H^2 on X_Δ(Q_N) localized at m_N. Hypothesis (6) of Theorem 9.1 only covers X_i(Q), and §5.2 defines K_i(Q) only for i = 0, 1. Vanishing on X_1 gives vanishing on X_Δ by trace only when p does not divide [X_1(Q_N) : X_Δ(Q_N)] = ∏(x−1)/p^N. Proposition 4.10(2) only gives x ≡ 1 mod p^N, so this can fail. Nothing in the paper checks the hypothesis. Remark 7.8 and Theorem 5.1 cover p ≥ a ≥ 4 only, not a = 2 or 3.

(2) Defence: the proof of Theorem 7.11 never uses the X_Δ vanishing. By Definition 3.1, and since Tor^O_p vanishes for p ≥ 2, d_S(M) = rank_O(M_Δ) − dim_k Tor_1^S(M,O)/ϖ for any finite M. This is the formula printed, with r the rank of M_Δ, which is H_0(X_0(Q), L)_m. Hochschild–Serre gives a surjection H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m → Tor_1^S(M,O). So one needs H_1(X_0(Q), L)_m to be torsion-free, which is Lemma 7.9 with Δ trivial and so needs Assumption 7.7 for X_0(Q). The rest is a characteristic-0 argument on X_0(Q) (Lemma 7.10 and Arthur's classification). Hypothesis (6) with i = 0 supplies exactly this, as explained in the correction. So Theorem 9.1 is fully supported by its own hypotheses. The fault is only that Theorem 7.11 states a hypothesis (X_Δ) other than the one its proof uses (X_0), and that step (c) leaves the check implicit.

(3) Is Theorem 7.11 correct as stated? Vanishing on X_Δ does not formally give vanishing on X_0. The Hochschild–Serre terms H^2(Δ, H^0) and H^1(Δ, H^1) with k-coefficients need not vanish for a p-group Δ. So Theorem 7.11 is proved under the X_0 hypothesis, not under the one it states. Its only use is step (c), where the X_0 hypothesis is available.

(4) One detail in the candidate's reason needs care. "Does not descend" should read "the trace argument does not apply"; nobody has shown the vanishing actually fails.

(5) A separate point, not part of this candidate and not assessed here: H_N is the (α,β)-ordinary part, while Theorem 7.11 is stated for the whole m-localized module.

issues.printed: (2) A is ordinary at p, and if α, β are the unit root eigenvalues of D_cris(V), then (α^2 − 1)(β^2 − 1)(α − β)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≢ 0 mod p. Then H^1_f(Q, asp^0(r) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p) = 0, where asp^0(r) is the 10-dimensional adjoint representation of PGSp(4).
issues.correction: State that V = V_p(A) (equivalently H^1_et(A_{Q̄}, Q_p)) is the p-adic Galois representation of A, and that r: G_Q → GSp_4(Z_p) is the associated integral representation (Tate module), with mod-p reduction r̄_p as in §A.3.2. asp^0(r) is r composed with the adjoint action on the 10-dimensional Lie algebra of PGSp_4.
issues.reason: Neither V nor r is introduced in Theorem A.1. Earlier in §A.1, V denotes an arbitrary pure de Rham representation ('for any pure de Rham representation V'), and r denotes 'a p-adic representation r: G_Q → GL_n(O) coming from M' for an automorphic compatible system M. The intended objects (the p-adic realisation of A and its integral model) are clear from Theorem 9.1(1) and from §A.3.2, where r̄_p is 'the corresponding semisimple representation' of the abelian surface A. The ambiguity between H^1 and the Tate module does not matter. Their crystalline Frobenius eigenvalues differ by x ↦ p/x on H^1 versus x ↦ 1/x after the Tate twist, so the unit roots α, β are replaced by 1/α, 1/β. A direct computation gives (α^{-2}−1)(β^{-2}−1)(α^{-1}−β^{-1})(α^{-2}β^{-2}−1) = unit × (α^2−1)(β^2−1)(β−α)(α^2β^2−1), so the non-vanishing condition is the same either way. This is an omitted definition in a theorem statement whose meaning is clear from context.

issues.locator: §A.1, paragraph after Theorem A.2, parenthetical remark, p. 882. The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, p. 3, is identical (with [ACC+18] for [1]).
issues.printed: (The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)
issues.correction: '(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for an extension F′/F for which restriction H^1_f(F, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) → H^1_f(F′, ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O) is injective. This holds, for example, if p ∤ [F′:F], or if (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0 for the Galois closure F″ of F′/F, e.g. F′/F Galois with r̄|G_{F′} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, as for the linearly disjoint CM fields supplied by [1] ...)'. The 'F/F' slip is recorded separately.
issues.reason: Restriction preserves the Bloch–Kato local conditions, so vanishing over F′ implies vanishing over F exactly when restriction on H^1 is injective. By inflation–restriction, the kernel of H^1(F, M) → H^1(F″, M), with M = ad^0(r) ⊗ K/O and F″ the Galois closure, is H^1(Gal(F″/F), M^{G_{F″}}). The kernel to G_{F′} is contained in it. If p ∤ [F′:F], cor∘res = [F′:F] also gives injectivity. M^{G_{F″}} = 0 iff (ad^0 r̄)^{G_{F″}} = 0, since M[λ] = ad^0 r̄. With r̄|G_{F″} absolutely irreducible and p ∤ n, Schur's lemma gives this. These conditions are not automatic for 'any extension': if p | [F″:F] and ad^0 r̄ acquires G_{F″}-invariants, the kernel can be nonzero, and the remark gives no hypothesis excluding this. In the intended example (symmetric powers of a non-CM E, p large, F′ a Galois CM extension linearly disjoint from F(r̄, ζ_p) as potential-automorphy theorems provide), the condition holds, so nothing downstream is affected. This is an unjustified, over-general reduction in an informal remark, not a false theorem. I could not build an explicit counterexample within the theorem's setting, hence low confidence.

issues.printed: "(The conclusion of the theorem holds for F if it holds for any extension F′/F, and any symmetric power of E/F is potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [1].)"
issues.correction: "... is potentially modular over some CM extension F′/F in this case by [1]." That is, F/F should read F′/F, the same auxiliary extension as in the preceding clause.
issues.reason:
I checked this against page images: p. 882 at 110 dpi, plus a 300 dpi crop of the passage. The same sentence first has "extension F′/F" with a visible prime. Two lines later it has "CM extension F/F" with no prime. pdftotext gives "F=F" on line 3965, and a grep for "CM extension" finds no other occurrence.

Theorem A.2 (p. 881) fixes F as a CM field. The remark says the theorem's conclusion over F follows from the conclusion over any extension F′/F. It then says symmetric powers of a non-CM elliptic curve E/F are potentially modular by ACC+18 [1], which gives modularity over some CM extension F′/F. Read as F/F, the extension would be trivial. That would make the "potentially" and the preceding base-change clause pointless, and it would claim more than [1] proves. No convention in the paper gives F/F a meaning, so this is a missing prime and not an intended statement.

The arXiv appendix (1907.08694v1) has the same slip. I rendered page 3 and it reads "potentially modular over some CM extension F/F in this case by [ACC+18]." Line 109 of the arXiv text shows the same.

Impact: the sentence is a parenthetical in the appendix introduction. It explains which examples Theorem A.2 would apply to. It is not a hypothesis or a step in any proof. Theorem A.2 and its proof in §A.3 (p. 888) do not use it, and neither do Theorem A.1 or the main text.

issues.printed: If one chooses a prime p, and supposes that ρ has a model over O, then the finiteness of the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is a consequence of the finiteness of the p-class group of Q(ker(ρ)). (The former is a quotient of the latter.)
issues.correction: Replace the parenthetical by: '(With L = Q(ker ρ), restriction to G_L maps the former, with kernel inside the finite group H^1(Gal(L/Q), ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), which is zero if p ∤ [L:Q], into Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O).)' The finiteness claim itself is correct.
issues.reason: G_L acts trivially on ad^0(ρ). A Bloch–Kato class restricted to G_L is a homomorphism G_L → ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O that is unramified everywhere. At w | p this holds because H^1_f(L_w, Q_p) = H^1_ur for trivial coefficients. At infinite places nothing is needed since p is odd. So the class factors through Cl(L)[p^∞], and by inflation–restriction the kernel is H^1(Gal(L/Q), M), a finite group since it is |Gal(L/Q)|-torsion and cofinitely generated. This gives finiteness, as the paper says. The parenthetical 'quotient' claim is false as stated. When p ∤ [L:Q] and ρ is unramified at p, the Selmer group equals Hom_{Gal(L/Q)}(Cl(L)[p^∞], ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O), and enlarging K by degree d raises its order to the d-th power, while Cl(L)[p^∞] does not depend on K. Take any case with a nonzero Selmer group, which the paper itself discusses ('there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(...) is nonzero'). For a large enough coefficient field its order then exceeds |Cl(L)[p^∞]|, so it cannot be a quotient of that group. The accurate relation is an embedding, up to finite kernel, into a Hom group out of the class group; dually, the Pontryagin dual is roughly a quotient. The error is in an informal justification, and the conclusion drawn is unaffected.

issues.locator: Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris), §A.2 'Relation with special values of periods', p. 883, second half of the page, in the test-case paragraph about an odd irreducible ρ: G_Q → GL_2(C). arXiv:1907.08694v1 (the appendix preprint), §2, has the same words, citing [CG18] in place of [16].
issues.printed: The methods of this paper (following [16]) show that, at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified, the Selmer group H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is detected by congruences between the modular form f and other Katz modular forms of weight 1 which may not lift to characteristic 0. In particular, there exist such congruences if and only if H^1_f(Q, ad^0(ρ) ⊗ K/O) is nonzero.
issues.correction: "... at all primes p > 2 such that ρ is unramified at p, the reduction ρ̄ is irreducible, and ρ is a minimal deformation of ρ̄ (in the sense of [16, Corollary 1.5(1)]; for example, at all p > 2 with p ∤ N(ρ)·|ρ(G_Q)|, so for all but finitely many p) ...". Adding "ρ̄ irreducible", as the candidate does, is necessary but not sufficient: minimality must also be assumed.
issues.reason:
Printed text checked on the rendered p. 883; it matches the transcription.

(1) What [16] gives. [16] is CG18, Invent. Math. 211. I read its Theorem 1.4 (p. 303): 'Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... Assume that ρ̄ is unramified at p. ... R^min ⥲ T_m'. The theorem needs ρ̄ irreducible, and it covers only minimal deformations. The Taylor–Wiles patching behind it also needs ρ̄ absolutely irreducible. So the methods cited say nothing at a prime p where ρ̄ is reducible (m Eisenstein), or where ρ is not minimal.

(2) Such primes exist. Let H be the splitting field of x³−x−1 (discriminant −23), and let ρ be the 2-dimensional representation of S_3. It is irreducible and odd, and it is ramified only at 23, so it is unramified at p = 3. In characteristic 3 every irreducible representation of S_3 is 1-dimensional, so ρ̄ is reducible. Both stable lattices check this explicitly: on the sum-zero lattice, b1+2b2 is fixed mod 3. So the sentence covers (ρ, p = 3), but [16] does not apply there. Primes of this kind all divide |ρ(G_Q)|, so the exceptions are finite. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)|, ρ̄ is irreducible and ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v).

(3) The 'iff' can fail in this example. f = η(z)η(23z) satisfies f ≡ E_1(1, χ_{−23}) (mod 3) coefficient by coefficient: the traces are 2, 0, −1 against 1+χ = 2, 0, 2, and a_23 = 1 on both sides. The constant term h/2 = 3/2 ≡ 0, so the two agree as mod-3 Katz forms by the q-expansion principle. On the other side, H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ Q_3/Z_3) = 0:
- h(H) = 1. The Minkowski bound is ≈ 3.51, and the primes of H above 2 and 3 have norms 8 and 27, because they lie over non-principal primes of Q(√−23).
- So a Selmer class dies on G_H, and the group is H^1(S_3, M) ≅ Ĥ^0(C_3, ad^0 L)^{C_2}.
- I computed this for both stable lattices L. In each case N_{C_3}(ad^0 L) = (ad^0 L)^{C_3}, so the group is 0.
- The local conditions at 23 and 3 add nothing: D_23 = C_2, which has no 3-torsion cohomology, and the classes at 3 are unramified.
So if Eisenstein series count as 'other Katz modular forms of weight 1', the 'iff' is false at (ρ, 3). If only cusp forms count (T in [16] acts on H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ), which is dual to cusp forms), I cannot decide the statement at such p. It is simply unproved there. That is why I class this as a gap and not an error.

The authors know these conditions matter: on p. 882 they say they 'do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible' and 'whether r is a minimal deformation'. Nothing in §A.2 assumes either condition. The remark is informal and nothing later uses it. The printed text is confirmed from the rendered p. 883. The claim rests on [16] = Calegari–Geraghty, Invent. Math. 2018, Theorem 1.4: "Suppose that p ≥ 3. Let ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) be an odd continuous irreducible Galois representation ... unramified at p. Let R^min denote the universal minimal unramified-at-p deformation ring of ρ̄ ... R^min ≅ T_m." To read H^1_f(Q, ad^0ρ ⊗ K/O) off R^min = T_m, two things are needed. (i) ρ̄ must be irreducible. (ii) ρ must be a point of R^min, i.e. minimally ramified; this is [16, Cor. 1.5(1)]: "either ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1".

Both conditions can fail at primes p > 2 where ρ is unramified.
(i) Take the S_3 representation cut out by x^3 − x − 1. The discriminant is −23 (computed), and the splitting field is the Hilbert class field of Q(√−23), ramified only at 23. So ρ is odd, irreducible, and unramified at 3. Its reduction mod 3 is reducible: in the reflection representation, (1,1,1) lies in {Σx_i = 0} mod 3 and is S_3-fixed, and Brauer–Nesbitt gives ρ̄^ss = 1 ⊕ ε_{−23}. Here m is Eisenstein, and indeed η(z)η(23z) ≡ E_1(1, ε_{−23}) mod 3. So [16] does not apply.
(ii) Take ρ = Ind_K^Q ψ with K = Q(√−47) (class number 5) and ψ a ring class character of order 15. The order-3 part should have conductor ℓ, with ℓ ≡ 1 mod 3 split in K. Then ρ is unramified at 3, and ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ with ψ̄ of order 5 is irreducible. But ρ|I_ℓ = ω ⊕ ω^{-1} with ω of order 3, while ρ̄|I_ℓ is trivial. So ρ is not minimal and is not a point of R^min.

Defence attempted, without success. No charitable reading restricts p. The paper's own methods also assume residual irreducibility (big image). The authors are aware of both conditions. On p. 882, about Theorem A.2, they write: "we do not even know that the representations r̄ are irreducible for sufficiently large p. Another is that we do not know whether r is a minimal deformation of r̄ at ramified primes v". §A.2 simply omits these conditions. For p ∤ |ρ(G_Q)| the reduction of the finite image group is injective and preserves irreducibility, so both conditions hold for all but finitely many p. I cannot show that the "iff" statement is actually false at the excluded p; in the S_3 example both sides are nonzero, since the 3-class group of K gives a Selmer class. The fault is an unsupported claim of scope, so the kind is gap, not error.

Consequences: §A.2 is a discussion remark. Nothing in the paper cites it; grep finds no reference to Section A.2, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 and §A.3 do not use it. So affects = nothing.

issues.locator: Appendix A, §A.3.1, Theorem A.4 and its proof, pp. 885–886; setup of r̄_v on pp. 884–885
issues.printed: p. 85: "THEOREM A.4 Suppose that H^i(Y, O/ϖ^n)_m = 0 unless i ∈ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0]. Let Q be a finite collection of primes x such that r̄(Frob_x) has distinct eigenvalues and N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. Then H^i(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^n)_{m_α} = 0 for all i ∉ [q_0, …, q_0 + l_0], where" p. 86: "(1) α = {α_x} is a choice of eigenvalues of r̄(Frob_x) for each x dividing Q; (2) the localization takes place with respect to the Hecke algebra T_Q consisting of the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x for all x ∈ Q. In particular, the conclusions of this theorem apply for all sufficiently large p. Proof. We first note that the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄ ensures that the cohomology of the boundary vanishes after localization at m. This is because the cohomology of the boundary may be computed inductively from the cohomology of Levi subgroups and then of GL_{n_i} for n_i < n (see, e.g., Section 3 and in particular Proposition 3.3 of [17]), and so the corresponding Galois representations associated to these classes are reducible. By Poincaré duality (and the discussion above concerning the vanishing of the boundary cohomology localized at m), it suffices to prove the result for i < q_0. Let i be the smallest integer for which the inequality is violated. Then, by the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence, we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. As in [16, Section 9.4] (see also [46, Lemma 6.25(4)]), we deduce that H^i(Y_0(Q), k)_{m_α} ≃ H^i(Y, k)_m. The result then follows by Lemma A.3." Setup, pp. 84–85: "For a prime v of O_E, let r̄_v : G_F → GL_n(k) be the corresponding semisimple Galois representation, and let m denote the corresponding maximal ideal of T." p. 82: "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p."
issues.correction:
Minimal fix: add one hypothesis to Theorem A.4, or to the §A.3.1 setup: "Suppose moreover that r̄ (= r̄_v) is absolutely irreducible." This is what the proof calls "the assumption", and it matches the parallel coherent Lemma A.6, which does say "Suppose, moreover, that r̄_p is absolutely irreducible." The last sentence then needs a qualifier: "the conclusions apply for all sufficiently large p [for which r̄ is absolutely irreducible]". Lemma A.3 supplies the vanishing hypothesis for large p. It does not supply irreducibility, which p. 882 says is not known.

H-h3-21's extra hypothesis at m^∨ is not needed. Absolute irreducibility of r̄ gives it for r̄^∨ as well, so boundary cohomology vanishes at both m and m^∨. Poincaré duality on Y then turns the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0 into vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0. [16, Remark 9.3] uses the same "by duality, considering both m and m^*".

Alternative fix that keeps the statement as printed: skip the boundary step and run the i < q0 argument on H_c at m_α^∨. Hochschild–Serre and the Taylor–Wiles isomorphism apply to H_c in the same way. Poincaré duality on Y gives H_c^j(Y,k)_{m^∨} = H^{D−j}(Y,k)_m^∨ = 0 for j < q0. Or use the minimal-complex argument over k[Δ_Q]. The application to A.2 still needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)]. That comes from irreducibility, which A.2(1) supplies.
issues.reason:
Checked on the page images (p. 881, 884–886). The core claim holds:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the setup of §A.3.1 assumes r̄ absolutely irreducible. There r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits that irreducibility for large p is unknown.
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m (needed for the Poincaré duality reduction), uses "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄", which the statement does not contain.
- arXiv:1907.08694v1, Theorem 3.2 and its proof, has word-for-word the same text, including "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r".

The candidate's second point is wrong. They say the upper degrees need the hypothesis at m^∨ as well. Given boundary vanishing at m and m^∨ (both follow from absolute irreducibility of r̄), Poincaré duality on Y derives vanishing at m^∨ for i < q0 from the stated vanishing at m for i > q0+l0. So "suffices to prove i < q0" is legitimate, and the added m^∨ hypothesis is redundant.

Impact: downstream results are fine. Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]"). There, hypothesis (1) (r̄|F(ζp) has enormous image, which includes CHT bigness) forces absolute irreducibility. That application also silently needs the boundary vanishing of [16, Conj. B(4)(b)], which the proof of A.4 supplies under this hypothesis.

Minor side slips:
- The proof ends with "follows by Lemma A.3" where the theorem's own hypothesis suffices.
- Theorem A.2 cites "[16, Section 9.2]" for "enormous", but [16] discusses it in §9.4. Checked on the page images (pp. 881–889) and in arXiv v1.

What is missing:
- Neither Theorem A.4 nor the §A.3.1 setup assumes r̄ is irreducible. r̄_v is only "the corresponding semisimple Galois representation", and p. 882 admits "we do not even know that the representations r_λ are irreducible for sufficiently large p".
- Yet the proof's first step, boundary vanishing at m, rests on "the assumption (of absolute irreducibility) on r̄". The Poincaré-duality reduction to i < q0 uses that step.
- The theorem's last sentence claims the conclusions hold "for all sufficiently large p", which the printed proof does not cover when r̄ is reducible.

Defences tried:
(a) The inherited setting. §A.3.1 works "in [16, Section 9]". In [16] (arXiv 1207.4224v2), §8.5 fixes "a continuous absolutely irreducible representation r̄", and Conjecture B(1)–(5) is stated only for non-Eisenstein m with r̄_m ≅ r̄. A.4 is meant to replace B(4). So the "assumption" is plausibly this imported standing hypothesis. That explains the intent, but it does not make the text correct: §A.3.1 redefines r̄_v for every v as merely semisimple, and the "all sufficiently large p" sentence contradicts p. 882.
(b) The parallel coherent Lemma A.6 (p. 887; v1 Lemma 3.4) states irreducibility explicitly. This confirms the omission in A.4 is a slip.
(c) The conclusion itself is probably true without irreducibility, using the H_c or minimal-complex argument and the same cited inputs. So the statement is not shown false; only the proof's first step relies on the missing hypothesis.

Consequences: Theorem A.4 is used only in the proof of Theorem A.2 (pp. 888–889: "we use Theorem A.4 as a substitute for the vanishing assumption required in [16, Conjecture B]") and in the remark on p. 886.
- In A.2, hypothesis (1) is enormous image, which [16] §9.2 defines as "in addition to bigness".
- Bigness gives H^0(r̄(G_{F(ζp)}), ad^0) = 0. With p ∤ n and r̄ semisimple, this forces r̄ to be absolutely irreducible.
- A.2 also assumes the rest of Conjecture B, which is set in the irreducible case.
So A.2 stands. Theorem A.1 does not use A.4; it uses Lemma A.6. The references to "Theorem A.4" on p. 889 that should read A.1 are a separate slip, already filed as X-K8-13.

issues.correction: 'The result then follows by Lemma A.3' should read 'The result then follows from the hypothesis'. The hypothesis gives H^i(Y, k)_𝔪 = 0 for i < q_0: take n = 1, or use a lowest-degree dévissage along 0 → k → 𝒪/ϖ^n → 𝒪/ϖ^{n−1} → 0, under which H^i(Y,k)_𝔪 injects into H^i(Y,𝒪/ϖ^n)_𝔪 once the lower degrees vanish. Lemma A.3 only shows that the hypothesis holds for all sufficiently large p, which is the 'In particular' clause.
issues.reason: Theorem A.4 is stated under a vanishing hypothesis for an arbitrary p, and its main conclusion does not assume p is large. The proof reduces to showing H^i(Y, k)_𝔪 = 0 for the smallest offending i < q_0. Lemma A.3 gives this only 'for all sufficiently large v', so citing it literally proves only the final 'In particular' clause. The needed vanishing comes directly from the theorem's own hypothesis, which is word for word the conclusion of Lemma A.3. So the intended meaning is clear and the fix is routine. This is a wrong cross-reference, not a mathematical error or a real gap.

issues.correction: Betti case (Theorem A.4). State and prove the theorem for the subcover Y_Δ(Q) → Y_0(Q), where Δ is the maximal p-power quotient of Δ_Q (any p-power quotient also works). The Hochschild–Serre lowest-degree argument then goes through word for word, because a p-group acting on a non-zero k-vector space has non-zero invariants. The alternative is to keep Y_1(Q) and add the missing input: the prime-to-p part of Δ_Q acts trivially on H^*(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α}. That input is local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q, relating diamond operators to inertia, as in [16, Conj. B(2)] and condition (d) of [16, Thm 6.3]. Note that the candidate's first option (going through Y_Δ(Q)) proves the statement for Y_Δ(Q), not for Y_1(Q). Getting back to Y_1(Q) again needs the prime-to-p invariants to be non-zero. So the diamond operators are central, and for y ∉ S∪Q∪{p} the operator S_y = T_{y,0} (which lies in the localising Hecke algebra) equals y^w⟨y^{-1}⟩_S⟨y^{-1}⟩_Q. Localising at m_α fixes S_y ≡ s̄_y, the same value as at level X. By Dirichlet (CRT on (Z/Q)^× × (Z/N)^×) every prime-to-p character of Δ_Q in H^*(X_1(Q),·)_{m_α} is trivial. I rendered pp. 884–889 and checked the printed text above against the images; the arXiv v1 appendix reads the same.

(1) Which cover Y_1(Q) is. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q), Y_0(Q), X_1(Q) or X_0(Q); it relies on [16, §9] and the main text. The main text, §5.2 (p. 822) and p. 834, says "X_{K_1(Q)} → X_{K_0(Q)} is then finite étale with Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×". So in both cases the Galois group is the full ∏(O_F/x)^×. That group is essentially never a p-group: N(x)−1 is even whenever N(x) is odd, so for odd p there is always a 2-part. For example, x = 7 and p = 3 give (Z/7)^× ≅ Z/6.

(2) The step. Let i be the least degree with H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} ≠ 0. Hochschild–Serre gives H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} ≅ E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. For a p-group acting on a nonzero k-vector space, the invariants are nonzero. For Δ_Q = Δ'×Δ_p with |Δ'| > 1 prime to p they need not be. Decompose V = ⊕_χ V_χ over characters of Δ'. Then H^a(Δ_Q, V_χ) = 0 for every a whenever χ ≠ 1. Toy check: Z/6 acting on k = F_3 through the quadratic character has V^G = 0 and no group cohomology at all. So the spectral sequence only brings the χ = 1 part down to Y_0(Q). Components with nontrivial prime-to-p nebentypus in degree < q_0 are left untreated.

(3) Localisation does not remove those components. Theorem A.4(2) defines T_Q explicitly as "the Hecke operators prime to p and prime to the level together with U_x − α_x", so there are no diamond operators, and m_α does not cut out χ = 1. Showing that the χ ≠ 1 components vanish requires local–global compatibility at x for torsion classes (inertia acting through χ, which is nontrivial mod p, would contradict r̄ being unramified at x). The proof never mentions this. Lemma A.6 has the same pattern; its m_α is described only as "any collection of eigenvalues", as in A.4.

(4) Status. The stated results are very probably true, since they follow from local–global compatibility. The p-power subcover version, which is all that [16, §7/§9.5] and Theorem 7.11 need, is proved by the printed argument as it stands. So this is a gap in the proofs of A.4 and A.6 as stated for Y_1/X_1, not a false statement, and Theorems A.1 and A.2 are unaffected.

One minor imprecision in the candidate: the "[16, Conjecture B(2)]" attribution is loose, because the local–global compatibility needed is really the diamond-operator/inertia link. The core claim stands. Lowest-degree Hochschild–Serre: when H^b(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α} = 0 for b < i, we get H^i(Y_0(Q),k)_{m_α} = E_2^{0,i} = (H^i(Y_1(Q),k)_{m_α})^{Δ_Q}. The argument therefore needs these invariants to be non-zero. The appendix never defines Y_1(Q). It takes Y from [16, §9], says 'As in [16, Section 9.4]', and calls Thm A.4 'a replacement for Conjecture B(4) of [16]'. In [16] (arXiv v2, §9.0.1), Y_1(Q) = Y(L_Q), with K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The Galois group of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q) is Δ̃ = ∏_{x∈Q}(O_F/x)^× ([16] §9.3), and this group is not a p-group. The main text uses the same convention for X_1(Q) (p. 822: Galois group Δ_Q := (Z/Q)^×; p. 833). An element of prime order ℓ ≠ p acting on k through a non-trivial character has no invariants. So the step is valid only if prime-to-p characters of Δ_Q cannot occur in the m_α-localisation. The localising algebra T_Q in Thm A.4(2) contains no diamond operators. In PGL_n the centre is trivial (T_{α,n} = 1), so no Hecke operator away from Q controls them. With only A.4's hypotheses (vanishing at level Y), ruling them out needs local–global compatibility at x ∈ Q for torsion classes, and A.4 does not assume it. So the Betti step is a real gap. Charitable reading: Khare–Thorne [46], which the proof cites, define U_1(Q) through the maximal p-power quotient (arXiv:1409.7007v1 p. 41: 'U_1(Q)_v is the pre-image ... of the maximal p-power quotient'). With that reading the proof is correct, but the text points to [16]'s full cover. Defence that succeeds for Lemma A.6: in GSp_4 with Klingen level, the Q-diamond operators are central elements, so the S_y in the localising algebra, together with Dirichlet, kill prime-to-p characters (details in the correction). That part of the candidate is only an omitted routine sentence. Consequences: Thm A.4 is used only in the proof of Thm A.2 (pp. 888–889, as a substitute for [16, Conj. B(4)]). The patching in [16] (proof of Thm 9.19) uses only the p-power subcovers Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), for which the corrected argument is complete. Thm A.2 also assumes Conj. B apart from (4), which supplies the missing compatibility. Lemma A.6 feeds Thm A.1 through Assumption 7.7, which concerns X_Δ(Q) with Δ of p-power order (Thm 7.11). Thms A.1 and A.2 are not affected. Only Thm A.4 in the form stated (unconditional, for the full Y_1(Q)) is left without a complete proof.

Equivalently, it suffices to show that, if i denotes the smallest integer such that H^i(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} is nonzero, then H^i(X, ω(−∞))_{m_Q} is also nonzero. ... issues.correction: The simplest fix is to assume H^i(X, ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_Q} = 0 for i = 2 and 3, which is exactly what Lemma A.5 gives. Alternatively, keep the H^2 hypothesis and add the missing step: H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0 follows from what is already assumed. The H^2 vanishing kills the ϖ-torsion of H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m, and H^3(X, ω^2_K)_m = 0 for non-Eisenstein m in characteristic 0, by the main text's §5.2 and §7.2 (argued below). The Serre-duality reduction then goes through. Separately, "eigenvalues of ρ(Frob_x)" should read r̄_p(Frob_x), and "this theorem" should read "this lemma".
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 886–888 (and arXiv p. 7) and checked them. The transcription above is exact. In the arXiv appendix v1, Lemma 3.4 on p. 7 has the same text, including 'H^2' alone and 'ρ(Frob_x)'.

1. Serre duality. The main text (§7.3) says ω^3(−∞) is the dualizing sheaf. So H^i(X, ω^2)^∨ ≅ H^{3−i}(X, ω(−∞)), and the case i ≥ 2 becomes degrees 3−i ∈ {0, 1}, as the proof says.

2. The written proof needs more than it assumes. It takes the smallest i0 with H^{i0}(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*} ≠ 0 and deduces H^{i0}(X, ω(−∞))_{m*} ≠ 0. A contradiction needs H^0 and H^1 of ω(−∞) at level X to vanish after localizing. These are dual to H^3 and H^2 of ω^2. The lemma assumes only H^2. If i0 = 0, the argument says nothing, not even about the i = 2 conclusion for X_1(Q).

3. The statement is affected too. The proof uses the identification H^i(X_0(Q), ·)_{mα} ≅ H^i(X, ·)_m 'for all i' ([13, Prop. 7.9.8]). So the i = 3 conclusion for X_0(Q) is equivalent to H^3(X, ω^2_k)_m = 0, which is not assumed. The stated hypotheses do not force it. From 0 → H^2(O)/ϖ^n → H^2(O/ϖ^n) → H^3(O)[ϖ^n] → 0, H^2 vanishing for all n only makes H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m torsion-free. H^3(X, ω^2_k)_m = H^3(O)_m ⊗ k is still nonzero whenever there is a characteristic-0 class in H^3(X, ω^2_K)_m. That is a weight-1 cusp eigensystem congruent to m. The paper rules this out only for sufficiently large p, in Lemma A.5, which is why that lemma states 'i = 2 and 3'. The Betti analogue, Theorem A.4, likewise assumes vanishing in every degree outside [q0, q0+l0]. The intended hypothesis ('as in the statement of Lemma A.5') is clearly both degrees.

4. A nuance. The i = 2 conclusion can in fact be recovered from the H^2 hypothesis alone by a different argument. For X_0(Q) use the identification. For X_1(Q), the Tor spectral sequence for RΓ(X_1(Q)) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k in degrees at most 3 forces H^3(X_1(Q)) to be free over k[Δ] and then H^2(X_1(Q)) = 0. The paper's proof does not do this, and the stated i = 3 case still needs H^3.

Downstream: Theorem A.1 (p. 889) uses Lemma A.6 only for sufficiently large p, where Lemma A.5 supplies both H^2 and H^3. So no later result is affected; the defect is confined to the lemma as stated. The ρ → r̄_p fix is a notational misprint. I rendered pp. 824–830, 886–888 and p. 7 of the arXiv appendix; the quoted text is exact.

1. The gap is real. Serre duality with dualizing sheaf ω^3(−∞) gives H^i(ω^2)^∨ ≅ H^{3−i}(ω(−∞)). The proof says it is "equivalent" to show that the least nonzero degree i ≤ 1 for X_1(Q) is also nonzero for X. That only produces a contradiction if both H^0 and H^1 of ω(−∞)_k at level X vanish after localization. Those are dual to H^3 and H^2 of ω^2_k. The lemma assumes only H^2, and the appendix never proves H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0. The case i = 0 is left open, and the i = 3 conclusion for X_0(Q) needs this vanishing outright. The proof identifies H^i(X_0(Q))_{m_α} with H^i(X)_m for all i, via [13, Prop. 7.9.8].

2. Defence: the stated lemma is still true. The missing H^3 vanishing follows from the stated hypotheses and results the paper itself proves.
(a) X is proper over O of relative dimension 3, so H^3(X, ω^2_k) = H^3(X, ω^2_O)/ϖ. There is an exact sequence 0 → H^2(O)/ϖ → H^2(k) → H^3(O)[ϖ] → 0, so H^2(X, ω^2_k)_m = 0 makes H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m torsion-free.
(b) Assuming r̄_p absolutely irreducible makes m non-Eisenstein (definition on p. 844). In characteristic 0, H^3(X, ω(2,2)_K)_m = 0:
- Lemma 7.10 (boundary cohomology vanishes after localizing at m) shows the localized cohomology equals interior cohomology.
- By Theorem 5.2(2), that interior cohomology comes from A_(2)(G).
- The classification argument in the proof of Theorem 7.11 (pp. 854–855) excludes classes (b)–(f), because they have reducible Galois representations. By Clozel's purity lemma the remaining class (a) is essentially tempered at infinity.
- Theorem 5.6(3) and Theorem 5.5 then leave only degrees i with (a−1, b−2) = (1, 0) ∈ C_i, that is i = 0 or 1. p. 830 states H^i(X(C), ω(a,2))_{(2),temp} = 0 for i = 2, 3.
(c) By (a) and (b), H^3(X, ω^2_O)_m is torsion-free and zero after tensoring with K, so it is 0, and H^3(X, ω^2_k)_{m_Q} = 0. With both degrees in hand, the paper's least-degree argument works as written. (The i = 2 conclusion alone can also be obtained from the Tor spectral sequence for RΓ(X_1(Q)) ⊗^L_{k[Δ]} k: H^2(X_0(Q)) = 0 forces H^3(X_1(Q)) to be free over k[Δ] and then H^2(X_1(Q)) = 0.)

So the prior verdict's claim, that the hypotheses do not force H^3 vanishing and that the paper rules it out only for large p, is wrong. Large p is needed in Lemma A.5 only to control torsion affecting H^2.

3. Consequences. The only downstream use is on p. 889: "Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above, where the vanishing result of Lemma A.6 replaces the vanishing results of Lan and Suh". The main text needs only H^2 vanishing: Assumption 7.7 is used in Lemma 7.9 and Theorem 7.11, and §1.2 says "The only point ... is to deduce that H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) = 0". Theorem A.1 in any case assumes p sufficiently large, where Lemma A.5 supplies both degrees.

Conclusion: this is a genuine but fillable omission in the proof. The lemma as stated is correct. Both proposed corrections (adding H^3 to the hypothesis) are right, minimal and harmless, but the paper does not need the stronger hypothesis. The ρ misprint is notational only.

issues.locator: Appendix, §A.4 (Proofs), item (1), p. 888
issues.printed: "(1) Coherent case: R is the minimal ordinary deformation ring denoted by R^min = R_∅ in [16, Section 4]." (checked on the p. 88 image. [16] is F. Calegari and D. Geraghty, Modularity lifting beyond the Taylor–Wiles method, Invent. Math. 211 (2018), 297–433; this is the bibliography on p. 91 onward, and the entry's back-references include p. 88.)
issues.correction: "… denoted by R^min = R_∅ in Section 4 above" (Definition 4.6 with Q = ∅; p. 816 says "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min"; Theorem 9.1 on p. 878 uses the same R^min). In the arXiv appendix the reference should be [CG] (the main paper), not [CG18].
issues.reason: The citation is wrong. The coherent case of the appendix is Theorem A.1, about a semistable modular abelian surface with a GSp4-valued r and the ordinary condition at p. The deformation ring meant is the one in §4 of this paper. On p. 815, Definition 4.6 defines deformations that are "minimal outside Q", and item (6) is the ordinary condition at p. On p. 816 the paper says "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min". Theorem 9.1 (p. 878) uses "R^min … in the sense of Definition 4.6 (with Q taken to be empty)". In the cited paper [16], §4 is "Complements", made up of 4.1 "Multiplicity two" (canonical modules, and a GL2 ordinary ring R_φ for multiplicity in Jacobians) and 4.2 "Finiteness of deformation rings" (Lemma 4.14). It has no R_∅ or R^min and nothing about GSp4. Where [16] does write "If Q = ∅, we will sometimes denote R_Q by R^min", that is in §3.1 (weight-one GL2, unramified at p) and in §5.1 (imaginary quadratic fields), not in §4. The other [16] citations in the same paragraph are correct: §8.5.1 of [16] defines R_v^1, and Theorem 5.16 and Theorem 6.4 exist there. So this is one isolated slip. It comes from the arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1, which was a separate preprint citing the main paper as [CG] and the Invent. paper as [CG18]. There, §4 item (1) reads "Coherent Case: R is the minimal ordinary deformation ring denoted by Rmin = R∅ in §4 of [CG18]", and [CG18] is the Invent. paper. So the arXiv version has the same slip; "§4 of [CG]" was intended. It changes nothing: the ring is clear from context. On p. 889, Theorem A.1 "follows as in Theorem 1.2 above", which uses this paper's R^min, and no later result depends on the wrong pointer.

issues.locator: Appendix §A.4, proof of Theorem A.1, p. 889. Related: §A.3.2 and Lemma A.6 with its proof, pp. 886–888; Theorem 9.1(6), p. 878; Assumption 7.7, p. 851; Theorem 5.1, p. 822; Lemma 7.10, pp. 852–853.
issues.printed: Equally, Theorem A.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 above, where the vanishing result of Lemma A.6 replaces the vanishing results of Lan and Suh [53] for other low-weight local systems.
issues.correction:
Weight a = 2 needs the vanishing for the subcanonical sheaf: H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(2,2)(−∞)_k)_m = 0 (Assumption 7.7 / Theorem 9.1(6)), at the level and localization used there. Lemma A.6 gives this for the canonical ω^2 instead.

The minimal fix is to state and prove Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞); both arguments carry over.
- Lemma A.5: the characteristic-0 class then lies in H^i(X, ω^2(−∞)_C). Since the eigensystem of π is non-Eisenstein, the boundary argument of Lemma 7.10 identifies this group with the canonical H^i. That is L²/tempered cohomology, which vanishes in degrees 2 and 3 (see p. 830).
- Lemma A.6: the Serre dual of ω^2(−∞) is the canonical ω, not ω(−∞). The Khare–Thorne/BCGP descent from X_1(Q) to X_0(Q) to X applies unchanged.

The alternative is a mod-p statement that the paper does not contain: H^1(D, ω^2|_D ⊗ k)_m = 0 on the toroidal boundary D, which makes the canonical and subcanonical H^2 agree. The results to follow are Theorem 9.1 with a = 2, whose hypothesis p − 1 > a ≥ 2 allows it; "as in Theorem 1.2" (j ≥ 4) is only loose wording.
issues.reason:
Checked on the rendered pages (pp. 886–889, 878, 851, 804, 822). The text of §A.3.2 is "by abuse of notation, also let ω denote the canonical extension of ω to X". Lemma A.6 states that H^i(X_1(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = H^i(X_0(Q), ω^2_{O/ϖ^n})_{m_α} = 0 for i ≥ 2. Its proof "use[s] Serre duality to reduce the problem to vanishing of H^i(X_1(Q), ω(−∞))_{m*_α} for i ≤ 1".

I redid the duality. By §5.2, ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b E, so ω(2,2) = ω^2. The dualizing sheaf is ω^3(−∞) (§7.2). So the dual of canonical ω^2 is ω^{−2} ⊗ ω^3(−∞) = ω(−∞), which confirms that Lemma A.6 concerns the canonical ω(2,2).

What the main argument needs is different. Theorem 9.1(6) requires H^2(X_i(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_{m_∅} = {0}. Assumption 7.7 requires H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m trivial, and it is used in Lemma 7.9 to make H^1(ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m divisible, which Theorem 7.11's balancedness needs. The Lan–Suh input that Lemma A.6 is meant to replace, Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.8, is also stated for ω(a,b)(−∞)_k. So the substitution swaps a canonical-extension statement for a subcanonical one without argument. The dual form of the needed statement is H^1 of the canonical ω, while Lemma A.6's proof treats ω(−∞).

The two differ by boundary cohomology: H^1(D, ω^2|_D) → H^2(ω^2(−D)) → H^2(ω^2). The paper kills the localized boundary cohomology only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10, statement p. 852). There is no mod-p boundary result anywhere in the text.

Strongest counterargument: §1.2 (p. 804) says one "need[s] only the weaker result that the image of H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^can) in H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) is zero" after localization. If that meant the interior H^2, Lemma A.6 would imply it. But that reduction is only asserted, never proved; the literal map can → sub does not exist; and Section 7 (Lemma 7.9) uses the full subcanonical H^2(·_k)_m = 0. In the same passage the authors call the H^2 vanishing unresolved and say only that one "should be able to" handle weight (2,2) by Khare–Thorne.

Verdict: a genuine gap. It is probably fixable by rerunning Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞), but that argument is not in the paper. The candidate's remark about Theorem 1.2 is also right: it assumes p − 1 > j ≥ 4, so the operative statement is Theorem 9.1 with a = 2. The candidate's suggested boundary vanishing is a sufficient condition; it is correct, but it is one of the two routes.

arXiv: appendix v1 (1907.08694v1) has the same text, with its §3.2 using the same canonical convention and its Lemma 3.4 being Lemma A.6. Its §4 reads "Equally, Theorem 1.1 follows as in Theorem 1.2 of [CG], where the vanishing result of Lemma 3.4 replaces the vanishing results of Lan–Suh [LS13] for other low weight local systems used in [CG]." In main-text v1 (1907.08691v1), Theorem 9.1(6) and Assumption 7.7 are identical to the published text.

Scope: Theorem A.1 is the appendix's main result and nothing later in the paper depends on it. It is not shown to be false, so the defect is in the proof only. Checked on the rendered p. 803, 804, 822, 823, 830, 851–853, 878–889.

(1) The appendix's ω^2 is the canonical extension. §A.3.2 says so explicitly. The main text also writes ω(a,b) = W^can_μ (p. 823), with ω(a,b)(−∞) for the subcanonical sheaf. Serre duality confirms it: the dualizing sheaf is ω^3(−∞) (p. 851), so the dual of the canonical ω^2 is ω(−∞), exactly as in the proof of Lemma A.6. For the subcanonical ω^2(−∞) the dual would have been the canonical ω. Two independent passages agree, so a charitable misprint reading (appendix ω meaning subcanonical) is not available.

(2) The main argument needs the subcanonical sheaf. Theorem 9.1(6) reads "H^2(X_i(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_{m_∅} = {0}", and Assumption 7.7 reads "H^2(X_Δ(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_k)_m is trivial". The proof of Theorem 9.1 uses these only through Theorem 7.11 ("H_N is finite and balanced over S_N by Theorem 7.11", p. 880). Theorem 7.11 uses Lemma 7.9: H^1(ω(a,2)(−∞)_{K/O})_m is divisible, which is equivalent to H^2(X_0(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)_O)_m being torsion-free. The Lan–Suh input being replaced (Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.8) is also stated for ω(a,b)(−∞)_k.

(3) Canonical vanishing does not give the subcanonical statement. Take a = 2 and 0 → ω^2(−D) → ω^2 → ω^2|_D → 0. Lemma A.6 plus Lemma 7.10 (⊗K) make H^2(sub_O)_m torsion, equal to coker(H^1(can_O)_m → H^1(D, ω^2|_D)_m). Lemma 7.9 needs this cokernel to vanish. That is a mod-p boundary statement, and the paper proves boundary vanishing only after ⊗K (Lemma 7.10).

Defences tried:
(a) §1.2 (p. 804) says one needs "only the weaker result that the image of H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^can) in H^2(X_1(N), ω(j,2)^sub) is zero after localization". The printed direction is reversed, since the natural map goes sub→can. Read as interior H^2, it would follow from Lemma A.6. But this is only asserted: the same paragraph says "we were not able to prove it". Also, by (3), interior vanishing is automatic once the canonical H^2_m = 0, yet it does not give Lemma 7.9.
(b) Could the patching be rerun with canonical sheaves? Then Section 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 (which use W^sub) and the H^0 comparison would need mod-p boundary input, which is also not in the paper.
(c) Cited sources: [13, Prop. 7.9.8] is invoked only for the level-lowering step, not for any comparison between canonical and subcanonical cohomology.

So this is a genuine gap, but a routine one. Rerunning Lemmas A.5 and A.6 for ω^2(−∞) works, with Lemma 7.10's characteristic-0 boundary argument added in Lemma A.5. There is also a minor mismatch in level and localization: Lemma A.6 uses X_0(Q)/X_1(Q) at m_α, while Assumption 7.7 uses X_Δ(Q) at m. The earlier verdict's two routes and its remark about Theorem 1.2 are confirmed.

Consequences: Lemma A.6 is used only in this sentence, to prove Theorem A.1. Theorem A.2 goes through Theorem A.4 (Betti cohomology) and is unaffected, and nothing after Theorem A.1 depends on it. Theorem A.1 is not shown to be false, and the fix is expected to work, so only its proof is affected.

issues.correction: Replace 'Theorem A.4' by 'Theorem A.1' in both places: '...which we are required to prove (for sufficiently large p) for Theorem A.1. Furthermore, we must justify the claim in Theorem A.1 that the assumptions hold for a set of primes p of density 1.'

issues.locator: Appendix, §A.4, proof of Lemma A.8, p. 890, lines 1–2 of the proof
issues.printed: Proof. From such an equality, we can build two finite-dimensional representations A_ℓ and B_ℓ built out of copies of ∧²V_ℓ, Q_p, Q_p(1), V_ℓ, and V_ℓ ⊗ V_ℓ, respectively, which have equal trace on Frob_p for infinitely many p. (Checked on a 400 dpi render of p. 90: both constituents have bold Q with subscript p, the same italic p as in Frob_p, not ℓ.)
issues.correction: Replace "Q_p, Q_p(1)" with "Q_ℓ, Q_ℓ(1)". On p. 889 the paper defines V_ℓ = H^1(A, Q̄_ℓ), so the matching form is Q̄_ℓ and Q̄_ℓ(1). These are the ℓ-adic trivial and cyclotomic characters of G_Q, whose Frob_p-traces are 1 and p. A pedantic point: with V_ℓ = H^1 and geometric Frobenius (the normalisation that gives the printed characteristic polynomial, whose roots have absolute value √p), the Tate twist with trace p is Q_ℓ(−1). With arithmetic Frobenius on the Tate module it is Q_ℓ(1). This is a convention question. What matters is the subscript: it should be ℓ, not p.
issues.reason: Rendered pp. 889–890. Lemma A.8 (p. 889) says there is no fixed linear relation between 1, p, b_p, a_p and a_p^2 holding for p in a set S of positive density. The proof moves the terms with positive coefficients to one side and those with negative coefficients to the other, then realises each side as the Frob_p-trace of a single G_Q-representation. The term 2p + b_p comes from ∧²V_ℓ, ±a_p from V_ℓ and a_p^2 from V_ℓ⊗V_ℓ. The constants 1 and p need 1-dimensional representations whose Frob_p-trace is 1 and p for every p. These are the trivial and cyclotomic characters with coefficients in Q_ℓ (or Q̄_ℓ). They are summed with the ℓ-adic V_ℓ into A_ℓ and B_ℓ, the argument then uses the image of G_Q on V_ℓ being GSp_4(Z_ℓ) together with Chebotarev, and so every summand must be ℓ-adic. "Q_p" has no sensible meaning here: p is the prime that varies over S, so Q_p and Q_p(1) are not fixed representations. A p-adic Q_p(1) would also be ramified at p, so it has no Frob_p-trace, and it cannot be combined with ℓ-adic representations. No convention in the paper makes Q_p denote an ℓ-adic coefficient field. The same Q_p appears in arXiv:1907.08694v1 (appendix), Lemma 4.2 proof, p. 8, where I checked the render: "built out of copies of ∧²V_ℓ, Q_p, Q_p(1), V_ℓ, and V_ℓ ⊗ V_ℓ respectively". The main arXiv preprint 1907.08691v1 does not contain the passage. Effect: nothing depends on it. The evident intended reading, ℓ-adic trivial and cyclotomic characters, is what the rest of the proof uses. Lemma A.8 is used only for Lemma A.7(2), and through it for the density-1 claim of Theorem A.4. Neither statement changes. Aside, not part of this item: the proof of Lemma A.8 is sketchy in other places, e.g. it says "for infinitely many p" where it means the positive-density set S. The candidate's claim is exactly this misprint.

issues.locator: Appendix, §A.4 (Proofs), proof of Lemma A.7(2), case (3), p. 890. The characteristic polynomial is on p. 889. In the arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1 it is the proof of Lemma 4.1, case (3), p. 9.
issues.printed: (3) Suppose that α = ε mod p for some fixed ε ∈ {±1}. Then b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p.
issues.correction: b_p + εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p (equivalently ε^2 + a_p ε + b_p ≡ 0).
issues.reason:
I checked this on the page images at 130 and 250 dpi. p. 889 prints the characteristic polynomial as "X^4 + a_pX^3 + (2p + b_p)X^2 + pa_pX + p^2", with roots "α, β, α^{-1}p and β^{-1}p". p. 890, case (3), prints "Suppose that α = ε mod p for some fixed ε ∈ {±1}. Then b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p." The "=" instead of "≡" is also as printed.

My computation from the printed polynomial:
- The roots sum to −a_p, so a_p = −(α + β + p/α + p/β).
- The X^2 coefficient is 2p + b_p, so b_p = αβ + p^2/(αβ) + p(α/β + β/α).
- In this case α and β are units at the prime above p. That is forced by the factor αβ in Lemma A.7(2), after using case (1) and the α↔β, β↔p/β relabelling. So mod p we get a_p ≡ −(α + β) and b_p ≡ αβ. Equivalently, the polynomial is ≡ X^2(X^2 + a_pX + b_p) mod p.
- So α ≡ ε gives ε^2 + εa_p + b_p ≡ 0, that is b_p + εa_p + 1 ≡ 0.
- For the printed expression: b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ εβ + (1 + εβ) + 1 = 2(1 + εβ). This is not ≡ 0 unless β ≡ −ε.

Concrete counterexample: p = 7, with polynomial (X^2 − X + 7)(X^2 − 3X + 7) = X^4 − 4X^3 + 17X^2 − 28X + 49. So a_p = −4 and b_p = 3. The unit root α ≡ 1 mod 7, so ε = 1. The printed expression gives 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 ≢ 0 mod 7. The corrected one gives 3 − 4 + 1 = 0.

A script over every product (X^2 − t1X + p)(X^2 − t2X + p) with p = 7, 11, 13 and unit t_i gave these results. The corrected congruence held in all 72 cases with α ≡ ε. The printed one failed in 66 of them.

No convention in the paper rescues the printed sign. The error does not depend on arithmetic versus geometric Frobenius: it is fixed by the printed polynomial, which is invariant under x ↦ p/x. It would be correct only if the cubic coefficient were −a_p, i.e. if a_p were the trace. The paper's remark that a_p^2 is the trace on V⊗V is sign-blind.

The arXiv appendix 1907.08694v1 (Lemma 4.1, case (3), p. 9) prints the same "b_p − εa_p + 1 ≡ 0 mod p", with the same characteristic polynomial "X^4 + a_pX^3 + (2p+b_p)X^2 + pa_pX + p^2".

issues.reason: I rendered p. 893 at 110 dpi, and entry [38] reads exactly as quoted. I also rendered p. 881; the only citations of [38] are the two quoted in the locator. I checked Crossref for doi:10.1186/s40687-016-0078-5. It gives the title "On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties", the authors Michael Harris, Kai-Wen Lan, Richard Taylor and Jack Thorne, the journal Research in the Mathematical Sciences, volume 3, article number 37, published online 26 Oct 2016 and in print Dec 2016. It is the same work. The arXiv abstract of 1411.6717 says: "We construct the compatible system of l-adic representations associated to a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n over a CM (or totally real) field … we impose no self-duality hypothesis". This is exactly the family r_λ(π) that Theorem A.2 uses. So the 2020 paper cites, as "in preparation" and under an old working title, a work that had been on arXiv under its final title since Nov 2014 and in print since 2016. The paper's own wording, "was only recently proved to exist in [38]", also treats the work as finished. The entry does not say where to find the cited work, but the intended reference is clear from the authors and context. That makes it a bibliographic slip ("misprint" in the sense of PROTOCOL §18), not a mathematical error. This matches earlier accepted bibliography misprints such as PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18/E217. No correction exists: Crossref's deposit for doi:10.1215/00127094-2019-0044 (the final issue version, vol. 169, no. 5, 1 Apr 2020) still lists "[38] … Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation." issues.printed: "If p > 0, we can find nonnegative integers λ and t such that 0 < λ ≤ v² and |disc(NS(X))| = p^t λ |disc(NS(M_H(v)))|." Proof: "… we have a natural injection of lattices with torsion cokernel Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X). Since the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ is v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), this implies by the same argument that |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))|."
issues.correction: λ need not be an integer. With I = [N(X) : Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X))], one has |disc NS(X)| = p^t (v²/I²) |disc NS(M_H(v))| with t ≥ 0. So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.
issues.reason: Take v = (1, 0, −1), the Mukai vector of ideal sheaves of length-two subschemes, so M_H(v) = X^[2]. It satisfies condition (C): it is primitive, of rank 1, v² = 2, and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1. Then v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = NS(X) ⊕ Z(1, 0, 1) with (1, 0, 1)² = −2, so |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = 2|disc NS(X)|. The proof's first step gives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|. Hence |disc NS(X)| = ½ p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|, which is not of the form p^t λ with λ a positive integer when p is odd. The proof passes from the equality disc(Zv ⊕ K) = I² disc N(X) to an integer multiplier without controlling I, here I = 2. The inequality stated for p = 0 is correct. Checked on the page image. issues.locator: §4.3, Remark 4.5, p. 863 (also in arXiv v1, §4.3)
issues.printed: “Let I be the kernel of φ′ : T_m → E[π]/(π^{r_an+1}).”
issues.correction: The homomorphism φ′ on T_m is not constructed. Either it must be constructed, or the remark must be read with the φ′ of Remark 3.4, whose domain is the subalgebra T′ ⊂ T and whose target is E[π]/π^{r+1}, in which case the ideal I, the isomorphism T_m/I ≅ E[π]/(π^{r_an+1}) and the faithfulness of B as a module over the corresponding ring all have to be restated.
issues.reason: The only φ′ defined in the paper is that of Remark 3.4, p. 852, which has a different domain and a different target. A map of the stated shape need not exist: any Λ-algebra homomorphism W → E[π]/(π^{r_an+1}) must send each ε_i into the annihilator of π, i.e. into E·π^{r_an}, so for r ≥ 2 the product ε_1 ⋯ ε_r maps to 0 while the relation ε_1 ⋯ ε_r + (−1)^{r_an} L*_an(χ)π^{r_an} = 0 forces L*_an(χ) = 0. So no such φ′ factors through ϕ_m except when L*_an(χ) = 0 or r = 1.

issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.

issues.printed: "Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪_ε r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, (6.6) where … φ is any even Hecke–Maass cusp form with Laplace eigenvalue 1/4 + r²." Proof: "Part (6.6) of Proposition 2 follows straight from Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 of [12]."
issues.correction: State (6.6) for the unit vector u = φ/‖φ‖: Weyl(u, χ) ≪_ε r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}. It follows from Theorem 4 and [12, Theorem 5] together with the Rankin–Selberg size of ‖φ‖ for the normalization a(1) = 1. It is also what the proof of Theorem 2 uses, since c(φ)⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f, u⟩u.
issues.reason: The forms φ are normalized by a(1) = 1 in (5.7), p.962, and the Shimura relation in Theorem 4 forces this too. [12, Theorem 5] (Duke 1988, p.85, read on the page image) bounds the coefficients of a spectral weight-1/2 form with eigenvalue 1/4 + t² by |λ|^A ch(πt/2)|n|^{−2/7+ε}. Here t = r/2, so Theorem 4 gives |Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ)| ≪ r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{3/4−2/7+ε}. That bound has an exponential factor, which (6.6) omits. The factor cannot simply be dropped. For a(1) = 1, Rankin–Selberg unfolding gives ⟨φ, φ⟩ ≍ L(1, sym²φ)/cosh(πr), so ⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ is about e^{πr/2} times the unit vector u. As printed, (6.6) would therefore make the Weyl integrals of u exponentially small in r, which the cited results do not give. For u the two exponentials cancel: Weyl(u, χ) = ‖φ‖ Weyl(⟨φ, φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪ L(1, sym²φ)^{1/2} r^C |D|^{13/28+ε}, and L(1, sym²φ) ≪ r^ε. The coefficient bound "c(φ) ≪ |r|^{−A}" used for Theorem 2 on p.969 holds for u, so Theorem 2 stands. Noted by the extraction ("The spectral norm gate").

issues.printed: An irreducible flat connection (E,∇) with torsion determinant L is called cohomologically rigid, if [(E,∇)] is a reduced isolated point of M_dR(X,L,r). This is equivalent to vanishing of  H¹_dR(X,(End(E),∇)) = 0,  and hence explains the nomenclature.

For every X with b₁(X) > 0 — every curve of positive genus, and every variety the paper is really about — the printed condition therefore holds for no connection at all, and the notion it defines would be empty. The invariant that is canonical is the one the proof has just built: the characteristic polynomial of the Morita-reduced Higgs sheaf π′_*F, which is independent of the splitting because F is unique up to unique isomorphism. Theorem 2.17 should require of M that this reduced invariant equal a, rather than only that M be supported on Z′_a with π′_*M of characteristic polynomial a^{p^d}; the descent of a should be deduced from that canonicity, not from uniqueness of p^d-th roots.

Witness for the two printed claims (r=2): let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, Z′ an elliptic curve over k with a nowhere-vanishing ω ∈ H⁰(Z′,Ω¹), and S = Spec k[ε]/(ε²). Then a = λ² + εω² and a₀ = λ² are distinct monic elements of A_{Z′,2}(S) with a^{p} = λ^{2p} + ε^pω^{2p} = λ^{2p} = a₀^{p}, so b = λ^{2p} has two monic degree-2 roots. Witness for the statement (r=3, d=1): take a = λ³ + εω²λ and a₀ = λ³, again with a^p = a₀^p. Since a vanishes on the zero section, Z′ ×_k S ⊂ Z′_a, so the D_{Z′}-module M of the constant family (F^*V,∇_can) with V of rank 3 — whose p-curvature is zero — is scheme-theoretically supported on Z′_a, and π′_*M is locally free of rank 3p with characteristic polynomial λ^{3p} = a^{p}. M therefore satisfies every condition on the right-hand side of Theorem 2.17 for this a, while the connection it corresponds to has Hitchin invariant a₀ ≠ a: the asserted equivalence of groupoids fails. issues.printed: One denotes by Def_ϱ: Art_F → Sets the functor sending a finite-dimensional commutative local F-algebra A to the set of isomorphism classes of continuous representations ϱ′: Γ→GL(r,A), such that there exists a finite field extension F′/F, an F-morphism A→F′, and an isomorphism (ϱ′)_{F′}≃ϱ_{F′}. The character functor A ↦ Hom_cont(Γ,1+m_A) is corepresented by the completed group algebra F_q[[Γ^ab ⊗ Z_p]] ≅ F_q[[x_1,…,x_b]] with b = b₁(X), so it acts freely on Def_ϱ and forces the hull of Def_ϱ to have dimension at least b₁(X). For X a curve of genus g ⩾ 1 no absolutely irreducible ϱ would then be rigid, and Lemma 5.6 — whose right-hand side is the completion of the moduli space M_B(X/C,det(ϱ),r) with the determinant fixed — would be false. issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.1, published p. 146, lines 3–5
issues.printed: Since there are infinitely many prime numbers p such that there exists a good closed point s∈S (Lemma 5.11), we conclude that the Kodaira–Spencer class vanishes everywhere on X_S.
issues.correction: Apply Lemma 5.11 after inverting a non-zero coefficient of gr(∇_S) — equivalently, after shrinking S — which its own proof allows, since the finitely generated ring R₁ ⊂ C chosen there may be enlarged at will and Cassels's theorem then sends the adjoined inverse to a p-adic unit. Infinitude of residue characteristics on its own does not give the density the deduction needs.
issues.reason: The good points of Lemma 5.11(c) are closed points of S of pairwise distinct residue characteristics, and such a family need not meet every non-empty open subset of a positive-dimensional arithmetic base: in Spec Z[t] the closed points (p,t), p prime, realise every residue characteristic and all lie in V(t), where the non-zero section t vanishes. The vanishing of a section at all of them therefore does not make it zero. What is true, and is what the proof needs, is this: gr(∇_S) is a section of a coherent sheaf on the integral scheme X_S, so it is non-zero if and only if it is non-zero on the generic fibre; if gr(∇_C) ≠ 0 there is a non-empty open V ⊂ S over which it is non-zero, and a good point inside V contradicts the vanishing established for every good s. The rest of the proof is unaffected: on the reduced fibre X_s the identity gr(∇_s) = ω·id together with nilpotency does force ω = 0.

issues.locator: Remark 2.16(a) and (b), published pp. 116–117
issues.printed: (a) The vector space of degree-r sections in H⁰(Z′, Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′}[λ]) is isomorphic to A_{Z′,r}(k). … (b) For a∈A_{Z′,r}(S) we define the spectral cover Z′_a to be the closed subscheme of T^*Z′×_kS defined by the sheaf of ideals generated by the section θ^r+a₂θ^{r−2}+…+(−1)^r a_r in (π′×_k Id)_*O_{T^*Z′×_kS} = (Sym^• T_{Z′})⊗_k O_S.
issues.correction: In (a): the space of *monic* degree-r sections whose λ^{r−1}-coefficient vanishes — an affine space over A_{Z′,r}(k) — or, kept linear, the degree-r sections whose λ^r- and λ^{r−1}-coefficients both vanish. In (b): that section lives in H⁰(T^*Z′×_kS, (π′×Id)^* Sym^r Ω¹_{Z′}), as the display on p. 117 correctly states, and for dim Z′ > 1 the ideal is the one generated by its components.
issues.reason: A degree-r section of Sym^• Ω¹_{Z′}[λ] is ⨁_{i=0}^{r} H⁰(Z′,Sym^i Ω¹_{Z′})·λ^{r−i}, which contains the i = 0 summand k·λ^r and the i = 1 summand H⁰(Z′,Ω¹_{Z′}); (2.5) defines A_{Z′,r} as ⨁_{i=2}^{r}, the paper having just noted that "the definition above omits the i=1 term, since our Higgs fields are trace-free by assumption". The two spaces are therefore never equal: for Z′ = P¹ one has H⁰(Sym^iΩ¹) = 0 for all i ⩾ 1, so A_{Z′,r}(k) = 0 while the degree-r sections are k·λ^r ≠ 0. Part (b) itself uses the corrected description, its element being monic with no λ^{r−1} term. This is the remark the authors introduce with "Since it is central to our approach, we give a more detailed description", which is why the imprecision is worth recording rather than passing over.

issues.printed: "We will work a little more generally: for any 2g-dimensional abelian variety A, the dimension of any commutative Q-subalgebra of End(A)⊗Q is at most g. If equality holds, then A is said to have “complex multiplication” (or CM for short), and the ring End(A) is necessarily a CM order"
issues.correction: For a g-dimensional abelian variety A, every commutative semisimple Q-subalgebra of End(A) ⊗ Q has dimension at most 2g; A has CM when one of dimension 2g exists, and it is that subalgebra's intersection with End(A), not End(A), which is a CM order (when A is simple, End(A) itself is one).
issues.reason: The bound for a g-dimensional abelian variety is 2g (the subalgebra acts faithfully on H_1(A, Q), of dimension 2g); for the printed '2g-dimensional' A the bound would be 4g, not g. The paper only uses abelian varieties L_R/L_Z with O_E-action, for which the intended statement is correct.

issues.locator: §8.1, proof of Theorem 8.4, p. 299
issues.printed: "A general X = Ω^∞E may be replaced by its Postnikov truncation τ_{≤2p−2}X, which splits as a product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces, up to homotopy equivalence of loop spaces. Indeed, the deloop Ω^∞ΣE can have non-vanishing homotopy in degrees ∗ ≥ 2 only, and the shortest possible k-invariant is 𝒫^1 : K(Z/p, 2) → K(Z/p, 2p). Hence τ_{≤2p−2}X splits as a product of Eilenberg–MacLane spaces, and this splitting respects the H-space structure."
issues.correction: The loop-space (H-space) splitting of τ_{≤2p−2}X can fail. The reduction to Eilenberg–MacLane spaces needs another argument, e.g. treat the single possible 𝒫^1-extension between π_1 and π_{2p−2} directly, or truncate at 2p − 3 and handle degree 2p − 2 separately.
issues.reason: The k-invariant 𝒫^1 : K(Z/p, 2) → K(Z/p, 2p) of the deloop connects π_2(Ω^∞ΣE) = π_1(X) to π_{2p−1}(Ω^∞ΣE) = π_{2p−2}(X), inside the range of the truncation. For E = ΣS^∧_p (p odd), α_1 ∈ π_{2p−3}(S) is detected by 𝒫^1, so τ_{≤2p−1}QS² has non-trivial k-invariant 𝒫^1ι_2 = ι_2^p, and τ_{≤2p−2}QS¹ is not a product of Eilenberg–MacLane loop spaces. The conclusion of Theorem 8.4 is not contradicted in this example: the Hurewicz image of α_1 survives in the indecomposables. But the argument as written does not prove it, and Lemma 8.5 needs an H-space splitting.

For self-dual ρ (S_φ ≅ S_3) a separate parametrisation is needed; Theorem 9.1(i) predicts it: the two characters of S_3 trivial on μ_3 go to the lifts from PGL_3 ⋊ Z/2Z, the 2-dimensional representation to the lift from PD^×.

For such φ, S_[φ] does not have order 3; C_[φ] = Z_{G_2}(S_3) is the fixed group of an outer involution of SL_3(C), isomorphic to SO_3(C), not simply connected of type A_2; and Irr(S_3) has three elements, so the bijection j : Irr(S_[φ]) → Z/3Z and the map η ↦ π_η of (b)–(c) are not defined. issues.locator: §9, p. 30 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: “This looks like a D_3 root system; however, the Weyl-invariant quadratic form in this case is q(s_1, s_2, s_3) = s_1² + s_2² + s_3³ − ¼(s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² rather than the usual dot product, and with this form, we have a realization of the C_3 root system with simple roots α_1 = (0, 1, −1), α_2 = (1, −1, 0), α_3 = (0, 2, 2).”
issues.correction: On the space of characters (s_1, s_2, s_3), where the paper has just written the Weyl action, the invariant form is s_1² + s_2² + s_3² + (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², and the simple roots are (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1), of type C_3. The printed form, with s_3² for the misprinted s_3³, is the invariant form on the dual space of cocharacters (u_1, u_2, u_3). There the vectors (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (0, 2, 2) are the images 2α^∨/q(α^∨) of the simple roots, and α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1).
issues.reason: The paper's reflection for α_3 is r_3(s) = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3, −s_3, −s_2), which is s − ⟨s, α_3^∨⟩α_3 with α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1) and α_3 = (−1, 1, 1). The computation gives q(r_3 s) − q(s) = (5/4)((s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² − s_1²) ≠ 0, so q is not invariant on characters. A form a|s|² + b(Σs)² is invariant under r_1, r_2, r_3 exactly when a = b. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. All this was checked by computation in exact arithmetic. The positive chamber stated next, Re s_1 > Re s_2 > |Re s_3|, is correct, and nothing later uses q.

issues.printed: "We can apply Proposition 5.1 to X and (A′, L|A′) … Hence the conclusion follows by applying the induction hypothesis to each irreducible component of X′ and appropriately adjusting c3 and c2."
issues.correction: Prove the statement for all irreducible X of degree ≤ d in abelian varieties of dimension ≤ g, not only generating ones. If some component X_i of X′ has a point P₁ ∈ X_i° with ĥ(P₁) ≤ c, apply the induction hypothesis to X_i − P₁ ⊆ B_i := ⟨X_i − X_i⟩. Take the Proposition 5.1 constants as min/max over l ≤ c(g)d^{2g} and dim B_i ≤ g, as in the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 5.1 also depends on the exact l = deg_L A′. The repair uses only the parallelogram law and Lemma 2.5, so Theorem 1.3 holds.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 6.1, §6.2 (p = 3) and §6.3 (p = 2), p.21 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: "So assume 9|k, in which case (3,0,0) is a non-singular solution modulo 9 and so lifts to solutions modulo 3ⁿ, n ≥ 2." … "So assume k ≡ 1 (mod 4) and we find the non-singular solution (1,0,0) modulo 4 … This then lifts to higher powers of 2."
issues.correction: The two lifts exist only in part of the stated classes: every x ≡ (3,0,0) mod 9 has M(x) ≡ 9 mod 27, and every x ≡ (1,0,0) mod 4 has M(x) ≡ 1 mod 8. Complete the argument with further points. For p = 2 and k ≡ 5 mod 8, use (x₁, 0, 2) with x₁² = k − 4 ≡ 1 mod 8, a 2-adic square. For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.
issues.reason: The gradient of M at (3,0,0) is 6 and at (1,0,0) it is 2, so the lifting needs M(a) ≡ k modulo 27, resp. 8 (Hensel's lemma in the form ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖²). A direct check confirms the two failing classes, k ≡ 18 mod 27 and k ≡ 5 mod 8 (e.g. k = 18, 5). Counting solutions modulo 3⁴ and 2⁶ confirms that Proposition 6.1 itself holds in every admissible class.

issues.correction: Restrict the claim to odd x₁, the only case in which it is used. Then x₁ − 2 and x₁ + 2 are odd and ≡ ±2 (mod 5), so each has an odd prime factor ≡ ±2 (mod 5).
issues.reason: For even x₁ the claim is false: x₁ = 60 gives x₁² − 4 = 3596 = 2²·29·31, with no odd prime factor ≡ ±2 (mod 5). The prime 2 gives no contradiction. The proof uses 5 ∤ x₁x₂x₃ only in the all-odd case (the other cases are reduced to it by a Vieta move or treated through (8.9)), so the conclusion is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proposition B.12, p.50 (arXiv v3)
issues.correction: Only the qualitative statement is right: δ₂(k) = 0 iff k ≡ 3 (mod 4), and otherwise δ₂(k) ≥ 3/4. In (1), δ₂(k) = (3/8)(1 + χ₄(k))(2 − χ₈(k)), i.e. 3/4 for k ≡ 1 (mod 8) and 9/4 for k ≡ 5 (mod 8); (2) and (3)(a), (c), (e) are consistent with direct counts. (3)(b) and (4)(b) involve 2^{−(η−6)/2} with η odd, which is irrational. (3)(d) fails: δ₂ = 7/4 for 4 − k = 16w with w ≡ 1, 3, 5 mod 8 and 11/4 for w ≡ 7. In (4), (c) holds only for w ≡ 1 (mod 4) (δ₂ = 1 when w ≡ 3 mod 4), and (a), (d), (e) fail in every class tested: for example δ₂ = 11/8 at η = 4, 5 with w ≡ 1 (mod 4), and δ₂(k) → 1 as η → ∞ (35/32 at η = 8), whereas the printed values tend to 5/2. ((3)(e) is read with (−1)^w = −1 for odd w.) The formulas must be re-derived from Lemmas B.9–B.10.
issues.reason: Brute-force counts modulo 2⁶, 2⁷ and 2⁸ give δ₂(1) = 3/4, δ₂(5) = 9/4, δ₂(16) = 11/8 and δ₂(24) = 1, against the printed 3/2, 9/2, 5/4 and 5/2. A table modulo 2¹² for |k| < 4000 fixes the values by 2-adic class. Lemma B.9 is consistent with the odd-k values (1 + N₁ + N₂ + N₃ = 3/4 or 9/4), so the error is in combining the lemmas. §9.1 uses only δ₂ ≥ 3/4 for admissible k, which holds, so Theorem 1.2(ii) is unaffected.

issues.reason: Let C be an algebraically closed characteristic-p perfectoid field, F=underline Zp times Spa(C,OC), and let the DISCRETE locally profinite group Z act by translations. Scholze11.12 realizes F as a perfectoid space; the free pro-etale relation coproduct_Z F defines a quotient diamond G and a Z-torsor. Scholze12.7–12.9 give |G|=Zp/Z with quotient topology. Every integer orbit is dense. Any nonempty saturated open has closed invariant complement, which would contain a dense orbit if nonempty; hence the quotient is indiscrete. It has more than one point (Zp is uncountable, Z countable), so it is connected, whereas pi0(F)/Z=Zp/Z has many elements. Proposition3.12 and6.6(2) use this false generality. This disproves the lemma, not by itself the geometric main theorems.

issues.printed: After replacing R by a finite étale extension R′ there exist rth roots Q_ℓ(1/r) of the Tate twist Q_ℓ(1) as lisse ℓ-adic sheaves on Spec R for all r ≥ 1 … For r ≥ 1 we define another continuous ℓ-adic representation of π_1^ét(Spec R′, C) by the formula exp((1/r) log(ρ|π_1^ét(Spec R′,C)))

The lemma holds for all r with Q̄_ℓ-coefficients: ρ(π_1(R′)) is procyclic with a generator u; choose compatible principal-unit roots u_k of u with u_k^ℓ = u_{k−1}, and set Q_ℓ(1/ℓ^k) = (g ↦ u_k^{a(g)}) where ρ(g) = u^{a(g)}. Theorem 2.18 needs only the finitely many r dividing the denominators of the α_i, β_j, so its proof survives with Q̄_ℓ-coefficients or with ℓ chosen prime to those denominators. The sheaves live on Spec R′[1/ℓ], not Spec R.
issues.reason: Let R ⊂ C be of finite type over Z. The fraction field of R′ is finitely generated over Q, so the cyclotomic character ρ of π_1(Spec R′[1/ℓ]) has open image, which contains 1 + ℓ^m for some m. A Q_ℓ-valued character χ is Z_ℓ^×-valued, and for odd ℓ, (Z_ℓ^×)^{ℓ^k} ⊂ μ_{ℓ−1}·(1 + ℓ^{k+1}Z_ℓ). For k ≥ m, 1 + ℓ^m ∉ μ_{ℓ−1}·(1 + ℓ^{k+1}Z_ℓ), so χ^{ℓ^k} = ρ is impossible. The same bound applies over any fixed finite extension of Q_ℓ.

issues.locator: §2.1(a), p. 9, with Corollary 9, p. 12, Theorem A/§0.3, p. 3, and §5.2, p. 20 (both versions)
issues.printed: (a) Each θ-twisted conjugacy class of W̃ intersects only finitely many W_a cosets. [Justified by: 'Since the action of θ on V is of finite order, each θ-orbit on Ω is a finite set.']
issues.correction: The statement needs a hypothesis: that (1 − θ)Ω is finite — equivalently, that the fibres of Ω → Ω_θ are finite. It holds automatically for θ = id and whenever Ω is finite (for instance G semisimple), but not in general.
issues.reason: The image in W̃/W_a ≅ Ω of the θ-twisted conjugacy class of w′ is κ(w′) + (1 − θ)Ω, not the θ-orbit of κ(w′), because w ·_θ w′ = w w′ θ(w)^{-1} changes the W_a-coset by ω − θ(ω). Two instances. (i) G = G_m and θ inversion: W̃ = Ω = Z, W_a = 1, all lengths are 0, twisted conjugation sends m to m + 2k, so each of the two classes 2Z and 1 + 2Z meets infinitely many W_a-cosets; every element is of minimal length in its class, so Corollary 9 fails and X_ν is the set of elements of F^× of a fixed parity of valuation, which is not compact. (ii) The case the paper is written for: G = GL_n with the twisted-endoscopy automorphism g ↦ J·(ᵗg)^{-1}·J^{-1} that preserves the standard Iwahori. Then Ω ≅ Z through the valuation of the determinant, θ acts on it by −1, and the twisted class of 1 contains τ^{2k} for every k, where τ generates Ω; all of these have length 0, hence are of minimal length, and all have the same invariants π = (0,0). So again Corollary 9 and the compactness of X_ν fail. The Newton decomposition of Theorem 3 itself is unaffected, and the compactness can be restored by replacing X_ν with a compact core inside one chosen Ω-coset, which the items of this extraction do (see C17 and N20): every minimal element of a Newton fibre is θ-conjugate by an element of Ω into that coset.

issues.reason: The cited theorem reads (arXiv:1511.01386, Theorem 2.27, the numbering of the published survey, cross-checked through its Theorems 2.28, 2.30 and 2.34, which this paper cites for the results they carry): 'Assume that G is simple. Let w ∈ W̃ such that wσ(a) is contained in a Shrunken Weyl chamber. Then for any basic σ-conjugacy class [b], Ĭ ẇ Ĭ ∩ [b] ≠ ∅ if and only if κ(w) = κ(b) and η_σ(w) is not contained in W_M for any proper standard ς-stable Levi M.' The element it is applied to is the a t^γ produced by Theorem 5.5, and that element is not shrunken whenever γ is not regular: if ⟨γ, α⟩ = 0 for a root α, then every point v of the alcove a t^γ(a) satisfies ⟨v, a(α)⟩ = ⟨u, α⟩ for a point u of the base alcove, so 0 < |⟨v, a(α)⟩| < 1 and v lies in the critical strip of ±a(α). Non-regular γ is the normal case, not an edge case: the proof of Theorem 5.5 introduces K = {s ∈ S; s(γ) = γ} and y′ ∈ W_0^K for exactly this reason, and §6.4 discusses λ_w = nω^∨ for a fundamental coweight ω^∨, where γ lies on the walls. A worked instance in split adjoint type A_2: λ = ω_2^∨, y = 1, x = s_2s_1 give J = ∅, J′ = {s_1}, x′ = s_2, z = s_1, γ = λ, y′ = 1 and a = s_1 ∗ s_2 = s_1s_2; on the base alcove {u < 0, v < 0, u + v > −1} the element w = x t^λ y is outside every critical strip, while a t^γ sends (u,v) to (1−u−v, u), whose second coordinate lies in (−1,0), so a t^γ is not shrunken although both finite parts have full support. The conclusion is not contradicted — [GHN15, Theorem A] is available for every w — but the step as written applies its source outside its hypothesis.

issues.locator: Proposition 5.1 with its proof, p. 8 (both versions)
issues.printed: Then the set {μ'; μ' is dominant, μ' + λ' ≥_Z λ} contains a unique minimal element with respect the dominance order ≥_Z. … [proof] The statement is proved.
issues.correction: Two steps have to be added: that the set is nonempty, and that it has a minimal element at all.
issues.reason: What the printed proof establishes is that the set is lower directed: for any two of its elements μ'_1, μ'_2 it produces a dominant μ in the set with μ'_1 ≥_Z μ and μ'_2 ≥_Z μ. Both missing steps are standard: μ' = λ − λ' + NΣ_{α∈Δ}α^∨ is dominant and feasible for N large, which gives nonemptiness; and for a fixed feasible μ'_0 the dominant coweights μ with μ'_0 ≥_Z μ form a finite set, so a minimal element exists.
