issues.locator: §2.2, p. 5, the standing reduction, with §5.2, p. 9 and §5.4, pp. 10–11 (both versions)
issues.printed: As discussed in [GHN15, §2], the study of the nonemptiness pattern and dimension formula of affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties for an arbitrary reductive group may be reduced to simple and quasi-split groups over F. From now on, we assume that G is simple and quasi-split over F.
issues.correction: The reduction must also carry 'of adjoint type', as the cited section does: [GHN15, p. 648] reduces 'to the case where G is quasi-split and semisimple of adjoint type' (§2.2 Reduction to adjoint groups, §2.3, §2.4).
issues.reason: Adjointness is what makes §5 well defined. §5.2 introduces ρ^∨_J, the dominant coweight with ⟨ρ^∨_J, α_s⟩ = 1 for s ∈ J and 0 otherwise — that is, Σ_{s∈J} ω^∨_s — and §5.4 uses the elements w_1 = x z^{-1} t^{λ_w − ρ^∨_J} y' and w_2 = (y')^{-1} z t^{ρ^∨_J} y of W̃ and the element a t^γ of W̃. These require ρ^∨_J ∈ X_*(T)_{Γ_0}, which fails as soon as that lattice is smaller than the coweight lattice: for G = SL_3, split, X_*(T) is the coroot lattice of A_2, and y = s_1 gives J = {s_1} and ρ^∨_J = ω^∨_1 = (2α^∨_1 + α^∨_2)/3 ∉ X_*(T), so t^{ρ^∨_J} is not an element of W̃ at all. The twisted case shifts γ itself out of the lattice: in unramified simply connected ²A_2, with P^∨/Q^∨ = Z/3 and σ acting by −1, taking λ = 3ρ^∨, x = 1, y = s_1 gives J = {s_1}, σ^{-1}(ρ^∨_J) = ρ^∨_{σ^{-1}(J)} = ω^∨_2, and the class of γ in P^∨/Q^∨ is that of ω^∨_2 − ω^∨_1 ≠ 0, so no W_0-translate of it is a coweight of G. That this is a slip in summarising the reduction, and not a restriction the author intends, is clear from §1.2, which describes W̃ as 'the semidirect product of the coweight lattice with the relative Weyl group' — the coweight lattice being X_*(T) exactly for adjoint groups. Two consequences are worth recording: the cited reduction to adjoint groups holds under char k ∤ |π_1(G_ad)| and, after the authors' erratum, only component by component (see E13), and the descent of Theorem 6.1 from G_ad back to G is not written out.

issues.printed: (We note that since the action of Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ) on the components of Sh_{𝒢̃_B} is trivial, the class c is Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ)-invariant.)
issues.correction: Choose c in the ℚ-subspace of Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ)-invariant combinations of fundamental classes of components. It is defined over ℚ because Galois permutes the components, and it contains c_η after extension of scalars to ℚ(η): Galois acts on Sh(T_1, h_1) through the reciprocity law of (T_1, μ_1), i.e. by translation by the central elements ([s, s], s), s ∈ 𝔸_{ℚ,f}^×, and η([s, s], s) = η(s^{-1}) = 1 because η is trivial on 𝔸_F^×. The determinant argument then yields a Galois-invariant ℚ-rational c with Res(Ξ_τ(d)) an isomorphism.
issues.reason: Galois does not act trivially on the components of Sh_{𝒢̃_B,K} in general: through the map to Sh(T_1, h_1) it acts by translation by ([s, s], s), and the closure of T_1(ℚ) meets the compact open subgroup in the closure of a finitely generated unit group, which cannot contain the image of an open subgroup of Ẑ^×; so for small K some components are not defined over F_Σ. The Galois-invariance of ξ_0 in Theorem 12.4(ii), and hence Theorems 1(ii) and 3.2(ii), rests on this step; the correction restores it.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.9, p. 24
issues.printed: “By construction, η_M is the composition of maps Ext^c_A(O, A) ⊗_A M −→ Ext^c_A(O, M) −→ Ext^c_A(O, M)^tf. … We identify η_M with the map on the left. … We leave it to the reader to verify that η_M identifies with the map H^c N(O, M)”

issues.reason: The sources differ when M/p_A M has O-torsion. Example (c = 0): A = O[[x]]/(ϖx) is a Gorenstein hypersurface in C_O(0), and M = A/ϖA ≅ k[[x]] is maximal Cohen–Macaulay. issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 10.6(1), pp. 46–47
issues.printed: “Let R′ denote the image of R∞ in End_{S∞}(P(C)). Then dim R′ = dim R∞, as the R∞-module P(C) is maximal Cohen–Macaulay. Moreover, R′ is a finite S∞-algebra. At this point, one can readily adapt the proof of [8, Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7] to deduce that the lift S∞ → R∞ of the map S∞ → R′ can be chosen to ensure that R∞ is finite as an S∞-module.”
issues.correction: Choose ϕ∞ independently of 𝔆: lift S∞ → Q̄ := lim_{s,a} R(s, a, ∞), which is finite over S∞ (Q̄/(n, ϖ) ≅ R_0/ϖ). Then modify the lifts of y, w by elements of K = Ker(R∞ → Q̄) one at a time so that, with ϖ, they cut out a finite-length quotient of R∞ (prime avoidance on R∞/(ϖ, earlier lifts), using dim R∞/ϖ = dim S∞/ϖ − ℓ_0 and dim Q̄ = dim R∞). The theorem's claim is true, but the printed step does not prove it.
issues.reason: [8, Lemma 3.6] (arXiv:2108.09729v2, p. 11) assumes (P): S ↪ R making R finite free, and (CI): R̃ a complete intersection, O-flat and equidimensional; neither holds for S∞ → R∞ here (dim R∞ = dim S∞ − ℓ_0 < dim S∞ when ℓ_0 > 0, and R∞ need not be Cohen–Macaulay), so the lemma does not apply as stated. The proof also takes R′ from an unspecified 𝔆, although ϕ∞ must serve the whole functor P, and dim R′ = dim R∞ needs P(𝔆) ≠ 0. Finiteness of R∞ over S∞ is not used later in an essential way (Theorem 11.3 can pass through R′).

issues.locator: Remark 12.2, second paragraph, second sentence, p. 55
issues.printed: “If the projective image of ρ̄ is PSL_2(k) (for |k| ≥ 5) and [F(ζ_ℓ) : F] > 2 then there are places v such that ρ̄(Frob_v) has eigenvalues with ratio q_v and q_v ≢ ±1 (mod ℓ); these are again level raising primes in our sense.”
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that some a ∈ F_ℓ^× ∖ {±1} is a square in k (e.g. ℓ ≥ 7, or [k : F_ℓ] even). Then choose λ ∈ k with λ² = a and use Chebotarev in the compositum of F(proj ρ̄) and F(ζ_ℓ), which are linearly disjoint because PSL_2(k) is simple.

So a ratio in F_ℓ ∖ {±1} must be a square in k. Either define the Taylor–Wiles levels through ad^{−1} as in §13.4 (keeping d ≡ 1 mod t²), which makes ⟨d⟩_v the diamond operators of the O[Δ_Q]-structure and the determinant ψ; or keep the d-type level, state Theorem 14.5(ii) with x² − T_v x + ⟨v⟩, and in Theorem 14.6 twist ρ_{Σ,Q} by the square root of the ℓ-power-order character ψ·det(ρ_{Σ,Q})^{−1} (ℓ odd), as in Calegari–Geraghty [17, Thm 3.11], before mapping from R^𝔇_{Σ,Q} (whose lifts have determinant ψ).
issues.reason: Forms with a nontrivial Δ_v-character have central character ramified at v ∈ Q, and in weight one det ρ_π is the central character. Patching needs H_0(C^𝔇_{Σ,Q}) to be free over O[Δ_Q] (Proposition 14.1(2)), so such forms occur after localizing at m; but ψ is unramified outside S and ℓ, so the printed characteristic polynomial, and the existence of R^𝔇_{Σ,Q} ↠ T^𝔇_{Σ,Q} with determinant ψ, fail as printed. At level Q = ∅ with prime-to-ℓ nebentypus the two agree, so the minimal-level statements are unaffected once the Taylor–Wiles levels are corrected.

issues.locator: Theorem G, Introduction p. 7 (and footnote 1), and the sentence before Conjecture A, p. 60
issues.printed: p. 7: “When F is a CM field and ℓ is sufficiently large, Conjecture A is known by [45, Theorem 1.3]. … Theorem G. … For ℓ > 20, there exists an integer µ ≥ 1 …” Footnote 1: “The precise bound is given in [45, (1.2)], in our situation, ℓ > 20 is sufficient if [F : Q] = 2.” p. 60: “part (ii) is known for sufficiently large ℓ; see [45, Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.3].”
issues.correction: [45, Theorem 1.3] gives ρ_m only modulo an ideal I with I^4 = 0, so it does not give Conjecture A(ii). The nilpotent-free result, whose bound is (1.2), is [45, Theorem 1.4 = Theorem 5.13]; it assumes ℓ unramified in F and a strictly regular weight (λ_{τ,1} > λ_{τ,2} for every τ), whereas the complexes C_K of §13 have trivial coefficients (λ = 0). So the cited results do not supply Conjecture A(ii) for C_K; Theorem G should also assume Conjecture A(ii) (and ℓ unramified in F), or cite a result covering trivial weight.
issues.reason: For n = 2 and F imaginary quadratic, the left side of [45, (1.2)] is 16 + 3(a_1 − a_2) + (b_1 − b_2) for λ_τ̃ = (a_1, a_2), λ_τ̃c = (b_1, b_2); its minimum over regular weights is 20, at λ = ((1,0),(1,0)), which is the footnote's ℓ > 20. At λ = 0 the Lan–Suh vanishing behind [45, Thm 5.10] fails already in degree 0. Also ℓ = 23 with F = Q(√−23) meets ℓ > 20 but is ramified in F. Theorem G as stated therefore rests on an input the citation does not provide; its other inputs (Conjectures C, D via Theorem 13.12) need only ℓ > 3.

issues.printed: "Now let r > 1. Then Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1} Y_i is a divisor with normal crossings on X which fulfills all the assumptions of the theorem, and the same is true for Z_r = Y_r ∩ Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1}(Y_r ∩ Y_i) on Y_r."
issues.correction: State and prove Theorem 3.1 for smooth divisors Y_i that are not necessarily irreducible (or connected), and discard empty intersections. The base case r = 1 works verbatim: for d = 1, Y is a finite set of closed points with separable residue fields, and 0 → C → ⊕_x Ind_{K(x)}^K Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → 0 stays exact on G_K-coinvariants because H_1(G, Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ) = 0 for finite G. Z_r is non-empty when d ≥ 2, because X ∖ Y_1 is affine and Y_r is proper of positive dimension, so Y_r meets Y_1. When d = 1 the right-hand column is trivially exact.
issues.reason: The theorem assumes the Y_i are smooth irreducible divisors, and the base case r = 1, d = 1 uses 'the unique point x ∈ Y'. The divisors Y_r ∩ Y_i on Y_r are smooth but in general reducible, and can be empty. For example, on a surface two smooth curves meeting transversally in two points have Y_r ∩ Y_i equal to two points. So the induction applies the theorem outside its stated hypotheses. The argument itself never uses irreducibility beyond the base case, which extends as stated.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.1.9 and its proof, printed p. 166
issues.printed: Lemma 3.1.9. — Let a_R = m²_R + pR. There is a canonical commutative diagram [M̃₁ ⊗_{Ŵ(R)} Ŵ(R/a_R) → φ*(M_{R/a_R}); D̃₁ ⊗_W Ŵ(R/a_R) → φ*(D) ⊗_W Ŵ(R/a_R)] where the horizontal maps are induced by the natural inclusions M̃₁ → φ*(M_R) and D̃₁ → φ*(D). Proof. — L ⊕ T be a normal decomposition for (M_{R/a_R}, M_{R/a_R,1}), and let L₀ ⊕ T₀ be the induced normal decomposition for (D, D₁).
issues.correction: The construction has to be replaced by the one of KPZ26 Lemma 5.1.15, which follows [Ho23] and, in essence, Zink's [Zi99, Theorem 3].
issues.reason: The map produced by the printed proof depends on the chosen normal decomposition M = L ⊕ T, so it is not canonical and the diagram does not characterise it: as KPZ26 Remark 5.1.17(a) puts it, « the isomorphism which is given by the construction of [KP18, Lem. 3.1.9] is not canonical and hence not “correct” », and the diagram does not determine c because its horizontal maps are not always injective, which can happen even when cW(R) is p-torsion free. Consequently [KP18, Lem. 3.1.12] does not hold with c defined as in the proof of Lemma 3.1.9.
issues.known: Known and corrected by the authors themselves: KPZ26 §1.3.1 and Remark 5.1.17(a)–(b); the replacement is KPZ26 Lemma 5.1.15. Pointed out by M. Hoff, [Ho23, Rem. 2.29].

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.1.17, printed p. 169
issues.printed: Hence, it suffices to give a complete separated topology τ on Ŵ(A) ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p such that for any x ∈ W(m_A), p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0. Indeed, then the sum s̃ = s + Σ_{m≥0} Φ^{m+1} ∘ s ∘ Φ₀^{−m−1} − Φ^m ∘ s ∘ Φ₀^{−m} converges to an element of Hom_W(D,M) ⊗ Q_p in τ and is Frobenius invariant.
issues.correction: The ring cW(A)[1/p] is not complete for the topology τ defined there, so establishing p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0 in τ does not finish the proof. KPZ26 show instead that cW(A)[1/p] is p-adically complete and separated and that p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0 in the p-adic topology for x ∈ cW(M_A), which does finish it, using Zink's logarithmic coordinates on cW(pN) and [Zi01, Prop. 2.3, 2.4].
issues.reason: The convergence argument needs completeness of the ring in the topology in which the series is summed; the printed topology τ does not have it.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.6.13 (printed p. 202) and Corollary 4.6.15 (printed p. 203)
issues.printed: Lemma 4.6.13. — There is an isomorphism of Ē-schemes with G₂(A^p_f) × Gal(Ē/E′)-action Sh_{K°_{2,p}}(G₂,X₂) ≅ [[Sh_{K°_p}(G,X)⁺ × A(G_{2,Z_{(p)}})]/A(G_{Z_{(p)}})°]^{|J|}.
issues.correction: The connected Shimura varieties in the disjoint union must carry different levels, conjugated by the elements j ∈ J of §4.6.12: writing Sh_{K°_p}(G,X)^{j,+} for the connected component containing (j,X⁺), which is isomorphic to Sh_{jK°_p j^{−1}}(G,X)⁺, the correct description is Sh_{K°_{2,p}}(G₂,X₂) ≅ ⨆_{j∈J} [Sh_{K°_p}(G,X)^{j,+} × A(G_{2,Z_{(p)}})]/A(G_{Z_{(p)}})°, and correspondingly the integral model of Corollary 4.6.15 is ⨆_{j∈J} [S_{K°_p}(G,X)^{j,+} × A(G_{2,Z_{(p)}})]/A(G_{Z_{(p)}})°, with S_{K°_p}(G,X)^{j,+} the Zariski closure of Sh_{K°_p}(G,X)^{j,+}.
issues.reason: As printed the union is the |J|-fold power of one space at the single level K°_p, which is not what the quotient by K°_{2,p} produces; the stabiliser computation Stab(jA(G_{2,Z_{(p)}})) = jK°_p j^{−1} ∩ Ã(G_{Z_{(p)}})° is what forces the conjugated levels. The same proof as Corollary 4.6.15 then works, the corrected scheme having the right generic fibre.

issues.locator: Journal §2 p312, after Lemma2.1; v2 §2 p8
issues.printed: There exists an open (dense) immersion
issues.correction: Add quasi-projectivity of X_F, or make the existence of the stated smooth projective SNC compactification an explicit hypothesis as v1 did.
issues.reason: The preceding hypothesis is only smooth geometrically connected finite type. An open subscheme of a projective scheme is quasi-projective, whereas smooth proper nonprojective varieties exist (for example the split smooth complete toric threefolds of Fujino–Payne, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0510679). A proper open immersion into a projective compactification would make such a variety projective. Shimura varieties here are quasi-projective, so this does not change that application.

issues.locator: Journal Lemma3.9 p327 first proof paragraph; Theorem3.10 p331; Proposition3.7(3) pp324–326; same step in v2
issues.printed: the Q[Γ_Q]-modules X•(T_x,i)_Q are irreducible and non-isomorphic
issues.correction: Retain pairwise nonisogeny, or inequivalence of rational character representations, as the separation property. At the auxiliary split primes in Proposition3.7 choose a split torus in one factor and an anisotropic torus in the other; prove this stronger property survives the twist.
issues.reason: The printed hypotheses only assert nonisomorphism of Q-tori, i.e. of integral Galois lattices. Nonisomorphic lattices can become isomorphic over Q. For example A₂ root and weight lattices under S₃ have index3 and the same irreducible rational representation; their integral intertwiner determinants are 3m², so none is unimodular. Pairwise integral nonisomorphism alone does not justify injectivity of the direct sum. This identifies a gap in the stated inference, not a counterexample to Theorem3.10; the stronger allowed local separation repairs the needed inference.

issues.locator: Journal Lemma3.6 p323 first sentence of proof; v2 §3.3
issues.printed: each T_v and K_v canonically decompose as products
issues.correction: Replace each arbitrary open subgroup K_v by a product of sufficiently small open subgroups contained in it, then apply the factorwise argument. The tori do decompose.
issues.reason: An open subgroup of a finite product need not be a product: the inverse image of the diagonal under two copies of a nontrivial finite quotient is open and proper while projecting onto both factors. issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, p.9 (published version)
issues.printed: "Let t_i := Σ_{v|w_i} x_v. Then since |x_{v_{i,j}} − x_{v_{i,j′}}| ≤ 2, we have x_{v_{i,j}} = t_i/k_i + O_k(1). We have Σ_i t_i = 0, since u, α_r, and α_s all have norm 1. Thus Σ_{i,j} max(x_{v_{i,j}}, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O_k(1) = O_k(1)."
issues.correction: Normalise the α_i first. Their relative norms η_i = Nm_{L/K}(α_i) are units of K, since the ideal (α_i) has trivial relative norm. Pigeonhole the α_i by the class of η_i in O_K^*/(O_K^*)^d, which has at most d^{[K:ℚ]} = O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) classes. Within one class, η_i = η₀e_i^d with e_i ∈ O_K^*; replace α_i by α_i/e_i, which leaves the ideal unchanged. Then Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s) = 1, so every t_i = log|Nm_{L/K}(uα_r/α_s)|_{w_i} vanishes, and the stated height bound follows. The loss is a factor O_{[L:ℚ]}(1) in N + 1, so (2.1) is unchanged.
issues.reason: The boxes control only PUL(α_i), i.e. the differences of coordinates within each block, because P drops the block sums t_i. Units u ∈ O* = ker(Nm_{L/K}) have t_i = 0, but an arbitrary generator α_i of ℘_i^{ℓa_i}℘̄_i^{−ℓb_i}℘₀^{−ℓa₀}℘̄₀^{ℓb₀} has t_i(α_i) = log|Nm_{L/K}(α_i)|_{w_i}, the logarithm of a unit of K, which need not be bounded. "Norm 1" in the absolute sense gives only Σ_i t_i = 0. The step Σ max(x_v, 0) = Σ_i t_i + O(1) needs each t_i = O(1) (for example t₁ = T, t₂ = −T gives Σ max ≈ T). So the claimed bound on H(uα_r/α_s) is not justified as written, though the repair costs only a constant depending on [L : ℚ].

issues.locator: Lemma 2.9, p. 394
issues.printed: "Suppose αi, ci ∈ C for i ∈ N satisfy the condition that the series defining φ(s) := Σ αi ci^s converges absolutely for s = s0 ∈ R and equals to 0 for all but finitely many s ∈ Z_{>s0}. Then we have Σ_{ci = c} αi = 0 for any c ∈ C^×."
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that for every ε > 0 only finitely many i have |ci| ≥ ε (equivalently, the moduli |ci| can be listed in decreasing order with finite multiplicities). The proof, which starts by arranging |c1| = |cm| > |c_{m+1}| ≥ …, then works.
issues.reason: Without the hypothesis the lemma is false. Let F(x) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − x/2^k), an entire function with Taylor coefficients αi, and let ci = 2^i and s0 = 0. Then Σ|αi| < ∞ and φ(s) = F(2^s) = 0 for every s ≥ 1, yet α0 = 1 with c0 = 1 unique (checked numerically). The applications are unaffected: in Corollary 2.11 with s0 > 0 the hypothesis follows from absolute convergence, and in Lemmas 3.2–3.3 the ci are values c(β, τ0)^{−𝔯}, which tend to 0 because the Eisenstein series converge.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.1, p. 404
issues.printed: "By the discussion and Lemma 31.32.4(3) in [Stacks, Tag 01OF] and Lemma 29.38.2 in [Tag 01VL], we know that O_X̃(−E) = O_X̃(1) is π-relatively ample."
issues.correction: Replace the boundary divisor E by the exceptional Cartier divisor D = V(I·O_X̃) of the (normalized) blow-up. D is supported on E but in general has multiplicities aσ ≥ 1, given by the polarization function of the admissible decomposition. Then O(−D) ⊗ π*L^k is ample, and Theorem 4.1 holds with L̃_k(−D). In Proposition 4.2 take ℓ0 ≥ n0·k·max aσ, so that g^{ℓ0}, which vanishes to order ≥ ℓ0 along every boundary component, gives a section twisted by −n0k′D.
issues.reason: The Stacks lemma gives O(1) = I·O_X̃ = O(−D) for the exceptional divisor of the ideal I of AMRT IV Thm. 2.2, not for the reduced boundary E. On a Hirzebruch cusp resolution (d = 2), −E is not π-ample whenever some boundary curve has self-intersection −2, since (−E)·Eσ = bσ − 2 = 0. The conclusion survives with D in place of E.

issues.printed: "When r is even, this follows from the discussion in Example 2.7 and Theorem 1.7. When r is odd and d1 is fundamental, Theorem 7.13 of [BEY21] gives the algebraicity … Using this and proceeding with the rest of the argument in the proof of Theorem 1.7 gives Theorem 1.1."

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 8.2.1, p.59
issues.printed: "We may further assume that L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ is integral and has a basis (e′_1, …, e′_n) such that val(e′_i) = a′_i. Let L′^♭ = ⟨e′_1, …, e′_{n−1}⟩. Then we have Int_{L^♭,V}(x) = Int_{L′^♭,V}(x′), and ∂Den_{L^♭,V}(x) = ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}(x′), where x′ = e′_n."
issues.correction: Replace the two claimed equalities by the equality of differences: with φ = Int_{L^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L^♭,V} and φ′ = Int_{L′^♭,V} − ∂Den_{L′^♭,V}, Theorem 6.1.3 cancels the horizontal parts, so φ(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) − ∂Den(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) = Int(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) − ∂Den(L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩) = φ′(x′). The induction hypothesis φ′ = 0 then gives φ(x) = 0 for x ∉ M(L^♭), which is all the rest of the proof uses.
issues.reason: Only the full functions Int_{L^♭}(x) = Int(L^♭ + ⟨x⟩) and ∂Den_{L^♭}(x) depend on the lattice L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ alone. Their horizontal and vertical parts depend on the hyperplane L^♭_F. By Definition 6.1.2, ∂Den_{L^♭,H}(x) and ∂Den_{L′^♭,H}(x′) are sums over integral L″ ⊇ L^♭ + ⟨x⟩ = L′^♭ + ⟨x′⟩ with the different conditions t(L″ ∩ L^♭_F) ≤ 1 and t(L″ ∩ L′^♭_F) ≤ 1; geometrically, Z(L^♭)_H ≠ Z(L′^♭)_H. So the two stated equalities do not follow from what precedes them. The step is repaired in one line and the theorem stands.

issues.locator: Remark 4.11.5, p.30 (final version; also arXiv v1); used in the proof of Lemma 9.2.2 (i), p.64
issues.printed: "If L, L′ ⊆ V are isometric O_F-lattices of rank n, then we may find g ∈ SO(V)(F) such that L = gL′. We may further lift g to g̃ ∈ GSpin(V)(F) = J(F) such that η(g) = 1. Then the automorphism g̃ of N (see §4.4, 4.5) carries ^𝕃Z(L′) to ^𝕃Z(L). In particular, Int(L) only depends on the isometry class of L."
issues.correction: A lift g̃ ∈ J(F) of g ∈ SO(V)(F) has spinor norm η(g̃) = sn(g) in F^×/(F^×)², so η(g̃) = 1 forces sn(g) = 1. What the argument needs is only val η(g̃) = 0, since g̃ carries RZ^{(ℓ)}_G to RZ^{(ℓ + val η(g̃))}_G (§4.5) and N = RZ^{(0)}_G; that is available exactly when some isometry carrying L′ to L has spinor norm of even valuation, which the remark does not establish.
issues.reason: There are isometric pairs for which every isometry has spinor norm of odd valuation. Take m even and ε = −1: for m even and U unimodular, ϵ(ϖU) = χ(U), so V^−_m ≅ ϖ·H^−_{m,F}. Write H^−_m = M ⊥ ⟨w⟩ with M self-dual of rank n = m − 1, and let L ⊆ V be M with the scaled form, so that all its fundamental invariants are 1 and val(w) = 1. An element of SO(V)(F) stabilizing L preserves L_F and the line L^⊥_F, hence is a product of an even number of reflections in vectors of L or of L^⊥_F (for p odd the orthogonal group of a unimodular lattice is generated by the reflections in its vectors of unit norm, O'Meara 92:4); each such reflection has spinor norm of valuation 1, so the stabilizer has spinor norms of even valuation. Since V is isotropic, sn : SO(V)(F) → F^×/(F^×)² is surjective; choosing h with val sn(h) odd and L′ = hL gives isometric lattices such that every g ∈ SO(V)(F) with gL′ = L has val sn(g) odd. Remark 4.11.5 is the invariance input for Lemma 9.2.2 (i) (the O(W)(F)-invariance of Int^⊥_{L^♭,V}), hence for Proposition 9.2.3 and Theorem 9.3.2. The conclusion is presumably true — Theorem 4.15.1 asserts it, and for m = 4, ε = −1 it follows from Terstiege's explicit formulas (Remark 4.15.2) — and an automorphism of RZ_G outside J(F) shifting the components would supply it; but no such argument is given here, and this extraction did not settle it.

By (5.8), Ω′_ψ(n)φ′(Y) = ψ(tY_i)φ′(n ⋆ Y), with (n ⋆ Y)_i = Y_i since n ⋆ changes only the coordinate 7 − i. So the left side carries ψ(+tY_i). On the right side, (n, a).0 = atX_{e_i} has trace 0 and ⟨atX_{e_i}, atX_{e_i}⟩ = 0, leaving ψ(−⟨n ⋆ Y, atX_{e_i}⟩/a) = ψ(−tY_i). The proof of Theorem 5.9(3) (p. 29) writes the phase with +Σ Y_iA_i/a. Only with that sign does its germ constant ψ(2(Y_{2,0} − A_{15,0})(Y_{5,0} − A_{12,0}) + 2(Y_{3,0} − A_{14,0})(Y_{4,0} − A_{13,0})) equal I^+(φ, φ′) as defined with Y · A of Proposition 5.5. With the printed − sign the same computation gives (Y_{2,0} + A_{15,0})(Y_{5,0} + A_{12,0}) + …, and Theorem 5.9(3) would fail for general φ′. The alternative repair, a sign error in (5.8) instead, would force changes to Proposition 5.5 and to the computation on p. 29 as well, so the printed (5.13) is the likelier slip. Either way the paper is internally inconsistent here. The fundamental lemma (Theorem 5.9(2)) is unaffected, because 1_{Y′(𝒪_F)} is even. issues.locator: §7, in the proof of Proposition 7.17, the non-superspecial supersingular case (accepted version of 25 December 2021; the same expression is in arXiv:2011.08887v1)
issues.correction: the middle expression is 2(p² + p − 1)/(p(p² − 1)); the two summands of the numerator are transposed
issues.reason: The displayed series is (2/(1-p^{-2}))(h(p^{-1}+1)/p² + hp/p⁴ + hp²/p⁶ + ···). Summing the geometric tail, the bracket is h((p+1)/p³ + 1/(p²(p-1))) = h(p²+p-1)/(p³(p-1)), and multiplying by 2p²/(p²-1) gives exactly (h/(p-1))·2(p²+p-1)/(p(p²-1)). At p = 3 this is 22/24 = 11/12, which is where the constant 11/12 comes from and shows the bound is sharp there; numerically, with h = 1 and p = 3 the series is (9/4)(4/27 + 1/18) = 0.4583… = (11/12)·(1/2), confirming it. The printed 2(p²-p+1)/(p(p²-1)) equals 7/12 at p = 3, so as printed the first inequality of the chain is false, although the final bound 11/12 that the proof uses is correct. The same computation carried out for the two superspecial cases of the same proof reproduces the printed constants exactly, 61/62 at p = 5 in case (1) and 17/20 at p = 5 in case (2), which confirms the method.

Lemma 5.3 likewise, with the proof "we conclude by [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)], since both d_0 and k are independent of m." But: "Theorem 5.7. For every m representable by (L, Q) …" and "Theorem 5.8. For every positive integer m, we have the following bounds …", proved from Proposition 5.2.
issues.correction: For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.

Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:

issues.locator: §7.3, construction of μ, p.43
issues.printed: "We define the a_i as follows: suppose that a_n ≠ 0; we define a_i = 0 for n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}}, and we then define a_i = 1 for i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. This implies that Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}} – that is, there is an integer x_n of size O(p^n) that approximates μ mod p^N, with N double-exponential in the size of x_n. … the lattice Λ created this way must also have property 2."
issues.correction: Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.
issues.reason: Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results.

issues.reason: The proof bounds the ratio from below for each large q. It keeps only the multidegrees n in a set 𝒞 (all n_i large, with prescribed parities) on which the number of Frobenius-fixed components is |H_2(G′,c)[q−1]|, and discards the other components as nonnegative. That gives a lower bound for the liminf. It does not show the limit exists: the discarded components with small n_i and their Frobenius-fixed counts may depend on q, and nothing in the argument controls them. The good cases, where the limits are computed exactly, are unaffected. In Theorem 1.2 the passage from Ẽ to E divides by the positive constants of §2.1, |Aut_{G′}(G)| and A(G,G′), so the lower bound transfers with a smaller constant. The proof's remark that "the second statements of both theorems are the same" should be read that way. Noted by the extraction (items 97, 141 and 143). The continuation makes the remaining obligation precise: by /307–/309 the ordinary limit exists iff the total normalized fixed-component profile is eventually constant. Stable parity fibers themselves require the obstruction test /300–/304; do not assume all stable fibers are independent of q without that test. No admissible-type counterexample is asserted.

issues.reason: In characteristic p the tame fundamental group of P¹ minus a finite set S is not pro-prime-to-p. Grothendieck's comparison (SGA 1, XIII, 2.12, which the paper cites) describes only its maximal prime-to-p quotient as the prime-to-p completion of the topological fundamental group. For example, for p ≥ 5 the tame fundamental group of P¹ ∖ {0, 1728, ∞} has as quotients the groups PSL₂(F_ℓ), ℓ ≠ p, of modular covers X(ℓ) → X(1), ramified with indices 2, 3, ℓ, and these orders are divisible by p for suitable ℓ. The definition and the proof of Theorem 3.13 only use homomorphisms to F and its lift F̃_c, whose orders are prime to p. These factor through the prime-to-p quotient, so nothing changes. Noted by the extraction (item 56).

With u = 1 and h ≠ 1 the count in the numerator is zero for every X, so the limit is 0, not 1, whenever H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|] ≠ 1. The paper has such cases. For a generator u, evaluation at u identifies the homomorphisms μ_L → H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|] with H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|], since |μ_Q| divides |μ_L|, which is the intended stratification. issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14: close CM points of the same type with the same projection to X(1)×X(1) lie on a low-degree Hecke curve, stated for Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points alike. Remark 16: "Hecke curves do not pass through anti-Heegner CM points. Thus, …" anti-Heegner CM points repel. Footnote 4: the 2-to-1 ambiguity of [BT13] "can be rectified by using the stronger repulsion statement found in Proposition 14."
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves the hyperbolic metric and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points, so anti-Heegner points cannot all repel. In general no h₀ ∈ SL₂(Z) reduces to the non-identity coset of the stabilizer H in its normalizer, which is where the proof fails (erratum §§1–2). The appeal in footnote 4 therefore rests on the withdrawn part; the main theorems hold by the corrected argument of the erratum.

issues.locator: §4, the paragraph after Corollary 15 on parabolic curves, v3 p.11 (published p.141), in arXiv 2108.13397v3 (15 September 2023, the final author version; PDF SHA-256 e23989fb…b722); published page numbers are those the extraction recorded from the open-access publisher PDF (SHA-256 77c20bc7…e148), which could not be re-fetched here
issues.printed: "We say that a curve X is parabolic if it has genus 0 and the degree of X̄ ∖ X is at most 2. If X is proper of genus 0, then there is a unique Galois section, and it is geometric if and only if X = P¹. If X is parabolic affine, every Galois section of X is cuspidal (the only non-trivial case is settled by [Sch15, Theorem A]). Because of this, we can always assume that X is non-parabolic."
issues.correction: The sentence is false as stated. What the later reductions need is a statement about the t-birationally liftable (or birationally liftable) sections of a parabolic affine X, which have to be treated directly, including the case where X̄ ∖ X is a single point of degree 2. The reductions to non-parabolic X rest on this: "We may assume that X is non-parabolic" in the proof of Lemma 16, and "it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l." after Definition 18, where the identity map is not available for parabolic X.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let k = Q and X = P¹_Q ∖ V(T² − 2). Then X is affine, of genus 0, with boundary a single point of degree 2, so it is parabolic. The paper defines a Galois section to be cuspidal if it is associated with a k-rational point of X̄ ∖ X (§1). The boundary has no Q-rational point, so X has no cuspidal sections. But 0 ∈ X(Q), so X has a geometric section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the existence of rational points and splitting; it does not make a degree-2 boundary point rational. The paper's Theorems A–C are not claimed to fail here, only this justification of the reduction. Noted by the extraction (item 77, with the reduction gap in items 81, 96 and 112).

issues.printed: "Lemma 3.15. With the previous notation, we have Σ_{x∈D(k)} Σ_{j=1}^{r} #{y ∈ C̃_j(k^alg) : ν_j(y) = x} ≤ (q + 1)r + 2q^{1/2} · Σ_{j=1}^{r} g_g(C_j)."
issues.correction: The count of geometric branches over k-points needs an extra term for the non-rational branches through rational singular points. For a geometrically integral curve C with normalization of genus g and arithmetic genus p_a, one has Σ_{x∈C(k)} #ν^{−1}(x) ≤ #C̃(k) + 2 Σ_x δ_x ≤ q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g). The constant q + 4q^{1/2} + 3 in Theorem 9.1 and in Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 10.1 and Corollaries 1.11, 1.14, 1.15, obtained from Lemma 3.15 in (9.8), is not established by the v2 argument.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. The proof's flaw: Lemma 3.17 correctly relates the product of Z*_{D,k}(ζT) over ζ ∈ μ_d to the zeta functions of the C̃_j over k′. But the zeros and poles of Z*_{D,k} cannot be read off from that product. Here Z*_{D,k}(T) = (1 + T)/((1 − T)²(1 − qT)), and the extra factor (1 + T)/(1 − T) disappears under T ↦ −T. The bound with q + 1 + 2g q^{1/2} + 2(p_a − g) follows from Weil's bound for C̃ together with b_x ≤ δ_x + 1 ≤ 2δ_x at singular points, and it is attained in the example. The general reducible, weighted sum in (9.8) needs the analogous count, including intersections of Frobenius-conjugate components. Noted by the extraction (gap G1, items bad-branch-bound and global-sum-source), which checked the page image.

"Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^m/m) · Ψ^{[m]}_j(y), Exp^t_j(x) = Σ_{m≥1} (1/m!) · ψ^{[m]}_j(x)", with ψ^{[m]}_j the homogeneous part of degree m of Ψ^{[m]}_j.

issues.printed: "Proposition 2.2. For a finite, flat map R → R′ of local rings, an open subscheme V ⊂ Spec R, and an affine, smooth R-group scheme G, if (1) Γ(Spec R, O) ≅ Γ(V, O) via pullback; and (2) every G-torsor is trivial over R; then the following pullback is injective: H¹_et(V, G) ↪ H¹_et(V_{R′}, G). (2.2.1)" Proof: "… every element of X(V) lifts to (Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V), so, by [Gir71, III.3.2.2], the map H¹_et(V, G) → H¹_et(V, Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′})) (2.2.2) is injective."
issues.correction: State Proposition 2.2 for commutative G, which covers both of its uses (Proposition 2.3, with G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T, and Corollary 2.4, with G = T). For noncommutative G, supply the missing step: for every G-torsor P over V, the twisted map (^P Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}))(V) → (^P X)(V) must also be surjective.
issues.reason: Write H = Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}) and X = H/G. Surjectivity of H(V) → X(V) shows that the fibre of H¹(V, G) → H¹(V, H) over the trivial class is trivial. When G is commutative this is injectivity, because the map is a group homomorphism. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is only a pointed set. The fibre through the class of a torsor P is the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), for the twists by P (Giraud III.3.2; cf. Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.5.5, Cor. 2). The proof checks only the untwisted case. The twisted forms ^P X live only over V, so hypothesis (1) and the affineness of X give no control of their V-points. If P extends to R it is trivial by (2), so the problem is exactly the torsors on V that do not extend. Proposition 2.2 is used only in the proofs of Proposition 2.3 (G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T) and Corollary 2.4 (G = T, an R-torus), where G is commutative, so the main theorems are unaffected. Noted by the extraction (gap G-NONABELIAN, items h1-descent and h1-abelian), which did not claim the statement false; neither is it claimed false here.

issues.reason: Take a odd with a² + 4 squarefree, for example a = 13 or 101 (D = 173 or 10205 = 5·13·157). Then D = a² + 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) is a fundamental discriminant, and a² + 4 is squarefree for a positive proportion of a. For the principal class, (a + √D)/2 has regular continued fraction [a; a, a, …]. A regular partial quotient a in an odd position becomes a run of a − 1 twos in the minus continued fraction, so the reduced period is ((a + 2, 2, …, 2)) with a − 1 twos, and ℓ_A = a. Meanwhile ε_D = ((a + √D)/2)² = (a² + 2 + a√D)/2, so log ε_D ≈ 2 log a, and ℓ_A / log ε_D → ∞. A direct computation for a = 5, 7, 13, 21, 51, 101, 201, 401 gives ℓ_A = a. In each case the product of the reduced w over the period equals ε_D, as in (6.3), which confirms that ℓ_A is the paper's quantity. The remark is not used elsewhere in the paper.
issues.known: Partly: P. Humphries and A. C. Nordentoft, "Sparse equidistribution of geometric invariants of real quadratic fields", arXiv 2211.05890v2 (28 August 2025), Remark 3.22, observe that Eichler's argument bounds the geometric code of the geodesic and not ℓ_A (the arithmetic code), so the remark is unsupported. Every element of Frac(k[x][[t]]) therefore has x-poles growing at most linearly in n, while Σ t^n/x^{n!} has poles of order n!. issues.printed: "Corollary 1.1.15. Let G be an arbitrary connected reductive group over Q_p with a Q_p-rational Levi subgroup M. Let μ: G_m → M be a minuscule cocharacter and [b_M] ∈ B(M)_b such that ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible. Then there exists w ∈ W(G, M) := N_G(M)/M such that ([b_M], {w·μ}) is M-admissible." Proof: "(1.1.13) implies that there exists w* ∈ W(G*, M*) such that ([b_{M*}], {w*·μ*}) is M*-admissible."
issues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
issues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Then ([b_M], {μ}) is G-admissible: its Newton point (1,0,0) equals the dominant μ̄, and both have κ_G = 1. But κ_M(b_M) = (1,0), while κ_M(μ) = (0,1). Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 2, items N29 and N32), which also verified the Weyl-group computation by machine.

issues.printed: "Let G′ = G × T, equipped with the symplectic representation V′ = V ⊕ V. Let X′ = X × {h_T}. Then we have (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). … Restricting the action of I_{s′_0} to A_T induces a map of Q-groups I_{s′_0} → T, and we consider the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. By Corollary 2.1.9, I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} is surjective, so the map I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, as this is true over Q_ℓ for any ℓ ≠ p."
issues.correction: Take G′ = G ×_{G^ab} T, the pairs (g, t) with the same image in G^ab. This lies in GSp(V ⊕ V, ψ ⊕ ψ), and X′ = X × {h_T} still maps into it because h^ab is constant on X. The kernel of G′ → G is T ∩ G^der, which dies in G^ab, so the composite I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab does factor through I_{s_0}. The rest of the proof then goes through.
issues.reason: Read literally, the construction fails at two points. First, G × T acting on V ⊕ V does not preserve ψ ⊕ ψ up to a scalar when the similitude factors of g and t differ, so it is not a subgroup of G_{V′}. Second, the claimed factorization fails. The CM automorphisms (1, t), t ∈ T, act trivially on A_{s_0} and by t on A_T, and they preserve the tensors cutting out G × T. So 1 × T lies in I_{s′_0}, and also in the kernel of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0}. But under I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab it maps onto G^ab, as T is a maximal torus of G. So the map does not factor through I_{s_0} unless G^ab = 1. The same happens over Q_ℓ, so the justification "as this is true over Q_ℓ" fails too. Surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} alone cannot give a factorization. What is needed is that the kernel maps trivially, and the fibre product above provides this. Lemma 2.2.8 is used in the proof of Proposition 2.2.2 (p.28). Noted by the extraction (source discrepancy 7, item T23) as a descent gate; the analysis and the fibre-product repair are given here.

Let π : X → S be a smooth relative curve over S of genus g > 1 with maximal variation. Let α be a line bundle on X of positive degree on fibers of π. Then the following morphisms satisfy the relative Bogomolov conjecture: (1) the S-morphism i_α^m : X^m_{/S} → J^m_{/S} for any m ≥ dim S + 1 …", where (§1.6) maximal variation means that the moduli morphism S → M_{g,R} is generically finite.
issues.correction: For a function field K of a curve over k, the hypothesis must be maximal variation of a model over k (equivalently, as the proof says, bigness of the relevant adelic line bundles over k rather than over K), which excludes isotrivial families. With that hypothesis, or for K a number field, the statement stands.
issues.reason: Counterexample to the function-field case: k algebraically closed of characteristic 0, K = k(t), S = Spec K, X = C₀ ×_k K for a smooth projective curve C₀/k of genus > 1, and α of degree 1. The moduli morphism Spec K → M_{g,K} is a point, hence generically finite, so X → S has maximal variation in the sense of §1.6. But every point of C₀(k) has canonical height 0 in the constant Jacobian, and these points are Zariski dense in X, so part (1) fails for m = 1 = dim S + 1; constant products give the same failure for the other parts. The proof itself notes that "we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K", which a constant family does not have. The main uniform Bogomolov theorem excludes isotrivial families and is unaffected. Found by the extraction (items 185–189, 262–266).

Namely, K is a number field if k = Z; K is a function field of one variable over k if k is a field. … Recall that the relative Bogomolov conjecture of [DGH2, Conj. 1.2] asserts that, if dim Y < g, then there is a constant ε > 0 such that Y(L, ε) = {y ∈ Y(K̄) : ĥ_L(ι(y)) ≤ ε} is not Zariski dense in Y."
issues.correction: Over function fields the statement needs the usual exclusion of the constant part (for instance, that A has trivial trace or that Y is not constant); [DGH2] formulates the conjecture over number fields.
issues.reason: For a constant abelian scheme A = A₀ ×_k S and a constant subvariety Y generating it with dim Y < g (for example a constant curve of genus > 1 in its Jacobian), the constant points have canonical height 0 and are Zariski dense, so the conjecture as stated fails for function fields. No result depends on the conjecture itself; its function-field instances in Theorem 4.19 are E1. Found by the extraction (item 182).

issues.locator: §1.6, definition of stable curves, p.16, in the author manuscript dated 21 August 2024 (126 pp., the journal's revision date; SHA-256 b36f4860…813e)
issues.printed: "The curve is called stable if it is semistable with arithmetic genus g > 1, and any rational irreducible component of C_k̄ intersects other irreducible components at three or more points."
issues.correction: Count special points on the normalization: every rational component must have at least three points of its normalization lying over nodes, counting both branches of a self-node (the Deligne–Mumford condition). Equivalently, a smooth rational component meets the other components in at least three points, and a rational component with a self-node meets them in at least one.
issues.reason: The printed condition ignores self-nodes. For example, a rational curve with one node attached at one point to a smooth genus-one curve is a stable curve of genus 2 in the usual sense, but its nodal rational component meets the other component in only one point. The paper uses stable reduction and the moduli of stable curves from the literature, so the intended (standard) notion is clear. Found by the extraction (item 1 and report §8).
